Surah al-Ahzab

Al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, and others, related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he said: "Surat al-Ahzab was revealed at Madinah." Ibn Mardawayh related the same from Ibn al-Zubayr. It has seventy-three verses. Al-Tabarsi said: "By consensus." Al-Dani said: "This is agreed upon."

'Abd al-Razzaq in al-Musannaf, al-Tayalisi, Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in the Zawa'id al-Musnad, al-Nasa'i, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, al-Diya' in al-Mukhtara, and others related from Zirr ibn Hubaysh, who said: Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him, said to me: "How many do you recite of Surat al-Ahzab, or how many do you count it as?" I said: "Seventy-three verses." He said: "Stop! I saw it when it was equal to Surat al-Baqarah, and we used to recite in it: 'The aged man and the aged woman, if they commit adultery, stone them absolutely as an exemplary punishment from Allah, and Allah is Mighty and Wise.' Then it was lifted along with what was lifted." By this, may Allah be pleased with him, he meant abrogation (naskh). As for the claim that this addition was in a sheet kept with 'A'ishah which a domestic animal (da'ijn) ate, it is a fabrication of the heretics (malahidah) and their lies, in claiming that it was lost by the eating of a domestic animal without abrogation. Thus in al-Kashshaf.

Abu 'Ubayd in al-Fada'il, Ibn al-Anbari, and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'A'ishah, who said: "Surat al-Ahzab was recited in the time of the Prophet, may Allah's peace and blessings be upon him, as two hundred verses. When 'Uthman, may Allah be pleased with him, wrote the mushafs, he could not preserve from it except what is now present." This is clearly about the loss of part of the Qur'an, and what I have heard implies that it is fabricated. The truth is that every report whose apparent meaning is the loss of some part of the Qur'an is either fabricated or in need of interpretation. The connection of this surah with what precedes it, as al-Jalal al-Suyuti said, is the similarity between the opening of this one and the closing of that one. That one ended with the Prophet ﷺ being commanded to turn away from the disbelievers and await their punishment, and this one begins with his being commanded, upon him be blessings and peace, to be mindful of Allah, not to obey the disbelievers and hypocrites, to follow what is revealed to him, and to rely upon Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as He, glorified and exalted, says: (In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful) ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah﴾. He, Mighty and Exalted, addressed him by his attribute, upon him be blessings
صفحة 143
and peace, rather than by his name, as a sign of honour and exaltation for him. Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: Allah, exalted is He, made His address to him, among the prophets, peace be upon them, by his attribute, as a dignity for him, upon him be blessings and peace, and as an honour, elevating his station and proclaiming his excellence. He placed his name in statements such as: ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah﴾ [al-Fath: 29] and ﴿Muhammad is only a messenger﴾ [Al 'Imran: 144], to teach people that he is the Messenger of Allah and to instruct them to name him thus and call him by it. There is therefore no difference between address and statement. Do you not see that in statements not intended for teaching and instruction, He mentioned him in terms similar to those used in address, as in His saying: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 128], ﴿And the Messenger says: My Lord﴾ [al-Furqan: 30], ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6], and so on.

Al-Kashf critiqued this, saying that the teaching and instruction is evident in His saying ﴿Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah﴾, but not in His saying ﴿Muhammad is only a messenger﴾. Moreover, His saying ﴿And believe in what has been sent down upon Muhammad﴾ [Muhammad: 2] undermines what he built. Yes, address is consistent with exaltation, and perhaps the address of all the other prophets, peace be upon them, in their books was similarly so, and they were mentioned by their names in the Qur'an to prevent confusion. It is more likely that, since his name, upon him be Allah's blessings and peace, was mentioned rarely, this indicates that his station is greater, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him and upon all of them. But there is room for consideration.

Al-Tibi, may Allah make his dust fragrant, preferred that the address mentioned here is for safeguarding (ihtiras) and for correcting what the command and prohibition might imply, like His saying: ﴿Allah pardon you! Why did you give them leave?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43]. The apparent context of what follows indicates that the one addressed by the command to be mindful is the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, not his community, as has been said regarding similar passages. The intended meaning is persistence and steadfastness in it. It has also been said that it means increasing in it, since it has a wide door and broad expanse whose reach cannot be attained. ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers﴾, that is, those who openly disbelieve, ﴿and the hypocrites﴾, those who conceal that within what they intend of falsehood. Ibn Jarir related from al-Dahhak, from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The people of Makkah, among them al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah and Shaybah ibn Rabi'ah, asked the Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace, to retract his statement on condition that they give him half their wealth, and the hypocrites and the Jews in Madinah threatened him that if he did not retract they would kill him, so this was revealed."

Al-Tha'labi and al-Wahidi mentioned, without a chain: "Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, 'Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, and Abu al-A'war al-Sulami came to him, upon him be blessings and peace, during the truce that was between him, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and them. With them was 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy, Mu'tib ibn Qushayr, and al-Jadd ibn Qays. They said to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him: 'Abandon mention of our gods, and say that they intercede and benefit, and we will leave you and your Lord.' This grieved the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, and the believers, and they intended to kill them, so this was revealed." It was also said: "It was revealed concerning some people of Thaqif who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and asked him, upon him be blessings and peace, to allow them to enjoy al-Lat and al-'Uzza for a year. They said: 'So that Quraysh may know our standing with you.'" It is not far-fetched that the intended meaning of the prohibition is steadfastness in not obeying. Its mention after the command to be mindful is intended as persistence in it, as has been said, being a kind of specification after generalization, because the context calls for emphasis on it. It has also been said that it is a kind of emphasis. It has also been said that the object of each of mindfulness and obedience differs from the other, as narrated by al-Wahidi and al-Tha'labi. The meaning is: be mindful of Allah, Exalted, in breaking the covenant and renouncing the truce, and do not obey the disbelievers from the people of Makkah and the hypocrites from the people of Madinah in what they ask of you, namely abandoning mention of their gods and your saying that they intercede and benefit. It seems that He placed the command to be mindful of Allah concerning breaking the covenant first, because the believers had already intended what that required, unlike obedience, which is forbidden, and no one had intended anything that would require it at all. So the concern with the command was greater than the concern with that prohibition. ﴿Indeed Allah is ever Knowing and Wise﴾, exceedingly so in knowledge and wisdom. He knows things, their benefits and harms, so He does not command you except with what contains
صفحة 144
benefit, and does not forbid you except what contains harm, and does not decree except what wise purpose demands. So the sentence is a reason for the command and prohibition, confirming the obligation of complying with them.

It has also been said that the meaning is that Allah was Knowing of those who are mindful, so He rewards them with what befits them, and Wise in guiding whom He wills and misguiding whom He wills. Thus the sentence is consolation for him, upon him be blessings and peace, but this is not sound.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 2:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾ is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) with what preceded it, of the type of conjunction of the general (ʿāmm) to the specific (khāṣṣ). That is: follow, in every matter of the religion that you come to and leave, what is revealed to you of the verses, among which is this verse commanding the fear of God, exalted is He, and forbidding obedience to the disbelievers and the hypocrites. The mention of the title of Lordship (ʿunwān al-rubūbiyyah) is to emphasize the obligation of compliance with the command. ﴿Indeed, God is ever, of what you do, Acquainted⦆ (khabīran). It has been said: the address is to the Messenger, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, and the plural is for honour (taʿẓīm). Abu al-Baqa' said: he came with the plural because by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And follow what is revealed﴾ etc., he meant: follow, you and your companions. And it has been said:

It is for the absent ones among the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and by way of iltifat (shift of address), but its remoteness is not hidden. Yes, it is permissible that it be for all of them by a kind of taghlīb (predominance of one group over another). Whichever it is, the sentence is a reason for the command and an emphasis of its requirement. So it is as if it were said, on the first view: Indeed God knows what you do, so He guides you to what contains righteousness; therefore following the revelation and acting upon its requirement is absolutely necessary. On the second view: God is Acquainted with what the disbelievers and the hypocrites do of plotting and scheming, so He commands you, glorified is He, with what repels it; therefore following what He reveals to you, majestic and exalted is He, is absolutely necessary. On the third view: God is Acquainted with what you do and what the disbelievers and the hypocrites do; He guides you to what contains the righteousness of your condition, informs you of their plotting and scheming, and commands you, majestic is His station, with what repels and turns it back; therefore following His revelation, exalted is He, and acting upon its requirement is absolutely necessary. Abu ʿAmr read ﴿ya'malūna﴾ (they do) with the third-person ya' of absence, on the basis that the pronoun refers to the disbelievers and the hypocrites.

It has been permitted that it be general, so do not overlook this.

And put your trust in Allah. That is, entrust all your affairs to Him, Mighty and Majestic is He. ﴿And sufficient is Allah as Trustee﴾, a Guardian to whom all affairs are committed. The use of the explicit name (Allah) in place of a pronoun is for glorification, and so that the clause stands on its own like a proverb.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 4:

﴿Allah has not made for any man two hearts within his body.﴾ Aḥmad, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it ḥasan), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Ḥatim, al-Ḥakim (who graded it ṣaḥīḥ), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Ḍiyā' in al-Mukhtāra narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) stood one day praying, and he made a slight slip (in his recitation), and the hypocrites who prayed with him said: 'Do you not see that he has two hearts, one with you and one with them?' So this was revealed."

In another narration from him, may Allah be pleased with him: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) prayed a prayer and forgot in it, and a word escaped from him, which the hypocrites heard, and they made much of it, saying: 'Indeed he has two hearts. Did you not hear his saying and his speech in the prayer: "Indeed he has a heart with you and a heart with his companions"?' So this was revealed."

Muqatil in his tafsir, Ismaʿil ibn Abi Ziyad al-Shami, and others said: It was revealed concerning Abu Maʿmar al-Fihri. The people of Makkah used to say: "He has two hearts because of the strength of his memory." The Arabs used to claim that every intelligent, discerning person has two hearts in reality. This Abu Maʿmar was known among the people of Makkah as "Dhu al-Qalbayn" (the Possessor of Two Hearts). According to al-Iṣaba, he was Jamil ibn Usayd (a diminutive of al-Asad), though it is said he was Ibn Asad (in the full form). Ibn Duraid named him ʿAbd Allah ibn Wahb. It is also said that Dhu al-Qalbayn was Jamil ibn Maʿmar ibn Ḥabib ibn Wahb ibn Ḥudhafa ibn Jumaḥ al-Jumaḥi, and he is the one referred to in the saying:

(And how shall I dwell in the house?)

This has been mentioned previously in the tafsir of Surah Luqman. What is relied upon is what is in al-Iṣaba. It is related that he used to say: "I have two hearts, with one of which I understand more than Muhammad (ﷺ) does." Then it is narrated that he fled on the day of Badr and passed by Abu Sufyan, who was holding one of his sandals in his hand and the other on his foot. Abu Sufyan said to him: "What has become of the people?" He replied: "They are between slain and fleeing." Abu Sufyan said: "What is the matter with one of your sandals being on your foot and the other in your hand?" He said: "I did not think except that both were on my feet." So Allah refuted his statement and their statement.

And from al-Ḥasan: a group of them used to say, each one of them: "A soul commands me and a soul forbids me." So this was revealed. The "jaʿl" here means "khalq" (creation), and "from a sword of a preacher" (an idiom). The intended meaning is that Allah, glorified is He, did not create for anyone, or for any creature possessing a heart at all, two hearts. The specific mention of "man" is not intended; its specification by mention is due to the complete necessity of life in him. If this is not for him, then how about other than him, from females? As for children, they will become men. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿within his body﴾ is for emphasis and depiction, like the hearts in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿But it is hearts that are blind, which are in the breasts﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 46].

It has been mentioned, in explanation of Allah's not making two hearts in one body, based on what is apparent, that the intended "heart" is the conical lump (al-muḍgha al-ṣanawbariyya), that the rational soul and likewise the animal soul must have an attachment, and its attachment is the spirit (rūḥ), which is a subtle vaporous body formed from the finest parts of nourishment, because the tightening of the nerves nullifies the powers of sensation and movement beyond the place of tightening that is not on the side of the brain, and tightening only prevents the passage of bodies; medical experiments also bear witness to this. And since the soul is one, there must be one organ to which its attachment is first, and then to the rest of the organs through it.

Many have mentioned that the first organ to be created is the heart, for it is the gathering place of the spirit, so the attachment must be first to it, then through it to the brain, the liver, and the rest of the organs, so the source of all the powers is from it. This prevents plurality, for if it were multiple, such that there were two hearts, it would necessarily follow that each of them is a source of the powers and not a source of them, or that two causes converge upon one effect. Nothing is hidden from anyone who has a heart that this, along with being built upon premises that hardly establish themselves for most of the Islamic scholars of the pious predecessors and the later successors, even with great difficulty, is a persuasive matter and not a decisive proof. Moreover, the philosopher too has a statement on it. The heart may also be explained as the soul, based on the view that the cause of revelation is what was narrated from al-Ḥasan, using the attached (mutaʿallaq) for the attached-to (mutaʿallaq ʿalayhi). They have explained the unity of the soul, and that it is not permissible for two or more souls to be attached to one body, with matters whose mention would be lengthy, and there is room for investigation in it, so let it be referred to. Furthermore, this explanation, based on the view that the cause of revelation is what was mentioned, is not definitive; rather, it is permissible to explain the heart upon it by what is apparent and immediately understood as well. Since the heart is the object of attachment of the soul, the negation of making two hearts indicates the negation of making two souls, so reflect.

﴿Nor has He made your wives whom you divorce by ẓihār into your mothers﴾: a nullification of what was in the Jahiliyya of applying the rulings of motherhood to the one who makes ẓihār with them. Ẓihār linguistically is the verbal noun of ẓāhara, which is from the form of mufāʿala derived from ẓahr (back), and it is used in various meanings returning to it in meaning and wording according to the differences of purposes. It is said: "ẓāhartuhu" when you literally place your back against his back; likewise when you enrage him, on the basis that enraging requires this confrontation; and "ẓāhartuhu" when you help him, on the basis that it is said: "he strengthened his back" when he helped him; and "ẓāhartu bayna thawbayn" when you wear one of two garments over the other, on the basis that each of them makes the other, what is adjacent to it, a back for the garment. It is said: "ẓāhara min zawjatihi" when he says to her: "You are to me like the back of my mother," analogous to labbā when he says labbayka, and affa when he says uff. The word ẓahr being metaphorical in some of these constructions does not prevent deriving from it, and the derived form may also be metaphorical. What is intended here is the last meaning, and that was a divorce from them.

It was transitivized with "min" although it is transitive by itself, because it includes the meaning of distancing and similar things that carry the meaning of abstention, which take "min." The "ẓahr" in this is a metaphor, according to what has been said, for the belly, because only the belly is ridden; so his saying "like the back of my mother" means "like her belly," by the relation of contiguity. And because it is her pillar. Ibn al-Humam said: "But it does not appear what the diverting factor from the literal meaning is, among the subtleties." al-Azhari said something to the effect: "They specified the back because it is the place of riding, and the woman is ridden when she is covered, so it is an allusive metonymy (kināya talwīḥiyya), moving from the back to the thing ridden, and from it to the one covered. The meaning: you are forbidden to me, you are not to be ridden as the mother's back is not ridden." It has been said: "He specified the back because approaching a woman from her back into her front was forbidden among them, so approaching his mother from her back is more forbidden, and the severity became great." It has been said: "They used 'back' as a euphemism for 'belly,' because they find mentioning the private part and what is near it abominable, especially in the case of the mother and what resembles her." But that is not the case. In the Sharia, it is the likening of a wife, or of a part of her that is common or that stands for the whole, to what it is not permissible to look at of a woman who is permanently forbidden, whether by nursing or by affinity. In al-Nihaya he added the condition of consensus, so that likening to what it is not permissible to look at of one whose prohibition is disputed, such as a daughter from fornication, is excluded. The truth on this is in Fath al-Qadir. It is specifically named ẓihār by preference for "ẓahr" because it was the principal usage among them. Its condition in a woman is that she be a wife, and in a man that he be among those eligible for expiation (kaffāra). Its pillar is the utterance containing that likening, and its ruling is the prohibition of intercourse, and its incentive toward the existence of expiation. The full discussion of it is in the books of jurisprudence, and some of that will come, Allah willing, in its place.

Qalun and Qunbul recited here, and in al-Mujadila and al-Talaq, "al-lāʾ" with a hamza without a yāʾ; Warsh with a yāʾ of a briefly pronounced kasra; al-Bazzi and Abu ʿAmr "al-lāy" with a silent yāʾ in place of the hamza, and this is a transmitted (masmūʿ) substitution, not a analogical (maqīs) one, and it is the dialect of Quraysh. The people of Kufa other than ʿĀṣim recited "taẓāharūna" with a fatḥa on the tāʾ and a lightened ẓāʾ, and its origin is "tatẓāharūna," so one of the two tāʾs was deleted.

Ibn ʿĀmir recited "taẓẓāharūna" with a fatḥa on the tāʾ and a doubled ẓāʾ, and its origin is as mentioned before, except that the second tāʾ was assimilated into the ẓāʾ. al-Ḥasan recited "tuẓahhirūna" with a ḍamma on the tāʾ, a fatḥa on the lightened ẓāʾ, and a doubled kasra-bearing hāʾ, the present tense of ẓahhara, with the doubling of the hāʾ, in the sense of ẓāhara, like ʿaqada in the sense of ʿāqada. Ibn Wththāb, as transmitted by Ibn ʿAṭiyya, recited "taẓhirūna" with a ḍamma on the tāʾ, a sukūn on the ẓāʾ, and a kasra on the hāʾ, the present tense of aẓhara. Hārūn from Abu ʿAmr recited "taẓharūna" with a fatḥa on the tāʾ and the hāʾ, and a sukūn on the ẓāʾ, the present tense of ẓahara with the lightening of the hāʾ. In the codex of Ubayy: "tatẓahharūna" with two tāʾs. The meaning of all is one.

﴿Nor has He made your adopted sons your sons﴾: a nullification of what was also in the Jahiliyya and the early part of Islam, namely that when a man adopts another's son, the rulings of sonship are applied to him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had adopted Zayd ibn Ḥaritha before the mission, and al-Khattab adopted ʿĀmir ibn Rabiʿa, and Abu Ḥudhayfa, his freed slave, adopted Salim, and other examples. Ibn Abi Shayba, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Mujahid that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Nor has He made﴾ etc., was revealed concerning Zayd ibn Ḥaritha, may Allah be pleased with him.

"Adʿiyāʾ" is the plural of daʿī, which is one who is called a son; it is faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl. Its analogical plural would be faʿlā, like jarīḥ and jarḥā, not afʿilāʾ; for the plural of the defective-final faʿīl in the sense of fāʿil, like taqī and atqiyāʾ, is afʿilāʾ, so it was likened to it in form and was treated accordingly and given its plural, as they said for asīr and qatīl: usarāʾ and qutalāʾ. It is said that this plural is analogical for the defective in general, and there is discussion in it.

﴿That﴾: it is said to refer to what is understood from the three sentences, that there may be two hearts in one body, and ẓihār and adoption. It is said: to what is understood from the last two. It is said: to what is understood from the last one. ﴿is your saying with your mouths﴾ only, without its having any referent or reality in fact and actuality; hence it is far from acceptance or the consequence of rulings, as you claim.

﴿But Allah says the truth﴾, the established, verified in reality, ﴿and He guides to the way﴾, that is, the way of truth. So leave your saying and take by His saying, mighty and majestic is He.

Qatada, as mentioned in al-Bahr, recited "yahdī" with a ḍamma on the yāʾ, a fatḥa on the hāʾ, and a doubled dāl; and in al-Kashshaf it is said that he recited "wa-huwa alladhī yahdī al-sabīl."

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 5 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers﴾: that is, attribute them to their fathers and specify them by them.

Al-Bukhari and Muslim (al-Shaykhan), al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, and others narrated from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that: "Zayd ibn Haritha, the freedman of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, we did not call him except 'Zayd ibn Muhammad', until the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers﴾, etc. Then the Prophet ﷺ said: 'You are Zayd ibn Haritha ibn Sharahil.'"

Concerning his affair, may Allah be pleased with him, as narrated by Ibn Mardawayh from Ibn Abbas: "He was with his maternal relatives, Banu Ma'n of Banu Tha'l of Tayy. He was seized in a raid on Tayy, and was brought to the market of Ukaz. Hakim ibn Hizam ibn Khuwaylid went to Ukaz to trade there, and his aunt Khadija instructed him to buy her a handsome, Arab slave if he could find one. When he arrived, he found Zayd being sold there, and his good looks pleased him, so he bought him and brought him to her. He said to her: 'I have bought you a handsome, Arab slave. If you like him, take him; otherwise leave him, for he has pleased me.' When Khadija saw him, she liked him and took him. Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ married her while he was with her. The Prophet ﷺ was pleased with his good looks, so he asked her to give him to him. She said: 'I give him to you. If you wish to free him, the walā' (right of patronage) will be mine.' The Prophet ﷺ refused this condition, so she gave him to him, [saying] that he might free him if he wished, or keep him if he wished." He said: "Zayd grew up with the Prophet ﷺ. Then he went out with camels belonging to Abu Talib to the land of Syria, and passed by the land of his people. His uncle recognized him, stood up to him and said: 'Who are you, boy?' He said: 'A boy from the people of Makkah.' He said: 'From their own selves?' He said: 'No.' He said: 'Are you free or a slave?' He said: 'Rather, a slave.' He said: 'Belonging to whom?' He said: 'To Muhammad ibn Abd Allah ibn Abd al-Muttalib.' So [his uncle] said to him: 'Are you a bedouin Arab or a non-Arab?' He said: 'An Arab.' He said: 'From whom is your origin?' He said: 'From Kalb.' He said: 'From which Kalb?' He said: 'From Banu Abd Wudd.' He said: 'Woe to you! Whose son are you?' He said: 'The son of Haritha ibn Sharahil.' He said: 'Where were you captured?' He said: 'Among my maternal relatives.' He said: 'And who are your maternal relatives?' He said: 'Tayy.' He said: 'What is the name of your mother?' He said: 'Su'da.' Then he embraced him and said: 'The son of Haritha!' and he called his father, and said: 'O Haritha, this is your son!' Haritha came to him, and when he looked at him he recognized him, and said: 'How has your master treated you?' He said: 'He prefers me over his family and his children.' So his father, his uncle, and his brother rode with him until they reached Makkah, and they met the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Haritha said to him: 'O Muhammad, you are the people of the Sacred Precinct of Allah, and its neighbours, and at His House. You release the captive and feed the prisoner. My son is with you, so be gracious to us and be kind to us regarding his ransom, for you are the son of the chief of his people, and we will raise to you whatever ransom you wish.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him: 'I will give you something better than that.' They said: 'And what is that?' He said: 'I will let him choose. If he chooses you, take him without ransom; and if he chooses me, then leave him alone.' He said: 'May Allah reward you with good; you have done well.' So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ called him and said: 'O Zayd, do you know these people?' He said: 'Yes, this is my father, my uncle, and my brother.' The Prophet ﷺ, peace be upon him, said: 'They are as you know them. If you choose them, go with them; and if you choose me, then I am the one you know.' Zayd said to him: 'I will never choose anyone over you, ever. You are for me in the place of a father and an uncle.' His father and uncle said: 'O Zayd, do you choose slavery?' He said: 'I will not part from this man.' When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saw his eagerness to remain with him, he said: 'Bear witness that he is free, and that he is my son; he will inherit from me and I will inherit from him.' So the hearts of his father and uncle were content when they saw his high esteem with him, peace be upon him. He continued in the Jahiliyyah to be called Zayd ibn Muhammad, until the Qur'an was revealed: ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers﴾, and he was called Zayd ibn Haritha."

And in some narrations, his father heard that he was in Makkah, so he came to him with his uncle and his brother, and what happened, happened.

﴿That is more just in the sight of Allah﴾: this is a reason clause for the command. The pronoun refers to the verbal noun of "call" (ud'u), as in His saying: ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8].

"Aqsat" is an elative (af'al al-tafdil, comparative-superlative form) intended to express an absolute increase in justice, from "qist" meaning justice. What is meant is that which is most extreme in truthfulness. Thereby the objection is dismissed which might be imagined, that the context requires mention of truthfulness rather than justice. That is: your calling them by their fathers' names is most complete in justice and truthfulness, and it increases in that in the judgment and decree of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

It is also permissible for "aqsat" to be an elative in its common usage, and the meaning would be "more just than what they say"; and calling him by a name that is false, in which there is no justice at all, would then be by way of mockery (tahakkum). ﴿But if you do not know their fathers﴾, that is, you do not recognize their fathers so as to attribute them to them, ﴿then they are your brothers in religion and your clients﴾: that is, they are your brothers in religion and your allies in it. So call them by brotherhood and clientage (mawlawiyyah), interpreting these two (ta'wil, interpretation) as brotherhood and allegiance in religion. In this sense, after the revelation of the verse, Salim was called "the client of Hudhayfah", and Hudhayfah had previously adopted him. It was also said: "your clients" means the sons of your paternal uncles; and it was said: your manumitters and your liberators. It seems that calling them by these [titles] was to soothe their hearts, and for this reason they were not commanded to call them by their names alone.

﴿And there is no blame upon you﴾, that is, no sin, ﴿for what you have erred in﴾, that is, in what you did of that while in error and ignorance before the prohibition; ﴿but [blame is upon you for] what your hearts have intended﴾: that is, but the blame and sin are for what you have intended after the prohibition. Here "ma" is in the genitive position, in coordination with "ma" in ﴿for what you have erred in﴾. It was objected that a coordinated genitive noun may not be separated from what it is coordinated with. For this reason Sibawayh said, concerning their saying: "Not like the likeness of Abd Allah says that, nor of his brother", that the annexed noun was elided from the coordinated noun, and the annexed-to noun was kept in its i'rab (grammatical case), and the original was: "nor like the likeness of his brother", so that the coordination would be with a nominative noun. It was answered by distinguishing between "ma" here and the example, and that there is no separation in it, because the coordinated item is the relative pronoun together with its complement, namely "ma taʿammadat", on the model of "ma akhtatum"; or [the reading is] "but [blame is upon you for] what you have intended in it, the blame", with "ma" in the nominative position as the subject of a sentence, and its predicate being an implied clause. The attribution of intending to the hearts is in the manner of the attribution in His saying: ﴿Indeed, its heart is sinful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 283]. That the meaning in the first is before the prohibition and in the second after it has been narrated by al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim, from Mujahid. It was also said: both matters are after the prohibition, and error is the opposite of intention. The meaning is: there is no sin upon you if you say to the child of another "O my son" by way of error and lack of intention, as if you forgot or your tongue slipped; but the sin is upon you if you say that intentionally. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah that he said concerning the verse: "If you call a man by other than his father, while you think that he is his father, there is no harm upon you; but what you intend and purpose is calling him by other than his father." It is also permissible that what is meant by His saying ﴿And there is no blame upon you﴾ etc. is pardon for error but not for intention, in a general way.

[This is] based on the hadith of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'I do not fear for you error, but I fear for you intention.'"

And the hadith of Ibn Abbas, who said: The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Error, forgetfulness, and what they have been compelled to do have been lifted from my Ummah."

Then he took, by its generality, the error of adoption and its intentional form. The sentence, under both the specific and the general assumptions, comes as a parenthetical concluding statement (i'tiraḍ tadhyili, a concluding parenthetical insertion), emphasizing compliance with what they were recommended to, together with the incorporation of a ruling intended in itself. Some of them made it a coordinated clause, interpreted as an imperative sentence, meaning: "Call them by their fathers' names; that is more just for you, and do not call them your own [sons] intentionally,"

[p. 149]

so that you would incur sin under the specific assumption, and it would be a digressive clause under the general assumption. This was objected to, on the grounds that it is a forced interpretation for which there is a sufficient alternative. The apparent meaning of the verse is the prohibition of intentionally calling a person by other than his father. Perhaps that applies when the calling is in the manner that was practiced in the Jahiliyyah. As for when it is not in that manner, as when an elder says to a younger one, out of tenderness and affection, "O my son" (ya ibni), which happens frequently, the apparent meaning is that there is no prohibition.

In the glosses of al-Khafaji on the tafsir of al-Baydawi: "Sonship, even if the figurative interpretation applies to it as it does to brotherhood, is nonetheless forbidden by way of resemblance to the disbelievers, and the prohibition is for reprehension (tanzih)." End of quote. Perhaps this prohibition is not intended to be what the mentioned verse indicates, since what the verse indicates is a prohibition of the forbidden kind concerning calling in the manner of the Jahiliyyah. The better view is to say, in explaining the prohibition: to block entirely the avenue of resemblance to the disbelievers. What al-Khafaji mentioned about the disliked nature of a person saying to the child of another "O my son" was related to me by one I trust, from the Fatawa al-Kubra of Ibn Hajar. As for the ruling on adoption by saying "he is my son": if the speaker's slave is adopted, manumission is established in every case; and his lineage from him is not established except if he is of unknown lineage, and is of such an age that someone like him could be born to someone like the speaker, and he has not previously acknowledged a lineage from another. According to al-Shafi'i, adoption has no effect: it does not produce manumission, nor the establishment of lineage. The verification of this is in its proper place. Then, the apparent view is that there is no difference, when the father is unknown, between saying "O my brother" and saying "O my master" (ya mawlaya); both are permitted absolutely in that case. However, some have explicitly stated that it is forbidden to say to a wicked person "O my master", based on a report to that effect; and it was said that this is because it involves venerating him, which is forbidden. The implication is that saying "O my brother", when it involves veneration, such as when the person is of high standing, is also forbidden. Perhaps calling someone of unknown father in the manner mentioned is restricted to when he is not wicked, and the basis for the restriction is the basis for the prohibition of venerating the wicked; so reflect upon this. Likewise, the apparent view is that there is no difference in the matter of calling between the called person being male or female; but we have not found adoption of females to have occurred in the Jahiliyyah. And Allah knows best.

﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving﴾: so He forgives the one who intends when he repents, ﴿Merciful﴾. Therefore He, glorified be He, lifted the blame from the one who errs. It is known from the verse that it is not permissible for a person to attribute himself to other than his father. Some have counted this among the major sins, based on what al-Shaykhan and Abu Dawud narrated from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "Whoever claims to be [the son] of other than his father, while knowing that he is not his father, Paradise is forbidden to him."

Al-Shaykhan also narrated: "Whoever claims [descent] from other than his father, or attributes himself to other than his clients, upon him is the curse of Allah, and of the angels, and of all people. Allah will not accept from him any compensation or ransom."

And al-Shaykhan also narrated: "No man claims [descent] from other than his father, knowing [that he is not], except that he has disbelieved."

Al-Tabarani narrated in al-Saghir, from the hadith of Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, and its chain is good: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "He has disbelieved who disowns a lineage, however distant it is, or claims a lineage that is not known."

[Page 150]

...and other such reports. Now, the connection (*munasabah*, the thematic link between verses) of His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿God has not made for any man two hearts within his body﴾ and what follows it, to what precedes it, is that it begins a mention of some of the revelation which the Prophet (ﷺ) was commanded to follow. This is what has been said. It has also been said that when He, may He be exalted, commanded taqwa (God-consciousness), it was part of its due that there should not be in the heart any taqwa for other than God, may He be exalted. For a person does not have two hearts, with one of which he fears God, may He be exalted, and with the other fears someone other than Him, glorified is He. That would only happen by turning the heart away from the direction of God, may He be exalted, toward other than Him, may He be majestic and exalted. And that is not fitting for one who fears God with the fear due to Him.

It is also transmitted from Abu Muslim (al-Isfahani) that it is connected to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ [al-Ahzab: 48], since it was brought for the purpose of refuting them. The meaning is: no one has two hearts, believing with one and disbelieving with the other; rather, there is only one heart, so either it believes or it disbelieves.

It has also been said that it is connected to "do not obey" and "follow." The meaning is that it is not possible to combine two opposing followings: following the revelation and the Qur'an, and following the people of disbelief and transgression. So this is expressed by mentioning the two hearts, because following arises from belief, and it is one of the actions of the hearts. Just as two hearts cannot be gathered in one body, two opposing beliefs cannot be gathered in one heart.

It has also been said that it is connected to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And rely upon God; and sufficient is God as Disposer of affairs﴾, insofar as it indicates His oneness, glorified and exalted is He. So it is as if it were said: "Rely upon God, and sufficient is He as Disposer of affairs," for He, glorified and exalted is He alone, is the Manager of the affairs of the world. Then He, glorified and exalted is He, pointed out that the affairs of a single man are not ordered if he has two hearts; so how can the affairs of the world be ordered if it has two gods?

It has also been said that this (verse) is driven toward warning against obeying the disbelievers and hypocrites, by relating their falsehoods. It is mentioned that His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿God has not made...﴾ and so on, is an example for zihar (the pre-Islamic practice of likening one's wife to one's mother) and tabanni (adoption). That is, just as a man cannot have two hearts, the one who likens his wife to his mother cannot make her a mother, and the adopted one cannot become a son. And the three mentioned matters together are made into an example of what has no reality. Many have approved of this.

Al-Tibi said: This is more suited to the composition of the Qur'an, because He, may He be exalted, arranged the three negated matters in one order. He, glorified is He, made His saying, may He be majestic and exalted, ﴿That is your saying﴾ a summary conclusion of them. Then He judged that this is a saying having no reality. Then He, glorified and exalted is He, appended the whole with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And God says the truth, and He guides to the way.﴾

Al-Kashshaf (of al-Zamakhshari) objected to this, saying that the occasion of revelation, and His saying, glorified is He, after the appendix: ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers...﴾ (the verse), are witnesses of truthfulness that the first is an example for adoption. Moreover, they did not used to make wives into mothers; rather, they used to make the utterance a divorce. So placing it within the matter of adoption as a digression is the right view, and not that it is a saying with no reality, like the first.

Al-Khafaji supported the majority, saying: If it were an example only for adoption, it would not have been separated from it. That the two hearts belong to one man, and that the adopted one is made a son in all rulings, is among what has no reality in fact, nor in any apparent Shari'ah. Likewise, making wives like mothers in permanent prohibition absolutely is among their inventions for which they had no legal basis. So it has no reality either. Therefore, what he claimed does not apply to them, especially since it contradicts what has been transmitted from them. End.

And the hand of God is with the majority.

Al-Tibi explained the composition of the verses from the opening of the surah to this point, saying: The beginning with His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿O Prophet, fear God﴾ indicates that the address includes an alert to a matter of great concern, in which lies a sense of urging and inspiring. Hence He joined "do not obey" to it as the particular is joined to the general. He followed the prohibition with the command, in the manner of your saying: "Do not obey the one who forsakes you, and follow your helper." It is not far-fetched to call this (device) "reversal and direct" (*tard wa 'aks*). Then He commanded reliance as encouragement to oppose the enemies of the religion and to seek refuge in the sanctuary of God's majesty, so that He would suffice to ward off their evils. Then He, glorified is He, followed each of those commands, by way of completion (*tatmim*) and appendage (*tadhyil*), with what corresponds to it. And He gave the reason for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ by His saying, glorified and exalted is He: ﴿Indeed God is ever Knowing and Wise﴾, as a completion for restraint, meaning: fear God in what you do and leave undone, in your secret and in your public life, because He, may He be exalted, is Knowing of all conditions, and must be feared with respect to His displeasure, and He is Wise, who does not love that His beloved follow His enemies. He gave the reason for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And follow what is revealed to you from your Lord﴾ by His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed God is ever Acquainted with what you do﴾, also as a completion, meaning: follow the truth and do not follow their false desires and their deviant opinions, because God, may He be exalted, knows your deed and their deed, and so He recompenses each with what it deserves. He appended, glorified and exalted is He, His saying, blessed and exalted is He: ﴿And rely upon God﴾ with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And sufficient is God as Disposer of affairs﴾, as confirmation and emphasis, in the manner of: "So-and-so speaks the truth, and the truth is clear," meaning: it is the right of one who is sufficient for all affairs that you entrust your affairs to him and rely upon him. And He separated His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿God has not made for any man two hearts within his body﴾ by way of resumption (*isti'naf*), as an alert to some of their falsehoods and contrivances. And His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is your saying﴾ and so on, is a summary conclusion of those sayings, indicating that they are worthy of being judged as void, and deserving that their speaker be blamed, let alone obeyed. Then He, may He be exalted, connected ﴿And God says the truth﴾ and so on, to this summary conclusion, by the common ground of contrast, in the manner of what preceded in "do not obey" and "follow." And He separated His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers; that is more just in the sight of God﴾ and His saying, may He be exalted:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 6 (part 1 of 2):

﴿The Prophet﴾ etc., and so on to the end of the surah, as an elaboration of the word of truth and of being guided to the straight path, ended. So reflect upon this and do not be heedless. ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers﴾, meaning he has more right to them and is nearer to them, ﴿than their own selves﴾, or he is more worthy of their allegiance and support than they themselves are. For peace and blessings be upon him do not command them, nor are they pleased with them, except in what is good for them and what brings them success. This is unlike the self (nafs), for it is either one that commands to evil, and its condition is evident at first, or it may be ignorant of some of the benefits and some of the advantages may be hidden from it. The word "closer" (awla) is stated without restriction so that the sentence conveys his preferential right over them in all matters. And from the fact that the Prophet (ﷺ) is closer to them than their own selves, it follows that he is closer to them than any of the people.

Al-Bukhari and others narrated from Abu Hurayrah, from him (ﷺ), that he said: "There is no believer except that I am the closest of people to him in this world and the Hereafter. Recite if you wish: ﴿The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves﴾. So whichever believer leaves wealth, let his heirs by blood inherit it, whoever they may be. But if he leaves debt or dependants, let him come to me, for I am his guardian (mawla)."

It is not objectionable that "selves" here has the same sense as in His saying: ﴿And do not kill yourselves﴾ [al-Nisa larger: 29], because the implication of the verse in question for the claim is also evident. And since the Prophet (ﷺ) stands in this position with regard to the believers, it is necessary that he be more beloved to them than their own selves, his judgement over them is more binding than their own judgement over themselves, his right is preferred by them over their own rights, and their compassion for him is more prior than their compassion for themselves.

The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul) of the verse, as it is said, is what is reported: "The Prophet (ﷺ) intended the expedition to Tabuk, so he commanded the people to set out. Some of them said: 'We will seek permission from our fathers and our mothers.' So it was revealed."

The way it indicates the occasion is that if he (ﷺ) is closer to them than their own selves, then by a fortiori he is closer to them than their two parents. There is no need to interpret "selves" in this verse as something other than its apparent meaning, as we have indicated just above.

﴿And his wives are their mothers﴾, meaning they are placed in the station of their mothers with regard to the prohibition of marriage and the entitlement to honour. As for beyond that, such as looking at them, being alone with them, inheriting from them and similar matters, they are like non-mahram women. Al-Qastallani in al-Mawahib derived from this that it is not said of their daughters that they are "sisters of the believers," according to the more correct view. And al-Tabarsi, who is Shi'i, held that their brothers are not called "maternal uncles of the believers." It is not hidden that this is like sipping gently in order to gulp down. In al-Mawahib it is also stated that regarding the permissibility of looking at them there are two opinions, the more well-known of which is prohibition. And because the aspect of resemblance is the whole of what has been mentioned, 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, said to a woman who had called her "O mother": "I am the mother of your men, not the mother of your women." Ibn Sa'd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated it from her. This does not negate the entitlement to honour from them as well.

Ibn Sa'd narrated from Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, that she said: "I am the mother of the men among you, and of the women." According to this, what was mentioned is the aspect of resemblance with respect to the men, while with respect to the women it is the entitlement to honour. The apparent meaning is that by "his wives" is meant everyone who is called his wife (ﷺ), whether he divorced her or did not divorce her. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated this from Muqatil, so the ruling applies to all of them. This is what Imam al-Shafi'i explicitly stated, and al-Nawawi affirmed it in al-Rawdah. It was also said that the ruling does not apply to one who separated from him (ﷺ) during his lifetime, such as the one who sought refuge (al-Musta'idhah) and the one in whose flank he saw whiteness. Imam al-Haramayn and al-Rafi'i in al-Saghir affirmed the prohibition only for the one who had been consummated with, because it was narrated that al-Ash'ath ibn Qays married al-Musta'idhah during the time of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. 'Umar intended to stone him, but he informed him that she had not been consummated with, so he refrained. In another narration, 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, intended to stone her, and she said to him: "Why is that? No veil was placed upon me, nor was I named a mother to the Muslims," so he refrained from her.

In al-Mawahib it is also mentioned that regarding the permissibility of marrying those among them who chose this world, there are two paths: one is to extend the disagreement, and the second is to affirm definitively that it is permissible. This was chosen by Imam [al-Haramayn] and al-Ghazali.

It has been reported that the view that a divorced wife does not acquire this ruling is attributed to the Shi'ah. I have seen in some of their books the denial of motherhood from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her. They said: because the Prophet (ﷺ) delegated to 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, the authority to keep whichever of his wives he wished and to divorce whichever of them he wished after his death, as a deputy on his behalf (ﷺ). 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, divorced 'A'ishah on the Day of the Camel, so she departed from the wives and her ruling no longer applied to her.

After I wrote this, it happened that I looked into a book composed by Sulayman ibn Abdullah al-Bahrani, may Allah deal with him by His justice, which contains what he deserves regarding the blemishes of a group of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all. I saw in it the following text:

Abu Mansur Ahmad ibn Abi Talib al-Tabarsi narrated in the book al-Ihtijaj from Sa'd ibn Abdullah that he asked the Awaited Mahdi (al-Qa'im al-Muntazar) while he was a child during his father's lifetime, saying: "O our master and son of our master, it has been narrated to us that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made the divorce of his wives into the hands of the Commander of the Faithful 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, so much so that on the Day of the Camel he sent a messenger to 'A'ishah and said: 'You have brought destruction upon Islam and its people by the deception that came from you, and you have cast your children into a place of destruction through ignorance. So if you refrain, well and good; otherwise I will divorce you.' So inform us, O our master, about the meaning of the divorce which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) delegated to the Commander of the Faithful." He said: "Allah, exalted is His name, magnified the station of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), and favoured them with the honour of motherhood. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O Abu al-Hasan, this honour remains as long as we are upon the obedience of Allah. So whichever of them disobeys Allah after me by rising against you, divorce her from the wives and remove her from the honour of the Mothers of the Believers.'"

Then he said: al-Tabarsi also narrated in al-Ihtijaj from al-Baqir that he said: "When it was the Day of the Camel, and the howdah of 'A'ishah was struck with arrows, 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, said: 'By Allah, I think I will divorce her.' He adjured a man who had heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'O 'Ali, the matter of my wives is in your hand after me,' to stand and testify. Thirteen men stood and testified to that hadith." And I have seen in some reports that are not present with me now something explicit about the occurrence of the divorce. End of what al-Bahrani said; may Allah deal with him according to His justice.

By my life, this is among foolishness, impudence, and audacity against Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) to an extreme degree. Its falsehood is too evident to be hidden, and the weakness of its wording calls out its lie at the top of its voice. I do not think it is a view acceptable to anyone among them who has even a little intellect. So may Allah curse whoever fabricated it, and likewise whoever believes in it.

Al-Furyabi, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he used to recite: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and he is a father to them, and his wives are their mothers."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ikrimah that he said: "In the first recension it was: 'The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and he is their father.'" In the codex of Ubayy, may Allah be pleased with him, as narrated by Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves, and his wives are their mothers, and he is a father to them." The designation of "father" for him (ﷺ) is because he is the cause of eternal life, just as the father is also a cause of life; indeed he (ﷺ) has a greater claim to fatherhood than the father does. From Mujahid: "Every prophet is a father to his community." From this it was said regarding the words of Lut: ﴿These are my daughters﴾, that he meant the believing women. Its aspect is what has been mentioned. From this fatherhood, according to what is said, follows the brotherhood of the believers.

It is known from what was narrated from Mujahid that fatherhood is not among his particular distinctions (peace be upon him). This is unlike the motherhood of his wives, for it is, according to what is stated in al-Mawahib, among the particular distinctions. Therefore it is not forbidden for anyone other than him (ﷺ) among the prophets, peace be upon them, to marry the wives of those prophets after them, from any of their communities. ﴿And those of kinship (ulu al-arham)﴾, meaning those with blood relationships, which includes the agnatic relatives, ﴿are closer to one another﴾, not what stands opposite them, ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾, in benefit by inheritance and other forms of financial benefit, or in mutual inheritance. The later mentioned occasion of revelation supports this. ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾, meaning in what He recorded in the Preserved Tablet, or in what He sent down, which is the verse of inheritance or this verse, or in what He, glory be to Him, decreed, prescribed, and decided. ﴿from among the believers and the emigrants﴾: this is a complement to (awla). So the object of (min) is the one being preferred over, and it is a min of origin (ibtida'iyyah), like it is in your saying: "Zayd is more excellent than 'Amr," meaning: those of kinship are more entitled by the right of kinship to every benefit, or by inheritance, among the believers by the right of religion, and among the emigrants by the right of emigration.

Al-Zamakhshari said: It is permissible that this be an explanation of (ulu al-arham), meaning the relatives among these, some of them are more entitled to inherit from some than outsiders are. The first is the more apparent. In Medina there was inheritance by emigration and by allegiance in religion; that was by the verse at the end of al-Anfal, or by this verse. It was also said: by consensus (ijma'), and they intended by that to uncover the abrogating evidence (naskh); otherwise it cannot be an abrogating ruling, as is not hidden. The nominative ("some of them") may be either in apposition or as a subject. ("in the Book") is connected to (awla). It is permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (hal), with the governing element being the meaning of (awla). According to what Abu al-Baqa' said, it is not permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause of (ulu) because of the separation by the predicate, and because then there would be no governing element.

His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿except that you do kindness to your allies﴾ (illa an taf'alu ila awliyaikum ma'rufan) is either an exception that is connected (istithna' muttasil) from a more general category in which preference is conceived concerning benefit, as if it were said: the relative is more entitled than the stranger among the believers and the emigrants in every benefit, such as inheritance, charity, gifts, and similar things, except in the bequest, for it is what is meant by "kindness (ma'ruf)." So the stranger has more right to it than the heir relative, since it is not valid for an heir. Or it is a disconnected exception (istithna' munqati'), on the basis that what is meant by what contains preference is inheritance. Then the exception is from a category other than that which is implied by the overall sense, as if it were said: do not bequeath inheritance to anyone other than those of kinship; but your doing kindness to your allies among the believers and the emigrant strangers is ma'ruf, which is that you make a bequest to whomever you love among them with something permissible. So that is for him by bequest, not by inheritance. It is also permissible that ma'ruf be general for everything other than inheritance. What comes to the mind most readily is that the exception is disconnected, and Abu al-Baqa', Makki, and likewise al-Tabarsi limited themselves to this. The verbal noun was made a subject with an omitted predicate, as we have indicated.

Interpreting "the awliya'" as those who are among the believers and the emigrants is what the context requires. It is then a case of placing the apparent noun in the position of a pronoun, on the basis that "min" in what preceded is for the beginning of the limit (li-l-ibtida') and not for specification (li-l-bayan). Ibn Jarir and others related from Mujahid that it means "those who," and that the Prophet (ﷺ) made brotherhood between them, from among the emigrants and the Helpers. Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah that he said: this verse was revealed concerning the permissibility of a Muslim bequeathing to a Jew or a Christian. They also related from Qatadah that he said: "the awliya'" are the relatives from among the people of polytheism, and "al-ma'ruf" is the bequest. It is related in al-Bahr from a group including al-Hasan and Ata' that "the awliya'" includes both the relative and the stranger, the believer and the disbeliever, and that "al-ma'ruf" is more general than the bequest. A group of jurists and the Imamiyyah have permitted it for a disbelieving relative, and likewise for a stranger; they permit it for some of the disbelieving relatives, namely the parents and the child, and no others. The prohibition against taking disbelievers as awliya' does not require a prohibition against being good to them and kind to them.

"Tafa'alu" is transitivized with "ila" because it includes the meaning of conveying and bestowing, as if it were said: "Except that you do good conferring upon your awliya' a kindness." ﴿That﴾, i.e., what was mentioned in the two verses, namely "Call them by their fathers' names" and "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their own selves," is "written." It is also allowed that it refers to what came from the beginning of the surah up to here, or to what follows His words, exalted is He: "Allah has not made for any man two hearts," or to what was mentioned in the last verse, and in this there is a discussion. ﴿In the Book﴾, i.e., in the Preserved Tablet, or the Qur'an; it was said: in the Torah. ﴿Inscribed﴾, i.e., fixed by being written down. From Qatadah, that he said in one of the readings: "That was written with Allah, that a polytheist should not inherit from a believer." So do not be heedless.

The phrase ﴿And when We took from the prophets their covenant﴾ has an implied verb, (bidhkur) "remember", and it is treated as a direct object (maf'ul) rather than an adverb of time (zarf), because the meaning would otherwise be corrupted. It is conjoined to what precedes it as one narrative joined to another narrative, or it is conjoined to an implied element such as "take this." It has also been permitted that it be conjoined to the predicate (khabar) of kana, but this is distant, though it is close in some respects. Since what preceded contained rulings that Allah the Exalted legislated, some of which were from the Jahiliyyah and some from Islam, and some of which were nullified and abrogated (nusikhat, i.e. naskh, "abrogation"), He, glorified is He, followed it with what urges conveying the message. So He, Mighty and Majestic, said: ﴿And when﴾ etc. That is, remember the time when We took from all the prophets their covenants to convey the message and the laws, and to call to the true religion. According to al-Zajjaj and others, this was the time when the children of Adam were brought forth from the loins of Adam (peace be upon him) like atoms (kal-dharr).

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Qatadah that He, glorified is He, took from the prophets their covenants to confirm one another and to follow one another. In another narration from him, Allah the Exalted took their covenant to confirm one another, to proclaim that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah, and for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to proclaim that there is no prophet after him.

﴿And from you, and from Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, and Isa son of Maryam﴾: they are singled out for mention although they are clearly included among the prophets, to signal their greater distinction and merit, and that they are among the most renowned bearers of laws.

It is well known that they are the Ulu al-'Azm (the Messengers of firm resolve) among the Messengers, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them all. Al-Bazzar narrated from Abu Hurayrah that they are the best of the children of Adam (peace be upon them). The mention of our Prophet (ﷺ) first, although he is the last of them in being sent, is to signal his great and exalted rank, or because he preceded them in creation.

Ibn Abi 'Asim and al-Diya' in al-Mukhtarah narrated from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "I was begun with in creation, and I was the last of them in being sent."

A group narrated from al-Hasan, from Abu Hurayrah, from the Prophet (ﷺ) who said: "I was the first of the prophets in creation, and the last of them in being sent."

The same applies to the matter of being made a prophet (istinba'), for it has come in several narrations that he (peace be upon him) said: "I was a prophet while Adam was between the spirit and the body."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, who said: "It was said: O Messenger of Allah, when was your covenant taken? He said: 'While Adam was between the spirit and the body.'"

The mention of Nuh (peace be upon him) first in the verse of al-Shura, namely His saying: ﴿He has prescribed for you of the religion what He enjoined upon Nuh﴾ [al-Shura: 13], does not contradict this, since every context has its own speech. The context there is the description of the religion of Islam as original, and the fitting order there is to mention Nuh first. It is as if it were said: He has legislated for you the original religion with which Nuh was sent in the ancient covenant, with which Muhammad (peace be upon him), the Seal of the Prophets, was sent in the recent covenant, and with which were sent those prophets and renowned figures who lay between them. Ibn al-Munayyir said: the secret of placing the Prophet (ﷺ) first is that he is the one addressed and the one to whom this recited revelation was sent down, so he was more entitled to precedence. There is discussion on this point.

﴿And We took from them a firm covenant﴾: that is, a covenant of great importance, or a strong and solid one. This is the first covenant, and the taking of it is the taking of the one mentioned before. The conjunction is based on treating a difference in description (ta'ghayur 'unwani) as if it were a difference in essence (ta'ghayur dhati), as in His saying: ﴿And We saved them from a severe punishment﴾ [Hud: 58], following His saying: ﴿And when Our command came, We saved Hud and those who believed with him﴾ [Hud: 58]. There is in this an exaltation of the matter of which there is much. For this reason He, Mighty and Majestic, did not say: "And when We took from the prophets, and from you, and from Nuh, Ibrahim, Musa, and Isa son of Maryam, a covenant, firm" in a simple way, but He spoke in the noble arrangement that is in the text. It has been said: the firm covenant is an oath by Allah the Exalted. So after Allah, glorified is He, had taken from the prophets the covenant to convey the message and to call to the truth, He confirmed it with an oath by Allah the Exalted to fulfil what they had undertaken. Thus the two covenants are distinct in essence. As for His saying, Mighty and Majestic:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 8:

﴿That He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness﴾
Page 155
It has been said: it is connected to an implied, newly begun clause, brought to explain the reason (ʿillah) for the taking [of the covenant] mentioned and its purpose (ghayah), i.e., Allah the Exalted did that so that He may ask, etc. And it has been said: it is connected to (akhadhna, "We took"). This was objected to on the grounds that the aim is to remind of the covenant itself, and then to state its reason and purpose as an intended statement (bayan qasdi), as the change of style through the shift to the third person (iltifat ila al-ghaybah) indicates. The "truthful" (al-sadiqin) here means the Prophets whose covenant was taken, and the expression was placed in the position of their pronoun to signal from the outset that they were truthful in what they were asked about. The asking itself is for a wisdom that requires it, namely: so that Allah the Exalted may ask on the Day of Resurrection the Prophets who fulfilled their covenants about their true speech that they spoke to their peoples, or about their peoples' confirmation of them. Their asking, peace be upon them, about that in both cases is for the rebuke of the disbelieving deniers, as in His saying, ﴿On the Day when Allah will gather the messengers and say, "What was the response you received?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 109]. Or the intended meaning of "the truthful" is those who believed in the Prophets, and the sense is: that He may ask those who confirmed the Prophets about their confirmation of them, so it is said: "Did you confirm them?" It has also been said: it is said to them, "Was your confirmation done for the sake of Allah the Exalted?" The reason for understanding it this way is that one who confirms the truthful is truthful, and his confirmation is truth. It has also been said: the meaning is that He may ask the believers who fulfilled their pledge, when He made them testify against themselves, about the truthfulness of their pledge. This was objected to on the grounds that the context of reminding of the covenant of the Prophets rules it out.

﴿And He has prepared for the disbelievers a painful punishment﴾. It has been said: it is conjoined (ʿaṭf) to an implied verb connected to what precedes. It has been said: it is conjoined to an implied element indicated by ﴿li-yasʾala﴾, as if it were said: "So He rewarded the believers, and prepared for the disbelievers, etc." It has been said: it is conjoined to (akhadhna), and this is a semantic conjunction (ʿaṭf maʿnawi), as if it were said: Allah the Exalted affirmed upon the Prophets the call to His religion for the sake of rewarding the believers, and prepared for the disbelievers, etc. It has been said: it is conjoined to (yasʾala), by treating it as a present-tense verb, though a point of relevance must be noted so that the conjunction is apt. It has been said: it is conjoined to an implied element, and in the statement there is ihtibak (interlocking ellipsis), the estimate being: "That He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness, and prepare for them a great reward, and may ask the liars about their lying, and prepare for them a painful punishment," so that from each of the two parts was omitted what was mentioned in the other. It has been said: the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (yasʾala), with (qad) estimated or without it, and the least of these in artifice is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 9:**

﴿O you who believe, remember the favor of God upon you﴾. This begins the account of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), which is the Battle of the Trench (al-Khandaq). According to Ibn Ishaq, it took place in Shawwal of the fifth year (AH), and Malik said it was in the fourth year.

If "favor" (al-ni'mah) is a verbal noun (masdar) meaning "bestowal" (al-in'am), then the prepositional phrase "upon you" (alaykum) is connected to it. Otherwise, it is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of it, meaning "existing upon you." God's words ﴿when there came upon you armies﴾ are an adverbial clause of time (zarf) modifying the favor itself, or modifying its being established for them. It has been said that it is in the accusative governed by "remember" (udhkuru), as a substitution of inclusion (badal ishtimal) for "favor" (ni'mah). By "armies" (junud) is meant the Confederates (al-Ahzab): the Quraysh, led by Abu Sufyan; the Banu Asad, led by Tulayha; the Ghatafan, led by Uyayna; the Banu Amir, led by Amir ibn al-Tufayl; the Banu Sulaym, led by Abu al-A'war al-Sulami; the Banu al-Nadir, whose chiefs were Huyayy ibn Akhtab and the sons of Abu al-Haqiq; and the Banu Qurayza, whose leader was Ka'b ibn Asad. There had been a covenant between them and the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but they broke it at the instigation of Huyayy. Their total number was ten thousand according to one account, fifteen thousand according to another, and it has been said to be about twelve thousand. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) heard of their advance, he dug a trench near Medina, enclosing it, on the advice of Salman al-Farisi, assigning each ten men forty cubits (dhira') of it. Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out with three thousand Muslims and pitched his camp, with the trench between him and the people. He ordered the children and women to be sent into the fortresses (al-aatam), fear grew intense, the believers entertained every kind of thought, and hypocrisy showed itself, as God related. Nearly a month passed for both sides with no fighting between them except shooting arrows and throwing stones from behind the trench. However, some horsemen of the Quraysh, among them Amr ibn Abd Wudd, who was considered equal to a thousand horsemen, Ikrima ibn Abi Jahl, Dirar ibn al-Khattab, Hubayra ibn Abi Wahb, and Nawfal ibn Abd Allah, mounted their horses, sought a narrow place in the trench, struck their horses, and burst across. Their horses ran about with them in the salt flat between the trench and Sal'. Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God ennoble his face, went out with a group of Muslims, may God be pleased with them, until he took control of the gap through which they had crossed. The cavalry then came toward them, and Ali, may God ennoble his face, killed Amr in a well-known story. His horse fled and burst back across the trench in flight. Munabbih ibn Uthman ibn Abd al-Dar and Nawfal ibn Abd al-Uzza were killed along with Amr. It has also been said that Nawfal was found in the middle of the trench, and the Muslims began to pelt him with stones. He said to them: "A death more beautiful than this! Let one of you come down, and I will fight him," and al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam killed him.

Ibn Ishaq mentioned that Ali, may God ennoble his face, stabbed him in the collarbone until he drew it out from his ribs, and he died in the trench. The polytheists sent to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) offering to buy his corpse for ten thousand, and the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "It is yours; we do not eat the price of the dead." Then God sent down victory, and that is His words: ﴿So We sent upon them a wind﴾. [...]

This is a conjunction (atf) with "there came upon you" (ja'atkum), brought to explain the favor in summary. Its remainder will come, God willing, at the end of the story.

﴿And armies you did not see﴾, and these were the angels, peace be upon them. They were, as has been said, a thousand. It is narrated that God sent upon them a cold east wind on a cold night, which uprooted them and blew dust into their faces. God commanded the angels, peace be upon them, and they pulled up the tent pegs, cut the tent ropes, extinguished the fires, overturned the cooking pots, and the horses surged against one another. He cast terror into their hearts, and the angels shouted "Allahu akbar" around the sides of their camp. Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid al-Asadi said: "As for Muhammad, he has begun with magic. So flee, flee!" and they fled. Hudhayfa, may God be pleased with him, when he had gone to bring the Messenger of God (ﷺ) news of the people, said: "I went out until I came near the camp of the people. I looked by the light of a fire they had kindled, and there was a dark, large man placing his hand on the fire and wiping his side, saying: 'Depart, depart; there is no staying for you.' And there was the man in their camp, not going beyond their camp by a span. By God, I could hear the sound of stones in their saddlebags and bedding, and the wind was striking them. Then I went out toward the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace. When I was halfway, or about that, I found about twenty horsemen wearing turbans, and they said: 'Tell your companion that God has sufficed him against the people.'"

Al-Hasan read "wa-junudan" with a fatha on the jim. Abu Amr, in one transmission, and Abu Bakr, in one transmission as well, read "lam yarawha" with the ya' of the third person. ﴿And God is ever Seeing of what you do﴾, namely of the digging of the trench and the arrangement of the initial stages of war, to raise high the word of God, most high. It has been said that it refers to your turning to Him, most high, and your hoping for His bounty, mighty and majestic.

Abu Amr read "ya'maluna" with the ya' of the third person, meaning "what the disbelievers do" of guarding against, fighting, and urging some of them on against others, out of eagerness to nullify your right. It has been said that it refers to disbelief and sins. ﴿Seeing﴾, and for this reason He did what He did of giving you victory over them. The clause is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraD) that confirms what precedes it.

Page 157

﴿When they came upon you﴾ is a substitution (badal kull min kull, substitution of the whole for the whole) for ﴿when they came upon you﴾. It has also been said that it is connected to (ta'malun, "you do") or to (basiran, "seeing"). ﴿From above you﴾ means from the upper part of the valley, from the direction of the east. The attribution to them (the "you" in "above you") is due to the slightest connection. Those who came from that direction were the Banu Ghatafan, those who followed them from the people of Najd, the Banu Qurayzah, and the Banu al-Nadir. ﴿And from below you﴾ means from the lower part of the valley, from the direction of the west. Those who came from that direction were the Quraysh, those who supported them from the Ahabish, the Banu Kinanah, and the people of Tihamah. It has also been said that those who came from above were the Banu Qurayzah, and from below the Quraysh, Asad, Ghatafan, and Sulaym. And it has been said other than that.

It is possible that ﴿from above and from below﴾ is a metaphor (kinayah) for encirclement from all sides, as if it were said: "when they came upon you surrounding you"
Page 158

as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The punishment will overcome them from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 55]. ﴿And when the eyes swerved﴾ is coordinated with what precedes it and is included with it in the ruling of the reminder, meaning: when the eyes turned away from their usual course and deviated from their normal line of sight, out of bewilderment and dismay.

Al-Farra' said: that is, when they turned away from everything, so they did not look at anything except their enemy. ﴿And the hearts reached the throats﴾ means they were overcome with intense fear and were terrified with a great terror, because they moved from their place and rose toward the throats in order to come out.

Ibn Abi Shaybah narrated, from Ikrimah, that he said concerning the verse: if the hearts had moved and departed, his soul would have come out; but it is only fear, so the statement is hyperbole (mubalaghah). It has also been said: the heart, at anger, is driven outward, and at fear it gathers inward, so it constricts at the throat, and may lead to blocking the passage of breath, so that a person cannot breathe and dies of fear. It has also been said: the lung swells from the intensity of fear, anger, and severe grief, and when it swells it rises, and the heart is lifted with its rising to the top of the throat; for this reason it is said of a coward: "his lungs (sahr) have swollen." Qatadah went to taking the statement literally.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said concerning the verse: that is, they left their places, and had it not been that the windpipe was too narrow for them, they would have come out.

In the Musnad of Imam Ahmad, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, he said: "We said, O Messenger of Allah, is there anything we can say, since the hearts have reached the throats?"
