He said: "Yes, O Allah, conceal our faults and secure our fears." He said: "So Allah, exalted is He, struck the faces of His enemies with the wind, and Allah defeated them with the wind."

The address in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And you assumed about Allah assumptions﴾ is to those who openly show faith, without restriction. ﴿Assumptions (zunun)﴾ is the plural of ﴿assumption (zann)﴾, which is a verbal noun that applies to both little and much. It was made plural only to indicate the multiplicity of its kinds, and it has come thus in their poetry. Abu 'Amr recited in the Kitab al-Alhan:

"When al-Jawza' followed the Thurayya, I assumed about the family of Fatimah assumptions (al-zunun)."

That is: you assume about Allah, exalted is He, various kinds of different assumptions. The sincere among you, who are firm in the field of faith, assume that He, glorified is He, will fulfill His promise of raising His religion and supporting His Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; and this is expressed by what will be related of their saying: ﴿This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us﴾ [al-Ahzab: 22], and so on. Or they assume that He will test them, and so they fear that their feet may slip and they will not bear what has befallen them. This does not contradict sincerity and steadfastness, as is not hidden. And the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease assume what is reported of them in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when the hypocrites said﴾ [al-Ahzab: 12], and so on. Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from al-Hasan that he said concerning the verse: different assumptions. The hypocrites assumed that Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and his companions would be uprooted, while the believers were certain that what Allah and His Messenger promised is true, and that it would prevail over all religion.

It may also be chosen that the address is to the believers outwardly and inwardly, and the difference in their assumptions is due to the fact that they sometimes assume that Allah, glorified is He, will give them victory over the disbelievers without them first gaining control over them; at other times that He, mighty and majestic, will give the disbelievers victory over them, so that they take control of Medina, and then He gives them victory over them afterward; and at other times that He, glorified is He, will give the disbelievers victory to such an extent that they uproot them and the days of ignorance return; or because some of them assume this, some assume that, and some assume the other. It is required that the assumption that does not befit the state of the believer arose from the impulses of the soul that natural fear necessitated and that humans could not repel, and such is pardoned. Or it may be said: their differing assumptions are the assumption of victory without the enemy inflicting anything on them, their assumption after the enemy inflicts something, and the assumption of trial. On this view, no excuse is needed. In any case, the sentence is coordinated with (zaghat, "swerved"), and the use of the present tense is to bring the scene to mind and to indicate continuity. The word ﴿al-Zununa﴾ and similar definite accusatives ending in alif with lam, such as al-sabila and al-rasula, were written in the Mushaf with an alif at the end. Abu 'Amr omitted it both in pause and in continuation, and Ibn Kathir, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs omit it only in continuation, while the rest of the seven readers retain it in both states. Abu 'Ubayd and the expert scholars chose that one should pause on such a word with the alif and not connect it, so that it is neither omitted nor retained in continuation, because omitting it contradicts what the Mushafs of the regions agreed upon; and because retaining it in continuation is absent from the speech of the Arabs, in verse and prose, except under necessity, and not even under necessity. As for retaining it in pause, it conforms to the written form and agrees with some Arab dialects, because they retain this alif at the ends of lines of their poetry and at the hemistich endings; among these is the saying:

"Has the blamer and the reproach become weary of me?"

The verse-endings (fawasil) in speech are like the hemistich endings. Abu 'Ali said: the ends of verses (ru'us al-ayy) are likened to rhymes (qawafi) in that they are endings, just as rhymes are endings.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 11:**

﴿Hunālika﴾ (there, at that time) is an adverb of place (*ẓarf makān*, an adverbial complement of place), and it is also used for time. It was said that it is used figuratively (*majāz*), and this is the most fitting reading here. In either case, it is an adverbial complement governing what follows it, not governing *(litaẓunnūna)* ("you were thinking"), as some have said. That is, "at that dreadful time," or "in that place of trial." ﴿The believers were tested﴾, meaning Allah tested them. The statement is in the mode of figurative expression (*tamthīl*), and what is meant is that Allah, glorified and exalted, dealt with them as one who tests. Thereby the sincere was distinguished from the hypocrite, and the firm from the wavering. Their testing, according to what is related from al-Dahhak, was by hunger, and according to what is related from Mujahid, was by the severity of the siege. It was said that it was by steadfastness in faith.

﴿And they were shaken with a mighty shaking﴾, meaning they were violently agitated, from the intensity of fear and the multitude of enemies. From al-Dahhak: "They were shaken from their places, so that they had nothing but the place of the trench." It was also said: meaning they were stirred toward sedition, but they were protected.

Ahmad ibn Musa al-Lu'lu'i recited, from Abu 'Amr, *zilzilū* with a kasra on the first *zāy*. This is what Ibn Khalawayh reported. Al-Zamakhshari said: "From Abu 'Amr there is *ishmām* of the *zāy* of *(zulzilū)*," and it seems he meant that the *ishmām* was toward the kasra. The basis for the kasra is that the vowel of the first *zāy* was assimilated to the vowel of the second, and the quiescent letter was not counted, just as it was not counted by the one who said *mintin* with a kasra on the *mīm*, assimilating to the vowel of the *tā'*, and it is an active participle (*ism al-fā'il*) from *anta'a*. Al-Jahdari and Isa recited *zalzālan* with a fatha on the *zāy*. The verbal noun (*maṣdar*) of the *fa'lala* pattern of the geminate (*mudā'af*) root may take either fatha or kasra, as in *qalqala qalqālan*. The fatha form may also be used with the meaning of the active participle, as in *ṣalṣāl*, meaning *muṣalṣil*. If it is from a non-geminate root, then what is heard from it in the *fa'lāl* pattern has a kasra on the first letter, as in *sarhafahu sarhāfan*.

﴿And when the hypocrites said﴾ is coordinated with (*idh zāghat*, "when the eyes swerved"). The use of the present tense (*muḍāri'*) is for the indication, already mentioned, of the continuity of the saying and the bringing to mind of its scene.

﴿And those in whose hearts is a disease﴾. The apparent sense of the conjunction is that they were a people who were not hypocrites. It was said: they were a people whom the hypocrites tried to win over by introducing doubts to them. It was also said: they were a people whose belief was weak because their time in Islam was recent. It is permissible that what is meant by them is the hypocrites themselves, and the conjunction is for the difference of description, as in the verse: "To the king, the noble, and the son of the brave."

﴿What Allah and His Messenger promised us﴾, of victory and the elevation of the religion, ﴿was nothing but delusion﴾, meaning a promise of delusion. It was said: meaning a false statement. In *al-Bahr* (al-Bahr al-Muhit, by Abu Hayyan): meaning a matter that deceives us and throws us into what we have no capacity to bear.

It is related that "while the Companions were digging the trench, there appeared before them a white, round rock, extremely hard, into which the picks would not penetrate. They complained to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he took the pick from Salman (may Allah be pleased with him) and struck it a blow which split it, and a flash came from it that illuminated what lay between the two lava plains of Madinah, so that it was as if a lamp were in the midst of a dark night. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'Allahu akbar,' and the Muslims said, 'Allahu akbar.' Then he struck it a second time and broke off a piece, and a flash came from it that illuminated what lay between its two lava plains. He said, 'Allahu akbar,' and the Muslims said, 'Allahu akbar.' Then he struck it a third time and shattered it, and a flash came from it that illuminated what lay between its two lava plains. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said, 'Allahu akbar,' and the Muslims said, 'Allahu akbar.' He was asked about that, and he, peace be upon him, said: 'In the first, the palaces of al-Hira and the cities of Kisra were illuminated for me, as if they were the fangs of dogs, and Jibril, peace be upon him, informed me that my community will prevail over them. In the second, the red palaces of the land of Rome were illuminated for me, as if they were the fangs of dogs, and Jibril, peace be upon him, informed me that my community will prevail over them. In the third, the palaces of Sana'a were illuminated for me, as if they were the fangs of dogs, and Jibril, peace be upon him, informed me that my community will prevail over them. So rejoice in victory.' The Muslims rejoiced. A man from the Ansar called Mu'tab ibn Qushayr, who was a hypocrite, said: 'Does Muhammad promise us that he will conquer for us the cities of Yemen, the white cities and the palaces of Rome, while any one of us cannot relieve himself without being killed? This is by Allah sheer delusion!' So Allah, exalted is He, revealed this concerning that."

[Page 159]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 12:

﴿And when the hypocrites say﴾ etc.

In another narration, the hypocrites said when they heard that: "Do you not marvel? He tells you and promises you and gives you false hopes, that he sees from Yathrib the palaces of al-Hirah and the cities of Kisra, and that they will be conquered for you, while you are digging the trench and cannot even go out to relieve yourselves!" So Allah the Exalted revealed His saying, ﴿When the hypocrites say﴾.

The explanation of the plural form, given the view that the speaker was one person, is that the rest were content with it and endorsed it. The apparent sense is that the attribution of the promise to Allah the Exalted and His Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, under the title of Messengership, came from hypocrites who do not believe that he, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, possesses Messengership, and that the promise was not Allah the Exalted's promise, glory be to Him, made in the manner of mere conversation or mockery. Even if it was uttered by others, it is attributed to them by extension.

It is also possible that what is mentioned occurred within the narration itself and not in their speech. This may be supported by what occurred in some reports. Some scholars investigated the application of the title "Messenger" to him, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, and said: it is within the narration and not in their speech, as is witnessed by what was related from Mu'tib. Or it is taqiyyah (dissimulation), not mockery, because that is not valid with respect to non-hypocrites. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

﴿And when a party among them said﴾. Al-Suddi said:

They were ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and his companions. Muqatil said: they were the Banu Salima. Aws ibn Ruman said: they were Aws ibn Qayzi and his companions, the Banu Harithah. The pronoun in ﴿among them﴾ refers either to the hypocrites or to all of them. ﴿O people of Yathrib﴾: Yathrib is the name of the illustrious city (al-Madinah). Abu ʿUbaydah said: it is the name of a plot of land, and the city lies in one part of it. It was also said: it is the name of its land. As a proper noun it is a diptote (ممنوع من الصرف, a noun that takes only some of the case endings and no tanwin), on account of its being a proper name together with its form of a verb (wazn al-fiʿl), or on account of its feminine sense. It is not appropriate to call the city by this name.

Ahmad, Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from al-Bara' ibn ʿAzib, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever calls the city Yathrib, let him seek forgiveness from Allah. It is Taybah, it is Taybah, it is Taybah."

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him): "Do not call it Yathrib, for it is Taybah," meaning the city, "and whoever says Yathrib, let him seek forgiveness from Allah three times. It is Taybah, it is Taybah, it is Taybah."

In the al-Hawashi al-Khafajiyyah it is stated that calling it by this name is disliked (makruhah) in the sense of reprehensible but not forbidden (karahah tanzihiyyah). The reason given for this is that the name suggests tathrib, which means blame and reproach.

Al-Raghib said: tathrib means rebuking someone for a sin. Al-Thurb is a thin layer of fat. Yathrib may derive from this root, the yaʾ being an added letter in it. End of quotation. It was also said: Yathrib is the name of a man from the ʿAmaliqah, and the city was named after him. It was also called Athrab. Al-Tabarsi quoted al-Sharif al-Murtada that the city has names including Yathrib, Taybah, Tabah, al-Dar, al-Sakinah, Jabirah, al-Mahburah, al-Mahabbah, al-Mahbubah, al-ʿAdhra', al-Marhumah, al-Qasimah and Yandad. End of quotation. It seems that those who chose Yathrib from among these names did so in opposition to him (ﷺ), since they knew of his dislike of this name in particular among them. Their calling the people of Madinah by a title of their belonging to it is a preparation (tarshih) for what follows of the command to return to it.

﴿There is no place for you﴾: that is, no place of residence, or there is no residence for you. That is, it is not fitting or possible for you to reside here.

Abu Jaʿfar, Shaybah, Abu Raja', al-Hasan, Qatadah, al-Nakhaʿi, ʿAbd Allah ibn Muslim, Talhah and most of the Seven Readers read ﴿lā maqāma﴾ with a fatha on the mim. This may also mean a place, that is, "no place of standing," or it may be a verbal noun, that is, "no standing for you." The meaning is as stated above.

﴿So return﴾: that is, to your dwellings in Madinah, so that this will be safer for you from being killed, or so that you may have a hand with these confederates. It was said:

Their intention was to order them to flee, as what follows suggests. But they expressed it as a return to make their statement acceptable and to indicate that it is not the blameworthy kind of flight. It was also said: the meaning is, "There is no residence for you in the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ), so return to what you were upon of polytheism, or return from what you pledged to him and hand him over to his enemies (peace be upon him)." Or: "There is no residence for you after today in Yathrib or its environs, because of the enemies' victory, so return as unbelievers, so that residence there may become possible for you once enmity is lifted at that time."

It was also said: it is possible that they feared that the Prophet (ﷺ) would kill them after his victory over them, once it became clear that they were hypocrites. So they said, ﴿There is no place for you﴾, meaning there is no place for you with the Prophet (ﷺ), because if he is defeated he will kill you. So return from what you pledged to him and hand him over (peace be upon him), or return from Islam and unite with the confederates. Or: "You have no place of residence in this world at all if you remain as you are. So return from what you pledged to him (peace be upon him) and so on." The first is more apparent and better suited to what follows. Some of these interpretations are very far-fetched, as is not hidden.

﴿And a party among them asks the Prophet for leave﴾: this is coordinated (ʿatf) upon "said." The present tense is used because of what has passed concerning the bringing of the scene to mind (istihdar al-surah). The ones asking for leave, according to what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas and Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, were the Banu Harithah ibn al-Harith. It was said: they sent Aws ibn Qayzi, one of them, to ask for leave. Al-Suddi said: he came, along with another man from them called Abu ʿArabah ibn Aws. It was also said: those asking for leave were the Banu Harithah, and the Banu Salimah asked him (peace be upon him) for leave to return, obeying the command of those who had said, "O people of Yathrib."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿saying﴾ is either a substitute (badal) for "asks for leave," or a circumstantial clause (hal) from its subject, or a resumed statement (istinaf) answering the question of how they asked for leave. ﴿Indeed our houses are exposed﴾: that is, their walls are weak and exposed to thieves, as reported from al-Suddi. Al-Raghib said: that is, they are broken and open to anyone who wants them. Al-Kalbi said: that is, empty of men and neglected. Qatadah said: that is, exposed, fearing the enemy. Its origin, as has been said, is a verbal noun meaning a defect, and it is used as a description for intensification. It may be used of feminine, masculine, singular or other forms, as is the case with verbal nouns. It is also permitted that it be an adjective of quality (sifah mushabbahah), being a lightened form of ʿawrah with a kasra on the waw, as Ibn ʿAbbas, Abu Yaʿmar, Qatadah, Abu Raja', Abu Haywah, Ibn Abi ʿAblah, Abu Talut, Ibn Miqsam, and Isma'il ibn Sulayman recited it here and in what follows, from Ibn Kathir, from ʿawirat al-dar when it became defective. Ibn Jinni said: keeping the waw in this case is anomalous, and by analogy it should be changed to an alif, so one says ʿarah, as one says kabsh safin and naʿjah safah, yawm rah and rajul mal, the original being sawf, sawfah, rawh and mawl. This was objected to on the ground that analogy requires the change only when the change occurs in the verb, and ʿawira here has kept its ʿayn sound by analogy with iʿwarra (the intensive form). He preferred its being a verbal noun used as a description for intensification, on the ground that this is more suitable to the context of excuse, as the opening of their statement with the particle of certainty (harf al-tahqiq) makes clear. However, it should be said regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they are not exposed﴾, when this word is applied to it as it is applied to what came before, that the intention is intensification in negation, in the manner of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and your Lord is not unjust to the servants﴾ [Fussilat: 46]. The waw in it is for the circumstantial clause, meaning: they say this while the reality is that it is not so. ﴿They intend nothing﴾: that is, what they intend by asking for leave is nothing ﴿but flight﴾: that is, fleeing from fighting and from helping the believers, as a group has said. It was said: it is flight from the religion.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 14:**

﴿And if it had been entered﴾, i.e., the houses, as is the apparent meaning, ﴿upon them﴾, i.e., upon these speakers. The entering is attributed to their houses and is given the preposition "upon them" because the intended meaning is the supposition of its entry while they are inside it, not the supposition of its entry in absolute terms, which is what would be understood if the prepositional phrase were not mentioned. Nor is it the supposition of an entry upon them in absolute terms, which is what would be understood if the prepositional phrase and the subject of the entering were attributed to whoever among the people of corruption wished to enter, that is, if everyone among the people of debauchery and corruption who wished to enter their houses while they were in them had entered. ﴿From its every side﴾: "aqtar" is the plural of "qutr," meaning the region and the side. It is also said "qutr" with a ta' (qutr), a dialectal variant of it, meaning from all its sides. This happens when it is completely breached. This falls within the hypothetical supposition, so it does not contradict His saying, exalted is He: (﴿And they were not in danger﴾, then they were asked), i.e., they were requested by another group, at that terrifying calamity and tremendous quaking, ﴿the strife﴾, i.e., the fighting, as al-Dahhak said. ﴿They would have given it﴾, i.e., they would have given it to those who asked. It is as if He likened the strife, in which they were required to follow, to a precious thing requested from them to be surrendered, and He made their obedience and following equivalent to surrendering and giving what they were asked for. Nafi' and Ibn Kathir read "la-'atawha" (لَأتَوْها) with the short vowel, meaning they would have done it. ﴿And they would not have delayed with it﴾, i.e., with the strife. The ba' (با) is for transitivity, i.e., they did not stay with it nor postpone it. ﴿except briefly﴾, i.e., except a brief delay, or a brief time, which is the amount of time in which they would take up their weapons, according to what has been said. It was also said: the amount of time in which they would answer the request. Both of these, in my view, are of the nature of illustration. The intended meaning is that if someone other than you asked them to fight, while they were in the most severe state and the greatest anxiety, they would have hastened greatly, let alone making excuses about the breach of their houses while those houses were intact, as they did just now. The summary is that their request for permission to return was not due to the breach of their houses, but due to their hypocrisy and their aversion to supporting you.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: the meaning is: and if the city had been entered from its sides and the real war had intensified, then they were asked for the strife and the war on behalf of Muhammad (ﷺ), they would have flown toward it, and they would not have lingered in their houses to guard them except briefly. It was said: the amount of time in which they would take up their weapons, end quote. So the pronoun in (dukhilat, "it was entered") according to him refers to the city, and the ba' in (bi-ha, "with it") is for location (zarfiyya), as is apparent from his statement. It was also permitted that it be causal (sababiyya), and the meaning, with an implied noun, would be: and they did not delay because of guarding it. It was also said: it may be for accompaniment (mulabasa) as well, and the pronoun in every case refers to the houses, and in this there is what is called dislocation of pronouns (tafkik al-damair).

From al-Hasan, Mujahid, and Qatadah: "al-fitna" is shirk (polytheism). Within its meaning is what was said: it is apostasy and a return to the open display of disbelief. Some scholars made the two pronouns in (dukhilat, "it was entered") and (bi-ha, "with it") refer to the city, and claimed that the meaning is: and if the city had been entered upon them from all its sides, then they were asked to return to the open display of disbelief and polytheism, they would have done it, and they would not have stayed in the city after displaying their disbelief except briefly, for God, exalted is He, would destroy them or expel them along with the believers. It was also said: the pronoun in (dukhilat) refers to the houses or to the city, and the pronoun in (bi-ha) refers to the strife, in the sense of shirk, and the ba' is for transitivity. The meaning is: and if it had been entered upon them and then they were asked for shirk, they would have committed shirk, and they would not have delayed it except briefly. Close to this is Qatadah's statement: that is, if it had been entered upon them and then they were asked for shirk, they would have given it, their souls willingly consenting to it, and they would not have hesitated with it except briefly. It was also permitted that the ba' be for other than that.

It was said: the subject of the entering is those confederate armies. The possible interpretations of the verse are many, as is not hidden from one who has even slight reflection. What we mentioned first is the most apparent in my view.

Al-Hasan read "su'ulu" (سُولُوا) with a silent waw after the damma-vowelled sin. They said: it is from "sala yusalu," like "khafa yakhafu," a dialect form of "sa'ala" which has a hamza in its middle radical. Abu Zayd related: "they both yatasawalan." Abu Hayyan said: it is also permissible that its original form had a hamza, because "su'ulu" may be understood according to the view of one who says "daraba" in the passive form as "daraba," then he eased the hamza by converting it to a waw, according to the view of one who says in "bu's" (misery) "bus," converting the hamza to a waw because of the damma before it.

Abd al-Warith, from Abu 'Amr, and al-A'mash read "si'ulu" (سِيلُوا) with a kasra on the sin without hamza, like "qila." Mujahid read "suwiilu" (سُويِلُوا) with a silent waw after the damma-vowelled sin and a kasra-vowelled ya' replacing the hamza.

[Page 162]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 15:

﴿And indeed they had already made a covenant with Allah before, that they would not turn their backs.﴾ These are the group who sought permission (al-musta'dhinun), and they are the Banu Haritha according to the majority. It was also said: they are the Banu Salima, who had lost their nerve on the day of Uhud, then repented and made a covenant on that day, before the day of the Trench (al-Khandaq), that they would not flee. And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas that they were a people who had made a covenant in Mecca on the night of al-'Aqaba that they would protect him (ﷺ) from whatever they protect themselves from. It was also said: they were people who were absent from the battle of Badr and grieved over what they had missed of the honour that the people of Badr had received, so they said: "If Allah makes us witness a fight, we will surely fight." The word "covenant" (ʿAhada) was treated as an oath for this reason, and it was followed by His saying, ﴿they would not turn their backs﴾. It came in the third-person form according to meaning; had it come as they had uttered it, the construction would have been "the backs shall not be turned" (lā tuwallā al-adbār). Turning the backs (tawliyat al-adbar) is a metaphor (kināya) for fleeing and routing, since the one who flees turns his back to the one he flees from. ﴿And the covenant of Allah is ever to be questioned﴾ — he will be called to account for fulfilling it and will be recompensed for it, and that is on the Day of Resurrection. The use of the past tense, according to what is in Majma' al-Bayan, is to affirm that it will certainly occur. It was also said: meaning, it was ever questioned in the sight of Allah, the Exalted, concerning its fulfilment, or it was a demanded obligation until it is fulfilled.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 16:

﴿Say: Flight will not benefit you if you flee from death or slaying.﴾ That is, that flight will not benefit you, nor will it repel from you what has been decreed for you from eternity, whether one of you dies a natural death or is killed by a sword or the like, for what is decreed will certainly occur without doubt. ﴿And then you would not be given enjoyment except for a little.﴾ That is, even if flight did benefit you, by repelling what was decreed upon you, and you were granted enjoyment, that enjoyment would be only a small enjoyment, or a short time.

This is by way of supposing the impossible (fard al-muhal). He did not say "even if it benefited you" as a concession to the manner of speech (mumashah), nor "if flight benefits you and you are granted enjoyment through delay," meaning that this is contingent with God, Exalted, upon flight and tied to it. Enjoyment would then be only a little, for the days of life, however long, are short, and a lifespan that the particles of minutes consume, however much it grows, is little. Some of the eminent scholars said: the meaning is that flight does not benefit you a lasting or complete benefit in repelling the two matters mentioned, death or slaying, entirely. For every person must have a death by natural causes or a slaying at a specific time, not because the decree preceded it, since it follows what is decreed and therefore is not what causes it, but because it is the necessary result of the ordering of causes and effects according to the customary course, in accordance with wisdom. Therefore there is no indication in it that flight is of no avail at all, so as to be contradicted by the prohibition against casting oneself into destruction and the command to flee from harms. His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And then you would not be given enjoyment except for a little﴾ indicates that flight has some benefit in general, since the meaning is that you would not be given enjoyment, on the assumption of flight, except for a little enjoyment. There is more to this, so reflect.

Al-Zamakhshari mentioned that one of the Marwanids passed by a leaning wall and hurried past it, and this verse was recited to him. He said: "That little is what we seek." It seems he inclined to the second aspect, or to what some mentioned regarding the verse. The answer to the conditional "in" (in) is omitted, because what precedes it indicates it. ("Idhan") is preceded here by a conjunctive particle, so it is permissible to use it in its operative form or its non-operative form, but here it has only been read in the non-operative form.
Page 163
It was read in the operative form in His saying, Exalted is He, in Surat al-Isra' [17:76]: (wa-idhan la yalbathuna khilafaka). And "la yumatta'una" was read with the third-person yā' (yumatta'ūna).

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 33, verse 17:

﴿Say: "Who is it that can protect you from Allah if He intends harm for you, or intends mercy for you?"﴾ This is an interrogative (*istifham*, a question used for emphasis) with the meaning of negation. That is, no one can prevent you from Allah, mighty and majestic, and His decree, whether it be good or evil. Mercy has been placed alongside harm in the sense of protection, although protection is only from harm, because "protection" (*ismah*) carries the meaning of prevention. It is also permissible that there is an elision (*taqdir*) in the speech, and the original would be: "Say: Who is it that can protect you from Allah if He intends harm for you, or who will afflict you with harm if He intends mercy for you?" The second part was omitted, like the statement of the poet:

*And I saw your husband in the battle, girded with a sword and a spear*

Here the intended meaning is: "and carrying a spear," or "or holding a spear," and this runs in the same direction as the preceding explanation of the verse. Al-Tibi (al-Tibi, the commentator) permitted that the meaning be: "Who is it that can protect you from Allah if He intends harm for you, or who is it that can withhold the mercy of Allah from you if He intends mercy for you?" The indicator of the elision (*qarina*, a contextual sign) is the meaning of prevention in "yaʿsimukum" (protects you). The first interpretation was preferred because it avoids omitting a whole clause without necessity.

﴿And they will not find for themselves, besides Allah, any *walī* (protector)﴾ who benefits them, ﴿nor any *naṣīr* (helper)﴾ who repels harm from them. What is meant is the first (the harm), so they will find it, and so on. It is like the statement of the poet:

*And you do not see the lizard therein retreating into its burrow*

It is conjoined (*maʿṭūf*) in meaning to what precedes it. It is as if it were said: "They have no protector (*ʿāṣim*), no guardian (*walī*), and no helper (*naṣīr*)." Or the clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāliyyah*).

﴿Indeed, Allah knows those among you who hinder⦆ — that is, those who discourage (people) from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); ﴿and those who say to their brothers, "Come to us!"⦆ — that is, come over to us, or bring yourselves close to us. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: The verse was revealed concerning ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy, Muʿtib ibn Qushayr, and those hypocrites who returned from the Trench to Madinah. Whenever a hypocrite came to them, they would say to him, "Woe to you! Sit down and do not go out," and they would write to their brothers in the army, "Come to us, for we are waiting for you."

Qatadah said: It was revealed concerning the hypocrites who used to say to their brothers among the residents of Madinah, the helpers of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his companions are nothing but a mouthful. Had they been meat, Abu Sufyan and his companions would have devoured them, so let them be."

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn Zayd, who said: "A man returned from the presence of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the Day of the Confederates to his brother, and found with him roasted meat and date wine. He said to him, 'You are here while the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) is among the spears and swords!' The brother said, 'Come to me, for you and your companion have been surrounded. By the One by whom one swears, Muhammad will never face them again.' The man said, 'You lie! By the One by whom one swears, I will inform him of your matter.' He went to inform the Prophet (ﷺ), but found that Jibril (peace be upon him) had already descended with this verse."

It was also said: These were the Jews, who used to say to the people of Madinah, "Come to us and be with us." It seems that what is meant by the people of Madinah here are the hypocrites among them whose hypocrisy was known to the Jews. (Qad) is for emphasis (taḥqīq) or for diminution (taqlīl), and this depends on the context of the statement. (Min-kum) is an explanation of "those who hinder," not a complement of it, as has been indicated. The meaning of brotherhood here is sharing in a quality: it is hypocrisy according to the first view, disbelief in the Prophet (ﷺ) according to the last view, and companionship, neighbourhood, and residence in Madinah according to the second view. The same applies to the third view, for that is compatible with brotherhood by lineage. The apparent form of the plural indicates that the verse was not revealed concerning those two full brothers alone; perhaps it was revealed concerning them, and concerning the hypocrites who said that, and the sincere helpers to whom it was said. That it was revealed concerning a group of blood brothers is merely a possibility, although it has a textual basis; so brotherhood should be understood in that sense, and there is no harm in it. As for affirming all four views mentioned and understanding brotherhood as brotherhood in religion, brotherhood in companionship and neighbourhood, and brotherhood in lineage, its status is not hidden.

(Halumma): among the people of the Ḥijāz, it is used in the same form for the singular and the plural. However, among the Tamim, one says halumma yā rajul ("come, O man") and halumm�ū yā rijāl ("come, O men"). According to some scholars, it is a sound (ṣawt) that has been named as a verb (ism al-fiʿl). It is well known that it may be transitive, as in halumma shuhadāʾakum ("bring your witnesses"), meaning "bring forth" or "bring near," and intransitive, as in halumma ilaynā ("come to us"), based on interpreting it as "come over to us." As for interpreting it as "bring yourselves close to us," the apparent view is that it is transitive with its object omitted, though it has been permitted that it be intransitive. This is an explanation of the overall meaning. In al-Bahr it is stated that the grammarians hold that halumma is not a sound but a compound, whose original composition is disputed. It has been said that it is composed of hā, which is used for alerting, and mimm, meaning "intend" or "come forward." This is the view of the Basrans. It has also been said that it is composed of hal and umm. The discussion of the preferred view on this matter is detailed in its proper place.

﴿And they do not come to battle⦆ — that is, fighting and combat. The original meaning of the word is "severity." ﴿except a little⦆ — that is, coming a little, or for a little time. They would not come to the army except when they had no choice but to come, so they would come so that people might see their faces, and when people were distracted from them, they would return to their homes. It is also permissible that it be an adjective of an implied object, just as it is an adjective of the verbal noun or of the time, meaning: except a little harm, since they make excuses for much harm and go out only in a little. Coming to harm in these aspects is taken in its literal sense. It may also be a metonymy (kināyah) for fighting, and the meaning would be: they do not fight except a little fighting, like the saying of Allah, ﴿They did not fight except a little⦆. Its littleness is either due to the brevity of its duration or the scarcity of its benefit. In either case, the clause is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) of (the sayers). It has been said that it is also permissible for it to be an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) on (Allah knows). This, as you see, is weak. It has also been said that it is part of the speech being related, and the plural pronoun refers to the companions of the Prophet (ﷺ), meaning: the sayers of that, saying, "The companions of Muhammad (ﷺ) will not come to the battle of the Confederates, and they will not confront them except a little." This view is contrary to what is apparent, and it seems that whoever held that the verse concerns the Jews was inclined to it.

[p. 164]

[p. 165]

*"Stingy towards you"* (أشِحَّةً عَلَيْكُمْ): that is, miserly toward you with spending and support, as narrated from Mujahid and Qatadah. It was also said: stingy with themselves; and it was said: stingy with the spoils at the time of division; and it was said: stingy with everything that is of benefit to you. Abu Hayyan (Abu Hayyan al-Andalusi) endorsed this last view. Al-Zamakhshari held that the meaning is: "They are grudging toward you, hovering over you the way a man protects one who defends him and fights in his stead when he is afraid." This is because they feared for themselves should the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers with him prevail, since there would be no one to keep the confederates away from them or to protect their domain other than them. It was also said that they did this out of showing off (riya'). Most scholars went with what you have heard before, and the abridgers of his *Kashshaf* (al-Kashshaf) also adopted it. This is said because the meaning Zamakhshari chose corresponds to what follows in the sequence (فِي التَّفْرِيعِ), so it requires taking it as an explanation (تفسيرًا). Some of the eminent scholars preferred it over the view of most, saying: "He chose it so that it would match a meaning and correspond to His saying afterwards: *'stingy towards good'* (أشِحَّةً عَلى الخَيْرِ), and because usage requires it: stinginess over a thing (الشُّحُّ عَلى الشَّيْءِ) means wanting its survival, as in *al-Sihah* (al-Sihah fi al-Lughah), and he alluded to it with his words 'grudging toward you' (أضِنّاءُ بِكُمْ)." And what others have mentioned is not supported by usage. End of quote.

Al-Khafaji said: If the usage mentioned is accepted, then it is definitive; otherwise, each has its own direction, as is not hidden from one who knows the styles of speech.

*"Stingy"* (أشِحَّةً) is the plural of *shahih* (شَحِيحٍ), irregularly. The regular pattern for *fa'il* adjectives whose second and third radicals are doubled is to form the plural on *af'ila'* (أفْعِلاءَ), as in *danin / adnna'* (ضَنِينٍ / أضِنّاءَ) and *khalil / akhilla'* (خَلِيلٍ / أخِلّاءَ). So the regular form would be *ashihha'* (أشِحّاءُ), and that is also attested. Its accusative case (نَصْبُهُ) is, according to al-Zajjaj and Abu al-Baqa, a circumstantial accusative (حال) from the subject of *ya'tun* (يَأْتُونَ), meaning they abstained from coming, being stingy. Al-Farra' said it is in the accusative of dispraise (عَلى الذَّمِّ). It was also said that it is a circumstantial accusative from the pronoun in *"Come to us"* (﴿هَلُمَّ إلَيْنا﴾), or from an implied pronoun in *yu'awwiqun* (يُعَوِّقُونَ). The first of these was reported from al-Tabari, and it is as you see. It was also said that it is from *"those who hinder"* (﴿المُعَوِّقِينَ﴾), or from *"the sayers"* (القائِلِينَ). Both were rejected on the grounds that they involve separating parts of the relative clause, but this was challenged: the intervening element belongs to the relative clause's complements, and the rejection is only clear if it is a circumstantial accusative of *"those who hinder"*, since it was then coordinated with the relative pronoun before its clause was complete.

Ibn Abi Abla read *ashihhatun* (أشِحَّةٌ) with a nominative ending, supposing an implied subject: *"They are stingy."*

*"When fear comes"* (﴿فَإذا جاءَ الخَوْفُ﴾): from the enemy, and it was anticipated that the people of Medina would be wiped out.

*"You see them looking at you, their eyes rolling"* (﴿رَأيْتَهم يَنْظُرُونَ إلَيْكَ تَدُورُ أعْيُنُهُمْ﴾): that is, their eyeballs (أحْداقُهم), or with their eyeballs, with the preposition *bi* being transitive, so the meaning becomes "their eyeballs turn their eyes." The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase: their eyes rolling from intense fear.

*"Like one who swoons from death"* (﴿كالَّذِي يُغْشى عَلَيْهِ مِنَ المَوْتِ﴾): this is an adjectival phrase describing the verbal noun of *yanzurun* (يَنْظُرُونَ), or a circumstantial phrase from its subject, or describing the verbal noun of *taduru* (تَدُورُ), or a circumstantial phrase from *a'yunuhum* (أعْيُنُهُمْ). That is, they look with a look like that of one fainting from the agonies of death, out of dread, fear, and clinging to you. Or: they look while being like the one who... etc.; or: their eyes roll with a rolling like the rolling of the eye of one who... etc.; or: their eyes roll being like the eye of one who... etc.

It was also said that the meaning of the verse is: when fear of battle comes and the Muslims prevail over their enemies, you see them looking at you, their eyes rolling in their sight, wandering and restless, hoping that some sword-wielder would signal to them, because they attend with an evil intention, not a good one. The first view is the apparent one.

*"When fear departs, they lash you with sharp tongues"* (﴿فَإذا ذَهَبَ الخَوْفُ سَلَقُوكم بِألْسِنَةٍ حِدادٍ﴾): that is, they hurt you with speech and dispute with you with powerful, sharp tongues. This was said by al-Farra'. From Qatadah: they extended their tongues against you at the time of dividing the spoils, saying, "Give us, give us; you have no more right to them than we do." Yazid ibn Ruman said:

They extended their tongues against you in harm, abusing you and disparaging the religion you are upon.

Some eminent scholars said: The root of *salq* (السَّلْقُ) is extending and stretching a limb for subjugation, whether it is a hand or a tongue. So "lashing with the tongue" is the public display of attack and blame. *Salq* is here interpreted as striking, metaphorically, just as blame is called a "stab" (طَعْنٌ). What necessitates this is the description of the tongues as sharp (حِدادٍ). It is permissible to liken the tongue to a sword or the like by way of implicit metaphor (الاستعارة المكنية), and to attribute to it *salq* in the sense of striking, as an imaginative representation (تخييلًا).

Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, about *salq* in the verse. He said: "Stabbing with the tongue." He said: "Do the Arabs know that?" He said: "Yes. Have you not heard the words of al-A'sha:

*Among them are fertility, generosity, and courage;
among them is the eloquent, sharp-tongued orator.*"

Al-Zajjaj explained it as intense address: the meaning of *salaqukum* (سَلَقُوكم) is that they addressed you with the most intense and eloquent address concerning the spoils. It is said: *khatib mislaq* (خَطِيبٌ مِسْلاقٌ) or *sallaq* (سَلّاقٌ) when he is eloquent in his sermon. Some took *salq* to mean raising the voice, and on this basis came the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "He is not of us who *salaq* or *halaq*." In *al-Nihayah* (al-Nihayah fi Gharib al-Hadith) it is said: that is, he raised his voice at calamity. It was also said: that a woman slaps her face and tears it. The first is more correct.

Some claimed that the meaning in the verse is that they extended their tongues in deceiving you with what pleases you, by way of flattery and courtesy, but what is in this is not hidden.

Ibn Abi Abla read *salaqukum* (صَلَقُوكُمْ) with *sad* (الصّادِ).

*"Stingy towards good"* (﴿أشِحَّةً عَلى الخَيْرِ﴾): that is, miserly and greedy for the wealth of the spoils, as narrated from Qatadah. It was also said: stingy with their own wealth that they spend. Al-Jubba'i said: that is, stingy in speaking any word that contains good. Abu Hayyan went to the generality of "good." *"Stingy"* (أشِحَّةً) is in the accusative as a circumstantial phrase from the subject of *salaqukum* (سَلَقُوكُمْ), or in the accusative of dispraise. This is supported by Ibn Abi Abla's reading *ashihhatun* with nominative ending, since on that reading it is the predicate of an implied subject, meaning *"they are stingy,"* and the clause is then a new sentence, not a circumstantial one, as it is on the dispraise reading.

Some distinguished the stinginess mentioned here from the stinginess mentioned earlier, saying that what is here is restricted to the "good" meaning the spoils' wealth, while what came before is restricted to helping and supporting the believers, or to spending in the way of Allah, so this does not repeat what came before. Al-Zamakhshari, having taken the position he took there, said here: "When fear departs and the spoils are secured and the division takes place, they transfer that stinginess, that grudging, and that hovering over you to the good, which is the wealth and the spoils, and they forget that first state, and they become bold against you and strike you with their tongues," etc. You have heard what some eminent scholars said about this.

It is possible to say, in distinguishing this from what preceded, that what was meant earlier is blaming them for stinginess with everything that is of benefit, or with some kind of it, toward the believers, and from this comes blaming them for greed for wealth, or for whatever is of benefit in general, without regard to whether it is toward the believers or others. The latter is more emphatic in blaming them than the former.

*"Those"* (﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾): those described with the foregoing evil qualities, *"they have not believed"* (﴿لَمْ يُؤْمِنُوا﴾) with sincerity, for they are the hypocrites who displayed faith and concealed disbelief in their hearts. *"So Allah has nullified their deeds"* (﴿فَأحْبَطَ اللَّهُ أعْمالَهُمْ﴾): that is, He made their invalidity manifest, because they were invalid from the moment they were performed, since their validity is conditioned on sincere faith, and they were concealing disbelief. In *al-Bahr* (al-Bahr al-Muhit): that is, He did not accept them, so they were as if nullified. On both views, *"deeds"* means the acts of worship commanded. It is also permissible that what is meant is what they did in hypocrisy and pretense, even if it was not worship, and the meaning is: He, mighty and majestic, invalidated their artifice and hypocrisy, so that it no longer entailed any worldly benefit at all.

Some took "deeds" to mean acts of worship and "nullification" in its literal sense, based on what was narrated from Ibn Zayd, from his father, who said: The verse was revealed concerning a man of Badr who became a hypocrite after Badr, and what happened to him happened, so Allah nullified his deed at Badr and elsewhere. But the plural form makes this unlikely, and so does His saying *"they have not believed,"* for this man, as the apparent meaning of this report indicates, had believed before. Also, the Prophet's saying, peace and blessings be upon him: "Perhaps Allah looked upon the people of Badr and said: do what you wish, for I have forgiven you," refutes it. So the apparent view, and Allah knows best, is that this report is not authentic.

*"And that"* (﴿وكانَ ذَلِكَ﴾): that is, the nullification, *"is easy for Allah"* (﴿عَلَى اللَّهِ يَسِيرًا﴾): that is, effortless; He does not mind it, and He, glorified be He, does not fear any objection to Him. It was also said: that is, easy and simple for Him, mighty and majestic. The specific mention of its ease, although everything is easy for Him, the Exalted, is to make clear that their deeds are nullified as stated, because the wisdoms requiring it are fully in agreement, and nothing prevents it at all. It was also said: "that" refers to their condition of stinginess and the like, and the meaning is: that condition was easy for Him, mighty and majestic, He does not mind it, and He, glorified be He, does not make it a cause for abandoning the believers. But this is not the point, and what is intended by what has been mentioned is threat and warning.

They think the confederates have not departed. That is, due to their great cowardice and fear, they are so overwhelmed by panic and bewilderment that Allah repelled the confederates and they withdrew, yet they imagine that they have not withdrawn. It has also been said that the meaning is: because of their cowardice, they think the confederates have not been defeated, when in fact they have been defeated and have turned back from the trench toward Medina for that reason. If a report supports this, then so be it; otherwise, the apparent meaning is that it is derived from Allah's words: ﴿and those who say to their brothers, "Come to us"﴾, since this apparently indicates that they were outside the camp of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, urging their brothers to join them. That the meaning is "Come to our opinion" or "Come to our place, which is at an edge where an arrow does not reach" goes against the apparent meaning. Likewise, His words: ﴿And if they were among you﴾ are, as is also apparent, [to be understood as referring to being outside], since it is far-fetched to interpret it as the same location, even within the trench. ﴿And if the confederates come﴾ again (a second time) ﴿they would wish that they were in the desert among the Bedouins﴾: they wish that they were outside, in the desert, and with the Bedouins, who are the people of the herds. Abdullah, Ibn Abbas, Ibn Ya'mur and Talhah read "budda" (بُدًّى), the plural of bad (بادٍ), like ghazi and ghuzza. This is not a regular pattern for defective final-radical nouns (mu'tall al-lam, words whose last root letter is a weak letter), whose regular form is fu'ala, like qadi and qudat. In another report from Ibn Abbas it is read "badaw" (بَدَوْا) as a past-tense verb. In the report of the author of al-Iqlid, it is read "bada" (بَدى) on the pattern of "ada". ﴿They ask﴾, that is, every arrival from the direction of Medina ﴿about your news﴾, about what happened to you from the confederates, seeking to learn your condition through inquiry rather than by witnessing it,
Page 167
out of fear and cowardice. The choice of living in the desert is so that they would be safe from fighting. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the doer of (bādūn). Ibn Atiyyah reports that Abu Amr, Asim and al-A'mash read "yasalūn" (يَسَلُونَ) without a hamza, like the words of Allah: ﴿Ask the Children of Israel﴾ [al-Baqarah: 211]. This is not known from Abu Amr and Asim, and perhaps it is in their irregular readings (shādhdh). The author of al-Lawami' transmitted it from al-Hasan and al-A'mash. Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, Qatadah, al-Jahdari, al-Hasan, and Ya'qub, according to one transmission from them, read "yassalūn" (يَسّالُونَ) with a doubled sin and a long vowel. Its original form is yatasa'alūn, in which the ta' was assimilated into the sin; that is, some of them ask others, meaning some say to others: "What did you hear, and what reached you?" Or it means they ask the Bedouins, that is, they ask them, just as you say: "I saw the crescent and I looked at it," and "I perceived Zayd and I looked at him intently." ﴿And if they were among you﴾, that is, in this second attack that is supposed by His words: (﴿And if the confederates come﴾), or (﴿if they were among you﴾) in the first attack that preceded, and they had not returned to inside Medina, and there was fighting with swords and single combat in the ranks, ﴿they would not fight except a little﴾, out of ostentation, reputation-seeking, and fear of being blamed. Muqatil, al-Jayyani and al-Ba'labakki said: it is little insofar as it is for show, but had it been for Allah, it would have been much.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 21:**

﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example﴾. The apparent meaning is that the address is to the sincere believers, who were addressed earlier in His saying, ﴿about your news﴾, and in His saying, glorified is He, ﴿even if they had been among you﴾.

*Uswah* (exemplar, model), with a kasra on the hamza, as the majority of readers recited it, and with a damma, as ʿAsim recited it, means a quality. Al-Raghib said: it is the condition in which a person is. It is the subject of *kāna* (was), and *lakum* (for you) is the predicate. *Fī rasūli Allāh* (in the Messenger of Allah) is attached to what *lakum* is attached to, or it is in a position modifying *uswah*, since if it were placed after it, it could be a qualifier of it. Or it is attached to *kāna*, according to the view of one who permits, when it is a defective verb (*nāqisah*) and its sister verbs, that the adverbial complement operate on the adverb. It is also permitted that *fī rasūli Allāh* be the predicate and *lakum* be a clarification, meaning: I mean, for you. That is: by Allah, indeed in the Messenger of Allah you have a good quality, one which it is right to emulate and follow, such as steadfastness in war and bearing hardships.

It is also permitted that *uswah* be understood as *qudwah* (model) in the sense of the one who is followed, meaning: he, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, in himself is a model worthy of being emulated. In the speech there is the figure of *tajrīd* (abstraction), which is to derive from a person possessing a quality another who is similar to him in it, for emphasis of the attribute, as in: "I met from him a lion." It may mean *min* (from), and it may mean *fī* (in), as in the verse of poetry:

*They shed our blood unjustly, the sons of Marwan,*
*and in Allah, if they do not act justly, is a judgment of justice.*

And as in His saying: "In the egg are twenty *mann* of iron," meaning: it itself is this amount of iron.

Although the verse was brought for the purpose of following him, peace be upon him, in matters of war, such as steadfastness and the like, it is general in all his actions, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, when it is not known that they are among his particular privileges, such as marrying more than four wives.

Ibn Majah and Ibn Abi Hatim related, from Hafs ibn ʿAsim, who said: "I said to ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with them both: I see you on a journey not performing the prayer before the prayer nor after it. He said: O son of my brother, I accompanied the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, so-and-so, and I did not see him perform it before the prayer nor after it. And Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example﴾."

ʿAbd al-Razzaq related in *al-Musannaf* from Qatadah, who said: "ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, intended to forbid the *ḥibarah* (a striped garment). A man said: Did you not see the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, wearing it? ʿUmar said: Yes. The man said: Did not Allah say: ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example﴾? So ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, left that."

Al-Shaykhan, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah, and others related from Ibn ʿUmar that "he was asked about a man performing ʿumrah who had circumambulated the House, whether he could have intercourse with his wife before he had performed the running between al-Safa and al-Marwah. He said: The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, arrived, circumambulated the House, prayed two rakʿahs behind the Station (*al-Maqam*), ran between al-Safa and al-Marwah, and then recited: ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example﴾."

Al-Shaykhan and others related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: "If a man makes his wife forbidden to himself, it is an oath which he must expiate." And he recited: ﴿Indeed, in the Messenger of Allah you have a good example﴾. And there are other reports besides these. The full discussion is in the books of the principles of jurisprudence (*kutub al-usul*).

﴿For whoever hopes for Allah and the Last Day﴾: that is, whoever hopes for (*yu'ammil*) Allah, exalted is He, and for His reward, as an report from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, alludes to. Accordingly, He has placed *al-yawm al-akhir* (the Last Day), in the sense of the Day of Resurrection, in the position of the reward, because His reward occurs in it. So it is, as al-Tibi said, from the usage of naming the locus for what is in it. The expression is like your saying: "I hope for Zayd and his generosity," where mentioning the first object serves as a preparation for the second, which is the intended one, and in it there is a beauty and eloquence that are absent from saying: "I hope for Zayd, his generosity," as an apposition.

The author of *al-Fara'id* said: it is possible that the estimate is: he hopes for the mercy of Allah, or the pleasure of Allah, and the reward of the Last Day. So in the speech there are two elided genitive constructions. And from Muqatil: that is, he fears Allah, exalted is He, and fears the Resurrection in which the recompense of deeds is, on the basis that he placed *al-yawm al-akhir* in the position of the Resurrection, because it occurs in it. Hope in this case is in the sense of fear. The object of hope, in whatever sense it is taken, is a matter of the category of meanings, because it does not attach to essences. Some have estimated that the noun added to the Divine Name is the word *ayyam* (days), intended as events, because *al-yawm* is used for what occurs in it of wars and incidents, and this became well known until it was like a literal meaning. The conjoined phrase was made the indicator of this estimate, and the conjunction was taken as the conjunction of the specific over the general. The apparent meaning of hope on this view is fear. It is permitted that the speech be in this case like your saying: "I hope for Zayd and his generosity." It may be that hope here means expectation (*amal*), if what is meant is the victory and reward that are in the Day. It may mean both fear and expectation together, based on the permissibility of using a single expression in both its meanings, or in its literal and figurative senses, and the intention of what occurs in it of the agreeable and the disagreeable. In my view, the estimate of *ayyam* (days) is not immediately evident to the understanding.

Some interpreted *al-yawm al-akhir* as the Day of the context, and what is immediately understood from it is the Day of Resurrection. And *man* (whoever), as it has been said, is a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun of address in *lakum* (for you), and the governing element is repeated for emphasis. It is a substitution of whole for whole. The benefit of it is the urging to emulation. The substitution of an explicit noun for the pronoun of the addressee in this way is permitted according to the Kufans and al-Akhfash, and the following verse of poetry indicates it:

*By you, O Quraysh, we were sufficed against every difficulty,*
*and whoever was astray was guided to the path of guidance.*

But the majority of the Basrans prohibited it. Hence the author of *al-Taqrib* said: it is a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*), or a substitution of part for whole, and it cannot be realized except on the view that the address is general, which contradicts the apparent meaning, as you have heard. Even with this it requires the estimate of *minkum* (from you). Abu al-Baqa' said: it is permitted that *li-man* be attached to *ḥasanah* (good), or to an elided element which is a qualifier of it, because it occurs after an indefinite noun. It was also said: it is permitted that it be a qualifier of *uswah*. This was objected to on the grounds that the qualified verbal noun does not govern what comes after its qualifier, and that the multiplicity of qualifiers without a conjunction is not valid. Al-Imam al-Wahidi explicitly prohibited that. It is not hidden that the question is one of disagreement, so do not be heedless.

﴿And who remembers Allah much﴾: that is, a great remembrance. He, glorified is He, joined the abundance of remembrance with the hope, because persistence in much remembrance of Him, mighty and majestic is He, leads to the constancy of obedience, and by it the following of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, is realized. Among what it is fitting to know is that some eminent scholars, such as al-Nawawi, explicitly stated that the remembrance of Allah, exalted is He, which is legally valid, is what occurs within a complete sentence, such as "Glory be to Allah," "Praise be to Allah," "There is no god but Allah," "Allah is greatest," "There is no power and no strength except by Allah," and the like. What is not a single word, such as "Allah," or "Powerful," or "All-Hearing," or "All-Seeing," is not counted legally as remembrance, since there is no supposed element there by which the expression becomes a sentence. Most people are heedless of this. And they agreed that the remembrance whose meaning is intended as worship is not rewarded for its speaker unless he summons its meaning. So the one who utters words such as "Glory be to Allah" or "There is no god but Allah," when he is heedless of the meaning, not attending to it or summoning it, is not rewarded, by consensus. Most people are also heedless of this.

*Fa-inna li-llahi wa-inna ilayhi raji'un* (Indeed we belong to Allah, and indeed to Him we shall return).

When the believers saw the confederates: this explains what came from the sincere believers when affairs became confused and opinions were mixed, after the account of what came from others. That is, when they witnessed them as they had been described to them. ﴿They said﴾ this. According to some verifiers (muhaqqiqin), this is an indication of what they witnessed, without any word coming to mind that would denote it, let alone its masculine or feminine form, since those are properties of the word. Yet the masculine is permissible by considering the predicate, which is ﴿what Allah and His Messenger promised us﴾, since that title is the first thing to come to mind when they witness it. According to most, it is an indication of the calamity and the trial. "Ma" (what) is a relative pronoun (maw ṣūlah), whose returning pronoun is omitted, and it is the second object of "wa'ada" (promised), meaning: what Allah promised us. It is also permissible that it be a verbal-noun "ma" (maṣdariyyah), meaning: this is the promise of Allah the Exalted and His Messenger to us. They intended by this what is contained in the saying of Allah the Exalted in Surah al-Baqarah [2:214]: ﴿Or did you think that you would enter Paradise without there having come to you the example of those who passed away before you? Adversity and hardship touched them﴾. This was narrated by Ibn Jarir, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father. A group also narrated it from Qatadah. The verse of al-Baqarah was revealed a year before the battle, according to what Juwaybir narrated from al-Dahhak, from al-Habr (may Allah be pleased with him).

In al-Bahr: From Ibn Abbas, who said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) said to his companions: 'The confederates will march against you in nine or ten [days]'."

That is, at the end of nine or ten nights, from the time of the report, or from the beginning of the month. So when they saw them approaching at the appointed time, they said this. Their intention by this is what this report promised. Ibn Hajar criticized this, saying that it is not found in the books of hadith. It was also read with imalah (inclination) of the rā' in "ra'aa" toward the kasrah, with the hamzah opened and without imalah. It was also narrated with imalah of both (the rā' and the hamzah) and imalah of the hamzah without the rā', in detail that is in al-Nashr, so let it be consulted.

﴿And Allah and His Messenger spoke truly﴾. Apparently it falls within the scope of the saying, so it is permissible that it be coordinated with the clause ﴿This is what Allah and His Messenger promised us﴾, etc., or with the relative clause (ṣilah) of the relative pronoun. This, as you see, is (weak). It is also permissible that it be in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) with qad (already) implied, or without it.

In any case, the meaning is that the truthfulness of the report of Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (ﷺ) became manifest, because the truthfulness was established before that, and what results from seeing the confederates is its becoming manifest. It is also permissible that the meaning be: Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (peace be upon him) spoke truly regarding the victory and the reward, just as Allah the Exalted and His Messenger spoke truly regarding the trial. The explicit mention (of Allah and His Messenger) despite prior mention is for exaltation, and because if it had been given as a pronoun, and it was said "and He spoke truly", the joining of Allah the Exalted and someone else in one pronoun would occur, and omitting it is preferable. Or it was said "and He spoke truly, and His Messenger", the explicit form remaining in place of the pronoun, so the question is not dispelled, as it has been said. The issue of combining (in one pronoun) has already been discussed.

﴿And it did not increase them﴾, that is, what they saw, the concept understood from the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿When the believers saw﴾, etc. The return of the pronoun to the verbal noun understood from "ra'aa" is contradicted by the masculine form (of the pronoun). Some returned it to the witnessing understood from that. It is also permissible that it return to the promise, or to the calamity and trial understood from the context, or to the indication.

Ibn Abi Ablah read ﴿and they did not increase them﴾ with the plural pronoun returning to the confederates, ﴿except in faith﴾ in Allah the Exalted and His promises, may He be glorified and exalted, ﴿and submission﴾ to His commands, may His majesty be exalted, and His decrees, glory be to Him. The verse has been used as evidence for the permissibility of increase and decrease in faith. Whoever denied it said: the increase is in what one believes in, not in faith itself. The discussion of this is well known, and it is recorded in the books of theology in its most extensive form.

[p. 170]

﴿مِنَ المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ means: of the believers in sincerity, without restriction, not only those whose virtues have been specifically related.

﴿رِجالٌ﴾ means: men who were true to what they pledged to Allah, namely steadfastness alongside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and fighting the enemies. It was also said: [they were true to] acts of obedience in general. What is mentioned enters into this by primary inclusion, and the occasion of revelation is evident with regard to the first meaning.

Imam Ahmad, Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i and a group [of scholars] related from Anas, who said: "My paternal uncle Anas ibn al-Nadr was absent from Badr, and it grieved him. He said: 'The first engagement in which the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took part, I was absent from it. If Allah shows me an engagement alongside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the future, Allah will surely see what I do.' So he took part in the Day of Uhud. Sa'd ibn Mu'adh (may Allah be pleased with him) met him and said: 'O Abu 'Amr, where [are you going]?' He said: 'Wah! The fragrance of Paradise—I find it beyond Uhud.' He fought until he was killed, and there were found in his body more than eighty wounds from a blow, a stab, and an arrow. This verse was revealed: ﴿Among the believers are men who were true to what they pledged to Allah﴾, and they used to consider that it was revealed concerning him and his companions."

In al-Kashshaf: Some of the Companions vowed that when they met in battle alongside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they would hold firm and fight until they were martyred, that is, they vowed complete steadfastness and fighting that by customary course leads to attaining martyrdom. They were: 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, Talhah ibn 'Ubayd Allah, Sa'id ibn Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl, Hamzah, Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr, and others. It is related from al-Kalbi and Muqatil that these men were the seventy people of the 'Aqabah, the people of the pledge. Yazid ibn Ruman said: They were the Banu Harithah. The reliance I place upon is what I have already presented.

The meaning of ﴿صَدَقُوا﴾ ("were true") is: they brought truthfulness, from [the expression] "sadaqani" when he spoke the truth. The position of ﴿ما عاهَدُوا﴾ ("what they pledged") is in the accusative, either by removal of the preposition, which is "fi", and conveying the verb to it, as in their saying "sadaqani sinna bakrihi" according to the narration with the accusative, meaning "concerning the age of his young camel"; and the object is elided, and the original is: "they were true to Allah in what they pledged to Him." Or it is in the accusative because it is itself the explicit object.

[The phrase] "what they pledged to Him" is made as if it were a person pledged to, by way of implicit metaphor (istiʿārah makniyyah), and making it something that is truthfully [kept] is an imaginative depiction (takhyīl), and it is by attributive metaphor (al-isnād al-majāzī).

﴿فَمِنهم مَن قَضى نَحْبَهُ﴾ ("Among them is one who has fulfilled his vow") is an elaboration of the state of the truthful, and a division of them into two categories. Al-nahb, according to what al-Raghib said, is a vow that has been judged obligatory by its undertaking. It is said: "Fulan qada nahbahu," meaning he fulfilled his vow. Abu Hayyan said: It is a vow concerning a matter which a person binds himself to and believes he must fulfil. The poet said:

*In the evening when the Harithiyyun fled, after he had fulfilled his vow in the meeting-place of the people, was Hawbar.*

And Jarir said:

*At Takhfah we fought the kings, and our horses—*
*In the evening of Bastam they ran upon the vow.*

That is, upon a great matter which one undertook to carry out. And it became common to say "qada fulanun nahbahu," meaning he died. Either because al-nahb is used metaphorically for death by explicit metaphor (istiʿārah taṣrīḥiyyah), since it is like a vow binding upon the neck of every person, and the indicator is contextual, and "qada" is a complementary term (tarshīh); or because the fulfilment of the vow is used metaphorically for it.

It is permitted that al-nahb in the verse means the vow, and that it means death. Some of the great scholars said: It is permissible that it be used metaphorically for being bound to die as a martyr, either by treating the binding to its causes, which are voluntary acts of the vower, as if it were the binding to himself, or by treating himself as if it were its causes and attaching the binding to it; and this is the most suitable to the context of praise. Making it a metaphor for death, because it is like a vow that is binding, is a distortion of the metaphor and a removal of its brilliance, and a removal of the noble composition from the requirement of the context altogether, ends [the quotation]. In this there is a clear objection, as is not hidden from the fair-minded person.

What the apparent sense of some reports indicates is that al-nahb here means the vow, and its fulfilment (qada') is its performance and keeping of it. Ibn Abi 'Asim, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as hasan, Ibn Jarir, al-Tabarani, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Talhah that the Companions of the Prophet (ﷺ) said to a foolish Bedouin: "Ask him about the one who fulfilled his vow, who is he?" They did not dare to ask him, out of reverence and awe. So the Bedouin asked him, and then [the Prophet] looked out from the door of the mosque and said: "Where is the questioner about the one who fulfilled his vow?" The Bedouin said: "I am." He said: "This one is among those who fulfilled their vow." Ibn Mandah and Ibn 'Asakir related from Asma' bint Abi Bakr, who said: "Talhah ibn 'Ubayd Allah entered upon the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: 'O Talhah, you are among those who fulfilled their vow.'" al-Hakim related something similar from 'A'ishah.

al-Tirmidhi and others related from Mu'awiyah that he said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) say: 'Talhah is among those who fulfilled their vow.'" It seems that 'Ali (may Allah honour his face) intended praise of him by that in his saying, when he was asked: "Tell us about Talhah." He said: "He is a man concerning whom a verse of the Book of Allah was revealed: ﴿Among them is one who has fulfilled his vow, and among them is one who awaits﴾." Abu al-Shaykh and Ibn 'Asakir related this from him (may Allah honour his face). He (may Allah be pleased with him) had held firm on the Day of Uhud until his hand was struck.

Mujahid went to taking al-nahb in its literal sense. So the meaning is: "Among them is one who fulfilled his pledge and discharged his vow, and among them, that is, and some of them, is one who awaits a day in which there is jihad, so he fulfils his vow, discharges his obligation, and keeps his pledge." Whoever takes ﴿what they pledged to Allah﴾ in its general sense and keeps al-nahb in its literal sense, says: The meaning is: "Among them is one who fulfilled the covenants of Islam and what obedience requires; and among them is one who awaits attaining the highest levels of faith and righteousness." The keeping of al-nahb in its literal sense was found problematic, because fulfilling the vow is itself the same as truthfulness in the covenant. So the meaning returns to: "Among the believers are men who pledged to Allah and were true, that is, did and fulfilled what they pledged to Allah. Among them is one who did and fulfilled what he pledged." This involves dividing a thing into itself. What troubles this meaning is His saying: ﴿and among them is one who awaits﴾, for the one who awaits has not yet fulfilled, so how can he be made a category of those who were true, that is, who fulfilled? It was answered: What is meant by truthfulness in the verse is the correspondence of the verbal statement to the external reality. This statement that involves this correspondence is what their pledge to remain steadfast required, such as their saying: "If Allah shows us an engagement alongside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), we will certainly stand firm and certainly fight." The description of a report as truthful, and likewise what is reported, does not require more than the correspondence of its relation to reality at one of the times. So [a sentence] like "Zayd is standing" is true, and likewise what is reported at the time of reporting it, even if the standing occurs after a thousand years, for example. Likewise [a sentence] like "If the sun is rising, then the day exists" is true, even if it was spoken at night. So these men, when they reported about themselves that if Allah the Exalted showed them an engagement alongside His Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), they would stand firm and fight, and He, glorified be He, knew that this corresponds to reality, He the Exalted reported about them that they were true. Then He divided them, Mighty and Majestic, into two categories: a category that discharged what they reported about themselves that they would discharge, and a category that awaits a time in which to discharge it. This category is not described as lying unless it dies, and Allah the Exalted showed them that, and it did not discharge it. And as for those whom Allah the Exalted reported about as truthful, [it is so] before they died, when they had discharged it, then there is no difficulty. Yes, the difficulty is upon the supposition that by truthfulness in "what they pledged" is meant the realisation of the covenant in what they manifested of their actions, as al-Raghib explained, and by fulfilling the vow is meant the discharge of the vow or the pledge, as is not hidden. It was also said: What is meant by their truthfulness mentioned is the agreement of what is on their tongues with what is in their hearts, in contrast to the hypocrites who say with their mouths what is not in their hearts. There is then no difficulty in the division. It was also said: Truthfulness is in the meaning famous among the majority, except that what is meant by "they were true" is "they confirm," and the present tense is expressed by the past for the certainty of occurrence. Both of these opinions, as you see, [are weak].

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that Nafi' ibn al-Azraq asked him about the verse of Allah the Exalted: ﴿qada nahbahu﴾, and he said: "His appointed term that was decreed for him." He said: "Does the Arabic language know that?" He said: "Yes. Have you not heard the saying of Labid:

*Do you not ask the man what he is striving for:*
*Is it a vow that he fulfils, or error and falsehood?*"

Some related from him that he explained it as death, and something similar is related from Ibn 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with both of them). According to this, there is no obstacle to ﴿were true to what they pledged to Allah﴾ meaning, as mentioned from al-Raghib: they realised the covenant in what they manifested of their actions. The meaning then is: "Among the believers are men who pledged to Allah the Exalted to remain steadfast and to fight when they met battle alongside the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and they realised that and stood firm. Among them is one who died, and among them is one who awaits death." What the context requires is that the intended meaning of "qada nahbahu" is established, by his having been martyred, like Anas ibn al-Nadr and Mus'ab ibn 'Umayr. It may be intended to include more than that, so that whoever died after standing firm, by natural death before the revelation of the verse, is included, if there were any such. They counted among those who await 'Uthman and Talhah. The earliest report concerning Talhah, that he is among those who fulfilled their vow, is taken to mean that he is in the status of one who was martyred. They required this on the basis of what Sa'id ibn Mansur, Abu Ya'la, Ibn al-Mundhir, Abu Nu'aym, and Ibn Mardawayh related from 'A'ishah, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Whoever would be pleased to look at a man walking on the earth who has fulfilled his vow, let him look at Talhah." Ibn Mardawayh related something similar from the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah.
