In Irshad al-'Aql al-Salim, from 'A'ishah, with the wording: "Whoever would be pleased to look at a martyr walking on the earth, who has fulfilled his vow, let him look at Talhah."

In Majma' al-Bayan, from Abu Ishaq, from 'Ali (may Allah honour his face), that he said: "It was revealed concerning us: ﴿men who were true to what they pledged to Allah﴾, the verse. By Allah, I am the one who awaits."

In the description of them with awaiting, which indicates desire for the one awaited, there is a true testimony to the completeness of their longing for martyrdom. It was also said: for death in general, out of love for meeting Allah the Exalted and desire for what is with Him, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿وما بَدَّلُوا تَبْدِيلا﴾ ("and they did not change at all") is conjoined to "they were true," and its subject is the same subject, meaning: they did not change their covenant, nor altered it with any alteration, neither in essence nor in attribute; rather they remained upon it, desiring it, observing its rights in the best manner. As for those who fulfilled their vow, it is evident; and as for the rest, their awaiting bears witness to it with the truest testimony. The generalisation of the non-alteration to the first group, despite its state being evident, is to signify that the second group is equal to them in the ruling. It is also permitted that the pronoun in "they changed" refers to those who await specifically, on the basis that what needs clarification is their state. And in the speech there is an allusion to those among the hypocrites who changed, since they turned their backs, though they had pledged not to turn their backs. So it is as if it were said: "And they did not change at all as the hypocrites changed." So reflect upon all of that, and may Allah the Exalted guide you.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 24:

﴿That Allah may reward the truthful﴾ i.e., those who were true to what they pledged to Allah, the Exalted, concerning it, ﴿for their truthfulness﴾, i.e., because of their truthfulness. He stated this explicitly even though the ruling's attachment to a derivative (al-mushtaqq) necessitates it, out of concern for the matter of truthfulness. He is content with what the attachment implies in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and punish the hypocrites﴾, because it is the basic principle and there is no reason to depart from it. The intended meaning is: "and punish the hypocrites for their hypocrisy," ﴿if He wills﴾, i.e., to punish them, ﴿or turn to them in forgiveness﴾, i.e., so He does not punish them but has mercy on them, glorified is He, if He wills, the Mighty and Majestic; so it is said. Its apparent meaning is that each of the punishment and the mercy for the hypocrites on the Day of Resurrection, even if they die in hypocrisy, is contingent upon His will, the Exalted.

It has been objected that hypocrisy is the worst of disbelief, as His saying, the Exalted, indicates: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire﴾ [an-Nisa': 145]. Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, has informed that He, glorified is He, punishes disbelievers absolutely, decisively, without doubt. So how is this conditional phrasing (ta'liq)?

It was answered that there is no difficulty, for Allah, whose majesty is great, has nothing obligatory upon Him, and the conditional phrasing is for that: He, exalted is His majesty, if He wills, punishes the hypocrite, and if He wills, has mercy on him. But what is realized is that He, blessed and exalted, willed to punish him and did not will his mercy. So it is as if it was said: "If He wills, He punishes the hypocrites in the Hereafter; but He, glorified is He, has willed to punish them in it; or He turns to them in forgiveness if He wills; but He, majestic and exalted, has not willed." Negating the antecedent of the second conditional in such a matter yields the negation of the consequent.

The reason the reward of the truthful was not made contingent upon will, as He made the punishment of the hypocrites and turning to them in forgiveness contingent upon it,
صفحة 173
is that, although He, the Exalted, if He wills rewards the truthful and if He wills does not reward them, the combination of two matters negates any obligation upon Him, the Exalted: the realization of the will to reward, and that mercy is intended in itself, unlike punishment. It seems that for this latter reason He, glorified is He, did not say "to give a reward" or "to bestow favour," and in contrast He said: (and punish), i.e., in the opposing clause.

Some of the eminent scholars said: turning to them in forgiveness is conditional upon their repentance, and the meaning of His turning to the servants is accepting their repentance. So it is as if it was said: "or He accepts their repentance if they repent," and the condition was omitted because the mentioned clause clearly implies it. It is also permissible to interpret His turning to them as His granting them success (tawfiq) to turn to Him, glorified is He; both meanings of His turning are attested, as in al-Qamus. Whatever the case, the matter is contingent upon will, since it is not obligatory upon Him, glorified is He, to accept repentance or to grant success to it. The meaning of making the punishment of the hypocrites contingent upon will is that if He, the Exalted, wills, He punishes them by leaving them in hypocrisy, and if He, glorified is He, wills not to punish them, He strips from them the attribute of hypocrisy by granting success in sincerity of faith.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the punishment of the hypocrites is the fruit of their persistence in hypocrisy and dying upon it, and repentance is a counterpart to that persistence, and its fruit is leaving them without punishment. So there are two matters: persistence in hypocrisy and repentance from it, and from them two fruits: punishment and mercy. He, the Exalted, mentioned by way of brevity one of these two and one of these two, and what was mentioned indicates what was omitted. What shows that the meaning of His saying, the Exalted, ﴿to punish﴾ is "to perpetuate them in hypocrisy" is His saying, glorified is He: (if He wills), and its balancing with repentance, and the particle (or). End of quote. He intended by this to resolve the difficulty. It seems that what he mentioned amounts to: the estimate is "that they persist in hypocrisy and die upon it, if He wills, so He punishes them, or He turns to them in forgiveness, so He has mercy on them." He omitted the cause of punishment and mentioned the effect, which is punishment, and mentioned the cause of mercy and forgiveness, and omitted the effect, which is mercy and forgiveness. This is of the type of (ihtibak). In al-Bahr it is said: this is a fine brevity.

As-Suddi said: the meaning is: "and punish the hypocrites if He wills to cause them to die in their hypocrisy, or turn to them in forgiveness by transferring them from hypocrisy to faith." It seems he made the object of the will the causing of death in hypocrisy rather than the punishment, as is apparent from what you have heard regarding the difficulty of making the punishment of them contingent upon will, although it is decreed. It has also been said for this: the intended meaning is "He punishes them in this world if He wills, or turns to them in forgiveness so He does not punish them in it." This was related from al-Jubba'i, and the discussion on it is in the utmost clarity.

It may be said: the intended hypocrites are the specific group who said: ﴿Allah and His Messenger promised us nothing but delusion﴾ [al-Ahzab: 12]; this is as a proper name for them, so the derivational source is not considered in it, nor is it made a cause of the ruling; rather the cause for it is what is understood from the context of the speech. Thus the thing made contingent upon will is the punishment of particular people, and the meaning is: "He punishes so-and-so and so-and-so, for example, if He wills, by causing them to die insisting upon what they are upon of what calls for punishment, or He turns to them in forgiveness by granting them success in repentance, so He has mercy on them." It is also permissible that the truthful be interpreted similarly; and in that case His saying, glorified is He:

﴿for their truthfulness﴾ is an explicit statement of what is understood from the context. It is understood from the words of Shaykh al-Islam that mentioning truthfulness alone is by way of sufficiency, where he said regarding the meaning of the verse: "That Allah may reward the truthful for what proceeded from them of statements and fulfilment in word and deed, and punish the hypocrites for what proceeded from them of deeds and reported statements." It was said: he did not say, regarding the hypocrites, "for their hypocrisy," because of His saying, glorified is He: (or turn), etc., for it requires a specific act from them; so reflect. The apparent view is that the lam in (liyajziya) is for causation. The statement, according to many, is a causal explanation of the explicit statement regarding the absence of alteration on the part of those who were true to what they pledged to Allah, and of the implicit allusion to the inclusion of others besides them among the hypocrites; for the sense, as you have heard, is: ﴿and they did not alter any alteration﴾, as the hypocrites altered. So His saying: "that He may reward and punish" relates to the negated and the affirmed by way of the estimated laff wa nashr. Making the hypocrites' alteration a cause of the punishment is based on likening the hypocrites to those who aim at an evil end, by way of metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah), and the indicator is the affirmation of the meaning of causation. It was also said: the lam is literally causal with respect to the explicit statement, and metaphorical with respect to the implicit allusion, and it would be of the type of combining literal and metaphorical senses; and whoever permitted it has permitted it.

It was also said: it is not far to make (liyajziya) etc. a causal explanation of the explicit statement qualified by the implicit allusion, so that it is as if it was said: "they did not alter as others did, so that He might reward them for their truthfulness, and punish others if they do not repent," and that the excellence of their conduct manifests the ugliness of others, and by their opposites things are distinguished. It was also said:

it is a causal explanation of (sadaqu), and this was related from al-Zajjaj. It was said: it is a causal explanation of what is understood from His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And it only increased them in faith and submission﴾. It was also said: it is a causal explanation of what is derived from His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And when the believers saw the confederates﴾; as if it was said: Allah, the Exalted, tested them with seeing that calamity (liyajziya), etc. This was preferred by al-Tibi, who said: it is a path easier in its derivation and further from forced interpretation, and closer to the intended purpose than making it a causal explanation of the explicit and the implicit allusion. Shaykh al-Islam preferred that it be related to an omitted element, and the speech is a resumptive summary (fadhlakah) clarifying what is the motive for the occurrence of what has been related of statements and actions in detail, and it is a final purpose, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That He may ask the truthful about their truthfulness﴾ [al-Ahzab: 8]; as if it was said: all that occurred occurred so that Allah may reward, etc. In my view this is good, although it involves an omission; so reflect on that, and may Allah, the Exalted, guide you.

﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Forgiving, Merciful﴾, i.e., toward whoever repents. This is an interjection containing an incitement to repentance.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 25:

His exalted saying: ﴿And Allah turned back﴾ and so on, is a return to narrating the rest of the story and a detailing of the completion of the blessing alluded to in summary by His saying, ﴿So We sent against them a wind and hosts you did not see﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 9]. It is conjoined ('ma'tuf', coordinated with a preceding verb) to "We sent" (arsalna). Between them is an explanation that what befell them was a calamity by which minds and understandings were bewildered, and a catastrophe in which knees knocked together and feet slipped. There is also a detailing of the states and statements that came from the two groups, the People of Faith and the People of Disbelief and Hypocrisy, in order to show the greatness of the blessing and the grandeur of its value, by explaining that it reached them at the height of their need for it. That is: So We sent against them a wind and hosts you did not see, and by that We turned back ﴿those who disbelieved﴾. The turn to the august Name (Allah, instead of a pronoun) is to cultivate awe and to bring in dread.

Shaykh al-Islam (Abu al-Su'ud) permitted that it be conjoined in meaning to the implied clause before "that He may reward" (li-yajziya Allah), as if it were said after recounting the matters mentioned: "What happened, happened of events, and Allah turned back those who disbelieved." Perhaps his arrangement, in beginning with this, indicates that this is the preferable reading. It has also been said that it is conjoined in meaning to His saying, "that He may reward" (li-yajziya). As if it were said: "So the outcome for those who were true to what they pledged to Allah was that Allah rewarded them for their truthfulness and turned back their enemies, and this turning back is part of their reward for their truthfulness." But as you see, this is not the case.

By "those who disbelieved" is meant the confederates (al-Ahzab), according to what many have related from Mujahid. The apparent meaning, however, is that it refers to the polytheists and the Jews who formed the confederacy.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from al-Suddi that he interpreted it as referring to Abu Sufyan and his companions, and this is perhaps the better view. According to both views, the meaning is: Allah turned back those who disbelieved from their place of gathering around Medina and their alliance, to their dwellings, ﴿in their rage﴾. The phrase "in their rage" is a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the relative pronoun (alladhina), not to the pronoun in "disbelieved", and the preposition (ba') expresses accompaniment, meaning "being in their rage", which is the most intense anger. His saying, ﴿they gained no good﴾, is also a circumstantial clause relating to that same referent, or to the pronoun in "in their rage", meaning: not succeeding in any good whatsoever. Some interpreted "good" as achieving victory over the Prophet (peace and blessings of Allah be upon him) and the believers, and applying the term "good" to that is based on their own supposition. Others interpreted it as wealth, as in His saying, ﴿And indeed he is intensely fond of wealth﴾ [Al-'Adiyat: 8]. The better view is that it refers to every good that they hoped for, so the indefinite noun in the context of negation is general in scope. It has also been allowed that the sentence is a resumed statement (isti'naf) explaining the cause of their rage, or that it is a substitute (badal) clause.

﴿And Allah sufficed the believers in fighting﴾, meaning: He, glory be to Him, protected them from that. The verb "sufficed" (kafa) here is transitive to two objects. It has also been said that it means "enough" (aghna), transitive to one object.

The discussion here is based on ellipsis and transmission (al-hadhf wal-iisal). The original is: "And Allah sufficed the believers from fighting," that is, He, glory be to Him, made them independent of it. There is no basis for this.

[p. 175]

This sufficiency was, as Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Qatadah, by means of the wind and the angels, peace be upon them. It has also been said that it was by the killing of 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, of 'Amr ibn 'Abd Wudd.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh, and Ibn 'Asakir reported from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to recite this phrase as: "And Allah sufficed the believers in fighting through 'Ali ibn Abi Talib." In Majma' al-Bayan (Majma' al-Bayan, a Shi'i commentary): it is what is related from Abu 'Abd Allah, may Allah be pleased with him.

This hardly can be sound. The apparent meaning is what was related from Qatadah, because of His saying, ﴿So We sent against them a wind and hosts you did not see﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 9]. It seems that by "fighting" which Allah sufficed them from is meant fighting in the known manner of arranging ranks, shooting arrows, and clashing with swords, or the fighting that such an alliance and gathering necessarily entails by customary reasoning.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, by Abu Hayyan): there is what is clear in meaning that the intended sense is that Allah sufficed the believers from continuous fighting and its recurrence, since the Quraysh were defeated by the power and might of Allah, mighty and majestic, and did not attack the Muslims after that. Otherwise, fighting did occur in general, and there was killing among the polytheists, as is related from Ibn Ishaq: three men from the clan of 'Abd al-Dar ibn Qusayy: Munabbih ibn 'Uthman ibn 'Ubayd ibn al-Sabbaq ibn 'Abd al-Dar, struck by an arrow, of which he died in Mecca; and from the clan of Makhzum ibn Yaqaza, Nawfal ibn 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mughira, who plunged into the trench, became entangled in it, and was killed; and from the clan of 'Amir ibn Lu'ayy, then from the clan of Malik ibn Hisl, 'Amr ibn 'Abd Wudd, whom 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, engaged, as you know, and killed.

It is related from Ibn Shihab that he, may Allah be pleased with him, also killed on that day his son Hisl, so the number of polytheists killed becomes four. Among the believers who were martyred because of this expedition were: Sa'd ibn Mu'adh, Anas ibn Uways ibn 'Ateek, and 'Abd Allah ibn Sahl, who were from the clan of 'Abd al-Ashhal; al-Tufayl ibn al-Nu'man and Tha'laba ibn 'Athama, who were from the clan of Jushm ibn al-Khazraj from the clan of Salama; and Ka'b ibn Zayd, who was from the clan of al-Najjar, then from the clan of Dinar, struck by a stray arrow which killed him. Ibn Ishaq said: Only these six were martyred, may Allah be pleased with them.

﴿And Allah is ever Powerful﴾ over bringing into being everything He wills, exalted is His majesty, ﴿Mighty﴾, prevailing over everything.

﴿And He brought down those of the People of the Scripture who supported them﴾, that is, who aided the confederates who had been repulsed, ﴿from their fortresses﴾, meaning the Banu Qurayza according to the majority, while al-Hasan said they were the Banu al-Nadir. The first view is the one relied upon. ﴿From their fortresses﴾: the plural of *siyasiyah* (a strong point, a fortress), which is anything one defends oneself with. It is also applied to the horn of an ox or a gazelle, and to the spur of a cock on its leg, which is like a small horn. *Al-sayasi* is also applied to the iron-tipped comb-teeth used by weavers. Abu 'Ubayda said this. He recited the verse of Duraid ibn al-Simma al-Jushami:

I looked at him while the spears were tearing at him,
like the striking of the weaver's combs upon the stretched cloth.

It is also applied to roots. Abu 'Ubayda said: the Arabs say, "God cut off his *si'si'* (root)," meaning his origin.

﴿And He cast terror into their hearts﴾, that is, intense fear, to the extent that they surrendered themselves to being killed, and their wives and children to being taken captive, as His words indicate: ﴿a party you kill and a party you take captive﴾, without any movement on their part, let alone opposition or defiance. In al-Bahr it is said: the casting of terror was the cause of their coming down, but the effect was mentioned first because the joy at their coming down was greater and the report of it more important. The object of *taqtulun* (you kill) was placed first because the killing fell upon the men, who were well known, and concern for their condition was more important. There was no such concern for the captives; rather the concern there was greater with regard to the taking captive. Had it been said, "and a party you take captive," one might have thought, before hearing *ta'sirun*, that it would be followed by "you rout" or something similar. It is also said: the object was placed first in the first clause because the context of the discourse is for its detailing, and it was placed last in the second for the sake of the rhyme (*fawasil*). It is also said: the placement was for that reason, and as for the postponement, it was so that the killing would not be separated from its counterpart, the taking captive, by an intervening element. It is also said: the two clauses were varied in the composition because the condition of the two groups differed in reality: one of them was put forward and was killed, and the other was delayed and was taken captive.

Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read *al-ru'ub* (terror) with a damma on the ain, *al-Ru'ub*. Abu Haywa read *ta'surun* with a damma on the sin. Al-Yamani read *ya'sirun* with the third-person masculine prefix. Ibn Anas, on the authority of Ibn Dhakwan, read it that way in this place and in *yaqtulun*. I do not see a convincing reason for restricting the subject to the third-person form, so consider this carefully.

The detailed account of the story, in summary, is that when it was the morning of the night in which the confederates were defeated, or the noon of that day according to some narrations, and the Messenger of God ﷺ and the Muslims had returned to the inside of Medina, Gabriel, peace be upon him, came, wearing a turban of brocade, upon a mule with a saddle, over which was a silk cover, to the Messenger of God ﷺ. He was with Zaynab bint Jahsh, who was washing his noble head, having already washed one side of it. He said: "Have you put down the weapons, O Messenger of God?" He said: "Yes." He said: "May God pardon you. The angels, peace be upon them, have not put down their weapons yet. I have only just returned from pursuing the people. God the Exalted commands you to march against the Banu Qurayza, and I am setting out toward them, to shake their fortresses to the ground." So he, peace be upon him, ordered a caller, who called among the people: "Whoever is hearing and obeying, let him not pray the afternoon prayer except at the Banu Qurayza." He appointed Ibn Umm Maktum over Medina. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, may God honour his face, went forward with his banner toward them, and the people rushed to it. He, may God honour his face, proceeded until, when he drew near the fortresses, he heard from them an ugly saying about the Messenger of God ﷺ, so he returned until he met him, peace be upon him, and said: "O Messenger of God, it is not right for you to draw near to these wicked people." He said: "Why? Do you think you heard some harm from them?" He said: "Yes, O Messenger of God." He said: "If they had seen me, they would not have said any such thing." When the Messenger of God ﷺ drew near their fortresses, he said: "O brothers of the apes! Has God disgraced you and sent down His vengeance upon you?" They said: "O Abu al-Qasim, you were not ignorant." In another narration: "You were not foul-mouthed." Before he reached them, the Messenger, peace be upon him, had passed by a group of his Companions at al-Suwayrayn, and he said: "Has anyone passed by you?" They said: "O Messenger of God, Dihya ibn Khalifa al-Kalbi passed by us upon a white mule with a saddle, over which was a silk cover." The Messenger, peace be upon him, said: "That was Gabriel, peace be upon him. He was sent to the Banu Qurayza to shake their fortresses and to cast terror into their hearts." When he ﷺ came to them, he alighted at one of their wells, on the side of their properties, called Bi'r Anna. The people came in succession. Men arrived after the late evening prayer (*al-'isha' al-akhirah*), and they had not prayed the afternoon prayer, because of the saying of the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Let none pray the afternoon prayer except at the Banu Qurayza." What preoccupied them was something unavoidable for them in their fighting. When they came, they prayed it after the evening prayer, and God the Exalted did not blame them for that in His Book, nor did His Messenger, peace be upon him, reproach them.

He ﷺ besieged them for twenty-five nights. It is said twenty-one, and it is said fifteen. The siege wearied them, and they feared with the greatest fear. Huyayy ibn Akhtab had entered with them into their fortress when Quraysh and Ghatafan withdrew from them, fulfilling his pledge to Ka'b ibn Asad. When they became certain that the Messenger of God ﷺ would not turn away from them until he engaged them in battle, Ka'b said to them: "O assembly of Jews, what you see has befallen you. I am offering you some choices, so take whichever of them you wish." They said: "And what are they?" He said: "We follow this man and believe in him, for by God it has become clear to you that he is a sent prophet, and that he is the one you find in your Book, so you will be secure for your lives, your wealth, your children and your women." They said: "We will never abandon the judgment of the Torah or exchange it for anything else." He said: "If you refuse this, then let us kill our sons and our women, then go out to Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions as men with drawn swords, leaving behind us no burden, until God the Exalted judges between us and them. If we perish, we perish, and we will have left behind no offspring about whom we are concerned. If we prevail, then by my life we will acquire other women and sons." They said: "We would kill these poor people! What good is life after them?" He said: "If you refuse this, then tonight is the night of the Sabbath, and it may be that Muhammad ﷺ and his Companions feel secure from us on it. So come down, perhaps we may catch them off guard." They said: "We would profane our Sabbath and introduce into it what those before us did not introduce, except for those whom you know, and what befell them, which is not hidden from you, namely the transformation (*al-maskh*)." He said: "Then not a man among you has spent a single night since his mother bore him with resolve." Then they sent to the Messenger of God ﷺ: "Send us Abu Lubaba ibn 'Abd al-Mundhir, brother of the Banu 'Amr ibn 'Awf, who were allies of the Aws, so that we may consult him about our affair." He, peace be upon him, sent him to them. When they saw him, the men rose to him, and the women and children rushed to him, weeping in his face. He was moved with compassion for them, and they said to him: "O Abu Lubaba, do you think we should come down under the judgment of Muhammad ﷺ?" He said: "Yes," and he pointed with his hand to his throat, meaning that it was slaughter. He then knew that he had betrayed God and His Messenger, peace be upon him. He did not return to the Messenger of God ﷺ, but went to Medina, and tied himself to a pillar in the mosque until his repentance was revealed, may God be pleased with him.

Then he, peace be upon him, made them come down. The Aws leapt up and said: "O Messenger of God, they are our clients (*mawali*) rather than the Khazraj's, and you have done with the clients of our brothers yesterday what you know." The Messenger of God ﷺ had, before the Banu Qurayza, besieged the Banu Qaynuqa', who had been allies of the Khazraj, and they came down under his judgment. The Khazraj asked him for them, through 'Abd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, and he granted them to him. When the Aws spoke to him, he, peace be upon him, said: "Are you not content, O assembly of the Aws, that a man from among you should judge concerning them?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Then that is settled. It is for Sa'd ibn Mu'adh." The Messenger of God ﷺ had placed him in a tent in his mosque belonging to a woman of Aslam called Rufayda, who used to treat the wounded and devoted herself to serving whoever among the Muslims had a claim upon her. Sa'd, may God be pleased with him, had been struck on the Day of the Trench by a man of Quraysh called Ibn al-'Araqa with an arrow, which hit his arm-vein (*akhal*) and severed it. He prayed to God and said: "O God, do not let me die until my eye is comforted concerning Qurayza." It is related that the Banu Qurayza themselves chose to come down under the judgment of Sa'd, and the Messenger of God ﷺ approved of that. His people came to him while he was in the mosque, and they carried him on a donkey, having spread for him a cushion of leather. He was a tall, handsome man. Then they proceeded with him to the Messenger of God ﷺ, saying: "O Abu 'Amr, be good to your clients, for the Messenger of God ﷺ only appointed you over them so that you would be good to them." When they pressed him, he said: "The time has come for Sa'd that he should not fear the blame of any blamer in God's cause." Some of those who had been with him from his people returned to the house of the Banu 'Abd al-Ashhal and announced to them the death of the men of the Banu Qurayza, before Sa'd arrived, concerning the word he had heard from him. When Sa'd reached the Messenger of God ﷺ and the Muslims, the Messenger, peace be upon him, said: "Rise for your master." The Muhajirun of Quraysh said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ only meant the Ansar." The Ansar said: "He, peace be upon him, meant all the Muslims by it." They rose to him and said: "O Abu 'Amr, the Messenger of God ﷺ has appointed you over the affair of your clients so that you may judge concerning them." Sa'd said: "Do you pledge to me the covenant and compact of God that the judgment concerning them is as I decide?" They said: "Yes." He said: "And upon whoever is here in this part where the Messenger of God ﷺ is?" — and he was indicating the Messenger of God ﷺ, peace be upon him. The Prophet ﷺ said: "Yes." Sa'd said: "Then I judge concerning them that the men be killed, the property be divided, and the children and women be taken captive." The Prophet ﷺ then said "Allahu akbar," and said: "You have judged concerning them by the judgment of God from above the seven heavens." Then the Messenger of God ﷺ confined them in the house of Bint al-Harith, a woman of the Banu al-Najjar. Then he went out to the market of Medina, which is its market today, and dug trenches there. Then he sent for them, and struck their necks in those trenches, bringing them out to it in groups. Among them was the enemy of God, Huyayy ibn Akhtab, and Ka'b ibn Asad, the chief of the people.

They were six hundred or seven hundred; and one who wants to inflate the number says they were between eight hundred and nine hundred. When they were being led to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, they said to Ka'b, "In groups, O Ka'b! What do you think he will do with us?" He said, "In every situation you do not understand! Do you not see that the summoner does not give up, and whoever of you goes does not return? By Allah, it is death!" That continued in this manner until the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had finished with them. Then Huyayy ibn Akhtab, the enemy of Allah, was brought, wearing a fine garment of silk (tufahiyya) that had been cut open on every side, a finger's width at a time, so that it would not be taken as spoil; his hands were tied to his neck with a rope. When he looked at the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he said, "As for me, by Allah, I did not blame myself for my enmity toward you. But whoever forsakes Allah, Allah forsakes him." Then he turned to the people and said, "O people, there is no harm in the command of Allah: it is a decree, a destiny, and a great slaughter written upon the Children of Israel." Then he sat down, and his neck was struck. Jabal ibn Jidal al-Taghlibi said about him:

By your life, Ibn Akhtab did not blame himself,
but whoever forsakes Allah will be forsaken.
For the striver, until the soul has made its excuse,
and for the restless one who seeks glory, every restless one.

It is narrated that Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas, may Allah be pleased with him, asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to grant him al-Zubayr ibn Bata al-Qurazi, because he had done him a favour in the Jahiliyya on the day of Bu'ath. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "He is yours." So he went to him and said, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ has granted me your life, so it is yours." He said, "An old man, what will he do with life, with no family and no children?" So Thabit went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, "May my father and mother be ransom for you, O Messenger of Allah, his wife and his children." He said, "They are yours." So he went to him and said, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ has granted me your family and your children, so they are yours." The people of a household in the Hijaz said, "They have no property, so how will they survive in this state?" So he went to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said, "What is his situation?" He said, "He is yours." So he went to him and said, "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ has given me your property, so it is yours." Then he said, "O Thabit, what became of the one whose face was a Chinese mirror in which the maidens of the tribe would look at themselves, Ka'b ibn Asad?" He said, "He was killed." He said, "And what became of our vanguard when we advanced, and our rearguard when we retreated, Ghazal ibn Shamwal?" He said, "He was killed." He said, "And what became of the two assemblies?" meaning the Banu Ka'b ibn Qurayza and the Banu 'Amr ibn Qurayza. He said, "They were killed." He said, "Then I ask you, O Thabit, by my hand that is in your possession, to join me to the people, for by Allah there is no good in life after these." Thabit said, "I am not patient for Allah's sake with a killing of a sincere remembrance until I meet my beloved ones," so Thabit brought him forward and struck his neck. When the words "until I meet my beloved ones" reached Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, he said, "He will meet them, by Allah, in Hell, abiding therein forever."

Salma bint Qays, mother of al-Mundhir, sister of Suleyt ibn Qays, who was one of the maternal aunts of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and who had prayed with him facing both qiblas and had pledged allegiance to him with the pledge of women, asked for Rifa'a ibn Shamwal al-Qurazi, and said, "May my father and mother be ransom for you, O Prophet of Allah, grant me Rifa'a, for he claims that he will convert and eat the flesh of the camel." So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ granted him to her, and she spared him.

He killed every male of them who had grown pubic hair. As for the women, he killed only one woman, called Lubaba, wife of al-Hakam al-Qurazi, who had thrown a millstone on Khallad ibn Suwayd and killed him.

Ibn Ishaq related from Urwa ibn al-Zubayr, "from 'Aisha, who said: By Allah, this woman was with me, talking with me and laughing heartily, while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was killing her men with swords, when a caller called her by name: Where is so-and-so? She said, 'I am, by Allah.' I said to her, 'Woe to you, what is wrong with you?' She said, 'I am being killed.' I said, 'Why?' She said, 'For an offence I committed.' So she was taken away and her neck was struck. 'Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, used to say: By Allah, I do not forget her wonder, her contentment of soul and her great laughter, though she knew she was going to be killed." Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ divided

Page 179

their property, women and children among the Muslims. On that day the shares of horsemen and the shares of foot soldiers were made known, and the fifth was taken out of it. The horse received two shares, the rider received one share, and the foot soldier who had no horse received one share. The horses in that expedition were thirty-six, and it was the first spoil in which shares were distributed, and the fifth was taken out of it," according to what Ibn Ishaq mentioned. "Then the Messenger of Allah ﷺ sent Sa'd ibn Zayd al-Ansari, brother of the Banu 'Abd al-Ashhal, with captives from among the captives of the people, and all the captives were, as it is said, seven hundred and fifty, to Najd; he bought with them horses and weapons for them. The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, had chosen for himself from their women Rayhana bint 'Amr, and she remained in his possession until he died. He, peace and blessings be upon him, had offered to marry her and to veil her, but she said, 'O Messenger of Allah, rather leave me in possession, for that is lighter on me and on you.' So he left her, peace be upon him. When she was taken captive she had refused anything but Judaism, so he set her apart, peace and blessings be upon him, and he felt something in himself because of that. Then while he was with his companions, peace and blessings be upon him, he heard the sound of two sandals behind him, and he said, 'Surely these are the sandals of Ibn Shu'ba, who has come to give me the good news of Rayhana's conversion.' He came to him and said, 'O Messenger of Allah, Rayhana has become Muslim,' and that pleased him concerning her matter." The conquest, according to what is in al-Bahr, was at the end of Dhu al-Qa'da. This expedition and the expedition of the Trench occurred in one year, as what we have mentioned at the beginning of the story indicates, and this is the correct view, in contrast to whoever said that each of them was in a separate year. When the affair of the Banu Qurayza was over, Sa'd, may Allah be pleased with him, had his wound burst open and died as a martyr. The angels, peace be upon them, rejoiced at his spirit, and the Throne shook for him. Concerning that, a man of the Ansar said:

"The Throne of Allah did not tremble at the death of any dead man
that we have heard of, except for Sa'd, father of 'Amr."

It is said, according to what is narrated from Ibn Ishaq, that one of the Muslims was martyred on the day of the Banu Qurayza, then from the Banu al-Harith ibn al-Khazraj, Khallad ibn Suwayd ibn Tha'laba ibn 'Amr, on whom a millstone was thrown and crushed him severely. They mention that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, "Truly, he has the reward of two martyrs."

Abu Sinan ibn Mihsan ibn Harthan, brother of the Banu Asad ibn Khuzayma, died while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was besieging the Banu Qurayza, and he was buried in their graveyard in which they bury today, and to it they have buried their dead in Islam. The complete account of what occurred in this expedition is in the books of biography.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 27:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He caused you to inherit their land﴾ is coordinated (ʿatf) with His saying, exalted is He: "sent down" (anzala) and so on. By "their land" is meant their farmlands, and it was mentioned first because of the great benefit derived from it, from the palm trees and crops.

In His saying, mighty and majestic is He: "caused you to inherit" (awrathakum) there is an indication that this (land) passed to them after the death of those slain, and that their possession of it is a strong possession, not by way of a contract of rescission (faskh) or cancellation (iqalah). ﴿And their homes﴾, that is, their fortresses (ḥuṣūnahum), ﴿and their wealth﴾, their money, their livestock and their goods, which their land and their homes contained.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Qatadah, in a lengthy report, that "Sa'd, may Allah be pleased with him, ruled that their fighting men be killed and their offspring taken captive, and that their properties (a'qar) be given to the Muhajirun to the exclusion of the Ansar. His people said: 'Do you prefer the Muhajirun over us in the properties?' He said: 'You have properties, and the Muhajirun have no properties.' And the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, affirmed his ruling."

In al-Kashshaf: It is narrated that "the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, made their properties ('aqar) for the Muhajirun to the exclusion of the Ansar. The Ansar spoke about this, and he, upon him be blessings and peace, said: 'You are in your dwellings.' ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'Will you not take a fifth (tukhammis) as you took a fifth on the day of Badr?' He said: 'No, this was only made mine as a special provision (ṭuʿmah) apart from the people.' He said: 'We are pleased with what Allah and His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, have done.'"

Page 180.
Al-Jalal al-Suyuti mentioned that the report was related by al-Waqidi through the narration of Kharijah ibn Zayd, from Umm al-ʿAla, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, seized Banu al-Nadir, he made..." (the hadith), and through the route of al-Miswar ibn Rifa'ah, who said: "ʿUmar said: '(O Messenger of Allah, will you not take a fifth of what was obtained from Banu al-Nadir?)'" (the hadith), end of quote. In light of this, it is not fitting for al-Zamakhshari to mention it here, especially since the verses, according to him, concern Banu Qurayzah. The discussion of what befell Banu al-Nadir will come in the tafsir of Surah al-Hashr, if Allah the Exalted wills.

﴿And a land you have not trodden﴾. Muqatil, Yazid ibn Ruman and Ibn Zayd said: it is Khaybar, which was conquered after Banu Qurayzah. Qatadah said: he used to narrate that it is Makkah. al-Hasan said: it is the land of the Romans and Persia. It was also said: Yemen. ʿIkrimah said: it is whatever the Muslims prevail over until the Day of Resurrection, and al-Bahr chose this. ʿUrwah said: I think it is only every land Allah grants the Muslims victory over, or He, mighty and majestic is He, is its conqueror until the Day of Resurrection. The apparent view is that the coordination is with "their land", and it has been objected that the inheriting is past in reality with respect to the coordinated-to item, and figurative with respect to this coordinated item. It was answered that by "caused you to inherit" is meant: caused you to inherit in His knowledge and decree, and this is realized in what has occurred of inheritance, such as their land, homes and wealth, and in what has not yet occurred, such as the inheritance of what was not conquered at the time of the revelation of the verse. Some scholars held that "caused you to inherit" in the coordinated item is intended as "will cause you to inherit", but it used the past tense to indicate the certainty of occurrence, and the cited evidence; the indication of what was mentioned on this was considered remote because the two differ in reality and figuratively.

It was said: the evidence is what follows, from His saying: ﴿And Allah is ever over all things competent﴾, and so on. Then, if the land is taken to include what was conquered at the hands of those present and what was conquered at the hands of others who came after them, the address does not restrict itself to those present, as is not hidden. Among the strange interpretations is that by this land is meant their women, and according to this no difficulty arises in the coordination. Zayd ibn ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read "lam taṭawuhā" (لَمْ تَطَوُها), dropping the hamzah, changing the hamzah of taṭa'u into an alif, after the manner of his saying:

Indeed the beasts are guided in their lairs, but people are never guided away from their evil.

Then a sakin met the waw and it was dropped, like your saying "lam tarawuhā".

﴿And Allah is ever over all things competent﴾: He, glorified is He, is able to make you possess whatever He wills.

[p. 181]

﴿O Prophet, say to your wives: If you desire the worldly life﴾, meaning its abundance and luxury, ﴿and its adornment﴾, meaning its ornaments. This is a specification after a generalization. ﴿Then come, I will provide for you﴾. The imperative *fa-ta'alayna* means: come forward, by your own will and choice, to one of the two states, as one says: "He came to quarrel with me (*aqbala yukhasimuni*), went to speak with me (*dhahaba yukallimuni*), stood up to threaten me (*qama yuhaddiduni*)." The original meaning of *ta'ala* is a command to ascend to a high place, and then it became predominant in the sense of a command to come in general. The intended meaning here is what you have heard. Al-Raghib said: Some have said that its origin is from *'uluw*, which is elevation of rank, so it is as if it were a call to what contains elevation, like your saying "Do such-and-such without being humbled," honouring the one addressed. This meaning is not intended here, as is not hidden. ﴿I will provide for you﴾, meaning I will give you the provision of divorce (*mut'at al-talaq*). The provision (*mut'ah*, a gift given to a divorced woman) is for a divorced woman who has not been consummated and for whom no dowry was fixed in the contract; according to Imam Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, and his companions, it is obligatory. For the rest of the divorced women it is recommended. It is reported from al-Zuhri that there are two kinds of provision: one, which the ruler enforces and compels upon the one who divorced before a dowry was fixed and before consummation; and the second, which is a duty upon the God-fearing, for the one who divorced after a dowry was fixed and consummation occurred. A woman brought a dispute before Shurayh concerning the provision, and he said: "Provide for her if you are among the God-fearing," and he did not compel him. It is reported from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: the provision is an obligatory right. It is reported from al-Hasan: every divorced woman has a provision, except the one who divorced by *khul'* (the wife's redemption of marriage) and the one subjected to *li'an* (mutual oath of condemnation). The provision is a shirt, a donkey and a wrap, according to one's means and straitened circumstances, except that if half her dowry is less than that, then the lesser of the two is due to her, and it does not fall below five dirhams, since the least dowry is ten dirhams, so half of it does not fall below that. Thus it is in *al-Kashshaf*, and the full discussion is in the books of jurisprudence (*furu'*). The verb is jussive (*majzum*) because it is the answer to the imperative. Likewise is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and I will release you﴾. It is also permitted that the jussive be because it is the answer to the conditional, and that *fa-ta'alayna* be a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraD*) between the condition and its consequence. A parenthetical clause may be preceded by *fa*, as in his saying:

*"Know, for the knowledge of a man benefits him, that everything decreed will surely come."*

Hamid al-Kharraz read *"umatti'ukunna wa-usarri'ukunna"* with *raf'* (nominative), as a resumed statement (*isti'naf*). Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read *"umatti'ukunna"* with the lightened form from *amta'a*. *Tasrih* originally means unrestricted release, then it was used as a metaphor for divorce, that is: "and I will divorce you." ﴿A release﴾, meaning a divorce, ﴿beautiful﴾, meaning having much goodness, by being a divorce in accordance with the Sunnah (*sunni*) in which there is no harm, as in the innovated divorce (*talaq al-bid'i*) known among the jurists. In *Majma' al-Bayan* the beautiful release is interpreted as divorce free from contention and quarrel. The apparent order would be to place the provision after the release, since it is caused by it, but it was placed before it to show kindness to them and to cut off their excuses from the very beginning. This is similar to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah pardon you, why did you give them permission?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 43], in one respect. It is also because it corresponds to what precedes it, namely "the worldly life." It is also permitted that it be in its proper place, on the basis that the desire for the world is equivalent to divorce, and *al-sarah* is the removal from the houses. So it is as if it were said: "If you desire the world and are divorced, then come, I will give you the provision and remove you from the houses with a beautiful removal, without contention or harm." Its remoteness is not hidden. The occasion of revelation of the verse, as has been said, is that his wives, upon him be prayer and peace, asked him for garments of adornment and an increase in maintenance.

Ahmad, Muslim, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Mardawayh narrated through Abu al-Zubayr from Jabir, who said: "Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, came while people were sitting at his door, and the Prophet (ﷺ) was sitting, but he was not given permission. Then permission was given to Abu Bakr and Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and they entered while the Prophet (ﷺ) was sitting, with his wives around him, and he was silent. Umar said: 'I will speak to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), perhaps he will laugh.' He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if you had seen the daughter of Zayd,' meaning his wife, may Allah be pleased with him, 'who asked me for maintenance just now, and I struck her neck.' The Prophet (ﷺ) laughed until his molar teeth showed, and said: 'They are around me, they ask me for maintenance.' Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, got up to Aisha to strike her, and Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, got up to Hafsa, both saying: 'You ask the Prophet (ﷺ) for what he does not have.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) forbade them, and his wives said: 'By Allah, we will not ask the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) after this gathering for what he does not have.' Allah, Exalted, revealed the option (*takhyir*), and he began with Aisha, and upon him be prayer and peace said: '(I am mentioning to you a matter that I do not wish you to hasten into until you consult your parents.' She said: 'What is it?' He recited to her: ﴿O Prophet, say to your wives﴾ to the end of the verse. Aisha said: 'Should I consult my parents about you? Rather, I choose Allah, Exalted, and His Messenger (ﷺ), and I ask you not to mention to any of your wives what I have chosen.' Upon him be prayer and peace said: 'Allah, Exalted, did not send me as one who seeks to embarrass, but He sent me as a teacher and a bringer of good news. None of them will ask me about what you have told me except that I will inform her.'"

In a report narrated by Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim from Qatadah and al-Hasan: "When the verse of the option was revealed, he, upon him be prayer and peace, had nine wives: five from Quraysh: Aisha, Hafsa, Umm Habiba daughter of Abu Sufyan, Sawda daughter of Zam'a, and Umm Salama daughter of Abu Umayya. He also had Safiyya daughter of Huyayy al-Khaybariyya, Maymuna daughter of al-Harith al-Hilaliyya, Zaynab daughter of Jahsh al-Asadiyya, and Juwayriyya daughter of al-Harith from the Banu al-Mustaliq. He began with Aisha. When they chose Allah, Exalted, and His Messenger (ﷺ), and the Hereafter, joy was seen on the face of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and all of them followed suit. When he gave them the option and they chose Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and His Messenger (ﷺ), and the Hereafter, Allah, Majestic is His state, thanked them for that when He, Glorified is He, said: ﴿Women are not lawful for you after this, nor is it lawful to exchange them for other wives, even if their beauty pleases you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 52]. Thus Allah, Exalted, restricted it to them, and they are the nine who chose Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and His Messenger (ﷺ)."

Ibn Sa'd narrated from Amr ibn Sa'id, from his father, from his grandfather: "that he, upon him be prayer and peace, gave his wives the option, and they all chose Allah, Exalted, and His Messenger (ﷺ), except the Amiriyya, who chose her people."

[Afterward she used to say: "I am the unfortunate one." She used to gather dung and sell it, and she would seek permission to enter upon the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) saying: "I am the unfortunate one."]

He also narrated from Ibn Junah, who said: "They all chose him except the Amiriyya, who was deranged until she died." In some narrations from Ibn Jubayr it is: "except the Himyariyya, and she is the Amiriyya." This option, as is narrated from Aisha and Abu Ja'far, happened after he, upon him be prayer and peace, had abstained from them for a month of twenty-nine days.

In *al-Bahr* it is: "When Allah, Exalted, gave victory to His Prophet (ﷺ), repelled the confederates from him, and granted him the conquest of al-Nadir and Qurayza, his wives, upon him be prayer and peace, thought that he had singled out the precious things and treasures of the Jews, so they sat around him and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the daughters of Kisra and Caesar are in jewelry and fine garments, with female slaves and servants, while we are in the poverty and hardship that you see.' They pained his noble heart, upon him be prayer and peace, by demanding that he widen their circumstances and treat them as kings and the sons of this world treat their wives. So Allah, Exalted, commanded him to recite to them what had been revealed concerning their matter." How excellent is the placement of these verses in this context after the conclusion of the story of the confederates and the Banu Qurayza, as is not hidden. It is understood from the words of the Imam that they are connected to the beginning of the surah, because noble character is confined to two things: reverence for the command of Allah, Exalted, and compassion toward His creatures, Mighty and Majestic. Thus He, Glorified is He, began by guiding His beloved, upon him be prayer and peace, to what relates to the side of reverence toward Him, Exalted, saying, Glorified is He: ﴿O Prophet, fear Allah﴾ [al-Ahzab: 1] etc. Then He, Glorified is He, guided him to what relates to the side of compassion, and began with the wives because they are the most entitled to that. And He, Glorified is He, put the conditional mentioned before His saying, Exalted is He:

[p. 182]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 29:

﴿And if you desire Allah and His Messenger﴾ etc., because the occasion of revelation is what you have heard.

Al-Imam said: The placing of the mention (of Allah and His Messenger before the Abode of the Hereafter) is an indication that the Prophet ﷺ was not inclined at all towards this world and its pleasures. He mentioned that the description of the release (sarah) as "beautiful" is also an indication of this. The meaning of ﴿if you desire Allah and His Messenger﴾ is: if you desire the Messenger of Allah. He mentioned Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, only to announce the greatness of his station, peace and blessings be upon him, with Him, exalted is He. ﴿And the Hereafter﴾ means its everlasting bliss, before which there is no value for this world and what is in it. ﴿Then indeed Allah has prepared﴾, i.e., readied and facilitated, ﴿for the good-doers among you﴾, in return for their good conduct, ﴿a reward﴾ whose abundance cannot be counted, ﴿great﴾ whose greatness cannot be fully measured. And "min" (among) is for specification, because all of them were good-doers.

It has been said: It is also permissible to read it as partitive, so that "the good-doers" are those among them who chose Allah and His Messenger, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him. But the choice of all of them was not known at the time of the revelation, and this, as al-Khafaji, may Allah have mercy on him, said, is far-fetched. As for the answer to "in" (conditional particle) apparently it is what is joined with the fa', but it has been said: the past tense here has the meaning of the present indicating the future, and the expression with it rather than with the present is for the certainty of its occurrence. It has also been said: the answer is omitted, like: "you will be rewarded" or "you will attain good", and what has been mentioned is its evidence. The conditional clause of the first (part) is stripped of threat, for emphasis in establishing the meaning of
page 183
the choice and to guard against any trace of compulsion. It has been said: this is the secret of placing the enjoyment (tamtic) before the release (tasrih), and describing the release as "beautiful".

Furthermore, scholars differed regarding the choice that took place: was it a delegation of divorce to them, such that divorce occurs by the very act of choosing, or not? Al-Hasan, Qatadah, and most of the people of knowledge, as in Irshad al-Aql al-Salim, and this is the apparent view, held that it was not a delegation of divorce, but was rather an offering of choice to them between the two desires, on the basis that if they desired the worldly life, the Prophet ﷺ would separate from them, as his saying, Exalted is He, indicates: ﴿Come, I will provide for you and release you﴾. Others held that it was a delegation of divorce to them, such that if they chose themselves, that would be a divorce.

Likewise, scholars differed on the ruling of the option when a man says to his wife: "Choose", and she says: "I have chosen myself", or he says: "Choose yourself", and she says: "I have chosen." From Zayd ibn Thabit: that three divorces occur, and Malik adopted this for a woman who has been consummated; for others, the husband's claim of a single (divorce) is accepted. From Umar, Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Mas'ud: that one revocable divorce occurs; this is also the view of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz, Ibn Abi Layla, and Sufyan, and al-Shafi'i and Ahmad adopted it. From Ali, may Allah ennoble his face: that one irrevocable (ba'in) divorce occurs. Al-Tirmidhi narrated this from Ibn Mas'ud, and also from Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, adopted this view. If she chooses her husband, then from Zayd ibn Thabit: one divorce occurs. From Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, there are two reports: one that one revocable divorce occurs, and the other that nothing at all occurs; and this is the view of the jurists of the major cities.

Al-Tabarsi mentioned that what is transmitted from the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt, may the pleasure of Allah be upon them all, is that the option is specific to the Prophet ﷺ, and that for anyone other than him, peace be upon him, this is not valid for him. Scholars differed regarding the duration of the wife's ownership of the choice if the husband says that to her: it was said she retains it as long as she is in the session, and this is related from Umar, Uthman, and Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with them.

This was also the view of Jabir ibn Abd Allah, Jabir ibn Zayd, Ata, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Malik, Sufyan, al-Awza'i, Abu Hanifa, al-Shafi'i, and Abu Thawr. It was also said: she retains it both within the session and beyond it; this is the view of al-Zuhri, Qatadah, Abu Ubayda, and Ibn Nasr, and the author of al-Mughni related it from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face.

In the Baladat of Muhammad ibn al-Hasan, he (Ali, may Allah ennoble his face) is reported as saying that it is confined to the session, like the view of the majority, may Allah be pleased with them all. The full discussion of this issue, and what each of these opinions holds and what they rest upon, is to be sought in the books of furu' (positive law), such as the commentaries on al-Hidayah and what relates to them. However, I say: that what is in the verse is the issue mentioned in the furu' on which disagreement occurred is hardly attainable, and al-Khafaji's interpretation of those who cite it as evidence in this context is not free from objection in the eyes of those of understanding.

Furthermore, al-Imam mentioned, in discussing the interpretation of this verse, several issues. The first: that the offering of choice from him, peace and blessings be upon him, was undoubtedly obligatory upon him in terms of speech, since it is conveying the message; and in terms of meaning, likewise, according to the view that the imperative indicates obligation.

The second: that if all of them or one of them desired the worldly life, then, looking at the station of the Prophet ﷺ, it is apparent that enjoyment and release are obligatory upon him, because breaking a promise from him, peace be upon him, is not permissible.

The third: that it is apparent that the one who is chosen after the irrevocable separation is not forbidden to others besides him, peace be upon him; otherwise the offering of choice would not be possible in the sense of enjoying the adornment of the worldly life.

The fourth: that it is apparent that whoever chooses Allah, the Exalted, and His Messenger
page 184
peace and blessings of Allah be upon him, her divorce becomes forbidden for the Prophet ﷺ, in view of his noble station. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 30:

﴿O wives of the Prophet﴾ is a shift in address (talwin al-khitab), turning the speech toward them to show concern for their admonition. Their being addressed here and in what follows by their association with him, peace and blessings be upon him, is because he is the one around whom the rulings that come to them revolve. Considering them as women in both places is more eloquent than considering them as wives, as is not hidden from the reflective.

﴿Whoever of you commits﴾ is read with the yā' (third person masculine) in agreement with the wording of "man" (whoever). Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, al-Jahdari, 'Amr ibn Qa'id al-Aswari, and Ya'qub read it with the tā' (second person feminine), in agreement with its meaning. ﴿of you with a flagrant indecency﴾ means with a major sin, ﴿clearly evident﴾, of obvious ugliness, from bayyana in the sense of tabayyana (became evident). Ibn Kathir and Abu Bakr read (mubayyanatin), with a fatha on the yā'. What is meant by it, as has been said, is every major sin that is committed. Al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan narrated from Muqatil ibn Sulayman that it is disobedience to the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. It has also been said that it is that, and their demanding of him what burdens him, peace and blessings be upon him, or what straitens his chest and grieves him, peace and blessings be upon him, on account of it.

Al-Bahr prohibited that it means fornication (zina), saying: because the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, is protected from his wives committing that, and because the indecency is described as being "clearly evident," whereas fornication is something concealed; and its implication is the prohibition of the more general sense. Then he said: "It is appropriate to understand the indecency as disobedience to the husband and corruption of his companionship." His speech is not free of scrutiny. The Imam (al-Razi) explained it as that, and made the conditional clause of the kind of ﴿If you were to associate partners, your deeds would surely be nullified﴾ [al-Zumar: 65], in that such an occurrence is possible at first glance, yet it does not definitely occur, for Allah the Exalted protects the wives of the prophets from that. Some discussion of this matter has already preceded in Surat al-Nur, and some of what relates to both will come, Allah willing, the Exalted.

﴿The punishment will be doubled for her﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, according to what is narrated from Muqatil, or in it; and in this world, according to what is narrated from Qatadah, ﴿double﴾, meaning they will be punished with double the punishment of others, that is, twice it. So if others from among those who commit a clearly evident indecency remain in the Fire for one day, for example, they would remain, were they to commit the like of what he committed, two days. And if a prescribed punishment (hadd) is due to others for an indecency, two prescribed punishments would be due to them were they to commit the like of it. Abu 'Amr and Abu 'Ubaydah, as al-Tabari related from them, said the doubling means that one is made three, so that there would be three prescribed punishments upon them, or three times the punishment of others; but this is not so. The reason for doubling the punishment is that the sin from them is more grievous, for the increase in its ugliness follows the increase in the excellence of the sinner and the blessing upon him, and that is evident in them. For this reason the punishment of the free is made double the punishment of the slave. The prophets, upon them be peace, were rebuked with what others are not rebuked with, and likewise the state of the scholar in relation to the ignorant: "Are those who know equal to those who do not know?"

It is narrated from Zayn al-'Abidin, may Allah be pleased with him, that a man said to him: "You are a family for whom forgiveness is assured," so he became angry and said: "We are more deserving that what Allah the Exalted decreed for the wives of the Prophet, Allah bless him and grant him peace, should apply to us, rather than that we be as you say. Indeed we see for our doer of good double the reward, and for our doer of evil double the punishment," and he recited this verse and the one after it.

Al-Hasan, 'Isa, and Abu 'Amr read ﴿yudaʿʿaf﴾ with the yā' in the passive voice, without an alif; al-Jahdari, Ibn Kathir, and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿nudaʿʿif﴾ with the nūn in the active voice, also without an alif; Zayd ibn 'Ali, Ibn Muhaysin, and Kharijah from Abu 'Amr read ﴿nudaʿif﴾ with the nūn and the alif, in the active voice; and a group read ﴿yudaʿif﴾ with the yā' and the alif, in the active voice. The word ﴿the punishment﴾ is read in the nominative by those who read the passive voice, and in the accusative by those who read the active voice. ﴿And that was﴾, that is, the doubling of the punishment upon them, ﴿with Allah easy﴾, that is, easy, not prevented by them being wives of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, rather it is the cause of it.

(Completed by the grace of Allah is the twenty-first part; and after it, Allah willing, the twenty-second part, whose beginning is: ﴿And whoever of you is obedient﴾.)

[Page 2]

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Whoever of you is devoutly obedient (yaqnut) to God and His Messenger﴾, that is, whoever of you humbles herself and submits to God and His Messenger through action, ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾ such as prayer, fasting, pilgrimage and paying zakat. This righteous deed is other than the devout obedience (qunut) to God the Exalted, according to what you have heard of its explanation, so there is no repetition. Some have explained it as obedience, and they answered the objection of repetition by saying that what is meant is: ﴿whoever of you is devoutly obedient (yaqnut)﴾ to the Messenger of God, ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾ for God the Exalted. The mention of God is only to magnify the Messenger (ﷺ) by making his obedience inseparable from the obedience of God, Mighty and Majestic. Others explained it in the same way, but answered the objection of repetition by saying that the righteous deed means good service and the performance of the affairs of the household, not things like prayer and fasting, and that obedience (taat), by which qunut is explained, means carrying out commands and avoiding prohibitions. Others explained it as continuing in obedience, and so the objection of repetition was answered in the manner already mentioned. It was also said that what is meant is continuing in the obedience already given, and by righteous deeds are meant the acts of worship that they are henceforth obliged to perform.

It was said that qunut means silence, as was said of the words of God the Exalted: ﴿And stand before God in devotion﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238]. Here, what is meant is silence about requesting what God and His Messenger (ﷺ) have not permitted them, such as additional maintenance and adornment garments. It was also said that it means other than this.

﴿We will give her her reward﴾, which she deserves for that, as a favour and generosity, ﴿twice﴾, so her reward will be doubled. This is in contrast to the words ﴿the punishment for her will be doubled, twofold﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from al-Rabi' ibn Anas that he said, regarding the essential meaning of the two verses: whoever of you disobeys, her punishment will be double that of the other women of the believers, and whoever does righteous deeds, her reward will be double that of the other women of the Muslims. This implies that if the women of the Muslims are rewarded for a good deed tenfold, these women are rewarded twentyfold for it, and if something beyond ten is added for women, double of it is added for them. It seems, and God knows best, that the phrase ﴿We will give her her reward twice﴾ was used instead of "her reward will be doubled", just as the opposite was said, ﴿the punishment for her will be doubled, twofold﴾, because the basic doubling of reward is not a special privilege of theirs; rather, everyone among the men and women of this community who does righteous deeds has his reward doubled. So the speech was phrased differently from what the contrast would require, as a hint that the doubling of reward is of a different manner from the doubling of punishment. Moreover, the said speech includes an indication of their greater honour and abundant care for them, for repeated kindness is sweeter. Whoever reflects on the two clauses will see the preponderance of the side of mercy over the side of wrath. And it suffices, as a sign of the attention given to them, that the agent of giving the reward is explicitly mentioned, that it is the pronoun of majesty, and that what they receive of bliss is expressed as "reward" and attributed to their pronoun, whereas the clause on doubling the punishment is free of such features, as a witness to what has been mentioned. Then, the doubling of their reward is due to their greater honour, which God the Exalted, Mighty and Majestic, has granted them, by being associated with the best of creation (ﷺ), upon whom be the best blessings and the most complete greetings from God the Exalted. It is apparent that this is not only with regard to the righteous deeds they did during his lifetime (ﷺ), but their reward is doubled both for those and for the righteous deeds they do after his death, upon him be prayers and peace.

[Page 3]

Some eminent scholars said: these two doublings are, one for the obedience and the other for their seeking the Prophet's (ﷺ) pleasure through contentment and good companionship. In al-Bahr and elsewhere, this request and that obedience were made the cause of the doubling. It is not hidden that what they mentioned implies that there is no doubling with respect to what they did of righteous deeds after his death (ﷺ). Some careful scholars said: what he intended by making these the cause of the doubling of their rewards is the application to the wording of the verse, since devout obedience to God and His Messenger, together with what follows it, was made the cause. It is also implied that the doubling of the punishment arose from the fact that rebellion against the Messenger (ﷺ) and seeking what burdens him is not like rebellion against other spouses. For this reason the doubling of punishment is required. Likewise, obedience to him, good conduct with him and good companionship are the opposite of this. This confirms what they said, that the cause of doubling the punishment is the greater ugliness of the sin on their part. And it implies that the opposite entails the opposite, so reflect.

Some exegetes said: the punishment threatened as double is the punishment of this world and then the punishment of the Hereafter, and likewise the reward, so the two doublings are, one in this world and the second in the Hereafter. Its weakness is not hidden. Al-Jahdari, al-Aswari, Ya'qub in one narration, and likewise Ibn 'Amir read ﴿whoever of you is devoutly obedient (taqnut)﴾ with the feminine ta', taking the sense into account. Al-Sulami, Ibn Wathhab, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read the three verbs with the masculine ya' in front, so that the pronoun in ﴿We will give her (yu'tiha)﴾ refers to the name of God the Exalted. Abu al-Baqa' mentioned that some read ﴿whoever is devoutly obedient (taqnut)﴾ with the feminine ta' in front, taking the sense into account, and ﴿and does (ya'mal)﴾ with the masculine ya' in front, taking the wording into account. Some grammarians said: this is weak, because the masculine is the basic form, so it should not be made subordinate to the feminine. And what they gave as the reason for this has a parallel in the Qur'an, namely the words of God the Exalted: ﴿They are exclusively for our males and forbidden to our wives﴾ [al-An'am: 139]. The end of the quotation. So reflect.

﴿And We have prepared for her﴾ in Paradise, in addition to her doubled reward, ﴿a generous provision﴾, great in worth, lofty in standing, pleasing to its possessor. It was also said that a generous provision is one that is free from every blemish.

Ibn 'Atiyyah allowed that this might contain a promise of worldly provision, meaning that her provision in this world is upon God the Exalted, and it is generous insofar as it is lawful and attained with the pleasure of God the Exalted. But this, as you see, is weak.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 32:

﴿O wives of the Prophet, you are not like any one of the (other) women﴾ A group of men held that the meaning is: not each one of you is like a single individual among the women, that is, among the women of your era. That is, each one of you is superior to each one of them, because you are distinguished by the honour of being married to the Messenger of God and by the motherhood of the believers. (Fa-ahad) remains in its status as a description of the masculine, except that the noun it describes is omitted, and the omission must be considered on the side of the thing compared, as has been pointed out. Al-Zamakhshari said: "Ahad" originally has the meaning of wahid, which is "one." Then it was placed in general negation, where the masculine, the feminine, the singular and what goes beyond it are equal. The meaning is: "You are not like a single group from among the groups of women." That is, if the community of women were examined group by group, there would not be found among them a single group that equals you in merit and precedence. It has also been used in the sense of "plural" in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and they do not make any distinction between any of them﴾ [al-Nisa: 152], because of the presence of (bayn), which requires entry upon a plurality. Taking ahad to mean "group," as in al-Kashf, is so that it corresponds to the thing compared. The meaning, regarding the preference of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ over the wives of others, is not a consideration of preferring one individual over one individual of the women, for that is not intended by this context, nor does the apparent wording indicate it.

That this is more eloquent, because it entails the preference of their group over every group, while it does not entail the preference of each one of them over each one of the women individually, if this were granted, would be acceptable if the wording and context support it. Some have also objected to it, saying that it entails that each one of the wives of the Prophet ﷺ is superior to Fatimah, may God be pleased with her, although this is not the case.
Page 4

This has been answered by saying that there is no barrier to adopting it, but one commits to the superiority being from the aspect of the motherhood of the believers and the marriage to the Messenger of God ﷺ, not from all other aspects. Therefore it is not harmful that Fatimah, may God be pleased with her, is superior to each one of them in some other respects. Indeed, she is superior in some respects, such as the aspect of being the daughter of the Prophet (bid'iyyah), over each of the four caliphs, may God be pleased with them all.

Yes, I object to what is in al-Kashshaf that the hamzah of ahad, placed in general negation, is original and not converted from wahid. Abu 'Ali explicitly stated this, but al-Radi disagreed, and it is reported from him that the hamzah of ahad everywhere is a substitute for the waw. The well-known distinction is between its occurrence in general negation and its occurrence in affirmation: the hamzah of the former is original, and the hamzah of the latter is converted from waw.

In (al-'Iqd al-Manzum fi Alfaz al-'Umum) by the excellent al-Qarafi, this has become problematic for many scholars, because the two words have the same form and the meaning of unity encompasses both, and the waw in them is original. It therefore necessarily follows that the alif of ahad is converted from it absolutely, and that the alif of one of them is converted while the alif of the other is not. God Most High has granted me knowledge of his answer, which is that ahad, which is used only in negation, means "human being" by the consensus of the lexicographers, and ahad, which is used in affirmation, means "the single unit of number." When their referents differ, their derivations differ, for there must be a correspondence between the word and the meaning, and one of them does not suffice for it. So when the intended referent is a human being, it is the one used only in negation, and its hamzah is original. If the intended referent is number, half of two, it is the one suitable for affirmation and negation, and its alif is converted from waw, end of quote.

It is not hidden that if the stated distinction is accepted, the hamzah here should be original. Abu Hayyan went to the view that the hamzah of the word in general negation is original, and said: what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, his saying "then it was placed in general negation" and so on, is not correct, because what is used in general negation has a referent different from the referent of wahid, for wahid applies to everything characterized by unity, whereas ahad used in general negation is specific to whoever has reason. The grammarians mention that its root is hamzah, ha', dal, and the root of ahad in the sense of wahid is originally waw, ha', dal. They thus differ in root and in referent.

It is mentioned that what is in God's saying, exalted is He: ﴿We make no distinction between any of His messengers﴾ [al-Baqarah: 285], may be for general negation, and it may be in the sense of wahid, with a conjoined term omitted, meaning "between one and one of His messengers," as the poet said:

So there was not between the good, had Abu Hajr come safe, except a few nights.

al-Raghib said: Ahad is used in two ways. In negation, it encompasses the whole class of speakers, and it applies to the few and the many, whether together or separately, as in "there is no one (ahad) in the house," meaning: not one, nor two, nor more, neither gathered nor scattered. This meaning is not possible in affirmation, because the negation of two opposites is valid, but their affirmation is not valid. If it were said "there is an ahad in the house," it would be the affirmation of a single individual together with the affirmation of more than one, gathered and scattered, and this is absurd. Since it encompasses more than one, it is valid in His saying: ﴿So there is not any one of you who would withhold from Him﴾ [al-Haqqah: 47]. In affirmation it has three uses: its use for the unit combined with tens, as in ahad 'ashar (eleven) and ahad wa-'ishrin (twenty-one); its use as a noun, or as a noun in annexation, with the meaning of the first, as in ﴿As for one of you two, he will give drink﴾ [Yusuf: 41], and the saying "the day of al-Ahad" (Sunday); and its use as an attribute, and this is valid only in describing Him, exalted is His majesty. As for its origin, namely wahid, it may be used for other than Him, glorified is He, as in the saying of al-Nabighah:
