As if my saddle, when the day had departed with us at Dhi al-Jalil, were on a sociable and solitary (wahid) she-camel.

End of quote.

It admits both the claim that its hamzah is converted from waw absolutely, and the claim that it is converted from waw in the last usage.
Page 5

It is not hidden from the fair-minded that the meaning in the verse being what al-Zamakhshari mentioned is more evident, and that the preference of each one of his wives ﷺ over each single one of the rest of women does not follow from this verse; rather it follows from another proof, either rational or textual, such as His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and his wives are their mothers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 6]. It has been said that it may be that this is for them, for by the customary usage it conveys the preference of each of them over the rest of women, because the superiority of a group over a group generally corresponds to the superiority of each one of them.

﴿if you fear God﴾: the conditional clause negates their likeness to and superiority over women. Its answer is omitted, indicated by what has been mentioned. The taqwa (fear of God), in its well-known sense in the language of the Shari'ah, and the object is omitted, meaning: if you fear the violation of God's command and the pleasure of His Messenger ﷺ. The intended meaning is: if you persist in this taqwa; and similar usage is common. Or it is on its apparent sense, and what is intended is stirring them up, by making the pursuit of worldly things and inclining to what women incline toward, because of its distance from their station, equivalent to leaving taqwa. Or the conditional has as its answer the saying, exalted is He: ﴿so do not be soft in speech﴾. The taqwa is also in its legal sense. In al-Bahr it is said that it means "to face," i.e., if you face anyone, then do not be soft, and this meaning is well known in the language. Al-Nabighah said:

The veil fell and she did not intend to drop it, so she caught it and shielded us (ittaqat) with her hand.

That is, she faced us with her hand. This meaning would be more eloquent in praising them, since it does not make their superiority depend on taqwa, nor does it make their prohibition from softness depend on it, since they are already God-fearing within themselves. Conditioning implies that they are not adorned with taqwa. The objection to this is that ittaqa in the sense of "to face" is, though linguistically sound and frequent in the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Who would shield with his face from the evil of the punishment﴾ [al-Zumar: 24], not applicable here, because it is used in that sense only with a complement through which protection is achieved, such as His saying ﴿with his face﴾ and the saying of al-Nabighah "with the hand." What has been cited as evidence for it is easy to deal with. The apparent wording of al-Kashshaf favours that ﴿if you fear God﴾ is a conditional whose answer is "so do not be soft," and it interprets ﴿if you fear God﴾ as "if you desire taqwa" and "if you are God-fearing," indicating that there must be some figurative usage in the speech, because the reality is that those addressed are God-fearing. So either the primary intent is the intensification of the prohibition, and it is explained as "if you desire taqwa," or the intent is stirring and inciting, and it is explained as "if you are God-fearing." There is thus no combining of literal and figurative meaning, as is supposed. This has been established in al-Kashf. The meaning of ﴿do not be soft in speech﴾ is: do not answer with a speech that is yielding, that is, gentle and languid, in the manner of the speech of women who court and of prostitutes. Its sum is: do not soften speech or make it tender. This, as has been said, applies to speaking other than to a husband and the like, such as addressing strangers, even though they are forever forbidden to them.

It is related of some of the Mothers of the Believers that she would place her hand over her mouth when speaking to a stranger, and her voice would change for this reason, out of fear that it would be heard as soft and tender. Harshness of speech toward non-husbands is counted among the praiseworthy qualities of women, in the pre-Islamic period and in Islam, just as their stinginess with wealth and their cowardice are counted among the qualities. What occurs in poetry of praising the beloved for the sweetness of voice, the beauty of conversation and the softness of speech belongs to the category of foolishness, as is not hidden. It is reported from al-Hasan that the meaning is: do not speak with obscenity. This, as you see, ... ﴿so that he in whose heart is a sickness may covet﴾, that is, lechery and fornication. Ibn 'Abbas explained it thus and recited the verse of al-A'sha:

A guardian of chastity, content with piety, not of those whose heart has sickness in it.

What is meant is intention or desire for lechery and fornication. It is reported from Qatadah that it means hypocrisy. Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Zayd ibn 'Ali, may God be pleased with them both, that he said: "Sickness is of two kinds: the sickness of fornication and the sickness of hypocrisy." The verb (yatma') is in the accusative as an answer to the prohibition.
Page 6

Aban ibn 'Uthman and Ibn Hurmuz read "fa-yat'ma'" with jussive and kasra on the ayn, because of the meeting of two sukuns, and this is coordinated with the position of the prohibitive verb, on the basis that it is a prohibition to the one with sickness in his heart from coveting, following their prohibition from softness in speech, as if it were said: "So do not be soft in speech, lest he in whose heart is sickness covet." Abu 'Amr al-Dani said: al-A'raj and 'Isa read "fa-yat'imi'" with fatha on the ya' and kasra on the mim. Ibn Khalawayh transmitted it from Abu al-Sammal and said: it has also been reported from Ibn Muhaysin. It is mentioned that al-A'raj, who is Ibn Hurmuz, read "fa-yut'imi'" with damma on the ya', fatha on the ayn and kasra on the mim, meaning: he makes him covet, i.e., the softness in speech. The relative pronoun (alladhi) is the object or the subject, with the object omitted, meaning: "so that he in whose heart is sickness covets himself." ﴿And speak a good word﴾: good, distant from suspicion, not arousing desire in anyone. al-Kalbi said: that is, sound, without abandonment or softening. al-Dahhak said: rough. It has been said: that is, a word that you have been permitted to speak. It has been said: the remembrance of God, exalted is He, and what one needs of speech.

[p. 6]

﴿And stay in your houses﴾. It comes from *qarra yaqirru* (to remain, to settle), of the *'alima* pattern. Its original form was *iqrarna*. The first *ra'* was deleted and its vowel (fatha) was transferred to the letter before it. The hamza was deleted because the *qaf* was already vowelled.

Abu al-Fath al-Hamdani (*Abu al-Fath al-Hamdani*) mentioned another interpretation in his book *al-Tibyan*. He said: *qarra yuqarru* means "to gather together," and from it comes *al-qarra* (a group), because of its gathering. Do you not see the saying of 'Adal and al-Dish: "Gather together and become a group"? So the meaning is: "Gather yourselves in the houses."

Most readers recited *wa-qirna* with a kasra on the *qaf*, from *waqara yaqiru waqaran*, meaning "to be calm and steady." The original form is *uwqirna*, and what was done to *'idna* (from *wa'ada*) was done to it. Or it is from *qarra yaqirru*, the doubled verb of the *darab* pattern, whose original form is *iqrirna*. The first *ra'* was deleted, its kasra was transferred to the *qaf*, and the hamza was deleted because it was no longer needed.

Makki and Abu 'Ali said: the *ra'* which is the middle radical of the verb was changed into a *ya'* to avoid doubling. Then its vowel was transferred to the *qaf*, then it was deleted because it was sakin and the *ra'* after it was also sakin. The hamza fell away because the *qaf* was vowelled. This is an extreme case of forced explanation.

In *al-Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*) it is stated that *qarartu* and *qarirtu*, with fatha and with kasra, both come from *al-qarar* (settling) in a place, in the sense of remaining in it. Abu 'Ubayda, al-Zajjaj and others have reported this. But a group, including al-Mazini, denied that *qarirtu* (with kasra) in the sense of settling in a place, in the form *aqarru* (with fatha), occurs. They said that it only occurs as *qarrat 'aynuhu taqarru* (with kasra in the past and fatha in the present), and the affirmative is given precedence over the negative.

Ibn Abi 'Ablah recited *waqrirna* with a hamzat al-wasl and a kasra on the first *ra'*.

The meaning, according to all readings, is their command, may Allah be pleased with them, to remain in their houses. This is a command that applies to all women. Al-Tirmidhi and al-Bazzar reported from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Indeed the woman is 'awrah (something to be concealed). When she leaves her house, Satan looks at her with desire, and she is closest to the mercy of her Lord when she is in the innermost part of her house."

Al-Bazzar reported from Anas, who said: "The women came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the men have taken the virtue and jihad in the way of Allah. Is there a deed for us by which we can attain the virtue of those who strive in the way of Allah?' He (ﷺ) said: 'Whichever of you sits in her house, she attains the deed of those who strive in the way of Allah.'"

It may be forbidden for them to go out, and it may even be a major sin, such as going out to visit graves when the corruption it causes is great, or going out even to the mosque after perfuming and adorning themselves when temptation is certain. If it is only suspected, it is forbidden but not a major sin. As for the kinds of going out that are permitted, such as going out for Hajj, visiting one's parents, visiting the sick, and consoling relatives over the dead, and similar things, these are permitted subject to conditions mentioned in their proper place.

The apparent meaning of attributing the houses to the pronoun of the pure wives is that they were their property. This was stated by the hafiz Ghulam Muhammad al-Aslami, may Allah illuminate his grave, in *al-Tuhfa al-Ithna 'Ashariyya*. In it he mentions that the Prophet (ﷺ) built a room for each of the wives who lived in them, and each of them managed the room she lived in as an owner manages his property, with his presence (ﷺ).

The jurists have stated that whoever builds a house for his wife and hands it over to her is like one who gifts his wife a house and delivers it to her, so the house becomes her property. What supports the claim that the room in which 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, lived was her property, apart from the attribution in *buyutikunna* (your houses), which includes her room, is that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, asked her permission to be buried in it, in her presence, with the Companions present, and none of them objected, not even 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face. Al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, also asked her permission for this, which is established among the People of the Sunnah and the Shi'ah, as mentioned in *al-Fusul al-Muhimma fi Ma'rifat al-A'immah* and other of their books. If that room had belonged to the public treasury (*bayt al-mal*), according to the hadith "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from," then 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, would have asked permission from Marwan, because he was at that time the ruler of Madinah and the one who managed the public treasury. And if it belonged to the heirs, on the basis of the Shi'ah claim that the Prophet (ﷺ) was inherited from like others, it would also have been necessary to ask permission from the other wives, since their rights in it would be connected according to their claim. Indeed, it would also be necessary to ask permission from the Prophet's (ﷺ) relatives who are entitled to what remains after the half and the eighth, if we say they inherit. Since 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, asked permission only from her, it is known that it was hers alone.

The statement that the consent of all the others was known, so he asked her permission for that reason, cannot stand as proof for them. They have in this matter fabrications that no one relies upon and that no wise person pays attention to. Among them is the claim that 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, gave permission to al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, when he asked her to be buried in the blessed room, and then regretted this after his death, mounted her mule, came to the mosque, prevented the burial, shot arrows at his noble, pure funeral, and claimed the inheritance.

Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, composed the following lines:
"You adorned yourself and behaved like a stubborn mule, and if you live you will act like a stallion; for you have the ninth of the eighth, so how could you own the whole?"

The weakness of this poetry proclaims the falsity of its attribution to that learned companion, may Allah be pleased with him. I wonder what need she had to ride, when her residence was that blessed room. If she had intended to prevent it, she would have closed its door. Furthermore, how could it be imagined of her, when she has the greatest share of intellect compared to her sisters, the Mothers of the Believers, that she would claim the inheritance when she and her father, may Allah be pleased with both of them, narrated in the presence of the Companions, who did not fear the blame of any blamer in the cause of Allah: "We, the company of prophets, are not inherited from."

Moreover, the attribution of the houses to the pronoun of the pure wives may be based on the fact that they lived in them, were responsible for their affairs, and were their guardians. The use of the specific for the general is common in attributing houses to wives on this basis. Asking permission may have been because each house, after the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), passed to the ownership of the one who lived in it, from the side of the Caliph, who was in charge of the public treasury, when he saw the benefit in assigning each of them to her dwelling and leaving it to her as an iqta' (grant) from the public treasury.

Among what may be cited in support of the attribution to their pronoun on this basis, and not on the basis that the houses were their property, is the attribution of a house to the Prophet (ﷺ) in other reports. Indeed, if Allah wills, the attribution of houses to him (ﷺ) will come later in His saying: ﴿O you who believe, do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless permission is given to you﴾ (al-Ahzab: 53), and the verse. Attribution to ownership is more appropriate there, so let this question be examined and considered.

﴿And do not display yourselves as in the display of the former times of ignorance﴾. *Tabarruj* (display), according to what was reported from Mujahid, Qatadah and Ibn Abi Najih, is walking with swaying, affectation and coquetry. From Muqatil: that a woman throws her head-cover over her head without tying it, so that it does not cover her necklaces, earrings and neck, and all of that appears from her. Al-Mubarrad said: that she displays of her attractions what it is obligatory for her to cover. Al-Layth said: it is said "the woman displayed herself" when she revealed her attractions from her face and body, and a good look is seen from her eye along with that. Abu 'Ubayda said: that she brings out of her attractions what arouses desire in men.

Its root, according to *al-Bahr*, is from *baraj*, which means breadth and beauty of the eye. It is said: a *tan'ah barja'* (a wide spear wound), meaning wide. And there is *baraj* in his teeth when the space between them is spread apart. It has also been said: it is from *al-burj* in the sense of a palace, and the meaning of "the woman displayed herself" is that she appeared from her *burj*, that is, her palace. Al-Raghib made the use of *baraj* for the breadth and beauty of the eye a comparison with the *burj* (tower) in both respects. It is not hidden that if *tabarruj* were interpreted here as appearing from a *burj*, this sentence would be like an emphasis on what precedes it, so it is better not to interpret it that way. *Tabarruj* is a verbal noun used as a simile, like the saying "his voice is the voice of a donkey," meaning: do not display yourselves like the display of the former times of ignorance. It has also been said that there is an ellipsis of two elements, meaning: the display of women in the days of ignorance, with the construction of "women" in the sense of "in." The "former times of ignorance," according to what Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman* reported from Ibn 'Abbas, are the period between Nuh and Idris, peace be upon them, which lasted a thousand years. He said: two lineages of the children of Adam were such that one lived in the plain and the other lived in the mountains. The men of the mountains were handsome but the women were plain, and the women of the plain and its men were the opposite. The people of the plain made a festival that they gathered for each year, so the women displayed themselves to the men and the men to the women. A man from the people of the mountain attacked them during their festival, saw the women and their beauty, went to his companions and told them about it, so they moved to the women and settled among them, and indecency appeared among them. In another report: at that time a woman would be united between a husband and a lover.

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Hakam ibn 'Uyaynah, who said: between Adam and Nuh, peace be upon them, there were eight hundred years, and their women were among the ugliest of women, while their men were handsome, and a woman would solicit a man for himself. This is the "former ignorance." Similar was reported from 'Ikrimah.

Al-Kalbi said: it is what was between Nuh and Ibrahim, peace be upon them. Muqatil said: it was in the time of Nimrod, and in it there were prostitutes who wore the thinnest coats of mail and walked in the streets. It was also reported from him that the first ignorance was in the time of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, and the second in the time of Muhammad (ﷺ) before he was sent. Abu al-'Aliyah said: the first was in the time of Dawud and Sulayman, peace be upon them, when a woman had a shirt of pearls, not sewn at the sides, through which her flesh and private parts were visible.

Al-Mubarrad said: a woman would combine her husband and her lover; for the husband she had her lower half, and for the lover her upper half, to be enjoyed by kissing and sucking. It has also been said: it is what was between Musa and 'Isa, peace be upon them. Al-Sha'bi said: it is what was between 'Isa and Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon them both. Al-Zajjaj said: this is the most likely, because they are the well-known *jahiliyyah*, who used to take prostitutes.

It is called "the former" only because every one who precedes is called *awwal* and *ula* (first, former). Its interpretation is that they preceded the community of Muhammad (ﷺ). It was reported from Ibn 'Abbas something that clearly states that "the former" here is in contrast with "the latter." Al-Zamakhshari said: it may be that the former ignorance is the ignorance of disbelief before Islam, and the latter ignorance is the ignorance of wickedness and immorality in Islam. So the meaning is: do not speak of display as an ignorance in Islam, imitating the people of the ignorance of disbelief. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: what appears to me is that the former ignorance refers to the ignorance that is specific to them, so they were commanded to move away from their conduct in it, which was what existed before the Law (*shar'*) of disbelief, scarce jealousy, and similar things.

And in a hadith reported by the two Shaykhs [al-Bukhari and Muslim]

[p. 9]

Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi (narrated) that he (ﷺ) said to Abu Dharr, who had reproached a man for having a non-Arab mother and had complained about him to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "O Abu Dharr, you are a man in whom there is still jahiliyyah (the state of ignorance that preceded Islam)." Ibn al-Athir explained it as the condition the Arabs were in before Islam: ignorance of Allah the Exalted and His Messenger (peace be upon him), of the laws of the religion, boasting about lineage, arrogance, tyranny, and other things. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

The Rafidah (the "rejectors," a term for the Shi'ah) cling to this verse in their attack on the Mother of the Believers, 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), and far be it from her to suffer any attack, because she left Medina for Mecca and from there went to Basra, where the Battle of the Camel took place. They said: Allah the Exalted commanded the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), and she was among them, to remain in their houses and forbade them to go out, so by going out she disobeyed the command and prohibition of Allah the Exalted, Mighty and Majestic.

The answer to this is that the command to remain settled in the houses and the prohibition of going out are not absolute. Otherwise he (ﷺ) would not have taken them out after the revelation of the verse for Hajj and 'Umrah (the minor pilgrimage), would not have taken them with him on the military campaigns, and would not have permitted them to visit their parents, visit the sick, and console relatives. All of this occurred, as the reports attest. It is also established that all of them used to perform Hajj after the death of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), except Sawdah bint Zam'ah. In a narration from Ahmad on the authority of Abu Hurayrah: except Zaynab bint Jahsh and Sawdah. None of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them all) objected to them, including the Commander of the Faithful (Ali, may Allah honour his face) and others. It is also reported in the authentic hadith that after the revelation of the verse he (ﷺ) said to them: "You have been permitted to go out for your needs." Thus it is known that what is meant is the command to stay settled, by which their dignity and their distinction over the rest of women are achieved, namely that they should keep to their houses for most of their time, and not be those who go out and come in frequently, wandering in the streets, markets, and people's homes. This does not contradict their going out for Hajj or for something that carries a religious benefit, while being veiled and not displaying themselves. 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) left her house for Mecca only for Hajj, and Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her) went out with her for the same reason. Likewise Safiyyah, who is accepted by the Shi'ah. But when she heard of the killing of 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) and the alignment of his killers with Ali (may Allah honour his face), she grieved greatly and sensed the disruption of the affairs of the Muslims and the occurrence of corruption and strife among them. While she was in this state, Talhah, al-Zubayr, Nu'man ibn Bashir, Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, and others from among the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) came to her, fleeing from Medina in fear of the killers of 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him), because they had openly shown their boasting of their shameful deed and had announced their abuse of 'Uthman. The hearts of those noble men were constricted, and they began to denounce what had happened and to condemn those base men, blaming them for that most abominable act. So their resolve to follow 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) became firm, and they knew that they had no power to prevent them if they undertook that. So they went out to Mecca and sought refuge with the Mother of the Believers and informed her of the news. She said to them: "I see it as right that you do not return to Medina as long as those base men are there surrounding the council of the Commander Ali (may Allah honour his face), who is unable to exact retribution from them or drive them out. So settle in a land where you will be safe, wait for the affairs of the Commander of the Faithful (may Allah be pleased with him) to be put in order and his power to be strengthened, and strive to separate them from him and help him take revenge on them, so that they may be a lesson to those who come after them." They approved of this and found it good, so they chose Basra, because it was at that time a gathering place for the armies of the Muslims. They preferred it over other places and insisted that their mother (may Allah be pleased with her) accompany them until the strife was lifted, security was achieved, and the affairs of the caliphate were put in order. By this they intended to increase her esteem and strengthen their sense of security, because she was the Mother of the Believers, the wife most highly respected by the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), the one he loved most and who was most accepted by him, and the daughter of his first Caliph (may Allah be pleased with him). So she travelled with them with the intention of reform, the ordering of affairs, and the protection of a number of the senior Companions (may Allah be pleased with them). With her was her sister's son, 'Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, and others from her sisters' sons, Umm Kulthum, wife of Talhah, and Asma', wife of al-Zubayr. Indeed everyone who was with her was in the position of sons in terms of being unmarriageable kin (mahram). She was in a howdah of iron.

Then news reached the Commander (Ali, may Allah honour his face) that she was heading to Basra, and those killers, the base men, had conveyed this to him in a distorted way and urged him to go out to them and punish them. Al-Hasan, al-Husayn, 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far, and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them) advised him not to go out and to remain until the situation became clear. But he refused (may Allah be pleased with him), so that Allah might decree a matter that was to be done. He set out (may Allah honour his face) together with those evil men, the people of strife. When they reached near Basra, they sent al-Qa'qa' to the Mother of the Believers, Talhah, and al-Zubayr, so that he could learn their intentions and present them to the Commander (may Allah be pleased with him and honour his face). Al-Qa'qa' came to the Mother of the Believers and said: "O mother, what has brought you out and made you come to this town?" She said: "My son, reform among the people." Then she sent for Talhah and al-Zubayr. Al-Qa'qa' said: "Tell me what the right course is." They both said: "Carrying out the legal punishment on the killers of 'Uthman and pleasing the hearts of his supporters, so that this will be a cause of our security and a lesson to those who come after them." Al-Qa'qa' said: "This will not happen except after the Muslims unite and the strife subsides. So you must, at this moment, pursue reconciliation." They said: "You are right and you have done well." He returned to the Commander (may Allah honour his face) and informed him of this, and he was pleased and rejoiced. The people were on the verge of returning, and they stayed three days without doubting that reconciliation would be achieved. But when the night of the fourth day came, and the messengers and intermediaries had agreed to make the reconciliation public on the morning of that night, with the Commander (may Allah honour his face) meeting Talhah and al-Zubayr (may Allah be pleased with them both), while those killers were not present with him, they realised this. It weighed heavily on them, they were agitated, and the earth became too narrow for them despite its vastness. So they consulted among themselves to attack those Muslims who were with 'A'ishah, so that they would think the Commander had broken faith, so that they would attack his army, and then they would think that those who attacked were the ones who had broken faith, and fighting would break out. They did this. Those with 'A'ishah attacked the army of the Commander, and those killers shouted that treachery had been committed. The fighting flared up, and the Commander mounted in astonishment. He saw that the battle had grown hot and that men were swimming in blood. He (may Allah be pleased with him) could do nothing but busy himself with fighting, thrusting, and striking.

Al-Tabari and the majority of trustworthy historians have related the event as you have heard, and they reported it in that way through multiple chains from al-Hasan, 'Abd Allah ibn Ja'far, and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas. As for what lies beyond that, which the Shi'ah have transmitted from their predecessors, the killers of 'Uthman, it is not to be given any attention. The dominance of the killers and the strength of their power is shown by what is in *Nahj al-Balaghah* (The Peak of Eloquence), which is accepted by the Shi'ah: that one of the Commander's companions said to him: "If only you would punish the people who incited against 'Uthman." He said: "O my brothers, I am not ignorant of what you know, but how can I deal with them when those who incited are powerful, controlling us and we do not control them? Here they are, your slaves have risen with them, the Bedouins have joined them, and they are among you, afflicting you as they wish."

Since the going out was at first for Hajj, and those who were with her of her mahrams (unmarriageable male relatives) were with her, and the command to remain in the houses did not include a prohibition of the like of this, the criticism does not apply to it at all. The same goes for the journey to Basra for that purpose, for it is no less than a voluntary Hajj journey. What followed from it had not been in her calculation and had not occurred to her mind. That is why, when what happened occurred and what followed from it took place, she regretted it in the extreme. It is reported that whenever she mentioned the Day of the Camel she would weep until her headcloth was soaked. Indeed, 'Abd Allah ibn Ahmad in *Zawa'id al-Zuhd* (Additions to *al-Zuhd*), Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Shaybah, and Ibn Sa'd transmitted from Masruq, who said: Whenever 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her) recited "*And stay in your houses*" she would weep until her veil was wet. And this was only because her recitation reminded her of the event in which many Muslims were killed. This is like the Commander (may Allah honour his face) being saddened by that as well. It is established that when the defeat befell those with the Mother of the Believers and whoever was killed from both sides was killed, he (may Allah be pleased with him) walked through the field of the slain, striking his thighs and saying: "Would that I had died before this and had been a forgotten, forgotten thing." Her weeping at the recitation of the verse was not because she knew that she had misunderstood its meaning or had forgotten it on the day she set out, as has been imagined. The poet Kazim al-Azdi al-Baghdadi, one of the later poets of the Rafidah, said in mockery of this, in a long qasidah containing several blasphemous lines:

She memorised forty thousand hadiths,
Yet of the Remembrance (the Qur'an) she forgot a verse.

Yes, to the reason we have mentioned for her weeping may be added that the Prophet (ﷺ) said one day to his pure wives, among whom was 'A'ishah: "I see one of you, the dogs of al-Hawab will bark at her." In some narrations not regarded as reliable by the People of the Sunnah, with the addition: "Beware, O Humayra (little reddish one), that you should not be she." She had not asked before the journey whether al-Hawab lay on her route or not, until dogs barked at her during the journey near some water. She said to Muhammad ibn Talhah: "What is the name of this water?" He said: "They call it al-Hawab." She said: "Turn me back!" She mentioned the hadith and refused to continue and resolved to return. Most of those with her did not agree with her, and a dispute broke out until Marwan ibn al-Hakam, together with about eighty men from the landowners of that region, testified that this water was a different water and was not al-Hawab. So she continued on her affair because of that, return became impossible, and the matter happened. It seems that she (may Allah be pleased with her) saw her silence about asking and verifying the situation before the journey as a shortcoming and a sin on her part, given her station, so she wept over it.

In addition to what has preceded, and to what the Shi'ah claim, that she (may Allah be pleased with her) was the one who incited people to kill 'Uthman, saying: "Kill Na'thal, for he has committed sin," likening him to a Jew called Na'thal. Then when he was killed and the people pledged allegiance to Ali, she said: "I do not care if the sky falls upon the earth. He was killed, by Allah, unjustly, and I am seeking his blood." Someone reminded her of what she had been saying, and she said: "By Allah, I did say it, and so did the people." Then he recited:

From you comes the change of mind, and from you the shifting,
From you the winds, and from you the rain.
You ordered the killing of the Imam,
And you told us that he had sinned.

This is a lie without any basis, and it is one of the fabrications of Ibn Qutaybah, Ibn A'tham al-Kufi, and al-Sumsati, who were well known for lying and fabrication.

Of the same kind of lie is their claim that she (may Allah be pleased with her) did not go out and travel to Basra except out of hatred for Ali (may Allah honour his face). In fact she never ceased narrating his virtues and merits. Among that is what al-Daylami narrated, that she said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: The love of Ali is worship." She also said, after what happened: "By Allah, there was nothing between me and Ali except what is between a woman and her in-laws."

[Page 12]

Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, honored her, treated her well, showed great respect for her, and returned her to Medina with a group of women from the notable families of Basra, honored and dignified. This is among the things used to refute the Rafidah (Shi'a extremists), who claim her disbelief. Allah forbid, she did not do what they say. As for what has been reported from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays, that when Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, prevailed over the people of the Camel, he sent to Aisha, "Return to Medina," but she refused. He sent the messenger back to her and instructed him to say to her: "By Allah, you will return, or I will send to you women from Bakr ibn Wa'il with sharp blades who will seize you with them." When she saw this, she left. This report is not to be relied upon. Even if it is said that Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba related it in al-Musannaf, it contradicts what the more trustworthy reports have transmitted, to the point that it nearly reaches the level of tawatur (mass transmission).

Furthermore, what Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Muhammad ibn Sirin does not undermine the view that it is permissible for women to go out for Hajj and similar purposes. He said: It is established that it was said to Sawda, may Allah be pleased with her, the wife of the Prophet (ﷺ):
"Why do you not perform Hajj or Umrah as your sisters do?" She said: "I have performed Hajj and Umrah, and Allah has commanded me to remain in my house. By Allah, I will not leave my house until I die." He said: By Allah, she did not leave the door of her chamber until her funeral was carried out. This is because that matter is based on her own ijtihad (independent legal reasoning), just as the going out of her sisters is based on their ijtihad.

Yes, Ahmad narrated from Abu Hurayra that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to his wives in the year of the Farewell Pilgrimage: "This (pilgrimage), then remain in your mats (lit. reed mats)." He said: So all of them performed Hajj except Zaynab bint Jahsh and Sawda bint Zam'a, and the two of them used to say: "By Allah, no animal will move us after we heard that from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." The meaning of his saying (peace be upon him), "This (pilgrimage) etc.," is that you should no longer go out of your houses after this pilgrimage and should remain on the ḥuṣur (mats). The ḥuṣur is the plural of ḥaṣīr, which is spread in houses and made of reeds. The ṣād is pronounced with a ḍamma or sukūn for ease. This statement implies a prohibition against going out for Hajj, so what was mentioned first does not hold. Moreover, the going out of the rest of the wives for this purpose is problematic.

It is answered that the report is not an explicit text prohibiting going out for Hajj after that pilgrimage. Otherwise, the rest of the pure wives would not have gone out for it without objection from any of the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all. Rather, it is reported that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, sent them for Hajj during his caliphate, and appointed Uthman and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf to accompany them, saying to them: "You are two dutiful sons to them. Let one of you be in front of their mounts and the other behind them." No one objected, so this became a silent (sukūtī) ijma' (consensus) on permissibility. Thus it seems that Zaynab and Sawda understood from the report that this pilgrimage was a specific obligation or was permitted, but that this specific pilgrimage was for them, and that after it the obligation upon you is to remain in your houses. Hence they did not perform Hajj afterward for that reason. Others understood from it that the appropriate or suitable thing for you is this pilgrimage, meaning this type of pilgrimage or this kind of journey for Hajj or for an important religious matter. After the appropriate or suitable task is completed, the obligation is to remain in the houses. Its implication, then, is the permissibility of going out for that purpose.

Whoever is fair would hardly claim that the report indicates a command to remain in the houses and a prohibition against leaving them absolutely after that particular pilgrimage. For the Prophet (ﷺ) fell ill in the house of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, and remained ill there until he passed away, peace be upon him. No one doubts that the rest of the wives went out to visit him, nor can one imagine them remaining in their houses without being restless with longing to see his noble countenance until he (ﷺ) died. Such a thing would not be done even by the least of women in love with their husbands, who are of no great standing. How then could the pure wives do it with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who is who he is, and with their love for him being what it was? Moreover, the answer mentioned is only needed after the soundness of the report is granted, and affirming its soundness with certainty requires scrutiny and review. Let it be scrutinized and reviewed. And Allah knows best.

﴿And establish the prayer and give zakat﴾: they were commanded with these two because of their excellence over other acts and because they are the foundation of physical and financial worship.

﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger﴾: that is, in everything you do and refrain from, especially in what you have been commanded and forbidden.

﴿Allah only intends to remove from you the impurity, O people of the household, and to purify you with complete purification﴾: this is a resumptive explanatory clause (istinaf bayānī) indicating the reason for their commands and prohibitions. The word rijs (impurity) originally means a filthy thing, and here, according to many, it is used figuratively to mean sin. Al-Suddi said it means sin; al-Zajjaj said it means immorality (fisq); Ibn Zayd said it means Satan; al-Hasan said it means shirk (polytheism). It was also said it means doubt, and it was said it means stinginess and greed, and it was said it means desires and innovations. It was also said that rijs applies to sin, to punishment, to physical impurity, and to defects, and here it is meant to include all of these. Nothing is hidden from you about the weakness of some of these views. The alif-lām in al-rijs is either for the genus or for totality (istighrāq).

As for tathīr (purification), it was said it means adornment with taqwa (piety). The meaning, according to what has been said, is: Allah only intends to remove from you sins and disobedience in what He has forbidden, and to adorn you with piety in an eloquent manner in what He has commanded. It is also permitted that it means protection (ṣawn), and the meaning would then be: He, glorified be He, only intends to remove from you impurity and to safeguard you from acts of disobedience with an eloquent safeguarding in what He commanded and forbade.

The grammar of the lām in ﴿li-yudhhiba﴾ has been disputed. It was said it is an extra (zāʾida) lām, and what follows it occupies the position of the object of yurīd (intends), as if it were said: Allah intends the removal of impurity from you and your purification. It was also said it is a lām of causation (taʿlīl). Then those who held this differed. Some said the object is omitted, meaning: Allah only intends to command you and forbid you so that He may remove, or: He only intends from you what He intends in order to remove, or something similar. Al-Khalil, Sibawayh, and those who followed them said: the verb in this case is taken as a verbal noun (maṣdar) in the nominative, as the subject, and the lām with what follows is the predicate. That is, the intention of Allah, exalted is He, is for the removal, in the same manner as the saying, "You hear of al-Mu'idi and it is better than you see him." Thus there is no object for the verb. Al-Tabarsi said: the lām is connected to an omitted element whose estimate is "and His intention is to remove." This, as you see, is weak. What they have mentioned applies also to the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Allah intends to make clear to you﴾ [al-Nisa: 26] and ﴿We have been commanded to submit to the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-An'am: 71], and to the poet's saying:

I intend to forget her remembrance, but it is as if
Layla is depicted for me in every place.

The word ahl (people) is in the accusative as a vocative (nidāʾ). It is also permitted that it is accusative by way of praise, so one estimates "I praise" or "I mean." It may also be accusative by way of specification (ikhtiṣāṣ), which is rare in address, as in: "By You, O Allah, we hope for favor." It is most common in the first person, as in the saying: "We are the daughters of Tariq, walking upon the cushions."

The alif-lām in "al-bayt" (the house) is for familiarity (ʿahd). It was also said it is a substitute for the omitted genitive, meaning "the house of the Prophet (ﷺ)." Apparently the intended meaning is a house of mud and wood, not the house of kinship and lineage, and it is the dwelling house, not the Prophet's Mosque as some have said. In that case, the people of the house are his wives (ﷺ), the pure ones, because of the contextual indications from the preceding and following verses. Moreover, the Prophet (peace be upon him) had no house to live in except their dwelling. Many have narrated this. Ibn Abi Hatim and Ibn Asakir narrated through the chain of Ikrima from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that the verse "Allah only intends…" etc. was revealed specifically concerning the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn Mardawayh narrated through the chain of Ibn Jubayr from him the same, without the word "specifically." Ikrima said: "Whoever wishes, I will invoke a curse (mubāhala) upon him that it was revealed concerning the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ)." Ibn Jarir and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ikrima that he said about the verse: "It is not as you suppose. It is about the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ)." Ibn Jarir also narrated that Ikrima used to proclaim in the marketplace that the saying of the Exalted, ﴿Allah only intends to remove from you the impurity, O people of the household﴾, was revealed concerning the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn Sa'd narrated from Urwa concerning ﴿to remove from you the impurity, O people of the household﴾ that he said: "It means the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ)."

The singular form "bayt" (house) is used because the houses of the pure wives, with respect to their attribution to the Prophet (ﷺ), form one house, while the plural is used in what precedes and follows, with respect to their attribution to the pure wives, who were many. The plural is used in His saying, glorified be He, to come: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless permission is given to you﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53], to avert the suspicion that the house of Zaynab would be intended if it were singular, since the occasion of revelation concerned something that happened there, as you will come to know, Allah willing.

The masculine plural pronoun is used in "ʿankum" (from you) and in "wa-yuṭahhirakum" (and purify you), in consideration of the word "ahl" (people). The Arabs often use masculine forms in such cases out of regard for the wording. This is like the saying of the Exalted addressing Sarah, wife of the Friend (Abraham), peace be upon them both: ﴿Do you wonder at the command of Allah? The mercy of Allah and His blessings be upon you, O people of the house. Indeed, He is Praiseworthy and Glorious﴾ [Hud: 73]. Also, according to some, His saying, glorified be He: ﴿He said to his family, "Wait, indeed I have perceived a fire"﴾ is an address from Moses, peace be upon him, to his wife. Perhaps the consideration of the masculine here is more fitting for honor.

It has also been said that the intended people are the Prophet (ﷺ) and his pure wives, may Allah be pleased with them, and the masculine plural pronoun is used because it takes precedence over them, peace be upon him. It was also said that the house intended is the house of lineage, and therefore it is singular and not plural as in what precedes and follows.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nu'aym, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il, all together, narrated from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah divided creation into two divisions, and placed me in the better of the two divisions. Then He divided the two into three parts, and placed me in the best of the three parts. That is His saying, ﴿And the companions of the right hand﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 27] and ﴿And the companions of the left hand﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 41]. So I am of the companions of the right hand, and I am the best of the companions of the right hand. Then He made the divisions into thirds and placed me in the best of them. That is His saying: ﴿And the companions of the left hand, what are the companions of the left hand?﴾ and ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾ [al-Waqi'a: 9–10]. So I am among the foremost, and I am the best of the foremost. Then He made of the tribes three clans and placed me in the best of them. That is His saying: ﴿And We made you nations and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous of you﴾ [al-Hujurat: 13]. I am the most pious of the children of Adam and the most noble of them before Allah, the Exalted, and I say this without boasting. Then He made the tribes into houses and placed me in the best of them as a house. That is His saying: ﴿Allah only intends to remove from you the impurity, O people of the household, and to purify you with complete purification﴾. I and the people of my house are purified from sins."

The Qur'an verse is quoted with its meaning in the verse-marker brackets.

The usual meaning of "house" (al-bayt), which is a division of the tribe, is the house of lineage (al-bayt al-nisbi). Scholars differ over who is meant by its "people" (ahl). Al-Tha'labi held that it means all of the Banu Hashim, male and female. The apparent reading is that he meant the believing Banu Hashim, and this is what is meant by "the family" (al-al) according to the Hanafis. Some Shafi'is said that it means the family of the Prophet (ﷺ) who are believers from the Banu Hashim and the Muttalib. Al-Raghib mentioned that "the people of the house" (ahl al-bayt) became a general term for the household of the Prophet (ﷺ) without restriction. The household of a man (usrat al-rajul), according to the Qamus, is his clan (rahṭuhu), that is, his people and his nearest tribe. In another place he said: "The people of the house became a common term for his family, peace be upon him." It is authentically reported from Zayd ibn Arqam, in a hadith recorded by Muslim, that he was asked: "Are his wives (ﷺ) among the people of his house?" He said: "No, by Allah. A woman may be with a man for a time, then he divorces her and she returns to her father and her people. The people of his house are his origin (asl) and his kinsmen ('usbah) who were forbidden the charity after him (ﷺ)." In another report, also recorded by him, which explains who those forbidden charity are, he said: "They are the family of 'Ali, the family of 'Aqil, the family of Ja'far, and the family of 'Abbas." Some of the Shi'a said: "The people of the house," whether by "house" is meant the house of clay and wood or the house of kinship and lineage, is general. As for its generality on the second meaning, it is obvious. As for the first, it is because it includes the female slaves and servants, since the house of clay is also inhabited by them. But what has been authentically transmitted indicates that the generality is not intended.

Al-Tirmidhi, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related through several chains, from Umm Salamah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: "It was revealed in my house: ﴿Allah only wishes to remove from you the uncleanness, O People of the House, and to purify you thoroughly﴾. In the house were Fatimah, 'Ali, al-Hasan, and al-Husayn. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) covered them with a cloak that he had on, then said: 'These are the People of my House. So remove from them the uncleanness and purify them thoroughly.'"

Some reports mention that he (peace be upon him) brought his hand out from the cloak, pointed it toward the sky, and said: "O Allah, these are the People of my House and my close ones. So remove from them the uncleanness and purify them thoroughly," three times.

In another report: "He (peace be upon him) placed upon them a Fadakī cloak, then placed his hand upon them, then said: 'O Allah, these are the People of my House,' and in another wording, 'the family of Muhammad. So place Your prayers and blessings upon the family of Muhammad as You placed them upon the family of Ibrahim. Indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious.'"

It is reported in a narration recorded by al-Tabarani, from Umm Salamah, that she said: "I lifted the cloak to enter with them, but he (ﷺ) pulled it from my hand and said: 'You are upon good.'"

In another, related by Ibn Mardawayh from her, she said: "Am I not of the People of the House?" He (ﷺ) said: "You are upon good, you are of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ)." At its end, it is related by al-Tirmidhi and a group, from 'Umar ibn Abi Salamah, the stepson of the Prophet (peace be upon him), who said: "Umm Salamah said, and I was with them: 'O Prophet of Allah?' He said: 'You are in your place, and you are upon good.'"

The reports of his (ﷺ) bringing 'Ali, Fatimah, and their two sons (may Allah be pleased with them all) under the cloak, and his saying (peace be upon him):

Page 15

"O Allah, these are the People of my House," and his supplication for them, and the non-inclusion of Umm Salamah, are more than can be counted. She is the one who specifies the general term "people of the house," in whatever sense "house" is meant. So the intended are those whom the cloak covered, and his wives (ﷺ) are not included among them. Among the Shi'a, 'Abd Allah al-Mashhadi explicitly stated that they are not included. He said that the "house" means the house of prophethood. There is no doubt that "people of the house" linguistically includes the wives, and even the female servants who live in the house. But this linguistic meaning is not intended in this broad sense by agreement. So what is intended is the "people of the cloak" whom the hadith of the cloak specifies. He also said: The fact that "houses" appears in plural in ﹙your houses﹚ and "house" appears in singular in ﹙the people of the house﹚ indicates that their houses are other than the house of the Prophet (ﷺ). Done.

In this there is what you will know, if Allah wills. It was also said that "house" means the house of residence and the house of lineage, and the people of each of the two houses are the people of both. You have heard what was said about it, and in it is the combining of the literal and the figurative.

Some verifying scholars said: "House" means the house of residence, and its people are as the context and the surrounding context of the verse require, and as the countless reports indicate. The custom also supports this for the one who has particular closeness to it, either by residing in it while taking care of its affairs and attending to its matters, and the resident not being in a state of change or transfer by the usual custom of sale or gift, as with wives. Or by residing in it in this way without attention to managing its affairs, as with children. Or by a closeness to its owner that by custom requires frequenting it and sitting in it without the owner's request. Or by not being prevented from that. So the children who do not reside in it are included, and like their children however far down, and like paternal uncles and the sons of paternal uncles. On this basis, the reports are reconciled. You have heard some of them, such as the hadith of the cloak, which has no indication of restriction. Also like the hadith of al-Hasan that "he (ﷺ) wrapped 'Abbas and his sons in a cloth, then said: 'O Lord, this is my uncle and the twin of my father, and these are the People of my House. So cover them from the Fire as I cover them with this cloth of mine.' Then the threshold and the walls of the house said: 'Amin' three times."

It is reported in some narrations that he (peace be upon him) added to the People of the Cloak, 'Ali, Fatimah, al-Hasan, and al-Husayn (may Allah be pleased with them all), the rest of his daughters, relatives, and wives. It is authentically reported from Umm Salamah in another report that she said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, am I not of the People of the House?' He said: 'Yes, if Allah wills.'" In yet another report she said to him (ﷺ): "Am I not of your family?" He said: "Yes." And that he (peace be upon him) admitted her under the cloak after he had finished his supplication for them.

It has been repeated, as al-Muhibb al-Tabari pointed out, that from him (ﷺ) there was gathering, his saying "these are the People of my House," and the supplication, in the house of Umm Salamah, the house of Fatimah (may Allah be pleased with them both), and others. By this the differences among the reports about the form of the gathering are reconciled, and about what he (ﷺ) covered the gathered ones with, what he supplicated for them, and what he answered Umm Salamah with. Her not being admitted under the cloak on some occasions is not because she is not of the People of the House at all, but because it is evident that she is of them, since she was of the wives whom the context and surrounding context of the verse require to be included. This is unlike those who were admitted under it (may Allah be pleased with them all), for if he (peace be upon him) had not admitted them and said what he said, it would have been thought that they were not included in the verse, since its context and surrounding context do not require that.

Ibn Hajar mentioned, on the assumption that some of the differing reports are authentic, that they can be understood as the revelation having occurred twice. And the Prophet (ﷺ) admitted some who had no causal (sababiyya) or lineage (nisbiyya) kinship with him among the People of the House, by way of extension and resemblance, such as Salman al-Farisi (may Allah be pleased with him), when the Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Salman is one of us, the People of the House." And in an authentic report: "Wathilah said: 'And am I of your family, O Messenger of Allah?' He (peace be upon him) said: 'And you are of my family.' So Wathilah used to say: 'Indeed it is among the most hopeful of what I hope for.'"

The report that by its apparent meaning indicates that "house" means the lineage house, I mean the report of al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and those with him from Ibn 'Abbas, may be understood as "house" meaning the house of clay. Animals are divided into Roman and Zanj, for example, just as humans are divided into them. Moreover, among its narrators is someone whom Ibn Ma'in declared reliable and others declared weak, and disparagement (jarh) takes precedence over commendation (ta'dil).

Page 16

As for what is reported from Zayd ibn Arqam (may Allah be pleased with him), of the denial that his wives (ﷺ) are the people of his house, and that the people of his house are his origin and his kinsmen who were forbidden charity after him (peace be upon him), the "people of the house" in that report means the people of the house whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) made the second of the two weighty things (al-thaqalayn), not the people of the house in the more general sense intended in the verse. This is supported by what is in Sahih Muslim: "From Yazid ibn Hayyan, who said: 'I went with Husayn ibn Sabrah and 'Umar ibn Muslim to Zayd ibn Arqam. When we sat with him, Husayn said to him: O Zayd, you have gained much good. You saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), heard his words, fought with him, and prayed behind him. You have gained much good, O Zayd. Narrate to us what you heard from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' He said: 'O my nephew, by Allah, my age has grown great, my time has long passed, and I have forgotten some of what I was aware of from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So accept what I narrate to you, and do not burden me with what I do not.' Then he said: 'The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood one day among us as a preacher, at a water called Khumm between Makkah and Madinah. He praised Allah, exalted Him, admonished, and reminded. Then he said: "Now then, O people, I am only a human. The messenger of my Lord is about to come to me and I will answer. I am leaving among you two weighty things. The first of them is the Book of Allah, in which is guidance and light. So take hold of the Book of Allah and hold fast to it." He urged the Book of Allah and encouraged it. Then he said: "And the People of my House, I remind you of Allah concerning the People of my House. I remind you of Allah concerning the People of my House. I remind you of Allah concerning the People of my House," three times. Husayn said to him: "And who are the People of his House, O Zayd? Are not his wives of the People of his House?" He said: "His wives are of the People of his House, but the People of his House are those who were forbidden charity after him." He said: "And who are they?" He said: "They are the family of 'Ali, the family of 'Aqil, the family of Ja'far, and the family of 'Abbas."' And the hadith continues."

The corrective addition (istidrak) after his making the wives among the People of his House (ﷺ) is clear that the purpose is to explain the intended meaning of "People of the House" in the hadith that was narrated from the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him), and in which they are the second of the two weighty things. So "People of the House" has two senses, one of which includes the wives and the other of which does not. By this, the reconciliation is achieved between this report and the previous report, which contains his (may Allah be pleased with him) denial that the wives are of the People of the House.

Some said: The apparent sense of his reasoning, denying that the wives are the People of the House, with his statement, "By Allah, a woman may be with a man for a time, then he divorces her and she returns to her father and her people," requires that they are not of the People of the House at all. Perhaps by his words in the previous report, "his wives are of the People of his House," he meant "are his wives...," with the interrogative hamza of denial, so that it means "his wives are not of the People of his House." This is as in most of the reports outside the Sahih of Muslim. And he (may Allah be pleased with him) would be among those who hold that the wives of the Prophet (peace be upon him) are not of the People of the House at all. We are not obliged to take God's religion according to his opinion, especially since the apparent sense of the verse is with us, as is the custom. In that case, it is permissible that the People of the House who are the one of the two weighty things are in the sense that includes the wives and others from his origin and his kinsmen (peace be upon him) who were forbidden charity after him. Nor does it harm this that the wives did not continue to remain, as the others continued to remain together with the Book, as is not hidden. Done.

You know that the apparent sense of what is authentically reported from his saying (ﷺ): "I am leaving among you two successors (in one report, two weighty things): the Book of Allah, a rope extended between the heaven and the earth, and my family, the People of my House. They will not separate until they come to me at the Basin," indicates that the pure wives are not included among the People of the House who are one of the two weighty things. For the "itrah" (family) of a man, as in the Sihah, is his offspring and his nearest kinsmen. And "People of my House" in the hadith is apparently an explanation of it, or a substitute for it, a substitution of the whole for the whole. And on both assumptions, it is identical with it. So since the wives are not included in the first, they are not included in the second.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 33 (part 5 of 6):

It is said in al-Nihaya that the ʿitrah (kin-folk) of the Prophet ﷺ are the Banu ʿAbd al-Muttalib. It is also said that they are his nearest household (ahl al-bayt), namely his children and ʿAli and his children, may Allah be pleased with them. And it is said: his ʿitrah are his nearest and more distant relatives. End of quotation.

What al-Qurtubi preferred is that they are those upon whom zakat is forbidden. Regarding whether the Pure Wives are included in this, there is a difference of opinion. Ibn Hajar said: "The view that zakat is forbidden to them is weak, even though Ibn ʿAbd al-Barr related a consensus on it, so consider this carefully."

Nor does the reading of "ahl al-bayt" in the verse in its more general sense get refuted by what Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim and al-Tabarani narrated from Abu Saʿid al-Khudri, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'This verse was revealed concerning five people: me, ʿAli, Fatimah, Hasan and Husayn: ﴿Allah only desires to remove from you the impurity, O people of the household, and to purify you thoroughly﴾.'" For there is no proof in it of restriction (hasr), and a number has no implied restriction (mafhum). Perhaps the limitation to those mentioned, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them, is because they are the most excellent of those included in the general meaning. This is on the assumption that the hadith is sound, but what predominates in my assessment is that it is not sound, since I have not known anything like it from him ﷺ in any of the sound hadiths I have come across in the reports on the occasions of revelation.

And by interpreting "ahl al-bayt" as those who have a special closeness to him, in the manner you have heard, the objection raised by al-Mashhadi is dispelled, namely that it would include the servants, maidservants and slaves who live in the house. For they are subject to change and transfer, passing from one owner to another by gift or sale, and they have no concern for his affairs, no care for his matters and no management of his affairs except where they are commanded to do so. Placing them in the same line as the wives, and claiming that the relation of all of them to the house is of one degree, is something no fair-minded person accepts and no one holds except a distorted thinker.

Some later scholars said: including them in the general meaning is not objectionable according to the Ahl al-Sunnah, because the verse, in their view, does not indicate infallibility (ʿismah), and there is no barrier to the mercy of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, and "for the sake of a thousand eyes, one eye is honoured." As for the matter of the plural and singular, you have heard what pertains to it. According to this view, the use of the masculine plural pronoun in ("ʿankum") is for the sake of prevalence (taghlib). It is mentioned that in ("ʿankum") there are two instances of prevalence: one is the prevalence of the masculine over the feminine, and the second is the prevalence of the addressed over the absent, since those of the household other than the Pure Wives had no prior mention and were not addressed with any command, prohibition or other thing in it. The reason for this is evident, though it is not as evident as it would be on the view that ahl al-bayt means the Pure Wives alone.

Al-Mashhadi excused the placement of the clause ﴿Allah only desires﴾ etc. in the middle by saying that similar things occur in the Noble Qur'an. For the Exalted said: ﴿Say: Obey Allah and obey the Messenger; but if they turn away, then upon him is only what he has been assigned﴾ [al-Nur: 54], then after the completion of the verse He said: ﴿And establish prayer and give zakat﴾ [al-Nur: 56], so He coordinated "aqimu" with "atiʿu" despite the great separation between them. But the reply is that "aqimu al-salah" etc. came after "wa-atiʿu al-rasul," so if the coordination were as he mentioned, it would necessitate coordinating "atiʿu" with "atiʿu," and that is as you see.

Even granting that there is no corruption in this, such a separation is not the matter in dispute, for it is a separation between the coordinated and that to which it is coordinated by something foreign in terms of grammatical function (iʿrab), and that does not contradict eloquence. What we are discussing, according to their view, is a separation by something foreign with regard to the contexts of the preceding and following verses, and denying that it contradicts Qur'anic eloquence is an obstinacy that is not hidden.

Among the things over which children laugh is his statement afterwards that there is a difference between the verses in terms of performative (inshaʾi) and informative (khabari) speech, because the verse of purification is a vocative and informative sentence, while what precedes and follows it of commands and prohibitions are performative sentences, and coordinating performative with informative is not permitted. By my life, this is among the most erroneous statements, comparable to the words of some common non-Arab folk: "Khasan and Khasin are the daughters of Mughawiya." And ﴿Whoever Allah does not give light, for him there is no light﴾ [al-Nur: 40].

Then the Shi'a relied on the verse after their claim that ahl al-bayt in it is restricted to those you have heard, and they made ﴿li-yudhhiba﴾ the direct object of ﴿yurid﴾, and they interpreted the impurity (rijs) as sins in the sense of infallibility. So they held that ʿAli, Fatimah and the two sons (Hasan and Husayn), may Allah be pleased with them, are infallible from sins, with the infallibility of the Prophet ﷺ from them.

Some eminent later scholars objected to this, saying: even if it were granted that all they claimed is determined, the verse's indication of infallibility is not established. Rather, it has an indication of its absence, since one does not say of someone who is already pure: "I want to purify him," because obtaining what is already obtained is impossible.

The most that can be said is that these persons, may Allah be pleased with them, being preserved from impurity and sins after the desire to remove their impurity has been attached to them, is established by the verse. But this too is on the principles of the Ahl al-Sunnah, not the principles of the Shi'a, because the occurrence of what Allah wills is not necessary in their view, since His will is absolute. In sum, if conveying the meaning of infallibility were intended, it would have been said: "Allah has removed the impurity from you, O people of the household, and purified you thoroughly."

Also, if it indicated infallibility, the Companions should be infallible, especially all those present at the Battle of Badr, given the Exalted's words concerning them: ﴿But He desires to purify you and to complete His favour upon you, that you may be grateful﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 6]. Indeed, this may be even more conclusive, because of His words: ﴿and to complete His favour upon you﴾, for this completion cannot be conceived without being preserved from sins and from the evil of Satan. End of quotation.

Al-Tabrisi explained the basis of the argument from it for infallibility as follows: ﴿innama﴾ is a particle that affirms what comes after it and negates what is not affirmed. Thus when one says, "Innama laka ʿindi dirham" (Only a dirham is yours with me), it indicates that the addressee has nothing with him except one dirham. So the verse affirms the realisation of the desire and negates anything other than it. The desire is either the bare desire or the desire that is followed by purification. The removal of impurity cannot be the bare desire, because Allah the Glorified and Exalted has desired that from every responsible person with bare desire, so it is not specific to the people of the household to the exclusion of all other responsible persons. Also, this statement necessarily implies praise and honour for them without doubt, and there is no praise in bare desire; so the second meaning is determined, and it is known that those other than the People of the Cloak are not intended, so infallibility is restricted to them. End of quotation. And this, as you see, is not sound. Moreover, the books of the Shi'a contain what indicates that the Commander (Amir), may Allah honour his face, was not infallible, and he is more excellent than being included under the cloak after the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. In Nahj al-Balagha it is related that he, may Allah honour his face, said to his companions: "Do not hold back from a statement of truth or counsel of justice, for I am not above making mistakes, nor am I safe from that in my actions, except that Allah the Exalted casts into my soul what He has more power over than I do." Also in it: he, may Allah honour his face, used to say in his supplication: "O Allah, forgive me what I have drawn near to You with and what my heart has opposed," and the intention of teaching, as in some prophetic supplications, is far-fetched, it is said. So reflect, and do not be heedless.

Some of the Ahl al-Sunnah explained the desire here as love (mahabbah). They said: if the desire meant were that by which the act is realised, then every member of the household until the Day of Resurrection would be preserved from every sin, and observation contradicts this. And restricting it to the People of the Cloak and the remaining twelve Imams, as the Imamiyya who claim their infallibility maintain, is something for which no proof stands in our view. The praise came from the concern with their status, the information that Allah loves for them this exalted matter, His addressing them with it, and His making it a Qur'an recited until the Day of Resurrection.

It may also be inferred that the desire here means the sense mentioned rather than the well-known sense by which the act is realised, from the fact that he ﷺ said when he brought ʿAli, Fatimah, Hasan and Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them, under the cloak: "O Allah, these are the people of my household, so remove from them the impurity and purify them thoroughly." For what need would there be for supplication if that were desired in the well-known sense? Is it not a claim of obtaining what must already be obtained?

Some have used this to argue that the verse was not revealed concerning them, and that the Prophet ﷺ only included them among the people of the household mentioned in the verse by his noble supplication, peace be upon him. But all that has been mentioned is not free from discussion. What appears to me is that by ahl al-bayt are meant those who have a greater connection with him ﷺ and a strong, close relationship to him, peace be upon him, such that it is not considered improper by custom for them to gather and dwell with him ﷺ in one house. This includes his wives and the Four People of the Cloak, and ʿAli, may Allah honour his face, along with his kinship to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who grew up in his house and under his care, peace be upon him, and never left him, and whom he treated as his own child when young, or whom he made his in-law and whose brother he became when grown.

The desire is in its true meaning, which entails the act, and the verse does not stand as proof of the infallibility of the people of his household, peace be upon him and them, those present at its revelation and others, nor of their preservation from sins as the Ahl al-Sunnah say, not because it is possible that the meaning is the directing of a command or prohibition or the like toward the removal of impurity and purification, by making the direct object of ("yurid") omitted and making ("li-yudhhiba") and ("yutahhira") in the position of the object of purpose. Although there is no harm in this, and some have taken this view, rather because the meaning, as the mind is drawn to and as the placement of the clause as a reason for the prohibition and command requires, is: Allah the Exalted has forbidden you and commanded you, for He desires by your prohibition and your command to remove impurity from you and purify you. There is in that the greatest benefit for you, and He does not desire by it to test you and impose obligations upon you without benefit returning to you. This is in the sense of a condition: that is, He desires by your prohibition and your command to remove impurity from you and purify you, if you refrain and comply. This is because the style of the verse is like the style of someone saying to a group, known to drink water, that it will surely remove their thirst: "Allah desires by the water to remove thirst from you," meaning that by the water He desires the removal of thirst from you if you drink it. So the meaning is removal of thirst on condition that the addressees drink the water, not removal absolutely. Thus the implication of the construction in the example is the realisation of the removal of thirst after drinking. In our case, the removal of impurity and purification occur after refraining and complying, because the intended removal is conditional upon them; its occurrence is thus certain after the condition is realised, but the realisation of the condition is not known, since it is a matter of choice and is not the object of the desire. The meaning of impurity is sin, and its removal means the eradication of its origins through refining the soul and making its powers, such as the appetitive power and the irascible power, such that there does not arise from them what arises from sins such as fornication, killing a soul which Allah has forbidden, and other things. It does not mean the removal of the very sin after it has been realised in external existence and proceeded from the person, for that is inconceivable except in the sense of erasing it from the records of deeds and not being held to account for it, and desiring that is, as you see, not the meaning.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 33 (part 6 of 6):

It seems that the outcome of *al-idhhab* (removal) is *al-takhliya* (emptying), and the outcome of *al-tathhir* (purification) is *al-tahliya* (adorning), with the *ha'* being the unpointed letter (ح). The verse contains a promise from Him, glorified and exalted, to the People of the House of His Prophet ﷺ: that if they refrain from what He forbids and comply with what He commands, He will certainly remove from them the beginnings of what is abhorrent and adorn them with the finest adornment of what is praiseworthy. It also implies the acceptance of their deeds and the certain consequence of beautiful effects upon them. This is a special distinction for them and a privilege over others, since those others, if they refrain and comply, are not assured that this will be achieved for them.

For this reason we find that the worship of the People of the House is more complete in state than that of the rest of the servants who share with them in outward worship, better in character, and purer in soul. The chains of the spiritual paths, whose foundation, as is not hidden from their travelers, is *al-takhliya* and *al-tahliya*, both of which are the two wings for flying to the enclosures of holiness and alighting upon the nests of intimacy, end in them. So much so that some people held that the *qutb* (spiritual pole) in every age is only from among them, contrary to Shaykh Abu al-Abbas al-Mursi, who held, as his disciple Taj ibn 'Ata Allah reported from him, that he may be from others. I have seen in the *Maktubat* of the Imam al-Faruqi al-Rabbani, the Renewer of the Second Millennium, may his secret be sanctified, what in summary means that the *qutbiyya* (the station of the pole) was not in the way of *asala* (original attainment) except for the well-known Imams of the House, and then it passed after them to others by way of *niyaba* (vicarious deputyship) on their behalf, until the turn came to the Sayyid al-Shaykh Abd al-Qadir al-Kaylani, may his luminous secret be sanctified, who attained the station of the *qutbiyya* by way of *asala*. When his holy spirit was raised to the highest of the 'Illiyyun, whoever attained that rank after him attained it by way of deputyship on his behalf. Then when the Mahdi comes, he will attain it by *asala*, as the others among the Imams attained it, may the good pleasure of God Most High be upon them all. [End of quotation] This is something for which there is no way to know or to ascertain its truth except by *kashf* (unveiling), and how could I attain that?

What prevails in my estimation is that the *qutb* may be from others, but the *qutb al-aqtab* (pole of the poles) is only from them, because they are the purest of people in origin and the most abundant in virtue. Whoever among them attains this rank attains it only by way of *asala*, not *niyaba* or *wikala* (agency). I do not conceive of deputyship in that station, and if I did conceive of it I would say: every *qutb* in every age is a deputy of our Prophet, upon him be the best of blessings from God Most High and the most perfect of peace, and there is no novelty in the deputyship of the poles after him ﷺ on his behalf, just as the prophets before him were deputies on his behalf. He, upon him be blessings and peace, is the Perfect One who perfects creation and the intermediary of the overflow upon them in reality. Every prophet who preceded him in time and every pole and saint who came after him are his deputies and draw their supply from him. I say that the Sayyid al-Shaykh Abd al-Qadir, may his secret be sanctified and may his goodness overwhelm us, attained what he attained of the *qutbiyya* through his grandfather, upon him be blessings and peace, in the most complete manner and the most perfect state.
