He, may God Most High be pleased with him, was among the noble ones of the People of the House, Hasani on his father's side and Husayni on his mother's side, in whom no deficiency was found, [not even in the sense of] *law anna* (if only), *'asa* (perhaps), or *layta* (would that). None denies this except a zindiq (heretic) or a Rafidi (extreme Shi'i) who denies the companionship of al-Siddiq. And I think that his statement, may God Most High be pleased with him:

*The suns of the earlier ones have set, but our sun*
*upon the sphere of exaltation never sets.*

does not indicate that whoever attains the *qutbiyya* after him from the People of the House, whose origin and his origin are one, is a deputy of his who has no overflow except from him. Rather, the most it indicates and alludes to is the continuing manifestation of his affair, the spread of his renown, the prevalence of his path, and the generality of his overflow to whoever draws benefit from him in the known manner among his people. This is something that can scarcely be denied, and it is clearer than the sun and the moon.

This is what I have to say on the noble verse, which contains a great virtue for the People of the House. From it is known the reason for the expression *yurid* (He wills) in the present tense (*sigha al-mudari'*), and the reason for placing the removal of *rijs* (impurity) before purification, and the reason for his ﷺ supplication for the People of the Cloak that the impurity be removed, without any need to say that this is a request for continuance, as has been said regarding His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, believe﴾ and the like. Much of what is objected to others is not objected to here. Nevertheless, there is latitude in the path of the mind, and there is no restriction upon the bounty of God, may He be glorified and exalted. So there is no obstacle to Him granting someone something better and greater than this. So reflect on that, and may God, glorified is He, guide you.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 34:**

﴿And remember what is recited in your houses﴾: that is, mention it to people by way of admonition and reminder. It was also said: that is, remember and do not forget what is recited in your houses ﴿of the signs of Allah﴾, that is, the Qur'an, ﴿and the wisdom﴾, which is the Sunnah (the Prophet's teachings and practice), as Ibn Jarir and others narrated from Qatadah. It has also been explained as his (ﷺ) admonitions. And from Ata', from Ibn Abbas, that in the codex (al-Mushaf) the word "the Sunnah" stood in place of "the wisdom." Muhammad ibn Abd al-Karim al-Shahrastani related this at the beginning of his tafsir, *Mafatih al-Asrar* (The Keys of Secrets). A group of scholars said: the intended meaning of "the signs" and "the wisdom" is the Qur'an. This is more fitting with His words, ﴿is recited﴾, that is, remember what is recited of the Book, which combines being the clear signs of Allah the Exalted, indicating the truthfulness of prophethood in many ways, and being wisdom comprising the various kinds of sciences and laws. This is a reminder of the favor He bestowed upon them by making them the People of the Prophet's House and the place of descent of revelation, and of what they witnessed of the hardships of revelation, which necessarily produces strength of faith and eagerness for obedience. It also contains an exhortation to refrain from what is forbidden and to comply with what they were charged with. It was also said: this is a command to perfect others after the command to perfect oneself, and from this the reason for the insertion of "Indeed, Allah only intends..." (*innama yurid*) etc. in between becomes clear. The mention of recitation in the houses, rather than descending in them, is notable, although descent would seem more suitable since they are the place of descent of revelation, because recitation is general to all the signs and occurs in every house and is repeated, which necessitates their being firmly able to remember and to remind, unlike descent. It was also said: this is for the sake of observing wisdom, on the basis that the intended meaning is the Sunnah, since it did not descend in the manner of the Qur'an. This was objected to, on the grounds that it is also not recited in the manner of the Qur'an. The non-specification of the reciter is so that it includes the recitation of Jibril and the recitation of the Prophet, upon both of them be peace, and their recitation and the recitation of others, by teaching and learning.

Zayd ibn Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, read *tutla* (تُتْلى) with the feminine *ta'* (تاء التأنيث), [meaning the verb agrees with the feminine subject, i.e., the houses being the grammatical subject, or the verse/revelation being feminine]. ﴿Indeed, Allah is ever Subtle, Acquainted with all things﴾: He knows and manages what is beneficial in the religion, and for this reason He did what He did of commands and prohibitions. Or: He knows who is fit for prophethood and who deserves to be of the People of His House. It was also said: He practices wisdom in sending down His Book, combining the two attributes. Some scholars permitted that *al-Latif* (the Subtle) refers to the signs, because of the fineness of their inimitability, and *al-Khabir* (the Acquainted) refers to the wisdom, because of its suitability to expertise (*khibrah*).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 35:

﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and the Muslim women﴾ i.e., those who have entered into submission (islam, al-silm) and who yield to the judgement of Allah, the Exalted, or who have entrusted their affairs to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, among the males and females. ﴿And the believing men and the believing women﴾ those who affirm what must be affirmed of the two groups.

﴿And the devoutly obedient men and the devoutly obedient women﴾ those who persevere in acts of obedience and perform them.

﴿And the truthful men and the truthful women﴾ in their statements, in which truthfulness is obligatory. It has been said: in speech and in action. Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Jubayr that he said: i.e., in their faith.

﴿And the patient men and the patient women﴾ in the face of hardships, in acts of worship, and in refraining from sins.

﴿And the humble men and the humble women﴾ those who are humbled before Allah, the Exalted, with their hearts and their limbs. It has been said: those who do not look at who is to their right or left while they are in prayer.

﴿And the almsgiving men and the almsgiving women﴾ giving in what is fitting to give in charity, whether obligatory or otherwise.

﴿And the fasting men and the fasting women﴾ fasting as prescribed by the Law, whether obligatory or voluntary. It is related from Ikrimah that it is restricted to fasting in Ramadan. It has been said: whoever gives a dirham in charity each week is among the almsgivers, and whoever fasts the white days (al-bid) of every month is among the fasting.

﴿And the men who guard their private parts and the women who guard them﴾ from what Allah, the Exalted, does not approve of.

﴿And the men who remember Allah much and the women who remember Allah much﴾ with the tongues and the hearts. The measure of "much" is custom (al-'urf) according to a group. ʿAbd al-Razzaq, Sa'id ibn Mansur, ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid that he said: a man is not recorded among those who remember Allah much until he remembers Allah while standing, sitting and lying down.

Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and others related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "If a man wakes his wife at night and they both pray two rak'ahs, they are recorded that night among those who remember Allah much and the women who remember Allah much." It has also been said that the intended meaning of the remembrance of Allah, the Exalted, is the mention of His blessings and favours, Glorified is He; this is related from Ikrimah, and its outcome returns to gratitude (shukr), though this is contrary to the apparent meaning.

﴿Allah has prepared for them﴾ because of their earning of the attributes mentioned ﴿forgiveness﴾ for what they committed of minor sins, since these are expiated by righteous deeds, as has been reported ﴿and a great reward﴾ for the acts of obedience they performed. The verse is a promise to the pure wives and others who possess these attributes. Ahmad, al-Nasa'i and others related from Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with her, who said:
Page 22
"I said to the Prophet (ﷺ): Why are we not mentioned in the Qur'an as men are mentioned?" Then one day I heard nothing from him (ﷺ) except his calling out on the pulpit while he was saying: ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and the Muslim women﴾ to the end of the verse.

The pronoun in "ma lana" (what is for us) refers to women in general. In another narration related by al-Nasa'i and a group from her as well, [she said]: "I said to the Prophet, peace be upon him: Why do I hear men being mentioned in the Qur'an while women are not mentioned? So Allah, the Exalted, revealed ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men and the Muslim women﴾ the verse."

Some reports indicate that the one who asked was someone other than her. At-Tirmidhi, who graded it sound (hasan), al-Tabarani, ʿAbd ibn Humayd and others related from Umm ʿUmara al-Ansariyya that she came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: "I see that everything is only for men, and I do not see women being mentioned for anything." So this verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men...﴾ etc.

Ibn Jarir related from Qatadah that he said: "Some women entered upon the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: Allah has mentioned you in the Qur'an, but He does not mention us for anything; is there nothing of what is mentioned in us? So Allah, the Exalted, revealed ﴿Indeed, the Muslim men...﴾ the verse." In another narration from him, he said: when the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) were mentioned, the women said: "If there were good in us, we would be mentioned." So Allah, the Exalted, revealed the verse.

There is no barrier to all of this being the case. The conjunction of females with males, like "the Muslim women" with "the Muslim men" and "the believing women" with "the believing men," is necessary, because the difference of the essences that share the ruling requires conjunction, unless the enumeration is intended as a listing. The conjunction of pairs, meaning the totality of each male and female together, like the conjunction of the totality of believing men and women over the totality of Muslim men and women, is not required; it has been employed here only to indicate that the basis for the preparation of what is prepared for them is their combining of these beautiful qualities.

Mentioning the private parts as the object of guarding is because they are the seat of dominant desire, and mentioning the Glorious Name as the object of remembrance is because it is the Greatest Name, which indicates all the sublime attributes. The object of both "the guarding women" and "the remembering women" is omitted, due to the indication of what precedes it. Placing remembrance last among the attributes is because of its generality and nobility. ﴿And the remembrance of Allah is greater﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45]. The pronoun in ﴿Allah has prepared for them﴾ is masculine to give precedence to males over females; otherwise the apparent form would be "for them and for them" (feminine as well). How excellent is the Revelation! It has indicated, at the beginning and end of the verse, the superiority of males over females.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 36:

﴿It is not for a believing man or a believing woman﴾ — that is, it is not proper or fitting for any man or woman among the believers ﴿when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter﴾ — that is, when the Messenger of Allah ﷺ has decided. The mention of Allah the Exalted here serves to magnify his command, by indicating that the Prophet (ﷺ) holds such a rank with Allah that his commands are counted as the commands of Allah, Mighty and Majestic; or it is to convey that whatever the Prophet (ﷺ) does, he does by His command, since "he does not speak from desire" [Surah al-Najm: 3–4]. So the construction is either of the type of ﴿and for Allah is one-fifth of it, and for the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], or of the type of ﴿and Allah and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 62].

﴿that they should have any choice in their affair﴾ — that is, that they should choose from their affair whatever they wish. Rather, it is obligatory upon them to make their opinion follow his opinion (ﷺ) and their choice follow his choice. Al-khiyarah (choice) is a verbal noun from takhayyara, like al-tiyarah is a verbal noun from tatayyara; and according to what has been said, no other verbal noun of this pattern has come besides these two. It has also been said that it is an adjective of the form ṣifah mushabbahah, interpreted as "the one chosen." ﴿from their affair﴾ is connected to it, or to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from it. The pronoun in ﴿lahum﴾ is plural in consideration of the meaning, since ﴿mu'min﴾ and ﴿mu'minah﴾ occur in a negative context, and an indefinite noun in a negative context is general. It should, according to what is in al-Kashshaf, have been singular, as you say: "No man or woman came to me except that it was from his affair such-and-such." Abu Hayyan criticised this, saying that this is a conjunction with waw, while singularity applies in conjunction with aw, like "whoever comes to you, noble or humble, honour him"; so the pronoun cannot be singular in that case except by way of an implied ellipsis. And its plurality in ﴿amrihim﴾, although it refers to the Messenger ﷺ at first and to Allah the Exalted, is for magnification, according to what has been said.
Page 23

Some eminent scholars said: It has not become clear to me that it is impossible for it to refer to what the first pronoun referred to, on the meaning that [the choice arises] from their affair, i.e., their motives that drive them to choose the opposite of what Allah and His Messenger ﷺ have commanded; or the meaning is choice in some part of their affair, i.e., their matters which they intend. Its reference to what was mentioned is preferred because of the absence of separation (tafkik) in the pronouns. It was rejected on the grounds that this is of little benefit, since choice arises from their motives or occurs in their affairs, and this is clear, needing no explanation. This is unlike the case where the meaning is in place of His command which the Prophet (ﷺ) decided, or going beyond his command, to emphasise and affirm the negation. This is what prevents its reference to what the first pronoun referred to. The truth is that there is no obstacle to that, on the meaning that it was not for the believers to have any choice in any part of their affairs when Allah and His Messenger decide a matter for them. We do not concede that what was counted as an obstacle is an obstacle, so reflect.

Perhaps the benefit of the shift away from the apparent reference in the first pronoun, according to al-Tibi, is to notify that just as it is not valid for each individual of the believers to have choice, likewise it is not valid for them to gather and agree upon one word, because the influence of a group and their agreement is stronger than the influence of one person. From this is derived the benefit of the plural in the second pronoun on the assumption that it refers to what the first referred to; and likewise the reason for the singular of "affair" when examined carefully. The two Ḥaramayn, the two Iraqi readers (al-ʿArabiyyān), Abu ʿAmr, Abu Jaʿfar, Shaybah, al-Aʿraj and ʿIsa read ﴿takūna﴾ with the feminine ta. The reasoning is clear. The reasoning for reading with the ya, which is the reading of the Kufans, al-Hasan, al-A'mash and al-Sulami, is that the subject of the verb is separated from it, while its feminine marking is not real. It was also read, as mentioned, by ʿIsa ibn Sulayman, "al-khīrah" with the ya sukun.

﴿And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger﴾ — in some matter of the affairs, and acts in it according to his own opinion — ﴿has certainly strayed﴾ from the path of truth ﴿into clear error﴾ — that is, manifestly deviating from the ways of rightness. It is apparent that this applies to matters that have been decided, as the context indicates. The verse, according to what is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, Mujahid and others: "It was revealed concerning Zaynab bint Jahsh, from his paternal aunt Umaymah bint ʿAbd al-Muttalib, and her brother ʿAbd Allah. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ proposed her for his freedman Zayd ibn Harithah and said: 'I wish to marry you to Zayd ibn Harithah, for I have approved him for you.' She refused and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I do not accept him for myself, and I am the most eminent woman of my people and the daughter of your paternal aunt; I would not do it.' In another narration, she said: 'I am better than him in lineage.' Her brother ʿAbd Allah agreed with her in that. When the verse was revealed, they both submitted and accepted. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then married her to Zayd, after she had placed her affair in his hand, and he gave her as dowry ten dinars, sixty dirhams, a veil, a head-covering, a wrapper, a shift, an izar, fifty mudd of food and thirty ṣāʿ of dates."

Ibn Abi Hatim reported "from Ibn Zayd that he said: It was revealed concerning Umm Kulthum bint ʿUqbah ibn Abi Muayt, and she was the first woman among the women to emigrate. She offered herself to the Prophet ﷺ, but he married her to Zayd ibn Harithah. She and her brother were displeased and said: 'We only wanted the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he married us to his slave.'"

[p. 24]

**"And when you said to the one on whom Allah had bestowed favor"**: This is an address to the Prophet (ﷺ). The meaning is: remember the time when you said to the one on whom Allah had bestowed favor, by guiding him to Islam and by your guidance to his good upbringing, his manumission, your care for him, your singling him out for adoption (tabanni), and his great nearness to you. **"And you bestowed favor upon him"** by acting upon what Allah, exalted is He, had enabled you to do of the various kinds of goodness, among which was his manumission. He is Zayd ibn Harithah, may Allah be pleased with him. Mentioning him with the aforementioned description, as Shaykh al-Islam (a title for a senior scholar) said, serves to show the incongruity of his situation with what proceeded from the Prophet (peace be upon him), namely the display of something contrary to what was in his noble heart. For that occurs only out of shyness and modesty, and both of these are inconceivable in the case of Zayd, may Allah be pleased with him. It has also been permitted that this is an explanation of the wisdom behind the Prophet's (ﷺ) concealment of what he concealed, because such a matter, together with its like, is something by which people might find fault, as it has been said:

"The most unjust of Allah's creation is one who spends the night envious of the one who lives amid his blessings."

**"Keep your wife to yourself"**: that is, Zaynab bint Jahsh. The reason was that she had a sharp tongue and kept boasting over Zayd of her nobility, and he would hear from her what he disliked. "One day he came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: O Messenger of Allah, Zaynab's tongue has become harsh toward me, and I want to divorce her. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said to him: ﴿Keep your wife to yourself and fear Allah﴾ regarding her matter, and do not divorce her out of harm and as a pretext because of her arrogance and the harshness of her tongue toward you." The construction of ﴿Amsik﴾ with ʿalā is because it is implicitly construed with the meaning of "restraining" (al-habs).

**"And you concealed within yourself what Allah was to disclose"**: this is coordinated with ﴿you said﴾. It has been permitted that it be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), with the supposition "(while you were concealing)," or without it, as is apparent from the words of al-Zamakhshari in various places of his Kashshaf. The intended meaning of the relative clause, according to what al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi and others transmitted from ʿAli ibn al-Husayn (may Allah be pleased with both of them), is: what Allah revealed to him, that Zaynab would be divorced by Zayd and would afterward be married by him (peace be upon him). This is the view of the verifying scholars among the exegetes (ahl al-tahqiq min al-mufassirin), such as al-Zuhri, Bakr ibn al-ʿAla', al-Qushayri, al-Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi, and others. **"And you feared the people"**: you feared their objection. It has been said that it means: you were ashamed of their saying that Muhammad (ﷺ) married his son's wife. By "the people" is meant the category as a whole, including the hypocrites. This is coordinated with what preceded or is a circumstantial clause. His saying: ﴿And Allah has more right that you fear Him﴾ is in a position of circumstantial clause only. The meaning is: Allah alone has more right that you fear Him in every matter, so that you do what He, glorified is He, has permitted you and authorized you to do. The reproach, in the view of whoever you have heard, is upon his (peace be upon him) saying that together with ﴿Keep﴾, while he knew that Zayd would divorce her and that he himself would marry her afterward. This reproach is for leaving what is preferable (tark al-awla). In such a matter, what was preferable for him (peace be upon him) was to remain silent, or to leave the matter to Zayd's judgment, may Allah be pleased with him.

Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabari and a group transmitted from Qatadah that he (ﷺ) was concealing his intention to divorce her and was fearing people's saying if he ordered her divorce; and that he (peace be upon him) said to him: ﴿Keep your wife to yourself and fear Allah﴾ while he loved her divorce. The reproach upon him is for displaying what contradicts the concealment. Al-Qadi ʿIyad refuted that in al-Shifa' and said: "Do not doubt in exonerating the Prophet (ﷺ) from this apparent meaning, namely that he would command Zayd to keep her while he loved his divorcing her," and so on to the end of what he said, as mentioned by a group of exegetes. Some of them mentioned that his (ﷺ) intention to divorce her and his love for it was merely a passing thought in his noble mind after knowing that Zayd intended to separate from her. There was no envy on his part, far be it from him, toward Zayd concerning her, so there is no harm. The safest view is what we have mentioned from Zayn al-ʿAbidin, may Allah be pleased with him, and the majority.

The summary of the reproach, according to what I say, is: "Keep your wife to yourself," while I had informed you that she would be among your wives. This agrees with the recitation, because Allah, exalted is He, informed that He would disclose what the Prophet (peace be upon him) had concealed, and He disclosed nothing except his marrying her. So He, glorified is He, said: ﴿We married her to you﴾. Had what was concealed been his love for her and his intention to divorce her and the like, He, exalted is He, would have disclosed it. There are speculations by the storytellers (quṣṣāṣ) regarding this story, which should not be placed within the scope of acceptance.

From among them is what Ibn Saʿd and al-Hakim transmitted from Muhammad ibn Yahya ibn Hibban: "that he (ﷺ) came to Zayd's house and did not find him, and Zaynab offered him to enter the house, but he refused to enter and went away returning, speaking words of which she understood nothing except: Glory be to Allah the Mighty, glory be to the Turner of hearts. Then Zayd came and she informed him of what had happened, so he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said to him: It reached me, O Messenger of Allah, that you came to my home; why did you not enter, O Messenger of Allah? Perhaps Zaynab pleased you, so I will part from her. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: ﴿Keep your wife to yourself and fear Allah﴾. So Zayd was not able to reach her afterward, and he separated from her."

In the tafsir of ʿAli ibn Ibrahim: "He (ﷺ) came to Zayd's house and saw Zaynab sitting in the middle of her room grinding perfume with her pestle. When he looked at her he said: Glory be to the Creator of light; blessed is Allah, the best of creators. Then he returned. Zayd came and she informed him of the news. He said to her: Perhaps you have fallen into the heart of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Would you like me to divorce you so that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) marries you? She said: I fear that you will divorce me and he will not marry me. So he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said to him: I want to divorce Zaynab. He answered him with what Allah, exalted is He, related." Besides that, there are many other reports which are not hidden from the one who investigates.

In Sharh al-Mawaqif it is said: "This story is among those things that must be kept far from the Prophet (ﷺ). If it is authentic, the inclination of the heart is not within one's capacity, together with what it involves of trial for both of them. The apparent meaning is that when Allah, exalted is He, wished to abrogate (naskh) the prohibition of the wife of an adopted son, He revealed to him (peace be upon him) that he should marry Zaynab once Zayd divorced her. He did not hasten to do so out of fear of the enemies' criticism, so he was reproached for it." This is a sound explanation stated by al-Khafaji, may Allah have mercy on him. Then he said: "The story resembles the story of Dawud (peace be upon him), especially since giving up a wife had been practiced among them at the beginning of the Hijrah without any blame attached to it." End of quote.

Some have gone too far, claiming that ﴿And you concealed﴾ and what follows is an address like its predecessor, from Allah, mighty and majestic, or from the Prophet (ﷺ) to Zayd, because he concealed his inclination toward her and showed his aversion from her when it entered his heart that the Prophet (ﷺ) wished she would be among his wives. Furthermore, in His saying: ﴿Keep your wife to yourself﴾ there is the joining of the verb that raises the attached pronoun to a pronoun in the genitive, while both refer to one person. It is like His saying: "Make it easy for yourself and leave off from yourself, a plunder shouted over in his chambers." They mention in such a construction that ʿalā and ʿan are nouns, and that they cannot be particles, because of the impossibility of "he was thought about in you" and "he was helped by you." Rather, this is among the constructions in which the self (nafs) is meant, i.e., "he was thought about in yourself" and "he was helped by yourself." My view is that this construction is permissible with ʿalā and ʿan being particles.

﴿So when Zayd had no longer any need of her﴾: that is, he divorced her, as was narrated from Qatadah, and it is a metaphor for that, like "I have no need of you." The meaning of waṭar is need. Al-Raghib restricted it to an important need. Abu ʿUbayda said: it is like adab (a strong need), and he recited for al-Rabiʿ ibn Dabʿ:

"He bade us farewell before we bade him farewell, when he had fulfilled from our youth its waṭar."

Adab is explained as a strong need that requires devising means to fend it off, and it is used sometimes for a single need and sometimes for a devised means even if it is not a need. Al-Mubarrad said: it is desire and love; one says: "I did not fulfill from your meeting a waṭar," meaning I did not enjoy you until my soul was satisfied. He recited:

"How could I stay in Medina after Jamil ibn Maʿmar had fulfilled from it a waṭar?"

From Ibn ʿAbbas, the interpretation of waṭar here is intercourse, and the meaning is that he no longer had need of her for intercourse, and he divorced her. In al-Bahr, quoting some scholars, it is said that he (may Allah be pleased with him) was not able to enjoy her. Abu ʿIsmat Nuh ibn Abi Maryam narrated with a chain that he traced to her that she said: "I was not refusing him, except that Allah, mighty and majestic, prevented me from him." It was also narrated that he would become swollen with that whenever he wanted to approach her, and he would refrain. It has been said: "It is not hidden that on this view it is very good to make the fulfilling of the waṭar a metaphor for divorce, so consider this."

[p. 25]

In the speech there is an omission, i.e., "So when Zayd had no longer any need of her, and her waiting period had ended." It has been said that fulfilling the waṭar implies the ending of the waiting period, because qaḍāʾ (fulfilling) means completion of a thing thoroughly. So it is as if it were said: "When Zayd fulfilled his need of marrying her, and divorced her, and her waiting period ended, and there remained in his heart no inclination to her and no dislike of her separation." ﴿We married her to you﴾: that is, We made her a wife for you without the mediation of a contract either by principal or by agent. It is authentically reported in the hadith of al-Bukhari and al-Tirmidhi that she, may Allah be pleased with her, used to boast over the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), saying: "Your families married you off, but Allah married me from above the seven heavens." Ibn Jarir transmitted from al-Shaʿbi, who said: she used to say to the Prophet (peace be upon him): "I take pride over you in three things, that none of your wives takes pride in them: my grandfather and your grandfather are one, I was given in marriage to you by Allah from the sky, and the envoy was Gabriel (peace be upon him)." Perhaps she meant his (peace be upon him) envoy between Allah, exalted is He, and His Messenger (ﷺ), otherwise the envoy between him (peace be upon him) and her was Zayd.

Ahmad, Muslim, al-Nasaʾi and others transmitted from Anas, who said: "When Zaynab's waiting period ended, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to Zayd: Go and mention her to me. So he went. He said: When I saw her, she became great in my chest. I said: O Zaynab, rejoice, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) has sent me to mention you. She said: I will do nothing until I consult my Lord. She stood up to her place of prayer, and the Qur'an was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came and entered upon her without permission."

From a hadith transmitted by al-Tabarani, al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan, and Ibn ʿAsakir through the route of Ibn Zayd al-Asadi, from Mudhakkir, the freedman of Zaynab: "She said: Zayd divorced me with a final divorce (battah). When my waiting period ended, I was not aware except that the Prophet (peace be upon him) had entered upon me while my hair was uncovered. I said: This is from heaven. You have entered, O Messenger of Allah, without a proposal or witnesses. He said: Allah, exalted is He, is the one who marries, and Gabriel is the witness." It is not hidden that this, in its apparent meaning, contradicts what preceded in the hadith, and the reliance is upon that. It has been said: the meaning of ﴿We married her﴾ is "We commanded you to marry her."

ʿAli and his two sons, the two fragrant herbs of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), al-Hasan and al-Husayn, and his son Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya, and Jaʿfar al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with them all, recited "zawwajtukahā" (I married her to you) with the tāʾ of the first person singular speaker alone.

﴿So that there will be no discomfort for the believers﴾: that is, no narrowness. It has also been said: sin. Some, such as al-Tabarsi, interpreted it with both meanings, based on the permissibility of using a homonym (mushtarak) in both of its meanings absolutely, as the Shafiʿis hold, or in negation, as the scholar Ibn al-Humam of the Hanafis holds. ﴿Concerning the wives of﴾: that is, concerning the marriage of the wives of ﴿their adopted sons﴾ whom they adopted ﴿when they have no longer any need of them﴾: that is, when the adopted sons have divorced them and their waiting periods have ended. For indeed, they have in the Messenger of Allah an excellent example. From this it has been deduced that the rulings established for him (ﷺ) are established for his community as well, except what is known to be among his special privileges (peace be upon him) by evidence. The full discussion of this question is recorded in the books of legal theory (uṣūl). The ruling here, as you heard at the beginning, means in general the marriage of the wives of adopted sons, and this, as has been said, is clear.

﴿And the command of Allah is ever executed﴾: that is, what He wills to bring into existence of affairs, or His commanded thing, which occurs by "Be" without fail. The clause is a concluding parenthetical statement that confirms what precedes it regarding the marriage of Zaynab, may Allah be pleased with her.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 38:**

﴿There is no restriction upon the Prophet in what Allah has ordained for him﴾. That is, it is not proper nor fitting in wisdom that there should be a restriction upon him ﴿in what Allah has ordained for him﴾, that is, what He has allotted and decreed for him (ﷺ). It derives from the saying, "He was assigned (faradha) such-and-such in the register (al-diwan)," and from it comes *furud al-asakir* (the allotments of the troops), meaning what the ruler grants them and records for them. Qatadah said: that is, in what He has made lawful for him. Al-Hasan said: in what He specifically granted him, namely the validity of marriage without a dowry (sadaq). Al-Dahhak said: from the increase beyond four (wives).

[p. 27]

﴿Sunnata Allah﴾ (the way of Allah): that is, Allah, exalted is He, has established that as a practice (sunnah). It is a verbal noun (masdar) in the accusative, governed by a verb implied from its own root, and the sentence serves to emphasize what precedes it, namely the negation of restriction. Al-Zamakhshari held that it is a noun placed in the position of the verbal noun, like their saying *turaban wa jandalan* (dust and gravel), meaning "may he be humbled, disgraced and disappointed." It seems that its status as a verbal noun was not established for him. It was also said that it is accusative by the implied verb "adhere to" (*ilzam*) or similar.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: it may be accusative by way of *al-ighra'* (urging/exhortation), as if it were said: "Upon him (is) the way of Allah." Abu Hayyan criticized this, saying it is not sound, because the governing element of a noun in *al-ighra'* may not be omitted; and also, the estimate "upon him, the way of Allah" with a third-person pronoun is impermissible, since an absent party is not urged. Their saying *'alayhi rajulan laysani* (upon him, a man, he is a rascal) is to be interpreted and is rare in any case. It was objected that his statement "the governing element of a noun in *al-ighra'* may not be omitted" is not accepted, and it contradicts what is understood from the books of grammar; and that what he mentioned regarding urging an absent person is granted, but it is possible to construe it here, as is not hidden. Then it was said: the apparent sense of Ibn 'Atiyyah's words implies that the accusative by the estimate "adhere to" is a division distinct from the accusative by urging, whereas in fact it is a subdivision of it. Consider this carefully.

﴿in the case of those who passed away﴾, that is, who went before, ﴿from before﴾, that is, from before you, among the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, in that He, exalted is His majesty, did not impose hardship upon them in proceeding with what He had made lawful for them, and He widened for them in the matter of marriage and other things. Indeed, they had concubines and many wives: David, peace be upon him, had a hundred wives and three hundred concubines, and Solomon, peace be upon him, had three hundred wives and seven hundred concubines.

Ibn Sa'd related from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that he, peace be upon him, had a thousand wives. The apparent meaning is that by "wife" he meant what is opposite to the concubine, but it is possible that he intended the more general sense, which would then agree with what came before.

It is related that the Jews, may Allah curse them, criticized him, and He is far above such blemish, ﴿ﷺ﴾, for his many marriages and multiplicity of wives. So Allah, exalted is He, answered them with His saying: ﴿the way of Allah﴾, and so on, the verse.

It was also said that by this, exalted is He and high is He, He pointed to what happened to David, peace be upon him, in his marriage to the wife of Uriah. Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Tabarani related this from Ibn Jurayj, and the name of that woman according to him is Alisiyah. This is not worth heeding, and the story, according to the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun), has no basis.

﴿And the command of Allah is a decree decreed﴾, that is, a determination (qadar) or possessing a determination. Describing it as "decreed" is like describing shade as "shady" (zalil) and night as "dark" (alyal), as in their saying *zill zalil* and *layl alyal*, for the purpose of emphasis. By "qadar", according to the commonly known meaning of *qada'* (decree), is intended the eternal will (al-irada al-azaliyyah) related to things as they are. It is also permissible that it means the commonly known sense of *qadar*, namely bringing things into existence in a particular measure and specific quantity, in accordance with aspects of benefit and other things. The first meaning is more apparent. Qada' and qadar are each used in the sense of the other. "Command" (amr) has been explained in a manner similar to what was said earlier. It is also permissible that it means the command which is one of the commands, without interpretation, and the meaning is that following the command of Allah, exalted is He, revealed to His prophets, peace be upon them, and acting upon its requirement, is necessary and decreed in itself, or it is as what is decreed in the necessity of following it. Its strain is not hidden. The apparent sense of the words of the Imam (al-Razi) is to choose that *amr* is one of the affairs (al-umur). He distinguished between qada' and qadar with something we have not found for anyone else; he said in summary: qada' is what is intended by Allah, exalted is He, in origin, and qadar is what is subsidiary; all good is by qada', and what harm exists in the world is by qadar, such as fornication and killing. Then he built upon this a subtle point: when He said, glorified is He, ﴿We gave her to you in marriage﴾, He followed it with (a command accomplished), because it is an original intended purpose and a decreed good. And when He, exalted is His majesty, said: ﴿the way of Allah in the case of those who passed away﴾, alluding to the story of David, peace be upon him, when he was tested by the wife of Uriah, He, glorified is He, said: ﴿a decree decreed﴾, because being tested is an evil not originally intended in the creation of the responsible person. There is much to discuss in this. The sentence is a parenthetical interjection (i'tiradh) between the two relative clauses, which function as one, for the sake of hastening to establish and confirm the negation of restriction.

[p. 28]

﴿Those who convey the messages of Allah﴾ is an attribute of "those who passed away," or it is in a place of nominative or accusative case by implicit supposition, or it is in the accusative as a term of praise. ʿAbdullah [ibn Masʿud] read *"balaghū"* (بَلَغُوا) as a past-tense verb. Ubayy [ibn Kaʿb] read *"risālata"* (رِسالَةَ) in the singular, treating the multiple messages as one because they agree in their foundations and because they all come from Allah, the Exalted, so they are like one thing, even though their rulings differ.

﴿And they fear Him﴾, that is, they fear Allah, the Exalted, in everything they do and leave undone, especially in the matter of conveying the message. ﴿And they fear none but Allah﴾. By restricting their fear to Allah, the Exalted, the verse contains an allusion to what proceeded from the Prophet (ﷺ) of avoiding the blame of people, since his fellow messengers did not have that conduct which should be followed. This is like an emphasis on what was stated explicitly earlier in His words: ﴿And you feared the people, while Allah has more right that you fear Him.﴾ Some have thought that the source of the allusion is the description of the prophets as conveying the messages, and they took the fear to be fear in the matter of conveying, because it occurs in its context. But there is in this what is not hidden.

﴿And sufficient is Allah as Reckoner﴾, that is, sufficient as a protector against what is feared, or as one who calls to account for the major and minor sins, whether of the heart or of the limbs. Therefore one should not fear anyone other than Him. The use of the explicit name in place of the pronoun has an effect that the pronoun does not have, due to the majesty of this name. The verse has been cited as evidence for the impermissibility of taqiyya (dissimulation, concealing one's faith under threat) for the prophets, peace be upon them, absolutely. Some Shiʿa restricted this to the conveying of the message, and they made what occurred from the Prophet (ﷺ) in this story, referred to by His words, ﴿And you feared the people, while Allah has more right that you fear Him,﴾ to be based on the fear in it meaning dread, not on the meaning that what is intended is shame before people's saying that he married the wife of his adopted son, as Ibn Furak said. They regard it as a permissible taqiyya, since it did not concern the conveying of the message. For them there is no distinction between fear of an ugly statement and bad suspicion, and fear of harms, in that each permits taqiyya in what does not concern conveying. They have a lengthy discussion on taqiyya, and it is, for their purposes, a dense shade. Whoever examines the books of the sects will know that excess and deficiency, correctness and confusion, have occurred in them, and that the People of the Sunna and the Community have taken the middle way in them, which is the safest path, whose traveler is secure from error and mistake. As for excess, it is attributed to the Shiʿa, since they permitted, and indeed made obligatory, as is reported from them, the outward display of disbelief for the slightest fear or greed. As for deficiency, it is attributed to the Khawarij and the Zaydiyya, since they do not permit, in exchange for religion, the preservation of honor, self, or property at all. The Khawarij have strange severities in this matter. They reviled and disparaged Buraydah al-Aslami, one of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), because he (may Allah be pleased with him) used to guard his horse during his prayer for fear that it would run away.

The doctrine of the People of the Sunna is that taqiyya, which is the preservation of the self, honor, or property from enemies by outwardly displaying a religiously forbidden matter, is legislated in general.

They divided the enemy into two categories:

The first: one whose enmity is based on difference of religion, such as the Muslim and the disbeliever. Attached to this is one whose enmity is due to difference of school of thought, a difference that leads to declaring the followers of one school to be disbelievers, such as the People of the Sunna and the Shiʿa.

The second: one whose enmity is based on worldly purposes, such as property and women. On this basis, taqiyya is also of two kinds.

As for the first: taqiyya from one whose enmity is based on difference of religion, whether in reality or in ruling. They have mentioned in this that whoever claims to be a believer, if he finds himself in a place where he cannot display his religion and what he holds because of the opposition of those who oppose him, it is obligatory for him to emigrate to a place where he can display it. It is not permissible for him to dwell there and conceal his religion under the excuse of weakness, for Allah's earth is wide. Yes, if he has another excuse, such as blindness, imprisonment, or intimidation by the opponent through killing him or killing his child, father, or mother, in any manner of killing, as intimidation that gives rise to the expectation that what he is threatened with will happen, then he is permitted to reside there and to comply to the extent of necessity, and it becomes obligatory for him to strive for a means of leaving. If the intimidation is not of that kind, such as intimidation by loss of benefit or by hardship that he is able to bear, such as imprisonment with food and light beating that does not destroy, then compliance is not permitted for him, and if death results from that he is a martyr.

As for the second: taqiyya from one whose enmity is based on worldly purposes. The scholars have differed on whether emigration is obligatory in this case or not. Some of them said: emigration is obligatory, for the preservation of property and honor is obligatory. A group said: it is not obligatory, since leaving that place is a worldly benefit among worldly benefits, and its abandonment does not bring any deficiency to religion, since the believing enemy, whatever he is, does not attack his weak believing opponent with evil merely because he is a believer. Some eminent scholars, by way of deliberation, said: the truth is that emigration here may also be obligatory, in the case where one fears the destruction of himself or of his relatives, or excessive violation of his sanctity. He said: even though it is obligatory, it is not an act of worship, for the truth is that not every obligation is an act of worship for which one is rewarded. Eating at the height of severe hunger, guarding against known or presumed harms in illness, avoiding poisons in health, and similar matters are obligatory acts, yet the one who performs them is not rewarded for them. End of quotation. In this there is a point for discussion.

The complete discussion on this matter is to be sought in the books of the eminent scholars. Perhaps we will return, if Allah, the Exalted, wills, to mention some of that. And Allah, the Exalted, is the guide to following the most upright paths.

There remains for us, regarding the verse, something: it is said that He, glorified is He, described the messengers, peace be upon them, who passed away, as not fearing anyone but Allah. He, the Mighty and Majestic, has informed us that Musa, peace be upon him, said: ﴿Indeed, we fear that he will hasten against us﴾ [Ta-Ha: 45]. Is the fear of that anything other than fear of someone other than Allah, the Exalted? So what is the way to reconcile them? I say: It has been answered that fear (khashya) is more specific than fear (khawf). Al-Raghib said: khashya is a fear mixed with veneration, and it is mostly from knowledge of what is feared. He cited several verses on this, among them this verse. The negation of the specific does not entail the negation of the general, for it may coexist with its affirmation. This is better than what has been said in answer, that khashya is more specific than khawf because it is intense fear, and what is negated in the verse here is that, not fear in general, which is affirmed in what is reported of Musa, peace be upon him. Another answered that what is meant by the negated khashya is the fear that arises after thought and reflection, and is not among the natural human accidents, while the affirmed fear is the fear that arises according to human nature at first impression. Many a time the like of it has come upon Musa, peace be upon him, and upon others of his brethren, and it is something in which there is no deficiency, as will not be hidden from the perfect. This is a good answer. It was also said: Musa, peace be upon him, feared only that Pharaoh would hasten against him with something that would prevent him from completing the call and displaying the miracle, so that the purpose of the mission would not be achieved. Thus it is fear of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. What is negated of the messengers is fear of other than Him, glorified is He, in the sense that one fears someone else, may He be exalted, so that he neglects His obedience or commits His disobedience. And where is this from that? So reflect. May Allah, the Exalted, take charge of your guidance.

[Page 29]

[p. 30]

*"Muhammad is not the father of any man among your men"* is a rejection of the cause of his ﷺ fear of people, for which he was rebuked, in the words of Allah the Exalted: *"And you feared the people, while Allah has more right that you fear Him."* This refers to their saying that Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, married the wife of his son Zayd, by denying that Zayd was his son, whose wife is forbidden to him ﷺ, in the most emphatic manner, as you will soon know, God willing.

The word *rijal* is the plural of *rajul*, with a *damma* on the *jim* as is well known, and also with a *sukun*. According to the *Qamus*, it means a male who has reached puberty, or a male from the moment of his birth. Some apparent meanings of the verses and reports support the second sense, such as the words of Allah the Exalted: *"For men there is a share of what the parents and close relatives leave"* [an-Nisa': 7], and His words: *"And if a man is inherited from in kalala (a person who leaves neither ascendants nor descendants)"* [an-Nisa': 12], and his ﷺ words, peace and blessings be upon him: *"Then to the nearest male man."*

The argument that some of the eminent later scholars made concerning the examples mentioned does not negate that the apparent meaning of them is this, to the impartial person. It may be cited in support of the first sense the words of Allah the Exalted: *"And of the oppressed men, women and children"* [an-Nisa': 98], for *rijal* there refers to those who have reached maturity, though this is open to discussion. Yes, the apparent meaning of the words of az-Zamakhshari, who is an imam with firm standing in the language and other Arabic sciences, indicates that *rajul* is the adult male. Whatever the case, the attribution of *rijal* to the pronoun of those addressed is in terms of begetting. If by *rijal* is meant the adult males, the meaning is: *"Muhammad is not the father of any of your sons, O people, the adult males whom you begot."* If by them is meant males in general, the meaning is: *"Muhammad is not the father of any of your sons whom you begot, in general, whether they were grown or young."*

*Ab* (father) is a literal meaning for the parent, as is understood from the words of many linguists. The fatherhood negated here is the true legal fatherhood, which entails the rulings of literal true fatherhood, such as inheritance, the obligation of maintenance, and the prohibition of marriage by affinity, whether it is by birth, by nursing, or by adoption (*tabanni*) of one who would be born like him to one like him, while he is of unknown lineage. So when it is negated that he ﷺ, may Allah the Exalted bless him and grant him peace, is the father of any man among their men, by whatever means fatherhood might be, and it is known that Zayd is one of their men, the negation of his ﷺ being his father in every sense is established. As for his ﷺ not being the father of Zayd by birth, this is not disputed, and no one imagined otherwise. Likewise, he ﷺ is not his father by nursing. As for his ﷺ not being the father of Zayd by adoption, though his adoption of him is established, this is because the fatherhood by adoption that is negated is only the true legal fatherhood, and what took place of adoption does not entail it, since it depends in law on conditions, among them that the adopter be of unknown lineage. That does not apply to Zayd, for he was of known lineage among them. It has already been explained to you that he was the son of Harithah. The generalization of the negation of his ﷺ fatherhood to any of their men, such that it includes the negation of fatherhood by birth, fatherhood by nursing, and fatherhood by adoption, is because there is no dispute about the negation of the first two. The dispute is only about the negation of the last, for it is the one that the one who says "Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, married his son's wife" claims, to exaggerate the negation of fatherhood by adoption, which they claimed entails the rulings of true fatherhood, by arranging what is hidden within a thread of what is not hidden at all.

Perhaps this is the secret in His words, the Exalted: *"Muhammad is not the father of any of your men,"* rather than "Muhammad is not the father of any of the men" or "Muhammad is not the father of any of you." Perhaps for this reason too he stated the negation of his ﷺ fatherhood to any of their men, so that it might be known from it that none of their men is his son, peace and blessings be upon him. He did not reverse the case by stating the negation of the sonship of any of their men to him, peace and blessings be upon him, so that the negation of his ﷺ fatherhood to any of their men might be known. What follows is brought in a manner that is coherent with what precedes it. By taking the negated fatherhood to mean true legal fatherhood, a difficulty in the verse is resolved, namely that its context is the negation of his, peace and blessings be upon him, fatherhood of Zayd, in order to refute by it those who object to the Prophet ﷺ for marrying his divorced wife. If by fatherhood is meant true literal fatherhood, which is by birth, it does not suit the context, and the stated refutation is not achieved by it, although it is the intended purpose, since no one claimed or imagined that he ﷺ was the father of Zayd by birth. If by it is meant metaphorical fatherhood, which is established by adoption and the like, then its negation is not correct, because he, peace and blessings be upon him, was the father of Zayd metaphorically, due to his adoption of him, and Zayd continued to be called "son of Muhammad" ﷺ until the words of Allah the Exalted were revealed: *"Call them by [the names of] their fathers"* [al-Ahzab: 5]. Then they called him "son of Harithah." The way this difficulty is resolved, by what we have mentioned, namely that the intended fatherhood is true legal fatherhood, is that this fatherhood occurs by birth, by nursing, and by adoption under its condition, and in all its types it is not realized in Zayd. As for it not being realized by the first two types, this is evident. As for it not being realized by the last type, this is because adoption, although it took place, lacks its condition, by which it entails true legal fatherhood, as you have learned. By making the attribution of *rijal* to the pronoun of those addressed in terms of birth, the objection to the stated negation is dispelled, namely that he, peace and blessings be upon him, had several sons born to him, so how is the negation valid? This is because whoever was born to him, peace and blessings be upon him, is not attributed to those addressed in terms of birth, but is attributed to him ﷺ in terms of that.

Whoever restricts *rijal* to adults says: the generality is not broken by this, because all who were born to him, peace and blessings be upon him, died young and did not reach the status of men. It is also said: there is no difficulty in this, because he, peace and blessings be upon him, had no son on the day the verse was revealed. The sura is Medinan, and it was revealed, as is reported from Ibn al-Athir in *Tarikh al-Kamil*, in the fifth year after the Hijra. In it the Messenger of Allah ﷺ married Zaynab. Those of his sons, other than Ibrahim, who were born to him ﷺ, were born in Mecca before the Hijra and died there. As for Ibrahim, although he was born in Medina, he was born in the eighth year after the Hijra. So he was not born on the day of revelation but after it. And this, as you see, is weak.

Just as the negation was objected to on the basis of what has been mentioned, it was also objected to on the basis of al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them both, for the Prophet ﷺ was their father in true legal sense. Some did not accept here the answer that they are excluded by the attribution, because they have a relation to those addressed in terms of birth, since Ali, may Allah honour his face, is included among them and they are his sons. Another accepted it on the basis that the attribution is for specificity in terms of birth, and there is no specificity of al-Hasan and al-Husayn to Ali, may Allah be pleased with them, in terms of birth, since they are also sons of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but through an intermediary. If this is accepted, then well and good; otherwise, the answer is as follows. As for what is said, that the intended men are the adults, and that they were not, may Allah be pleased with them both, adults on the day of revelation, this is not so. Al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him, was born in the third year after the Hijra, and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with him, was born in the fourth year after it, on the fifth night of Sha'ban, and his mother had conceived him fifty nights or less after the birth of his brother. The revelation was after their births, as you have heard just now. As for what is said, that the intended father in the verse is the biological father, and it is known that he ﷺ was not their biological father, then reflect.

It is also said: the meaning of the verse is nothing but the negation of his ﷺ fatherhood of any man by adoption, so that his, peace and blessings be upon him, fatherhood of Zayd, which the objector claims, is negated, as the context of the noble verse indicates. It is as if it were said: "Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, as you claimed, since you said he is the father of Zayd by his adoption of him," and it is silent about the negation of his ﷺ fatherhood of anyone by birth or by nursing, and about affirming it. So there is no question about those males born to him ﷺ, nor about al-Hasan and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them, and no answer is needed. The words of Abu Hayyan incline toward choosing this. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Some Shafi'is have used this verse as evidence that it is not permissible to call the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, "father of the believers." This is related by the author of *al-Rawda*, who then said: al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, explicitly stated that it is permissible to call him ﷺ "father of the believers," that is, in terms of the prohibition of marriage and the like. Ar-Raghib, after saying "the *ab* is the parent," said the following: "Every one who was a cause in bringing something into existence, or in its improvement, or in its appearance, is called a father. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ was called father of the believers. Allah the Exalted said: *'The Prophet is closer to the believers than themselves, and his wives are their mothers'* [al-Ahzab: 6]. In some readings: *'and he is a father to them.'*" It is also narrated that he ﷺ said to Ali, may Allah honour his face: "I and you are the two fathers of this community." To this he ﷺ alluded with his words: *"Every cause and every lineage will be cut off on the Day of Resurrection except my cause and my lineage."* End of quotation. So do not be heedless.

[Page 32 continues]

Those who permitted the unrestricted usage said: the words of God Most High, ﴿but the Messenger of God﴾, are a corrective transition (*istidrak*, a "but" that qualifies a preceding negation) from the negation of his being the father of any of their men, in the sense that would entail the prohibition of affinity by marriage (*musaharah*) and similar rulings, to the affirmation that he (ﷺ) is a father to every member of the Ummah in what pertains to the obligation of reverence and veneration toward him (ﷺ), and the obligation on him (ﷺ) to show compassion and sincere counsel to them. For every prophet is a father to his community in that regard. The sum of this is that it is a corrective transition from the negation of true legal fatherhood, upon which the prohibition of affinity by marriage and similar rulings are based, to the affirmation of metaphorical, linguistic fatherhood, which belongs to the station of the Messenger (ﷺ) and which entails reverence on their part and compassion on his part (ﷺ).

It has also been said, regarding the direction of the corrective transition, that when his (ﷺ) fatherhood to any of their men was negated, while it was well known that every prophet is a father to his community, and for this reason it has been said that Lot (peace be upon him), in his words ﴿These are my daughters; they are purer for you﴾ [Hud 11:78], meant by them the believing women of his community, there arose the supposition that the negation of his (ﷺ) prophethood follows from the assumed necessary connection between fatherhood and prophethood. So it was corrected by affirming the prophethood, as an alert that the negated fatherhood is one thing and the fatherhood affirmed for the Messenger is another.

As for His words, glorified is He, ﴿and the Seal of the Prophets﴾, it has been said that it was brought in to indicate the perfection of his (ﷺ) counsel and compassion. Thus it conveys that his (ﷺ) fatherhood toward the community referred to by God Most High's words ﴿but the Messenger of God﴾ is a perfect fatherhood, surpassing the fatherhood of all other messengers (peace be upon them) toward their communities. This is because a messenger who is followed by another messenger may not reach the utmost limit of compassion and the utmost limit of counsel, relying on the one who will come after him, as a true parent does when he knows that his child will have someone after him to take his place.

It has also been said that it was brought in to point to the extension of that fatherhood referred to earlier until the Day of Resurrection. It is as if it were said: ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any of your men﴾ in the sense that a relation of affinity by marriage is established between him and them; ﴿but he is the father of each one of you, and the father of your sons and the sons of your sons, and so on until the Day of Resurrection﴾, such that reverence and honoring of him is obligatory upon you and upon whoever descends from you, and compassion and complete counsel are obligatory upon him toward you and toward whoever descends from you.

It has also been said that it was brought in to repel what might be supposed from God Most High's words ﴿of your men﴾: that he (ﷺ) might be the father of one of the men who were born from him (peace be upon him), by a son being born to him who lives until he reaches manhood. This is because his (ﷺ) being the Seal of the Prophets indicates that no male child of his will live to reach maturity, for if he did reach it, his rank would be to be a prophet, and then he (ﷺ) would not be the Seal of the Prophets. By "father" here is meant the biological father, so that the objection of al-Hasanayn (may God be pleased with them both) is avoided.

The evidence for the conditional statement is what Ibrahim al-Suddi related from Anas, who said: Ibrahim, the son of the Prophet (ﷺ), had already filled the cradle, and had he remained alive he would have been a prophet, but he did not remain, because your Prophet is the last of the prophets (peace be upon them). Similar reports came in other narrations.

Al-Bukhari related through the route of Muhammad ibn Bishr, from Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid, who said: I said to Abdullah ibn Abi Awfa: Did you see Ibrahim, the son of the Prophet (ﷺ)? He said: He died as a young child. Had a prophet come after Muhammad (ﷺ), his son Ibrahim would have lived; but there is no prophet after him.

Ahmad related from Waki', from Isma'il, who said: I heard Ibn Abi Awfa say: Had there been a prophet after the Prophet (ﷺ), his son would not have died.

Ibn Majah and others related, from the hadith of Ibn Abbas: "When Ibrahim, the son of the Prophet (ﷺ), died, he said: 'Indeed he has a wet-nurse in Paradise. Had he lived, he would have been a truthful one (*siddiq*) and a prophet. Had he lived, his maternal uncles would have been freed from the Copts, and no Copt would have been enslaved.'"

In its chain is Abu Shaybah Ibrahim ibn Uthman al-Wasiti, who, according to al-Qastallani, is weak. Ibn Mandah related it by way of him in *al-Ma'rifah*, and said: it is gharib (a single-route report). It seems that al-Nawawi did not come upon this raised report or something similar to it, or he came upon it but did not find it authentic. So in *Tahdhib al-Asma' wa'l-Lughat* he said: As for what has been related from some of the earlier scholars, "Had Ibrahim lived, he would have been a prophet," it is false, a presumptuous speech about the unseen, a reckless gamble, and an assault upon a great matter. Ibn Abd al-Barr is similar; he said in *al-Tamhid*: I do not know what this is. Noah (peace be upon him) fathered sons who were not prophets, and if a prophet fathered only prophets, then everyone would be a prophet, since they all descend from Noah (peace be upon him). I say: it cannot be supposed of a Companion that he would presumptuously report on such a matter by conjecture. Therefore the apparent meaning is that he reported only on the basis of a stipulation from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). And if the raised hadith of Ibn Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) is authentic, the dispute is ended. However, the apparent meaning is that this ruling was specific to Ibrahim alone, namely that it had already been decided in the knowledge of God Most High that, had he lived, He would have made him a prophet, not because he was the son of the Prophet (ﷺ), but for a reason known only to Him, may His majesty be exalted: ﴿God knows best where to place His message﴾ [al-An'am 6:124]. In that case, the conditional premise stated earlier is refuted, namely his words "for, if he had reached maturity, his rank would have been to be a prophet": this is a plain prohibition (*man'*). The evidence presented earlier does not establish it, because its apparent sense is particularity, so it is possible that a male child of his (ﷺ), other than Ibrahim, might reach maturity without being a prophet, because he was not fit for prophethood in the knowledge of God Most High had he lived.

As for the statement of some eminent scholars: the basis of that conditional is not rational necessity or logical syllogism, but the requirement of divine wisdom, namely that God, glorified is He, honored some of the messengers (peace be upon them) by making their sons prophets, as with the Friend (*Khalil*, Abraham) (peace be upon him); and our Prophet (ﷺ) is the most honored by Him and the most excellent in His sight; so had his sons lived, God Most High's honoring of him and his excellence in His sight would have required that. This is nothing, because we say: honoring some of His messengers (peace be upon them) by making their sons prophets, and our Prophet (ﷺ) being more honored and more excellent than them, does not imply that his sons, had they lived and reached maturity, would necessarily be prophets, from the requirement of honor and excellence. For it might be said that the wisdom behind his (ﷺ) being the Seal of the Prophets, since it is greater and more magnificent, prevented them from living to be made prophets. Do you not see that God Most High honored some messengers by making some of their relatives, during their lifetimes and after their deaths, prophets to assist them and to support their law, without contradicting it in principle or in detail, as with Moses (peace be upon him)? Our Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) is more honored and more excellent than them, yet this was not granted to him.

If it is said: he (ﷺ) was compensated for this by God making for him, from among his relatives and the People of his House, eminent scholars like the prophets of the Children of Israel, such as Ali, may God ennoble his face, as is indicated by his (ﷺ) saying to him (may God be pleased with him): "You stand to me as Aaron stood to Moses, except that there is no prophet after me."

We say: then why could God, glorified is He, not allow for him (ﷺ) male children who reach maturity, and compensate him for their prophethood, which the wisdom of the Sealing prevented, in the same way that He compensated him for the prophethood of some of his relatives, which that wisdom prevented? That is closer to what honor requires, as is not hidden.

It has also been said: the implication (*mulazamah*) is derived from the verse, because if it were not so, the corrective transition would have no meaning. For "but" (*lakin*) comes between two opposites, so there must be an incompatibility between their being sons of his (ﷺ) and his being the Seal of the Prophets; and this incompatibility arises only if the sonship of such men entails their prophethood. The words of God Most High ﴿the Messenger of God﴾ do not undermine this, as might be supposed, because even if we grant that they were messengers, their messengership would be either in his time (ﷺ), in which case it would contradict his messengership, or after him, in which case it would contradict his being the Seal (end of quote).

It is to be said in reply: the implication in the words "and if that were not so, the corrective transition would have no meaning" is not established. The evidence cited does not establish it, since the meaning of the corrective transition may be what we mentioned at first. Moreover, what he said afterward contains what is not hidden. It has also been said regarding the direction of the corrective transition: since the absence of male offspring implies that his (ﷺ) rulings will not remain and his remembrance will not endure, it was corrected by what was mentioned. And this, as you see, is weak.

Some later scholars said: it is possible that the corrective transition is not from the particle "but" (*lakin*) with its usual sense, but here it has the sense of removing a supposition that arises from the beginning of the speech, as in your saying: "Zayd is not generous but brave," and it may carry the sense that a ruling opposed to what precedes it is established for what follows it, as in: "This is not still but moving," and "This is not white but black." Such usage has come in some verses of the Noble Book, as in His words: ﴿O my people, there is no foolishness in me, but I am a messenger from the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-A'raf 7:67]. For the negation of foolishness does not imply the negation of messengership, nor the negation of what follows from it of guidance and piety, so as to make it a corrective transition in the first sense. (End of quote.) So let it be considered.

Among the strange things is that Ibn Hajar al-Haytami said in his *al-Fatawa al-Hadithiyyah*: there is no remoteness in affirming prophethood for Ibrahim, the son of the Prophet (ﷺ), in his infancy, since it has been established in infancy for Jesus and John (peace be upon them both). Then he quoted from al-Subki a statement concerning the hadith: "I was a prophet while Adam was between the spirit and the body," the sum of which is that his (ﷺ) reality may have existed before Adam, and God Most High gave him prophethood by creating it prepared for it and bestowing it upon it from that time, and so he became a prophet. Then he said: by this the verification of the prophethood of our master Ibrahim in his childhood becomes known (end of quote). In this there is room for discussion.

As for the report that "he (ﷺ) put his hand into his grave after burial and said: 'Indeed, by God, he is a prophet, the son of a prophet,'" its chain contains one who is not strong, so it is not to be relied upon, nor is there need to strain to interpret it.

The word *khatam* (seal) is the name of an instrument for what is sealed with it, like a stamp for what is stamped with it. So the meaning of "Seal of the Prophets" is that by which the prophets were sealed, and its outcome is "the last of the prophets." Al-Mubarrad said: "*khatam*" is a past-tense verb on the pattern *fa'al*, meaning "sealed the prophets," so "the prophets" is in the accusative as its object. But this is not right. The majority of readers recited *wa-khatima* with a kasra on the ta', as an active participle, meaning "the one who sealed the prophets," and what is meant by it is also "the last of them." In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "but a prophet who sealed the prophets." By "prophet" is meant something more general than messenger, so from his (ﷺ) being the Seal of the Prophets it follows that he is the Seal of the Messengers. And what is meant by his (ﷺ) being their Seal is the cessation of the occurrence of the attribute of prophethood in anyone of the two species (humans and jinn), after he (ﷺ) was adorned with it in this present world.

[Page 35 begins here.]

This does not conflict with what the community (ummah) has agreed upon and what the reports about it have made widely known. Indeed, these reports may have reached the level of *tawatur ma'nawi* (mass transmission in meaning), and the scholars have spoken of it with one voice. Belief in it is obligatory, and whoever denies it is judged a disbeliever, like the philosophers, concerning the descent of Jesus, peace be upon him, at the end of time. This is because he was a prophet before our Prophet (ﷺ) was adorned with prophethood in this worldly life. The same applies to the continued life of al-Khidr, peace be upon him, according to the view that he is a prophet and that he still lives.

Then, when he, peace be upon him, descends, he remains upon his earlier prophethood and is not removed from it. [The scholar] said: "However, he will not be worshipped through it (i.e., he will not act on it as a binding law), because it has been abrogated (*naskh*) for him and for others, and he is obligated to the rulings of this Sharia, both fundamental and derivative. Therefore, no revelation (*wahy*) will come to him, peace be upon him, nor will he establish rulings. Rather, he will be a caliph (*khalifah*) of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and a ruler among the rulers of his religion (*millah*) over his community, judging by what he was taught in heaven before his descent of his law, peace be upon him, as in some reports. Or he will consult the Book and the Sunnah."

He, peace be upon him, does not fall short of the rank of *ijtihad* (independent legal reasoning) that leads to deriving what he needs during his days on earth of rulings, such as breaking the cross, killing the swine, imposing the jizyah (poll tax), and not accepting it, from what is known from our Sharia to be correct, in his saying (ﷺ):

[Page 36 begins here.]

"Indeed, Jesus will descend as a just judge. He will break the cross, kill the swine, and impose the jizyah."

So his descent, peace be upon him, is the end point for the disbelievers' acknowledgment of paying the jizyah under those conditions, and then he will accept only Islam. It does not abrogate it. This was stated by Shaykh al-Islam Ibrahim al-Laqani in (*Hidayat al-Murid li-Jawharat al-Tawhid*).

His statement, "He, peace be upon him, when he descends, remains upon his earlier prophethood and is not removed from it, but he will not be worshipped through it," etc., is better than the statement of al-Khafaji: "It appears that what is meant by his being upon the religion of our Prophet (ﷺ) is that he will be stripped of the description of prophethood and messengerhood, in that he will not convey what he conveys from revelation. Rather, he will judge by what he receives from our Prophet, peace be upon him. For this reason, he did not lead the prayer with al-Mahdi. I do not think he meant by being stripped of the description of prophethood and messengerhood that he would be removed from it, such that it would not be valid to call him Messenger and Prophet, peace be upon him. Allah forbid that a messenger or prophet be removed from messengerhood or prophethood! Indeed, I can hardly conceive of that. Perhaps he meant that the description of conveying rulings from revelation will not remain for him as it did before being raised up. Thus, he, peace be upon him, is a prophet and messenger before being raised, in heaven, after descending, and also after death. The continuation of prophethood and messengerhood after death, for him and for other prophets and messengers, peace be upon them, is real, as many have held. The one who is described by them, and likewise by faith, is the spirit, and it remains and is not changed by the death of the body."

"Yes, al-Ash'ari, as al-Nasafi said, held that these two (prophethood and messengerhood) remain after death in a legal sense." What al-Laqani's statement conveys, that he, peace be upon him, will judge by what was taught to him in heaven of the Sharia before his descent, was conveyed by al-Safarini in (*al-Buhur al-Zakhirah*), and this is what I incline toward. As for his performing ijtihad, considering the Book and the Sunnah, this is far-fetched, although he, peace be upon him, has been given much more than what was given to the mujtahids of the nations, of what ijtihad depends on. This is because most of the scholars hold that when he descends he will pray behind al-Mahdi, may Allah be pleased with him, the dawn prayer. That time is too short for deriving what that prayer contains of statements and actions from the Book and the Sunnah in the known manner.

Yes, it is not far-fetched that he, peace be upon him, has been taught some things in heaven and entrusted with ijtihad and taking from the Book and the Sunnah for other things. It was also said that he, peace be upon him, will take the rulings from our Prophet (ﷺ) directly (*shafahan*) after his descent, while he is in the noble grave, peace be upon him. This is supported by the hadith of Abu Ya'la: "By Him in whose hand my soul is, Jesus son of Mary will surely descend. Then, if he stands at my grave and says, 'O Muhammad,' I will surely answer him."

It is also allowed that this takes place through meeting with him, peace be upon him, in a spiritual manner (*ruhaniyyah*). There is no oddity in this, for the vision of him (ﷺ) after his death has occurred for many of the perfected ones of this community, and taking from him while awake (*yaqazah*) [is also reported]. Shaykh Siraj al-Din ibn al-Mulaqqin said in (*Tabaqat al-Awliya'*): Shaykh Abd al-Qadir al-Kaylani, may Allah sanctify his secret, said: "I saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) before noon, and he said to me: 'O my son, why do you not speak?' I said: 'O my father, I am a non-Arab man. How can I speak to the eloquent people of Baghdad?' He said: 'Open your mouth.' I opened it, and he spat into it seven times and said: 'Speak to the people and call to the path of your Lord with wisdom and good instruction' (﴿ادْعُ إلى سَبِيلِ رَبِّكَ بِالحِكْمَةِ والمَوْعِظَةِ الحَسَنَةِ﴾). So I prayed noon, sat down, and a great crowd gathered. I was tongue-tied, and then I saw Ali, may Allah honor his face, standing beside me in the assembly. He said to me: 'O my son, why do you not speak?' I said: 'O my father, I have become tongue-tied.' He said: 'Open your mouth,' and I opened it, and he spat into it six times. I said: 'Why do you not complete it to seven?' He said: 'Out of courtesy to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).' Then he disappeared from me."
