I said: "The seeker of thoughts dives into the sea of the heart for pearls of knowledge, extracts them to the shore of the chest, and the broker of the tongue's interpreter calls over them, and they are bought for precious prices, the goodness of obedience, in houses that Allah has permitted to be raised" (﴿فِي بُيُوتٍ أذِنَ اللَّهُ أنْ تُرْفَعَ﴾).

[Page 37 begins here.]

He also said, in the biography of Shaykh Khalifah ibn Musa (in *al-Nahr Milki*): "He often saw the Messenger of Allah, peace be upon him, while awake and in sleep. It was said that most of his actions were received from him (ﷺ), whether awake or asleep. He saw him in one night seventeen times. In one of those times he said to him: 'O Khalifah, do not be bored with me, for many of the saints died from the grief of not seeing me.'"

Shaykh Taj al-Din ibn Ata' Allah said in (*Lata'if al-Minan*): A man said to Shaykh Abu al-Abbas al-Mursi: "O my master, shake my hand with this hand of yours, for you have met men and lands." He said: "By Allah, I have not shaken hands with this hand of mine except with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." He said: The Shaykh also said: "If the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were hidden from me for the blink of an eye, I would not count myself among the Muslims."

Similar reports are very numerous in the books of this group.

In (*Tanwir al-Halak*) by Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti, which he wrote to refute those who deny seeing the Prophet (ﷺ) after his death while awake, there is a considerable amount of such material. He began the argument for this with what al-Bukhari, Muslim, and Abu Dawud reported from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever sees me in a dream will surely see me while awake, and Satan cannot take my form.'" al-Tabarani reported something similar from the hadith of Malik ibn Abd Allah al-Khath'ami and from the hadith of Abu Bakrah, and al-Darimi reported something similar from the hadith of Abu Qatadah.

The deniers have differed in interpreting it. It was said: the intended meaning is "he will see me on the Day of Resurrection," for there is the complete wakefulness, as people are asleep and when they die they awaken. This was challenged on the grounds that there is no benefit in this specification, since all of his community will see him on the Day of Resurrection, whether or not they saw him in a dream. It was also said: the intended meaning is seeing him in a special way of nearness and favor from him (ﷺ) on the Day of Resurrection, or obtaining intercession for him, or something similar; the above objection does not apply to this. It was also said: the intended meaning of "whoever" is one who believed in him during his lifetime without seeing him, because he was absent from him at that time. Then the report would be a good tiding to him that he will certainly see him while awake, meaning with the eyes of his head. It was also said: with the eye of the heart. Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi related both opinions.

Imam Abu Muhammad ibn Abi Jamrah said in his commentary on the hadiths he selected from Sahih al-Bukhari: "This hadith indicates that whoever sees him (ﷺ) in sleep will see him while awake. Does this apply generally, during his lifetime and after his death, or was it during his lifetime? And is this for everyone who saw him absolutely, or is it specific to those who have the qualification and follow his Sunnah (ﷺ)? The wording gives generality, and whoever claims specificity without a specifier from him (ﷺ) is being artificial." He spoke at length on this and then said: "It has been reported from the early and later generations, and so on, of those who saw him (ﷺ) in sleep and who believed in this hadith, that they then saw him while awake and asked him about things that troubled them, and he informed them of their relief and specified to them the ways by which relief would come, and the matter turned out just so, without addition or subtraction." End of what is intended from it.

Then, the vision of him (ﷺ) while awake, according to those who hold it, most often occurs with the heart, and then the state progresses until it is seen with the sight. They differed about the reality of what is seen. Some said: what is seen is the essence of the Chosen One (ﷺ) with his body and spirit. Most of the people of spiritual states hold that it is his likeness (*mithal*). Al-Ghazali explicitly stated this, saying: "It is not meant that one sees his body and frame. Rather, it is a likeness of him that becomes an instrument through which the meaning in his soul is conveyed. The instrument is sometimes real and sometimes imaginary, and the soul is other than the imagined likeness. So what one sees of the form is not the spirit of the Chosen One (ﷺ) nor his person, but rather a likeness of him in reality."

Qadi Abu Bakr ibn al-Arabi made a distinction, saying: "Seeing the Prophet (ﷺ) in his known description is perception in reality, and seeing him in other than his description is perception of a likeness." Jalal al-Din al-Suyuti approved of this, and after citing hadiths and reports he said the following: "From the totality of this discussion, the reports, and the hadiths, it is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) is alive with his body and spirit, that he moves and travels wherever he wills across the regions of the earth and in the kingdom (*malakut*), in the same form he had before his death, with nothing changed in him, and that he is hidden from sight just as the angels are hidden though they are living in their bodies. So when Allah the Exalted wills to lift the veil for whomever He wishes to honor with seeing him, he sees him in the form in which he (ﷺ) is. There is no obstacle to this, and no reason to restrict it to seeing a likeness." End of quote.

He, may Allah have mercy on him, went in a similar direction regarding all the prophets, peace be upon them. He said they are alive, their spirits having been returned to them after they had been taken, and they have been permitted to come out of their graves and to move in the upper and lower kingdoms. What he mentioned about coming out of the graves, he supported with many reports, including the following:

From these is what Ibn Hibban in his *Tarikh*, al-Tabarani in *al-Kabir*, and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* reported from Anas, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'No prophet dies and then remains in his grave except for forty mornings.'"

From these is what Abd al-Razzaq reported in his *Musannaf* from al-Thawri, from Abu al-Miqdam, from Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, who said: "No prophet stayed on earth more than forty days." Abu al-Miqdam is Thabit ibn Hurmuz, a trustworthy shaykh.

From these is what Imam al-Haramayn mentioned in *al-Nihayah*, and then al-Rafi'i in *al-Sharh*, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I am too honored in the sight of my Lord to leave me in my grave after three days." Imam al-Haramayn added: "It has been reported that it was more than two days."

The Prophet's appearance after his death to the eyes is, in my assessment most likely, not like the ordinary sight that people have of one another. It is a collective, transient state, a condition of the *barzakh* (the intermediate realm between death and resurrection), and a matter of direct experience, whose reality is known only to one who has undergone it. Because this vision closely resembles ordinary sight, the matter is confused for many of those who see him, so they think that they have seen him with their eyes in the ordinary way, when this is not so. It is sometimes said that it is a vision of the heart, and because of its intensity it resembles sight. What is seen is either his spirit (ﷺ), which is the most perfect of spirits in its detachment and holiness, having developed and appeared in a visible form in that vision, while its attachment to his noble body remains, alive in the exalted grave. This is in line with what some have said, that Gabriel, peace be upon him, although he appeared before the Prophet (ﷺ) in the form of Dihya al-Kalbi or another, did not leave the Lote Tree of the Utmost Boundary. Or what is seen is an imaginal body (*jasad mithali*) to which his pure, detached spirit (ﷺ) is attached, and there is no obstacle to the imaginal body multiplying into countless bodies, while his holy spirit remains attached to each of them, with a thousand thousand blessings and greetings from Allah, the Exalted, upon him through each of them. This attachment is of the kind of the one spirit's attachment to the parts of a single body, and in its perceptions and sensations in that attachment it does not need the instruments it needs in attaching to the body in the visible world. In light of what has been mentioned, the reasoning becomes clear behind what Shaykh Safi al-Din ibn Abi Mansur and Shaykh Abd al-Ghaffar transmitted from Shaykh Abu al-Abbas al-Tanji, that he saw the heaven, the earth, the Throne, and the Footstool filled with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Through this, the question of how many people can see him (ﷺ) at the same time in widely distant regions is resolved.

There is no need, with this, for what some have alluded to when asked about this, and who recited:

*Like the sun in the midst of the sky, whose light covers the lands, east and west.*

This vision generally occurs to the perfected people who have not fallen short of following the Sharia by the measure of a barley grain. Whenever the affinity between the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and a member of the community grows strong, the matter of seeing him (ﷺ) grows strong too. It may also occur to some of the righteous of this community at the time of death, due to the strength of collectedness at that moment. As for the vision that is wakeful for one who sees him (ﷺ) in a dream: if it is in this world, it is like the vision of some perfected people of him (ﷺ), and it is more perfect than a dream vision, although in both the one seen is the Messenger of Allah, upon him be blessings and peace. The last occasion for its realization is the time of death.

Perhaps the more common case for the general population is its realization in this way. If it is in the Hereafter, the matter is clear. I prefer the view that it occurs in the Hereafter in a special manner of nearness and favour and the like, because the good news in the report is more emphatic about this. Then the report

[p. 38]

mentioned earlier is recorded in Sahih Muslim with its chain going back to Abu Hurayrah, who said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'Whoever sees me in a dream will see me in wakefulness, or it is as if he saw me in wakefulness; Satan cannot take my form.'"

There is therefore no certainty in this narration that he (ﷺ) said "he will see me," so if the reality is that, the discussion of it is as you have heard. If the reality is "it is as if he saw me," then it is like his saying (ﷺ) in another report: "then he has seen me," and in yet another: "then he has seen the truth." The meaning is that his vision is true. As for what was previously mentioned, that the prophets, peace be upon them, come out of their graves, that is, with their bodies and spirits as is apparent, and that they dispose over the upper and lower realms of the dominion, this is something I do not affirm. The report previously cited, which Ibn Hibban, al-Tabarani and Abu Nu'aym narrated from Anas, namely his saying (ﷺ): "No prophet dies and then remains in his grave except for forty mornings," they transmitted via al-Hasan ibn Sufyan, from Hisham ibn Khalid al-Azraq, from al-Hasan ibn Yahya al-Khushani, from Sa'id ibn Abd al-Aziz, from Yazid ibn Abi Malik, from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him. Ibn Hibban said of it: "It is false, and al-Khushani is extremely unreliable in narration; he narrates from trustworthy transmitters what has no basis."

In al-Mizan, from al-Daraqutni: "al-Khushani is abandoned." For this reason Ibn al-Jawzi ruled the hadith fabricated, yet it is also part of a longer hadith. The complete hadith in al-Tabarani is: "No prophet dies and then remains in his grave except for forty mornings, until his spirit is returned to him. And on the night I was taken on the Night Journey I passed by Musa, and he was standing praying in his grave."

According to this, it does not indicate that after the forty days he does not remain in his grave, but rather that he goes out of it. It only indicates that he does not remain in the grave dead like all the other dead beyond forty mornings; rather his spirit is returned to him and he is alive. How far this is from the claim of coming out of the grave after forty days! Life in the grave does not entail coming out, and I affirm it for the prophets, peace be upon them. Al-Bayhaqi composed a treatise on their life in their graves and included in it a number of reports.

After it has become clear that the preceding hadith does not indicate coming out, the dispute about its description and its reaching the level of *hasan* (good) through its supporting evidence does not harm me. The reports mentioned afterwards, in what has preceded, all have as their meaning the affirmation of life in the grave through some kind of interpretation. The meaning of that life is a kind of life not comprehensible to us, and it is far above the life of the martyrs. The life of our Prophet (ﷺ) is more perfect and complete than the life of all of them, peace be upon them.

As for the report: "No Muslim greets me except that Allah returns my spirit to me until I return his greeting," it is to be understood as an affirmation of a special turning towards and spiritual attention, which arises from the noble prophetic presence towards the world and descends into the human realm, so that the return of the greeting takes place. There are other interpretations of it mentioned in their place. Then, although that life in the grave entails some of what life in the world known to us entails, such as prayer, the call to prayer, the iqamah, returning a greeting that is heard, and the like, it does not entail everything that could follow from that known life, and not everyone perceives or grasps it. So if the grave of one of the prophets, peace be upon them, were to be uncovered, people would not see the prophet in it except as they see all the other dead whose bodies the earth has not consumed. Perhaps Allah reveals to some of His servants and they see what people do not see. Were it not for this, the reports speaking of their life in their graves would conflict with the report of Abu Ya'la and others with a sound chain, as al-Haythami said, raised to the Prophet: that Musa moved Yusuf from his grave in Egypt.

Then I say after all this that what is attributed to some perfected people among the masters of spiritual states, of seeing the Prophet (ﷺ) after his death, asking him questions, and taking knowledge from him, we have not known of anything like it occurring in the earliest generation. Disagreement arose among the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, from the time he (ﷺ) died until whenever Allah wills, on religious matters and worldly affairs, and among them were Abu Bakr and Ali, may Allah be pleased with both of them.

[p. 39]

Most chains of the Sufis, to whom that vision is attributed, go back to them, yet it has not reached us that any of them claimed to have seen the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in wakefulness and took from him what he took. Likewise, it has not reached us that he (ﷺ) appeared to someone among those noble Companions who was perplexed about a matter, guided him, and removed his perplexity. It is authentically reported from Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said about some matters: "I wish I had asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it." It is not established for us that he sought to ask him (ﷺ) after his death, in the manner of what is related of some masters of spiritual states. You have learned of their disagreement over the ruling on the grandfather together with the brothers. Did you come to know that any of them was appeared to by the Messenger (ﷺ), who guided him to the truth in it? You have also heard of the great grief that befell Fatimah al-Batul, may Allah be pleased with her, after his death (ﷺ), and what happened to her regarding Fadak. Did it reach you that he, upon him be blessings and peace, appeared to her as he appears to the Sufis, soothed her anguish, lessened her sorrow, and clarified the situation for her? You have also heard of Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, going to Basra and what happened at the Battle of the Camel. Did you hear that he (ﷺ) confronted her before she departed and prevented her from it, lest it occur, or lest the proof be established against her in the most complete way? And other matters beyond counting in number.

In sum, it has not reached us that he, upon him be blessings and peace, appeared to any of his Companions or the people of his household, although they had the most urgent need for that. His appearance near the door of the Mosque of Quba, as some of the Shia relate, is pure fabrication and sheer falsehood. In general, his non-appearance to those noble ones, and his appearance to those after them, is something that requires an interpretation that will satisfy people of understanding. It would not be proper for me to say: "Everything related from the Sufis of this kind is a lie without basis, because of the multitude of those who relate it and the eminence of those who claim it." Nor would it be proper for me to say: "They only saw the Prophet (ﷺ) in a dream, and because of the lightness of sleep and its brevity they thought it was wakefulness, so they said: 'We saw him awake,' because of the distance involved." Perhaps their words contradict this. My utmost claim is that this vision is one of the extraordinary events of custom, like the other miracles of the saints and the miracles of the prophets, peace be upon them. Extraordinary events were very rare in the earliest generation, due to the proximity to the sun of prophethood. How can a star be seen under the rays, or a planet appear when the light of the sun has spread across the lands? It is possible that this happened to some of them in a rare manner, and that the public interest did not require its disclosure. It may also be said that it did not occur for the sake of testing, or out of fear of trial, or because among that people there was one who was like a mirror for him (ﷺ), or so that people would turn to the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and His Sunnah (ﷺ) for what concerns them, so that the gate of ijtihad (independent reasoning) would widen, the Sharia would spread, and the proof that anyone can understand would become great. Or for something of that kind.

Perhaps it may be claimed that he, upon him be blessings and peace, did appear, but he was veiled in his appearance, as it is reported that some of the Companions wished to see the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so he came to Maymunah, and she brought out her mirror for him. He looked into it and saw the image of the Messenger of Allah, upon him be blessings and peace, and did not see his own image. This is like the appearance that the Sufis claim, except that it is behind the veil of the mirror. It is not a matter of imagination that grew strong through looking into his mirror (ﷺ), and noticing that his image often appeared in it, as Ibn Khaldun supposed.

If my view and my explanation of this matter are accepted, then so be it, and well done. Otherwise, the matter remains problematic, so seek for yourself what resolves it. Allah, glorified is He, is the One who grants success in what is correct.

Furthermore, it has been said that it is permissible that Isa, peace be upon him, received from our Prophet (ﷺ) the rulings of his Sharia, which differ from what he was upon, and which is part of the Sharia during the time he was together with him before his death on earth, knowing that he would descend and would need that. Their meeting in this way has come in reports.

[p. 40]

Ibn Adi related from Anas: "While we were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), we saw a coolness and a hand, so we said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what is this coolness we saw, and the hand?' He said: 'You have seen it.' They said: 'Yes.' He said: 'That was Isa son of Maryam; he greeted me.'"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 40 (part 5 of 5):

In a narration of Ibn 'Asakir from him (Abu Hurayrah): "I was circumambulating the Kaaba with the Prophet (ﷺ) when I saw him shake hands with something which I did not see. We said: 'O Messenger of Allah, you shook hands with something and we do not see it.' He said: 'That is my brother 'Isa son of Maryam. I waited for him until he finished his circumambulation, and then I greeted him.'"

From here, he (peace be upon him) is counted among the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them. It has also been said that after his descent, he (peace be upon him) receives the rulings of our Shari'ah from the angel, by the angel teaching him them or informing him of them, not in the sense of their being revealed to him from the side of the Exalted and Majestic, and his sending with them so that in that there would be a new message containing a new prophethood. The saying of the Exalted: ﴿and the Seal of the Prophets﴾ has indicated the cessation of this, but rather (it is) like the teaching of a shaykh to his student what he has taught him of the Shari'ah. Mere meeting with the angel, receiving from him and conversing with him does not require prophethood. Whoever imagines that it requires it has, as al-Laqani said, deviated from the correct view. For angels, peace be upon them, spoke to Maryam and to the mother of Musa according to one opinion, and to a man who went out to visit a brother of his for the sake of Allah, and informed him that Allah, the Exalted and Majestic, loves him as he loves his brother for His sake.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in the Book of Remembrance (Kitab al-Dhikr) narrated from Anas, who said: "Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: 'I will certainly enter the mosque, pray, and praise Allah with praises that no one has praised Him with before.' When he prayed and sat to praise Allah and extol Him, behold, a loud voice from behind him said: 'O Allah, to You belongs all praise, to You belongs all sovereignty, in Your hand is all good, and to You returns all affair, its open and its secret. To You is praise, indeed You are capable of all things. Forgive me what has passed of my sins, preserve me in what remains of my life, provide me with pure deeds with which You will be pleased with me, and accept my repentance.' So he came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and related it to him, and he said: 'That was Jibril (peace be upon him).'" The reports are abundant concerning the Companions seeing the angel and hearing his speech, and as proof for what we are discussing is the saying of the Glorified: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast — the angels descend upon them, (saying), "Fear not and do not grieve, but receive good tidings of Paradise, which you were promised."﴾ [Fussilat: 30], for in it is the descent of the angel upon non-prophets in this world and his speaking to them, and no one among the people has said that this requires prophethood. That this descent and speech occur shortly before death does not benefit (the argument), as is not hidden. The Sufis have gone to something similar to what we have mentioned. The Proof of Islam al-Ghazali said in his book (al-Munqidh min al-Dalal), in the course of speaking about the praise of those masters: "Then, while awake, they witness the angels and the spirits of the prophets, and hear voices from them and derive benefits from them. Then the state rises from witnessing forms and images to degrees that the scope of speech cannot contain."

His student, the judge Abu Bakr ibn al-'Arabi, one of the imams of the Malikis, said in his book (Qanun al-Ta'wil): "The Sufis have held that when a person attains purity of the soul, purification of the heart, severing of attachments, and cutting off the sources of worldly causes such as status, wealth, and mixing with people, and turns entirely to Allah, the Exalted, with constant knowledge and continuous action, the hearts are unveiled for him, and he sees the angels, hears their speech, and gains knowledge of the spirits of the prophets and the angels. Hearing their speech is possible for the believer as a mark of honour and for the disbeliever as a punishment." End of quotation.

It is attributed to some of the imams of the Ahl al-Bayt that he said: "The angels crowd us in our houses in caravans." The apparent meaning of their statements is that meeting them and taking from them is only for the perfected people with holy souls, and that neglecting the Sunnah is a great barrier to that. This is indicated by what Muslim reported in his Sahih from Mutarrif, who said: 'Imran ibn Husayn said to me: "An angel used to greet me until I was cauterized; then he stopped. Then I stopped the cautery, and he returned."'

It is known from what we have mentioned that whoever claims this while opposing the judgment of the Book and the Sunnah is a liar who should not be listened to, and his claim is false and rejected. Where are the darknesses from the light, and the impure from the pure? Then there is no way to know that the one met is an angel, after the report of the truthful one, except by the necessary knowledge that Allah creates in the servant regarding that, and one is certain that he is not an angel whenever he contradicts what the angel brought, namely the Book, the Sunnah, or the consensus of the Ummah.

Similar to this, in my view, is speaking in a way that resembles raving, at which children laugh. Whoever experiences that should not spread it or announce it, because of what it entails of exposure to tribulation. Muslim reported also from Mutarrif by another route, who said: "'Imran ibn Husayn sent for me during his illness from which he died and said: 'I am going to relate to you something; if I live, keep it from me, and if I die, narrate it if you wish: he has greeted me.'" In the narration of al-Hakim in al-Mustadrak: "Know, O Mutarrif, that the angels used to greet me near my head, at the house, and at the door of the chamber. When I was cauterized, that stopped." He said: "When he recovered, he spoke to him." He said: "Know, O Mutarrif, that what I used to conceal has returned to me, until I die." Likewise, one should not say, regarding the angel's casting (something) upon him, that it is revelation, because of the vile misconception it contains, namely the misconception of the revelation of prophethood, whose claimant is declared a disbeliever after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) without any dispute among the Muslims. Some extremist Shi'ah have absolutely asserted revelation to the pure Imams, and they, may Allah be pleased with them, are far removed from accepting the words of those wicked ones.

It is narrated that Sudayr al-Sayrafi asked Ja'far al-Sadiq, may Allah be pleased with him: "May I be your ransom, your Shi'ah have differed concerning you and have multiplied (views), to the point that some of them say: 'The Imam has something blown into his ear'; others say: 'It is revealed to him'; others say: 'It is cast into his heart'; others say: 'He sees it in his dream'; and others say: 'He only issues fatwas from the books of his fathers.' So which of their answers should I take? May Allah, the Exalted, make me your ransom." He said: "Do not take anything of what they say, O Sudayr. We are the proofs of Allah, the Exalted, and His trustees over His creation. Our lawful is from the Book of Allah, the Exalted, and our unlawful is from it." This was related by Muhammad ibn 'Abd al-Karim al-Shahrastani at the beginning of his tafsir (Mafatih al-Asrar). And there has appeared in this age a group of extremist Shi'ah who have named themselves the Babis, and they have chapters on this matter, whose adherents are judged to be disbelievers by everyone who is counted among people of intellect. Their root had nearly become established in Iraq, had it not been for the determination of the noble governor, upon whose determination and piety the good fortune fell, when he defeated them — may Allah help him — and scattered their assembly, and Allah be pleased with him, and corrupted their work. May Allah reward him on behalf of Islam with good, and repel from him in both abodes harm and injury.

Some of them claimed revelation to 'Isa (peace be upon him) after his descent. Ibn Hajar al-Haytami was asked about this and said: "Yes, it is revealed to him (peace be upon him) with true revelation, as in the hadith of Muslim and others from al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an, and in a sound narration: 'While he is in that state, Allah the Exalted revealed: O 'Isa, I have brought forth servants of Mine whom no one has the power to fight; so take My servants to Mount Tur.' That revelation was through Jibril (peace be upon him), for he is the envoy between Allah, the Exalted, and His prophets." This is not known for anyone else. The report "There is no revelation after me" is false. What is famous, that Jibril (peace be upon him) does not descend to the earth after the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), has no basis, and it is refuted by the report of al-Tabarani: "I do not like that one in a state of major impurity should sleep until he performs ablution, for I fear that he may die, and Jibril (peace be upon him) does not attend him." This indicates that Jibril descends to the earth and attends the death of every believer whom Allah causes to die in a state of purity. End of quotation.

Perhaps whoever denies revelation to him (peace be upon him) after his descent meant the revelation of legislation, and what has been mentioned is a revelation without legislation in it. So reflect.

That he (ﷺ) is the Seal of the Prophets is among what the Book has declared, the Sunnah has proclaimed, and the Ummah has agreed upon. Whoever claims otherwise is declared a disbeliever and is to be killed if he persists.

Among the Sunnah is what Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Nasa'i and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "My example and the example of the prophets before me is like a man who built a house and made it good and beautiful, except for the place of one brick in a corner of its corners. People began to walk around it and marvel at it, and say: 'Why did you not place this brick?' I am the brick, and I am the Seal of the Prophets." A similar report has been authentically transmitted from Jabir, marfu', and likewise from Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, may Allah be pleased with them. The Shaykh Muhyi al-Din ibn al-'Arabi, may his secret be sanctified, has a statement concerning the hadith of the brick, which a group of eminent scholars have criticized. So hold fast to the Book and the Sunnah, and Allah, the Exalted, is the Protector from falling into trial.

The accusative of (رَسُولَ, rasula) is by implying kana (كانَ), indicated by the preceding kana, and the waw is conjunctive to the corrective clause after what precedes it. That lakin (لَكِنِ, "but") in its light form is for conjunction according to the majority only when there is no waw and what follows it is a single word. It is permitted that the accusative be by conjunction to ﴿abā aḥadin﴾ (father of anyone).

'Abd al-Warith narrated from Abu 'Amr a reading "wa-lakinna" with shaddah, so he put ﴿rasula﴾ in the accusative as the noun of lakinna, and the predicate is omitted, its estimate being: "but the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets is he," i.e., Muhammad (ﷺ). Al-Zamakhshari said: its estimate is: "but the Messenger of Allah is the one you know," i.e., he did not live to have a male child. Omitting the predicate of lakinna and its sisters is permissible when evidence indicates it. Among what has come with lakinna is the poet's saying:

"Had you been a Dabbi, you would have known my kinship, / But (you are) a Zanji with great lips."

That is: "but a Zanji with great lips are you." There is a discussion in this that is not hidden from one with knowledge. Zayd ibn 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them both, and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read "lakin" with lightening and "rasulu" and "khatamu" in the nominative, i.e., "but he is the Messenger of Allah," etc., as the poet said:

"I am not the boastful poet among them, / But I am the pillar of war with spears."

That is: "but I am a pillar."

﴿And Allah is, of all things﴾, more general than whether it exists or does not exist, ﴿Knowing﴾, so He, glorified be He, knows the rulings and wisdoms that were explained previously, and the wisdom in His being, peace and blessings be upon him, the Seal of the Prophets.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 41:

﴿O you who have believed, remember Allah with much remembrance﴾ by that with which He, exalted is He, is deserving of: [such as] declaring His oneness (tahlil), praising Him (tahmid), glorifying Him (tamjid), and sanctifying Him (taqdis). ﴿Much remembrance﴾ encompasses most times and conditions, as said by more than one [scholar]. And from Ibn Abbas: the much remembrance is that He, exalted is His status, is not forgotten. This is also narrated from Mujahid. It was also said: it is that He, glorified is He, is mentioned by His sublime attributes and His beautiful names, and is declared free of what is not befitting to Him. And from Muqatil: it is that one says: "Glory be to Allah," "All praise is due to Allah," "There is no god but Allah," and "Allah is greatest" in every condition. And from the pure progeny (al-'Itrah al-Tahirah), may Allah be pleased with them: whoever says this thirty times has indeed remembered Allah with much remembrance.

In (Majma' al-Bayan), from al-Wahidi with his chain to al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim, from Ibn Abbas, who said: "Jibril (peace be upon him) came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, say: Glory be to Allah, all praise is due to Allah, there is no god but Allah, Allah is greatest, and there is no power and no strength except through Allah, the Exalted, the Mighty, [as many as] the number of what is known, its weight, and its fill. Whoever says them, six qualities will be written for him: he will be written among those who remember Allah much, he will be the best of those who remember Him by night and day, a planting will be made for him in Paradise, his sins will fall away from him as the leaves of a dry tree fall, Allah will look upon him, and whoever Allah looks upon, He will not punish.'" Thus I saw it in its source, so do not be heedless. And some of them said: the basis of "much" is custom (al-'urf).

And glorify Him: exalt Him, far above whatever is unworthy of Him. ﴿Morning and evening﴾: that is, the beginning of the day and its end. Their being singled out for mention does not restrict glorification to these two times to the exclusion of all others. Rather, it is to show the excellence of these two times over the rest, because the angels of the night and the angels of the day attend them, and because glorification among the various forms of remembrance (dhikr) is distinguished in them, since it is the chief of those forms, although it is also included within dhikr in general. It has been said that both matters are intended, as when one says: "Fast and pray on Friday." And if the abundant remembrance (al-dhikr al-kathir) is explained as that which covers most of the times, there is no need to attach these two times to the first command. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that the intended meaning of glorification is prayer, that is, by mentioning a part to denote the whole. Thus, glorifying Him in the morning is the dawn prayer, and glorifying Him in the evening is the night prayer (ʿishaʾ). It is related from Qatadah something similar to what was related from Ibn ʿAbbas, except that he said: "By these two times he pointed to the morning prayer and the afternoon prayer (ʿasr), and this is more apparent than what was related from the scholar (al-Ḥabr)." What was related from the two of them has been criticized on the ground that it involves figurative usage (tajawwuz) without necessity. It may be said that glorification is in its literal sense (ḥaqīqa), but glorifying Him in the morning is by praying in it, and glorifying Him in the evening is by praying in it. So reflect. It is also permissible that the intended meaning of the remembrance commanded is the increase of acts of obedience and devotion to them, for every act of obedience is part of remembrance. Then glorification in the morning and evening is singled out from that, meaning prayer in all its times, or the dawn and afternoon prayers, or the dawn and night prayers, because of the excellence of prayer over other bodily acts of obedience. Its remoteness is not hidden.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 43:**

﴿He it is who sends blessings upon you﴾ etc. is a resumptive sentence (*isti'naf*) that serves as a reason (*ta'lil*) for what precedes it, namely the two matters mentioned earlier. ﴿And His angels﴾ is conjoined (*'atf*) to the pronoun in (*yusalli*, "sends blessings"), because of the intervening separation that makes unnecessary an emphasis by a detached pronoun. It is not conjoined to (*Huwa*, "He"). According to the well-known view, which is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas, the blessing (*salah*) is, from Allah the Exalted, mercy (*rahmah*); from the angels, seeking forgiveness (*istighfar*); and from the believers among mankind and the jinn, supplication (*du'a'*). According to the view of those who permit using a single word in two meanings, it is possible that the two first meanings are intended here by *salah*, so that it denotes first mercy and second seeking forgiveness. As for those who do not permit this, like our companions, they say that the metaphor is general (*'umum al-majaz*), in that *salah* is taken in a general figurative sense of which both meanings are a real instance. This general sense is either *i'tina'* (solicitous care), since in it there is the good of those addressed and the welfare of their affairs, for each of mercy and seeking forgiveness is a real instance of it. This metaphorical use of *salah* in the sense of supplication is either a metaphor (*isti'arah*), since solicitous care resembles supplication in that each involves the desire for good and a beloved matter, or a metonymic metaphor (*majaz mursal*), since supplication is caused by solicitous care. As for compassion and the inner inclination (*in'ita f ma'nawi*) derived from the well-known *salah*, which includes the outward inclination consisting of bowing (*ruku'*) and prostration (*sujud*): there is no doubt that the angels' seeking forgiveness for the believers and their supplicating for them is a form of compassion toward them. As for whether that is a cause of mercy because they are answered in supplication, as has been said, there is a question about it. The general meaning mentioned has been preferred, on the ground that it is closer to what follows, for it is explicitly stated there in His saying: ﴿And He has been merciful to the believers﴾. This shows that the intended meaning of *salah* is mercy. It has been objected that *rahima* is transitive while *salla* is intransitive, so it is not good to explain it by it; and that it implies that *rahima* may be used with *'ala* ("upon"); and that He, the Exalted, distinguished between them in His saying: ﴿Those—upon them are blessings from their Lord and mercy﴾ [al-Baqarah: 157], by the conjunction that clearly indicates difference. It has been answered that the purpose of explaining *salla* by *rahima* is only to show that the meaning assigned to *salla* is the meaning assigned to *rahima*, setting aside the notion of transitivity and intransitivity, for synonyms may differ in that respect, and this is not harmful. It was claimed that this is not good and that it entails the permissibility of *rahima 'alayhi*, but this claim is not well placed. Moreover, it is good to make *salla* transitive with *'ala* but not *rahima*, because the first carries the sense of tenderness, affection and compassion, since *salah* is a particular mercy; and this degree of difference suffices. It has also been said: when the agent is plural, the verb is treated as if it were transitive to more than one object, so that mercy is intended from one word and seeking forgiveness from another. Thus there is no need to say that the metaphor is general. There is no use of a single word in two meanings in reality and in judgment, and this, as you see, is weak. Similar is the view that ﴿His angels﴾ is a subject whose predicate is omitted, because what precedes indicates it, as if it were said: "He it is who sends blessings upon you, and His angels send blessings upon you." Then there are two words, each in reality with its own meaning. Allah willing, what will increase your knowledge about the matter of *salah* will come later.

The occasion of revelation of the verse is what 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated, saying: "When the verse was revealed: ﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ [al-Ahzab: 56], Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'Allah has revealed nothing good to you except that He has made us partners in it.' Then the verse was revealed: ﴿He it is who sends blessings upon you, and His angels, that He may bring you out from darknesses into light﴾." That is, from the darknesses of sins into the light of obedience. Al-Tabarsi said: from ignorance of Allah the Exalted into knowledge of Him, Mighty and Majestic, for ignorance is most like darkness, and knowledge is most like light. Ibn Zayd said: from error into guidance. Muqatil said: from disbelief into faith. It has been said: from the Fire into Paradise, related by al-Mawardi. It has been said: from the graves into the Resurrection, related by Abu Hayyan, but this is not correct. The *lam* (in *li-yukhrijakum*, "that He may bring you out") is connected to *yusalli*, meaning: He Himself and His angels show solicitous care for you, that He may bring you out, or: He, Mighty and Majestic, and His angels show compassion, that He may bring you out thereby from the darknesses into the light.

﴿And He has been merciful to the believers﴾ is a parenthetical clause (*i'tiraD*) confirming the content of what precedes it. That is, He, glory be to Him, has been perfectly merciful to all the believers, among whom you are included; and for this reason He does for you what He does, both directly and through intermediaries. Or: He has been merciful to you, and the word "the believers" is an apparent noun placed in the position of the pronoun, to praise them and to indicate the reason for the mercy.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 44:

And His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be, "Peace."﴾ is an explanation of the deferred rulings of His mercy toward them, after the explanation of its immediate effects, namely the bringing forth mentioned earlier. The taḥiyyah (greeting) is that one says, "Ḥayyākallāh," meaning, "God has granted you life." This is first a statement of information, and then it becomes a supplication. It is said, "Fulān ḥayyā Fulānan taḥiyyatan" when he says that to him. The origin of this word is from ḥayāh (life), and then every supplication was called a taḥiyyah because all of it does not fall outside of bringing about life or being a cause of life, whether for this world or the next.

Here it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) construed with its object, which is the subject (mubtada'), and salām, used to refer to its own wording, is the predicate (khabar). The meaning is: that with which God greets them and which He says to them on the Day they meet Him, Exalted is He, and they enter the abode of His honor, is "Salām," that is, this expression. It is narrated that God, Exalted is He, says: "Peace be upon you, My servants. I am pleased with you; so are you pleased with Me?" And they all say: "O our Lord, we are pleased with a complete pleasure." And it has been transmitted that God, Exalted is He, says: "Peace be upon you, welcome, My believing servants, who pleased Me in the abode of the world by following My command." It was also said: the angels, peace be upon them, greet them with that when they enter Paradise, as God, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And the angels will enter upon them from every gate﴾ ﴿"Peace be upon you."﴾ And it was said: they are greeted when they come out of the graves, so they greet them and give them the good news of Paradise. And it was said: at the time of death.

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: When the Angel of Death comes to seize the soul of the believer, he says: "Your Lord sends you His greetings of peace." It was said: according to this, the pronoun in ﴿yalqawnahu﴾ refers to something not mentioned, namely the Angel of Death. But there is no necessity for that, since there is no obstacle to the pronoun referring to God, Exalted is He, as it does according to all the other opinions. The meeting with God, Exalted is He, as the Imam (al-Razi) indicated, is an expression for turning wholly toward Him, such that nothing occurs to the person that occupies or distracts him or causes him to be heedless of Him, Mighty and Majestic. This occurs upon entering Paradise, within it, at the Resurrection, and at death.

Al-Raghib said: meeting God, Exalted is He, is an expression for the Resurrection and for returning to Him, Mighty and Majestic. Al-Tabarsi said: it is meeting His reward, Exalted is He. This is not apparent according to all the earlier opinions, but is apparent according to some of them, as is not hidden. And it is narrated from Qatadah concerning the verse that on the day they enter Paradise, some of them greet others with peace, meaning: "We are safe, and you are safe from every fear." The taḥiyyah here, according to what al-Khafaji said, is a verbal noun construed with the agent. In al-Bahr, it is said that it is a verbal noun construed with the one who greets, and the one greeted, not in the sense of the action, because a single pronoun cannot be both agent and object. Rather, it is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We were witnesses to their judgment﴾ [al-Anbiya': 78], meaning, to the judgment that took place among them.

Likewise it is said here: the greeting exchanged among them is "Salām," and the words of the one greeting on that Day, "Salām," are a statement of information, not a supplication, because it is more eloquent, according to what has been said. So reflect. And the most worthy of the opinions with acceptance in my view is that God, Exalted is He, greets them on the Day they meet Him, as an honor to them and a magnification of them.

﴿And He has prepared for them a generous reward﴾, meaning: Mighty and Majestic is He, who prepared for them a good reward. The apparent meaning is that the preparation occurs before entering Paradise and the greeting; and for this reason the sentence did not come in the form of what precedes it, such that it would be said "and their reward is a generous reward," meaning, "and for them is a generous reward." It was also said: it is after entering and the greeting, so the statement explains the effects of His mercy overflowing upon them after entering Paradise, following the explanation of the effects of His mercy that reached them before that. Perhaps the choice of the verbal sentence over the nominal one that would fit what precedes it is for the sake of emphasis in encouraging and kindling desire for what is promised, by explaining that the matter which is the ultimate goal among the rest of the effects of mercy exists in fact, prepared for them, together with what it contains of observing the rhyme endings (fawāṣil).

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 45:**

﴿O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness﴾ over those to whom you were sent, observing their conditions, witnessing their deeds, and bearing testimony (tahammul, the act of taking on witness) concerning what proceeds from them of affirmation and denial, and all else that they hold of guidance and misguidance. You will render that testimony (ada', the act of delivering it) on the Day of Resurrection in an acceptable manner, regarding what is in their favour and what is against them. This is a *hal muqaddarah* (a circumstantial clause describing a future state). If the sending is regarded as an extended action, given that bearing and rendering testimony are involved, then the sending, under that consideration, though it accompanies the bearing, does not accompany the rendering, even if extension is taken into account.

It has been said that if "witness" is taken to mean only bearing, then the circumstantial clause is contemporaneous, and the conditions mentioned afterwards are contemporaneous too, on the basis of extension. You may also disregard extension entirely, in which case all the conditions are future. Now, bearing witness over those who were contemporary with him (ﷺ) and who observed his deeds is an evident matter. As for bearing witness over those who came after him, individually, if that is also intended, then there is obscurity in it, because the apparent sense of the reports is that he (ﷺ) does not know the deeds of those who came after him individually. Abu Bakr, Anas, Hudhayfah, Samurah and Abu al-Darda' narrated from him (ﷺ): "Some of my companions will certainly come to me at the Basin, and when I see them and recognise them, they will be driven away from me. I will say, 'O Lord, my companions, my companions!' It will be said to me, 'You do not know what they innovated after you.'"

Yes, it may be said that he (ﷺ) knows the acts of obedience and disobedience that occur after him among his community, but he does not know the individuals who are obedient or disobedient. By this the aforementioned report is reconciled with the report of the deeds being presented to him (ﷺ) every week, or more or less often. It has also been said that it is reconciled by saying that he (ﷺ) also knows the individuals, but he forgot and said, "My companions," and to magnify the gravity of what they innovated, it was said to him, "You do not know what they innovated after you." It has also been said that everything other than disbelief is presented to him, and this, as you see, is weak. As for the claim that bearing witness over those who come after him until the Day of Resurrection is possible because he (ﷺ) is alive in his spirit and body, travelling wherever he wills across the regions of the earth and the malakut (the unseen realm), it is built upon what you have understood of his state. Perhaps these two reports refute it, as will not be hidden from one who reflects.

Some of the Sufi masters pointed out that God Most High had made him (ﷺ) aware of the deeds of His servants, so that he looked upon them, and for this reason he (ﷺ) was named *shahid*. Our master Jalal al-Din al-Rumi, may God sanctify his noble secret, said in his Mathnawi:

*In his sight were the stations of the servants;*
*for that reason God named him Witness.*

So reflect and do not be heedless.

It has also been said that the intended meaning is a witness over all nations on the Day of Resurrection, that their prophets had delivered the message to them and called them to God Most High, and his testimony to this is due to what he knew from the Glorious Book. It has also been said that the intended meaning is a witness that there is no god but God. ﴿And a bringer of good news﴾: you give good tidings to the obedient of Paradise. ﴿And a warner﴾: you warn the disbelievers and the disobedient of the Fire. Because warning is general and good tidings are specific, it has been said that "bringer of good news and warner" is in the form of intensification (mubalaghah), rather than "mundhir" (warner), even though the apparent sense of its conjunction with "bringer of good news" would require that. Good tidings are placed first because of the nobility of those who bring good news, and because it is the primary purpose, since he (ﷺ) is a mercy to the worlds. It seems that for this reason what was lost of intensification in the warning was compensated by His words, Most High: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 46:

﴿وداعِيًا إلى اللَّهِ﴾ That is, calling to the acknowledgement of Him, glorified is He, and of His oneness, and of all the attributes and acts in which belief is obligatory, mighty and majestic is He. Perhaps this is what Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah meant by their saying, that is, the testimony that there is no god but Allah.

﴿بِإذْنِهِ﴾ That is, by His facilitating and making easy, exalted is He. The word "permission" (idhn) is used for facilitation metaphorically, since it is among its causes, especially permission from Allah, mighty and majestic is He, and it is not taken in its literal sense. Yet it would be valid here that Allah, exalted is His majesty, grants permission to him, upon him be prayer and peace, literally in the call, since it has been understood from His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Indeed We have sent you as a witness and a bearer of good news and a warner, and as one calling to Allah by His permission and as a lamp giving light﴾ [al-Ahzab: 45–46], that he (ﷺ) is authorized in the call. From what has been mentioned it is known that (بِإذْنِهِ) belongs with (داعِيًا). The call is restricted by this to indicate that it is a matter difficult to attain and a grave affair of utmost difficulty, which cannot be accomplished except with support from the presence of His holiness. How could it not be, since it is the turning of faces away from the worshipped idols and the placing of necks into an unfamiliar necklace? It has been permitted that the restriction returns to all of the preceding, but the first is more apparent.

﴿وسِراجًا مُنِيرًا﴾ by which the misguided seek light in the darknesses of ignorance and error, and from whose light the lights of those guided to the paths of right direction and guidance are kindled. This is a simile, either a compound rational simile or a figurative simile abstracted from several matters, or a distributed one. Exaggeration is made in the description with illumination, because among lamps there are those that do not give light when their oil is little and their wick is thin.

Al-Zajjaj said: it is conjoined to (شاهِدًا) with an elided genitive, that is, one possessing a lamp that is bright. Al-Farra' said: if you wish, it is in the accusative, in the sense of "and one reciting a bright lamp." And according to both of them, the bright lamp is the Qur'an. When it is explained thus, it is possible, as has been said, that it is conjoined to the kaf in (أرْسَلْناكَ) in the sense of "We have sent you" and the Qur'an, either by way of following or by the mode of (متقلدا سيفا ورمحا). It has also been said that, on the assumption of (تالِيًا سِراجًا), this conjunction is permissible, that is, "Indeed We have sent you, and reciting a bright lamp," like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿reciting purified scriptures﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 2], on the basis that he combines the two matters, in the manner of: ﴿And We gave Moses and Aaron the criterion and a light﴾ [al-Anbiya': 48], that is, We sent by sending you, reciting.

It has been permitted that it means "and We made you reciting." It has also been said that by (ذا سِراجٍ) may be meant the lamp of the Qur'an, and in that case the sense would be: "Indeed We have sent you, and sent down upon you one possessing a lamp." It has been objected that making the Qur'an "possessing a lamp" is a forced reading, and the truth is that all that has been said in this manner is [of the same kind].

And give good news to the believers (ʿaṭf, coordination, on an implied element that the context requires and the flow of the discourse calls for), as if it were said: "So observe the conditions of the people and give good news to the believers." It is also permitted that it be coordinated with the preceding report (khabar), as the coordination of one narrative with another narrative. It was also said: it is coordinated with what precedes and is taken to have the sense of a command, because it has the meaning of "call them as a witness, a bringer of good news, and a warner," etc. "And give good news to the believers from among them ﴿that for them is from Allah a great bounty﴾," i.e., a generous gift. It is, as reported from al-Hasan and Qatada, Paradise and what they are given therein, and it is supported by His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And those who believe and do righteous deeds, in the gardens of Paradise they will have whatever they wish with their Lord. That is the great bounty﴾ [al-Shura: 22]. It was also said: the meaning is a bounty over the other nations in rank and nobility, or an increase over the rewards of their deeds by way of grace and kindness.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn ʿIkrima reported from al-Hasan: "When it was revealed, ﴿That Allah may forgive you your earlier and later sins﴾ [al-Fath: 2], they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we know what will be done with you, so what will be done with us?' So Allah, Exalted is He, revealed: ﴿And give good news to the believers that for them is from Allah a great bounty﴾."

Commentary of al-Alusi (*Ruh al-Ma'ani*) on surah 33, verse 48:

﴿And do not obey the disbelievers and the hypocrites.﴾ This is a prohibition against being lenient with them in matters of the call (*da'wah*), against being gentle in conveying the message, and against being lax in warning. It is expressed indirectly, through a prohibition against obeying them, in order to intensify the prohibition and the warning against what is forbidden, by placing it in the same thread and depicting it in its form. Many scholars took the prohibition as a means of stirring and inflaming (*tahyij wa-ilhab*), in that the Prophet (ﷺ) never obeyed them in the first place, so he needed to be forbidden. Some scholars made it fall under the pattern of "*It is you I mean, but hear me, O neighbour*" (*iyyaka a'ni wa-isma'i ya jarah*), so do not be heedless.

﴿And leave off their harm.﴾ That is: do not care about their harming you because of your warning them, and bear patiently what reaches you from them. This is what Qatadah said. Here *adhahum* (أذاهم) is a verbal noun (*masdar*) annexed to its subject (the one who harms). Abu Hayyan said: "The apparent meaning is that it is a verbal noun annexed to its object (i.e., the harm inflicted upon them)." When the Prophet (ﷺ) was forbidden to obey them, he was commanded to abandon harming them and punishing them. Some of what pertains specifically to the disbelievers was abrogated (*nusikh*, i.e., abrogation, *naskh*) by the verse of the sword. Something similar is narrated from Mujahid and al-Kalbi. The first view, however, is preferable.

﴿And rely upon Allah.﴾ In all that you do and leave undone of affairs, among which is this matter, for indeed He, Exalted and Majestic, suffices them. ﴿And Allah is sufficient as a Disposer of affairs.﴾ That is, the affairs are entrusted to Him in all circumstances. The mention of the Glorious Name in the place where a pronoun would be expected serves to give the reason for the ruling and to emphasize the independence of this concluding parenthetical statement (*i'tiraḍ tadhyili*).

When the Prophet (ﷺ) was described with five attributes, each one was matched with an address that suits it, except that what corresponds to the attribute of "witness" (*shahid*) was not explicitly mentioned. That corresponds to the command to watchfulness (*muraqabah*), relying on the clear indication of the attribute of "bringer of good tidings" (*mubashshir*), which is the command to give good tidings, as mentioned above. The attribute "warner" (*nadhir*) is matched with the prohibition against being lenient with the disbelievers and hypocrites and being tolerant in warning them. The attribute "caller" (*da'i*) with His permission is matched with the command to rely upon Him, insofar as that is an expression of seeking aid from Him, Exalted and Majestic. The "illuminating lamp" (*siraj munir*) is matched with sufficiency in Him, Exalted. Whoever Allah has supported with holy power, designated for prophethood, and made a bright proof, guiding creation from the darkness of error to the light of right guidance, is truly deserving of being sufficed by Him, Exalted, over anyone else.

Al-Zamakhshari made the counterpart of "witness" to be "and give good tidings to the believers," and the counterpart of turning away from the disbelievers and hypocrites to be "the one given good tidings" (*al-mubashshar*), namely the believers. He strained himself in this.

Al-Tibi (may Allah sanctify his resting place) said: The parallel to this verse is what al-Bukhari and Imam Ahmad narrated from ʿAta' ibn Yasar, who said: "I met ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, and I said: 'Tell me about the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the Torah.' He said: 'By Allah, he is indeed described in the Torah with some of his attributes mentioned in the Qur'an: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings, and a warner﴾ and a protection for the believers. You are My servant and My Messenger; I have named you "the one who relies upon Allah." He is not harsh, nor coarse, nor clamorous in the markets, nor does he repel evil with evil, but he pardons and forgives. Allah will not take him until He has set right through him the crooked religion, by making people say "There is no god but Allah," and opens through him blind eyes, deaf ears, and closed hearts.'" Al-Darimi narrated something similar from ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam.

So his saying "a protection for the believers" corresponds to His saying: ﴿and as a caller to Allah by His permission﴾, for his call (ﷺ) only bears its fruit among those whom Allah has enabled by His facilitation and ease. Therefore those people believed, and were saved from the calamities of this world and the severe trials of the Hereafter. Thus, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, he was in this respect a protection for them. His saying "I have named you the one who relies upon Allah," and so on, corresponds to His saying: ﴿and as an illuminating lamp﴾. It is thus known that His saying, Exalted: ﴿And rely upon Allah, and Allah is sufficient as a Disposer of affairs﴾ is appropriate to His saying: ﴿and as an illuminating lamp﴾, for the lamp shines in itself and gives light to others. Thus by being one who relies upon Allah, Exalted, he is perfect in himself. So it fits His saying: "You are My servant and My Messenger; I have named you the one who relies upon Allah," up to His saying: "he pardons and forgives." And his being illuminating, upon which Allah, Exalted, pours forth (light), makes him perfect for others, and this fits His saying: "until he sets right through him the crooked religion," etc.

Then he said: It is possible to arrange the ranks according to the language of the people of gnosis (*ahl al-irfan*). So His saying, Exalted: ﴿Indeed We have sent you as a witness, a bringer of good tidings, and a warner﴾ [al-Fath: 8] is the station of the Shariah, calling people to faith and abandoning disbelief, and the result of turning away from all other than Allah, Exalted, and embarking upon the journey and the path, and seeking refuge in the sanctuary of His subtle kindness, and relying upon Him, Glorified and Exalted. And His saying, Glorified be He: ﴿and as an illuminating lamp﴾ is the station of Reality (*al-haqiqah*), and its result is the annihilation (*fana'*) of the wayfarer and his subsistence through His self-subsisting (*qayyumiyyah*), Exalted. End of quotation. The weakness of what he established regarding the hadith is not hidden. And Allah, Exalted, knows best what He intends.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 49 (part 1 of 2):**

﴿O you who have believed, when you marry believing women and then divorce them before you have touched them, then you have no waiting period for them to count.﴾ This returns to the subject of women. Here *nikah* (marriage contract) means the contract, by general agreement. The scholars differed over its meaning in the lexical sense. It has been said that it is a homonym (*mushtarak lafzi*) shared between sexual intercourse (*wat'*) and the contract. It has been said that it is literally the contract and metaphorically sexual intercourse. It has also been said that the two meanings are reversed. And it has been said that it is shared between them as a common meaning (*mushtarak ma'nawi*), being one of the instances of what is graduated (*al-mushakkik*). Its underlying meaning is joining and combining, as in the verse:

*I pressed to my chest her perfumed breast,*
*as the mother of the boy embraces her child.*

Al-Mubarrad transmitted this view from the Basran grammarians, and Ghulam Tha'lab, Shaykh Umar and al-Zahid transmitted it from the Kufan grammarians. Then, what is immediately understood from the word *damm* (joining) is that it relates to bodies and not to statements, because statements are accidents (*a'rad*), the first of which vanishes before the second comes into existence, so the second never meets anything for it to be joined to. This requires that it be a metaphor for the contract. However, if joining is taken in the general sense, covering the joining of body to body and of statement to statement, then *nikah* may be literal for both sexual intercourse and the contract, or metaphorical according to the well-known distinction in using a general term for each of its individual instances.

Al-Raghib preferred the second of the earlier views and went to great lengths in rejecting the third. He said: it is literally the contract, then it was borrowed for intercourse. It is impossible that it was originally for intercourse and then borrowed for the contract, because all the terms for intercourse are euphemisms (*kinayat*), due to their finding its mention as offensive as its practice. And it is impossible that someone who does not intend indecency should borrow the name of something they find abhorrent for something they consider good.

Al-Zamakhshari preferred the third view and said: *nikah* means intercourse, and the naming of the contract as *nikah* is because of its association with it, in that it is a means to it. The parallel is the naming of wine as sin (*ithm*), because it is a cause of committing sin. The word *nikah* does not occur in the Book of God except in the sense of the contract, because in reference to intercourse it is explicit, and among the etiquettes of the Qur'an is to refer to it by euphemisms such as *mulamasa* (touching), *mumassa* (touching), *qurban* (approaching), *taghshshi* (covering) and *ityan* (coming to). He intended, as has been said, that in the contract it is a technical meaning (*haqiqa shar'iyya*) in which the lexical meaning has been effaced. His statement that the word *nikah* does not occur in the Book of God except in the sense of the contract has been challenged, with the argument that in God's words ﴿until she marries another husband﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:230] it means intercourse. This is the view of the majority, and Ibn al-Musayyab dissented on this point. The full discussion belongs in its proper place.

*Mass* (touching) in its basic sense is well known, and it is used here as a euphemism for sexual intercourse. *'Idda* (waiting period) is that which is counted, and the *'idda* of a woman means the days upon whose completion she becomes lawful for marriage again.

So the meaning is: O you who have believed, when you contract marriage with believing women and then consummate the marriage, and then divorce them before you have had intercourse with them, then you have no waiting period for them, with days in which they wait, that you must count and complete. The verb *ta'taddunaha* (you count it) may be a reflexive form (*mutawi'*) of *'adda* (to count): one says *'adda al-darahim fa-i'taddaha*, meaning he counted the coins and completed their number, like your saying *kiltuhu fa-iktaltuhu* (I measured it and so I took its measure) and *wazantuhu fa-ittazantuhu* (I weighed it and so I took its weight). Or it may be *ta'uddunaha*, with *if'al* in the sense of *fa'al*.

The attribution of the verb to men indicates that the waiting period is the right of the husbands, which is what is suggested by God's words ﴿then you have no waiting period﴾. It has been objected that what is mentioned in the books of jurisprudence (*furu'*), such as *al-Hidaya* and others, is that it is a right of the Law (*haqq al-shar'*). For this reason it is not dropped even if the husband waives it, and she may not leave the house even if he permits her, and two waiting periods may overlap, although overlapping does not apply to the right of the slave or the right of the child. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said: "It is not lawful for a man who believes in God and the Last Day to water his water (semen) with the field of another." Based on this they held that the two of them (the husband and wife) cannot nullify it by mutual agreement that there was no intercourse.

It has been answered that the intended meaning is not that it is a waiver of their right, but rather that its benefit and purpose return to them, because it serves to protect their waters and the lineages that trace back to them. Therefore this does not contradict its being a right of the Law and of the child, which prevents its waiver. Even if it were assumed to be a waiver of their right, it could be said that the fact that it is not dropped by their waiver does not contradict that, unless it were established that every right of a human being is dropped when he waives it. But this is not so, since some rights of a human being are not dropped by his waiving them, such as inheritance, the right to retract a gift, and the option of inspection. Moreover, there is room for reflection in using the hadith as evidence that it is a right of the child, as is not hidden.

The specification of believing women, although the ruling applies generally to women of the People of the Book (*kitabiyyat*), serves to alert that the believer ought to choose carefully for his seed, and not marry anyone but a believing woman. Its essence is that it indicates what is more appropriate and fitting, after the ruling on marrying women of the People of the Book was detailed in al-Baqarah.

The benefit of bringing in *thumma* (then) even though the ruling applies to a man who marries a woman and divorces her immediately, just as it applies to one who marries her and divorces her after a long period, is to remove what might be imagined, namely that the delay of the divorce has some role in making the waiting period obligatory, because of the possibility of secret meeting and intercourse, just as it has a role in lineage. It is also possible that the reference is to a sequence of rank (*tarakhi rutbi*): although divorce is permissible, with no reprehensibility in it according to what has been said, due to God's words ﴿There is no blame upon you if you divorce women while you have not yet touched them﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:236], it is nonetheless not beloved, like marriage, in that it leads to severing the bond and undoing the tie of marital union, which leads to fewer offspring, by which the community multiplies. For this reason there was reported what Abu Dawud, Ibn Majah, al-Hakim, al-Tabarani and Ibn 'Adi transmitted from Ibn 'Umar, may God be pleased with them both, as a raised (*marfu'*) report: "The most hated of lawful things to God is divorce." Al-Bayhaqi transmitted it as a *mursal* report without Ibn 'Umar. Indeed, the great scholar Ibn al-Humam said: the sounder view is that it is forbidden and reprehensible except for a need, because it involves ingratitude for the blessing of marriage, and because of the reports indicating that. The word "permissible" (*mubah*) in the aforementioned report is to be understood as what is permitted at certain times, namely the times when the permitting need is realized. This is clear in a version of Abu Dawud: "God has not made lawful anything more hateful to Him than divorce." The verb has no generality across times, and the permitting need is, for example, old age or suspicion. Among what permits it is her not being desired, to the point that he is unable, or he would harm himself by forcing himself to have intercourse with her, while she does not consent to remaining in his marital bond without intercourse or equal treatment (*qasam*).

As for what is reported from al-Hasan al-Sibt, may God be pleased with him, when he was asked about his frequent marriages and divorces, he said: "I love wealth (*ghina*)," since God says ﴿But if they separate, God will enrich each of them from His abundance﴾ [al-Nisa' 4:130]. This is his personal opinion, if it is taken at face value. And whatever is reported about the divorces of the Companions, may God be pleased with them, is to be understood as referring to the existence of a need.

The apparent meaning of the verse requires that a waiting period is not obligatory merely by seclusion (*khalwa*), because God negated the obligation of a waiting period when she is divorced before intercourse, and seclusion is not intercourse. According to us, however, if the seclusion is valid, in the manner explained in the books of jurisprudence, it is like intercourse in making the waiting period obligatory, so the waiting period is obligatory for it as a precaution against the suspicion of occupation (*shaghl*), in view of the real possibility of contact. Indeed they said it is like it in all its rulings except ten, which the most excellent of our contemporary jurists, Shaykh Muhammad Amin al-Shami, known as Ibn 'Abidin, versified, saying:

*Seclusion is like intercourse, except in ten matters:*
*claim to intercourse, permission for the former husband, iḥṣan (marital status for legal purposes), the lawful intermediary marriage (tahlil), return (fay'), the inheritance claim, reconciliation (raj'a), impotence (fayd 'unna), the prohibition of a daughter (tahrim bint), the contract for a virgin, and the ritual washing (taghsil).*

The apparent sense of their statement that a waiting period is obligatory due to seclusion is that it is obligatory judicially (*qada'*) and in religious matters (*diyana*). In *al-Fath*, al-'Itabi said: Our scholars discussed whether the waiting period obligated by valid seclusion is obligatory apparently or in reality. It was said: if she marries while certain there was no consummation, it is lawful for her in religious matters, but not judicially. End quote. He did not follow this with anything. Sa'di Jalabi mentioned it in the margins of *al-Baydawi* and said: the reliance should be on this view. Al-Shihab al-Khafaji criticized that, saying: although our jurists transmitted it, they explicitly stated that it is not to be relied upon, and we have not seen this explicit statement, so it should be investigated. Furthermore, it is not hidden that the non-obligation of a waiting period in divorce after seclusion is among what is counted as an explicit statement (*mantuq sarih*) in the verse, if *mass* is interpreted as intercourse, and it is not a matter of implication (*mafhum*), so that one could say: we do not hold it, as is imagined. Therefore, to establish that a waiting period is obligatory in this case, one needs evidence. Some people interpreted *mass* here as seclusion, taking the effect for the cause, since touching is customarily an effect of seclusion. It was objected that *mass* is not well known in the sense of seclusion, and there is no context in the speech indicating that it is intended. Also, it would follow that if he divorced her after having had intercourse with her in front of people, there would be no waiting period, because he divorced her before seclusion.

This was answered by saying that the waiting period in that case is obligatory by consensus. And if the waiting period is obligatory in divorce due to seclusion alone, it is obligatory in divorce due to intercourse all the more so. And how could it not be obligatory due to intercourse, when its obligation due to seclusion is because of the possibility of its occurrence within seclusion, not for its own sake. It has also been said that since *mass* does not have its apparent meaning, otherwise a waiting period would be required in the case where he divorced her after having touched her with his hand outside seclusion, even though by agreement there is no obligation in that case, it is known that it is a euphemism for another meaning among the implications of contact, which is intercourse and what is equivalent to it, namely valid seclusion. There is room for objection in this, because the impossibility of its apparent meaning being intended does not necessitate that it intends what includes both intercourse and seclusion. Why could it not be that intercourse is intended? And this is supported by the fame of the euphemism for intercourse with this and similar words. Its application to it is either because the name of the cause is applied to the effect, or because the name of the general is applied to a specific particular, and the latter is the more likely according to what Ibn al-Humam mentioned. In sum, the claim that the apparent meaning of the verse requires that a waiting period is not obligatory merely by seclusion is a firm claim and a clear truth. So reflect.

In *al-Bahr* by Abu Hayyan: the apparent view is that if a divorced woman's husband took her back before her waiting period ended, and then divorced her before he touched her, her waiting period from the first pronouncement is not completed, because she is a woman divorced before consummation, both before and after returning to her. Dawud said, and 'Ata' and a group said: she continues her waiting period from her first divorce, which is one of the two opinions of al-Shafi'i. Malik said: she does not build upon the waiting period of the first divorce, and she begins a new waiting period from the day of the second divorce. This is the view of the majority of the jurists of the cities.

The apparent view also is that if she was irrevocably divorced (*ba'in*) but not finally divorced (*mabtuta*), and he married her during the waiting period and then divorced her before consummation, then in Dawud's view she is like a revocably divorced woman: there is no waiting period upon her, neither the remainder of the first divorce's waiting period nor the beginning of a new waiting period for the second. She is entitled to half the dowry. Al-Hasan, 'Ata', 'Ikrima, Ibn Shihab, Malik, al-Shafi'i, 'Uthman al-Batti and Zufar said: she is entitled to half the dowry and completes the remainder of the first waiting period. Al-Thawri, al-Awza'i, Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf said: she is entitled to a full dowry for the second marriage, and a new waiting period, since they treated her as one who has been consummated, because she observes the waiting period of one hundred days. End quote.

Also in it: the apparent view is that divorce is only valid after the contract, so the divorce of one not yet contracted to is invalid. This is the view of the majority of the Companions and the Successors. However, a large group, including Malik, said it is valid. By divorce of one not yet contracted to, they meant a man's saying: "Every woman I marry is divorced," or "If I marry so-and-so, she is divorced."

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 49 (part 2 of 2):
