Many narrators have transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, that he was asked about this and said: "It is nothing." It was then said to him: "Ibn Mas'ud used to say that if a man divorces a woman he has not yet married, the divorce is valid." He said: "He erred in this," and he recited the verse. In some narrations, he said: "May Allah have mercy on Abu 'Abd al-Rahman. Had it been as he said, Allah would have said: 'O you who believe, when you divorce believing women and then marry them...' But He only said: ﴿When you marry believing women and then divorce them﴾."

In al-Durr al-Manthur there are several hadiths traced to the Prophet (ﷺ) stating clearly that there is no divorce before marriage. What is mentioned in our legal school (furu') is that this falls under the category of ta'liq (conditional divorce), whose condition is ownership (al-milk) or attribution to it. So if a man says: "If I marry a woman, then she is divorced," or "If I marry you, then you are divorced," or "Every woman I marry is divorced," the divorce takes effect when he marries, because this is a conditional statement and includes attribution to ownership. The meaning of a condition suffices, except for a specific woman identified by name and lineage, as when he says: "So-and-so, daughter of so-and-so, whom I will marry, is divorced," or by pointing to a present woman, as when he says: "This woman whom I will marry is divorced." In both cases she is not divorced, because she has been identified, so the descriptive phrase "whom I will marry" is void, and it becomes as if he had said: "So-and-so, daughter of so-and-so, is divorced," or "This woman is divorced," while she is a stranger (ajnabiyyah) and no attribution to ownership exists. So the divorce does not take effect if he marries her. Reflect on this.

"Tumassuhunna" was read with a damma on the ta' and an alif after the mim. From Ibn Kathir and other people of Makkah, "ta'taddunaha" was read with a light dal. Ibn Khalawayh and Abu al-Fadl al-Razzi in (al-Lawami') transmitted this from him and from the people of Makkah. Ibn 'Atiyyah said: Ibn Abi Bazzah reported from Ibn Kathir that he read with a light dal, from al-'udwan (transgression), as if he said: "What waiting period do you impose on them as transgression and injustice toward them?" The first reading is more well-known from him, and the light dal is a mistake by Ibn Abi Bazzah. But it is not a mistake, since a group other than him transmitted it from him. This was explained as: "ta'taddunaha" is from al-i'tida' in the sense of injustice, as in His saying: ﴿And do not hold them back to harm them, to transgress﴾ [al-Baqarah: 231]. The meaning is "you transgress in it," as in the poet's words:

"And a day we witnessed, Sulaym and 'Amir in it, / few, except for the piercing of spears, its surplus"

Meaning: "we witnessed in it," so he removed the preposition and attached the verb directly to the pronoun. Abu Hayyan said: i'tida' is transitive with 'ala, so the meaning is "you transgress against them in it." A parallel with 'ala omitted is the poet's words:

"She yearns and reveals what is in her of longing, / and conceals what, were it not for grief, would have killed me"

He meant: "it would have been decided against me." It was also allowed that this is by substituting one of the two dals with ta', and it was said against this: it is an unsound explanation, since 'adda, ya'uddu is of the pattern nasara, as in the books of lexicography, so there is no reason for a fatha on the ta' if it were substituted for the dal. Therefore the apparent interpretation is that one of the two dals is elided for lightness. al-Hasan read with a sukun on the 'ayn like the others, and with a shadda on the dal, combining the two sakins.

"Fa-matti'uhunna" means: give them the mut'ah (provision). In the well-known understanding, it is a dir' (a shirt/tunic) and khimar (what a woman covers her head with), and milhafah (what she wraps herself in from head to foot). Perhaps it is what is today called an izar. According to al-Bada'i', this is the minimum that a woman is clothed with and covers herself with when she goes out.

It is understood from the words of Fakhr al-Islam and al-Fadil al-Barr Jundi that the custom of each town is considered regarding what a woman is clothed with when she goes out. The opinion adopted and most fitting to jurisprudence is the statement of al-Khassaf: she is judged by their condition, so if both are wealthy she receives the best of garments, if both are poor the least, and if they differ, the middle. It is obligatory for a woman divorced before consummation and seclusion, according to its proponent, for whom no valid dowry was specified in the marriage in every respect, to have a dowry that does not exceed half the equivalent dowry (mahr al-mithl) and does not fall below five dirhams. If it equals half, that is what is obligatory; if half is less than it, the lesser is obligatory, unless it falls below five dirhams, in which case five dirhams is completed for her.

In al-Bada'i' it is stated: if the value of the mut'ah is given to her, she is compelled to accept it. So the meaning of the verse, as you have heard, and the command is for obligation: "mattri'uhunna" if no dowry was assigned for them in the marriage. This is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas. As for the woman for whom a dowry was assigned, if she is divorced before touching, what is obligatory for her is half of the assigned dowry only.

As for the mut'ah, according to al-Mabsut, al-Muhit and other authoritative works, it is recommended (mustahabbah). According to some copies of al-Qaduri, and as followed by the author of al-Durar, it is also not recommended. The more likely view is that it is recommended. In the old opinion of al-Shafi'i, it is obligatory, as in the case where no dowry was assigned. It was also allowed that the verse remains on its apparent meaning, and that the intended matter is the ruling for a woman divorced before touching, whether or not a dowry was assigned for her in the marriage. "Mut'ah" is meant as provision in general, so it includes half of the assigned dowry and the mut'ah known in jurisprudence, and the command is for obligation as well. Or "mut'ah" is taken in its well-known meaning, and the command is understood to cover both obligation and recommendation.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib claimed, as narrated by 'Abd ibn Humayd, that the verse is abrogated by the verse: ﴿And if you divorce them before you have touched them, while you have already set a dowry for them, then half of what you have set﴾ [al-Baqarah: 237]. He said: so she receives half the dowry and no provision. al-Hasan and Abu al-'Aliyah denied abrogation and said: she receives half the dowry and she has provision.

Another narration, transmitted by 'Abd ibn Humayd from al-Hasan as well, states that every divorced woman has provision, whether she was consummated or not, whether a dowry was assigned or not.

Its apparent meaning claims obligation in all cases, which contradicts our position. You have known the ruling in two cases, and in the remaining two cases it is recommendation. As for the claim of abrogation, its flaws are not hidden. The apparent view is that the fa' is for ordering what follows upon what precedes. It was also said that it is fa' of explanation (fasihah), meaning: if it is as mentioned, then give them provision.

﴿And release them﴾ means: send them out of your dwellings, since you have no waiting period over them. The original sense of tasrih is that camels graze on al-sarh, which is a tree bearing fruit; then it came to mean allowing release in grazing, then for every release and sending out. ﴿A fair release﴾ means one containing good speech, free from harm and from withholding what is obligatory. It was also said: the fair release is that they do not demand from them what they gave them. al-Jubba'i said: it is the sunni (proper, in accordance with the Sunnah) divorce. This is not correct, because that is linked by 'atf (conjunction) to the provision that comes after the fa', which is ordered upon the divorce; this would require that the sunni divorce be ordered upon the divorce, and the pronoun refers to women not yet consummated, so it is not possible that this be a divorce ordered upon a previous divorce, since for women not yet consummated, a subsequent divorce cannot apply after another divorce, and moreover, if she is divorced, she is separated (bana).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 50 (part 1 of 4):

﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful to you your wives whom you have given their bridal gifts (ujur)﴾, that is, their dowries (mahr), as Mujahid and others said. The word "ajr" (wage, reward) is applied to the mahr because it is a return for enjoyment of the body and for other enjoyments permitted by marriage. The restriction of the lawfulness to giving her the prompt portion of the mahr, as is understood from the meaning of "you have given" (ataita), is not apparent; the lawfulness does not depend on it. Rather, it is to prefer what is better for him (ﷺ), for in prompt payment there is the discharge of the obligation and the contentment of the soul. For this reason the custom (sunnah) of the predecessors (salaf) was that none of them was known to do otherwise. Al-Imam said: Some people have said that the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was obligated to give the mahr first, because the woman has the right to refrain from surrendering herself until she receives the mahr, and the Prophet (ﷺ) did not demand what was not owed to him. Intercourse before the giving of the dowry is not due, although it is lawful. And how could it be otherwise, since when the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, asked for something, refusing it became unlawful; so if he asked for submission before the giving of the mahr, it would follow that it is obligatory and not obligatory, which is impossible, whereas that is not the case for any of us. End of quote. There is in this a discussion that is not hidden. Interpreting "giving" (ita') as handing over and what is in its ruling, such as stipulating it in the contract, and making the restriction a matter of preferring what is better, is also (problematic), since stipulating the mahr is better than omitting it, even though the contract is valid without it and the mahr of the equivalent (mahr al-mithl) becomes due; this is contrary to the apparent meaning.

Abu al-Hasan al-Karkhi, one of our companions (the Hanafis), used as evidence the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Indeed We have made lawful to you your wives whom you have given their wages﴾, to show that marriage is concluded with the wording of hire (ijarah), just as it is concluded with the wording of marriage (tazwij), and that the word "ijarah" is used metaphorically for it, because what is established by each of them is the ownership of a usufruct (manfa'ah), so the common element is found. It was refuted: it does not follow from calling the mahr a wage that a marriage contract is valid with the wording of hire, and the metaphor mentioned is nothing, because hire is not a cause of ownership of a usufruct so that it could be used metaphorically for it. So said the author of (al-Hidayah). Some of them said: hire is not concluded except as time-limited, and marriage requires its negation, so they are contradictory, and therefore one cannot be borrowed for the other.

It was objected: if the two contradictory things are the two accidents that cannot coexist in one locus, then the same applies to sale, since it does not combine with marriage, yet the contract with it is valid according to the companions. Moreover, the truth is that time-limitation is not the concept of the word "ijarah" nor a part of it, but a condition for its being considered valid; so it lies outside it. It is therefore simply the granting of ownership of usufructs for a consideration, except that when it occurs without qualification, it is not considered valid in the law, like the prayer, which is the known sayings and actions; if they occur without purification, they are not considered valid. And one may not say that purification is part of the concept of prayer. This is the case.

Similar to the restriction of the lawfulness of wives by what has been mentioned, it is said, is the restriction of the lawfulness of the female slave to one who has personally taken her captive (sabi), and its witness is in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿and what your right hand possesses from what Allah has granted you as spoils (afa'a)﴾. For the purchased slave, the beginning of her affair and what happened to her cannot be verified, since the captivity may not have been lawful in its origin. For this reason some scrupulous people married slave-girls by contract after purchasing them, while holding that contract with slave-women is not valid. This was raised as a difficulty regarding Mariyah the Copt, daughter of Shamʻun, may Allah be pleased with her, for she was not a captive; rather the ruler of the Copts, Jurayj ibn Mina, lord of Alexandria and Egypt, gifted her to him (ﷺ). It was answered that this objection does not arise, because gifts from people of war to the Imam have the ruling of spoils (fay'). It may be said that it is also raised regarding another concubine of his (ﷺ), who was a slave-girl that Zaynab bint Jahsh, may Allah be pleased with her, gave him as a gift. He (ﷺ) had abandoned his wives for a period over the matter of Safiyyah bint Huyayy, during Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram and Safar. When the month of Rabi' al-Awwal came, in which he passed away, and he entered upon her, she said: "I do not know what to repay you with," so she gave her to him as a gift. They counted her among his concubines, peace and blessings be upon him,
[Page 53]
and the answer mentioned does not apply to her. Perhaps the answer to this is that he, peace and blessings be upon him, took her as a concubine to explain the permissibility, and it is not far-fetched that he had verified the beginning of her affair and what happened to her, in such a way that it was as if he had personally taken her captive and witnessed it. It is also possible that she was among what Allah the Exalted granted to him, peace and blessings be upon him, as spoils, and Zaynab came to own her by some means of ownership, then she gave her to him (ﷺ).

Despite this, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, was given lawful possession of slave-women afterwards without being restricted, according to the apparent meaning, to her being among what Allah granted him as spoils, in the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Women are not lawful to you after this, nor to exchange them for other wives, even if their beauty pleases you, except what your right hand possesses﴾.

Then, the gift of this slave-girl occurred in the month of his (ﷺ) death, and the verse was revealed before that, for it was revealed either in the year of the Confederates (al-Ahzab), which is the fifth year of the Hijrah, or after the conquest (al-Fath), which is the eighth year of it. On this basis, what happened concerning Mariyah precedes the revelation of the verse, because she was sent to him (ﷺ) in the seventh year of the Hijrah, for in that year he, peace and blessings be upon him, sent his messengers to the kings, among them Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah al-Lakhmi, whom he sent to al-Muqawqis, ruler of the Copts mentioned above. He came back from him with Mariyah, her sister Sirin, a brother or cousin of hers who was a eunuch called Mabur, a mule called Duldul, a donkey called Ya'fur or 'Afir, a thousand mithqals of gold, and other things. So reflect.

Similar to what has been mentioned, it is said, is the restriction of the female relatives to being emigrants with him (ﷺ), in the words of Allah the Glorified: ﴿and the daughters of your paternal uncles, the daughters of your paternal aunts, the daughters of your maternal uncles, and the daughters of your maternal aunts, who emigrated with you﴾. They are better than others. The "with" (ma'iyyah) indicates sharing in the emigration, not contemporaneity in time, like "I embraced Islam with Sulayman." Abu Hayyan said: It is said "so-and-so entered with me and went out with me," meaning his deed was like my deed, even if we did not coincide in time. If you say "we went out together," both meanings are implied: sharing in the action and coinciding in time, and that is a fine expression. Al-Mawardi reported an opinion that emigration is a condition for the lawfulness of wives absolutely, and it is very weak; and another opinion that it is a condition for the lawfulness of his (ﷺ) mentioned relatives. Evidence for this was taken from what Ibn Sa'd, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi (who graded it sound), Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim (who authenticated it), Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi transmitted from Umm Hani Fakhitah bint Abi Talib, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) proposed to me, and I excused myself to him, and he excused me. Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful to you your wives﴾ up to His words: ﴿who emigrated with you﴾." She said: "So I was not lawful to him, because I had not emigrated with him; I was among the freed ones (al-Tulaqa')."

It was answered: the non-lawfulness due to lack of emigration was only understood from the words of Umm Hani. Perhaps she said that according to her understanding of the verse, and that does not stand as proof against us unless it is transmitted from the Prophet (ﷺ). One may not say: Ibn Sa'd transmitted from Abu Salih, client of Umm Hani, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) proposed to Umm Hani bint Abi Talib, and she said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I am a widow and my children are young.' When her children grew up, she offered herself to him, peace and blessings be upon him, and he said: 'As for now, no. Allah the Exalted has revealed to me: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful to you your wives﴾ up to ﴿who emigrated with you﴾'" — and she was not among the emigrants. This indicates that he himself understood the prohibition; otherwise he would have married her. For we say, after granting the soundness of the report: we do not grant that he (ﷺ) understood the prohibition, and his not marrying her may be because it was contrary to what is better. The report of Umm Hani also indicates that this verse was revealed after the conquest, so do not be careless.

Some have claimed that the prohibition of marrying non-emigrant women to him (ﷺ) was first and then abrogated (naskh). It is related from Qatadah that the meaning of ﴿who emigrated with you﴾ is "who embraced Islam with you." It was said: On this basis, what is forbidden to him, peace and blessings be upon him, is only the disbelieving women, and this is extremely far-fetched, as is not hidden. The apparent meaning is that by "your wives whom you have given their bridal gifts"
[Page 54]
are meant his wives (ﷺ) who were under his protection and to whom he had given their mahr, such as Aishah, Hafsah and Sawdah; and by "what your right hand possesses from what Allah has granted you as spoils," such as Rayhanah, based on what Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: when he (ﷺ) conquered Qurayzah, he chose her for himself, and she remained with him until she died while in his ownership; and others agreed with him on this.

Al-Waqidi transmitted with his chain to Ayyub ibn Bashir, who said: "He, peace and blessings be upon him, sent her to the house of Salma bint Qays, mother of al-Mundhir, and she stayed with her until she menstruated and then became pure from her menstruation. Then Umm al-Mundhir came and informed the Prophet (ﷺ), and he came to her in the house of Umm al-Mundhir and said to her: 'If you wish, I will free you and marry you; and if you wish to remain in my ownership, I will have intercourse with you by ownership.' She said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I would like to lighten your burden and to remain in your ownership.' So she was in the ownership of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he would have intercourse with her until she died."

Some scholars held that the Prophet (ﷺ) manumitted her and married her. Al-Waqidi also reported this from Ibn Abi Dhi'b, from al-Zuhri, and then said: "This report is more firmly established according to us." It is also related from her that she said: "When the Banu Qurayza were taken captive, the captives were presented to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and I was among those presented to him. He ordered that I be set aside. He had the choice of every spoils (safi, the portion reserved for the leader), and when I was set aside, Allah chose for me. He sent me to the house of Umm al-Mundhir bint Qays for some days, until the prisoners were killed and the captives were distributed. Then he (ﷺ) entered upon me, and I withdrew from him out of modesty. He called me and seated me before him and said: 'If you choose Allah and His Messenger, the Messenger of Allah will choose you for himself.' I said: 'I choose Allah and His Messenger.' When I embraced Islam, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) manumitted me and married me, and he gave me a dowry of twelve ounces of gold, as he gave dowries to his wives. He held the wedding feast for me in the house of Umm al-Mundhir, he would divide (his time) for me as he divided it for his wives, and he placed the veil upon me." Ibn al-Athir mentioned only the view of manumission and marriage. Some held that she embraced Islam, and the Prophet (ﷺ) manumitted her, so she joined her people, and she used to veil herself among them and say: "No one shall see me after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Her joining her people is related from al-Zuhri. Some claimed that she remained alive after him (ﷺ) and died in the sixteenth year of the Hijra, during the caliphate of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him).

Ibn Kamal, in his tafsir, for the explanation of the relative clause (al-mawsul, the relative pronoun in the verse), mentioned Safiyya and Juwayriya. What is mentioned in most authoritative works concerning these two is that when the captives of Khaybar were gathered, Dihya took Safiyya. The Prophet (ﷺ) had said to him: "Go and take a (different) slave-girl." Then he (ﷺ) informed him that she was fit only for him, because she was the daughter of the chief of her people. So he said to Dihya: "Take another instead of her." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) took her, manumitted her, and married her, and her dowry was her own freedom. And concerning Juwayriya: during the expedition of Banu al-Mustaliq she fell to the share of Thabit ibn Qays ibn Shammas al-Ansari, and she made a contract of manumission (kitaba) with him for her own freedom. Then she came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I am Juwayriya bint al-Harith, and what has happened to me is not hidden from you. I fell to the share of Thabit ibn Qays, and I have made a contract for my freedom, so I have come to ask you for help with it." He (ﷺ) said: "Would you like something better than that?" She said: "And what is it, O Messenger of Allah?" He said: "I will pay your contract on your behalf, and I will marry you." She said: "I accept."

Ibn Hisham said: It is said that he (ﷺ) bought her from Thabit, manumitted her, married her, and gave her a dowry of four hundred dirhams.

It is not hidden from you that if the intended meaning is the permissibility of what his right hand possessed (ﷺ) at the moment of ownership, insofar as it was his property, even if no intercourse actually took place, then all the slave-girls he owned at the time of ownership are included. The subsequent manumission and marriage do no harm, and intercourse became lawful through marriage, not through ownership. But if the intended meaning is the permissibility of that together with actual intercourse, and the attribute of ownership remains, then the relative clause can be explained only by a slave-woman with whom he (ﷺ) had intercourse while she was his property, such as Rayhana according to one opinion, and a slave-girl he acquired among some of the captives, whom they counted among his concubines (ﷺ). Most (scholars) did not mention her name. Al-Jalabi counted among the concubines of the Prophet (ﷺ) a slave-girl whom he named Zulaykha al-Qurayziyya, so perhaps she is the one who was not named. (He also counted) Mariya al-Qibtiyya, and the slave-girl whom Zaynab gave to him (ﷺ). You have heard the discussion about these two earlier.

By "the daughters of his paternal uncles and the daughters of his paternal aunts" is meant the daughters of Qurashi men and the daughters of Qurashi women. For Qurashi men, whether near or distant, are called his paternal uncles (ﷺ), and for Qurashi women, whether near or distant, they are called his paternal aunts (ﷺ). By "the daughters of his maternal uncle and the daughters of his maternal aunts" is meant the daughters of the Banu Zuhra, males and females. This is the view of al-Tabarsi in Majma' al-Bayan, and he mentioned no other. The application of "paternal uncles" and "paternal aunts" to a person's relatives on his father's side, male and female, near or distant, and of "maternal uncles" and "maternal aunts" to his relatives on his mother's side in the same way, is common in usage and widespread in practice.

The women whom he (ﷺ) married and with whom he consummated the marriage from among the Qurashi women were six. His marriage to some of them was certainly before the revelation of the verse. His marriage to the rest is open to being either before or after, as will not be hidden from anyone who consults the books of biography and hears what has been said about the time of the revelation of the verse. We have not found that he (ﷺ) married anyone from the Zuhriyyat at all. So, by the permission of marrying those (women), what is meant is merely its permissibility, and that does not require that it actually occurred.

If "paternal uncle" is taken to mean the brother of the father, "paternal aunt" his sister, "maternal uncle" the brother of the mother, and "maternal aunt" her sister, then the apparent meaning of the verse requires that he (ﷺ) have paternal uncles, paternal aunts, maternal uncles, and maternal aunts of this kind, and that they have daughters. This is well known regarding the paternal uncles and paternal aunts and their daughters. The majority of the people of biography mention a number of his paternal uncles and a number of their daughters, such as al-Abbas. Among his daughters was Umm Habiba, whom Aswad al-Makhzumi married. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had proposed to her, according to what has been said, but he found that her father was his foster brother, whom Thuwayba, the freedwoman of Abu Lahab, had nursed along with him. Among them was also Abu Talib. Among his daughters was Umm Hani, and you have heard what has been said about her. Jumana was one of those who pledged allegiance to him (ﷺ), and she was under Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith, her paternal cousin. And Abu Lahab; among his daughters was Khalida, whom Uthman ibn Abi al-As al-Thaqafi married, and she bore him children. Durra embraced Islam and emigrated; she was under al-Harith ibn Nawfal, then under Dihya al-Kalbi. Azza was married to Awfa ibn Umayya. And (there was) al-Zubayr, among whose daughters were Dubaa, wife of al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, and Umm al-Hakam, who is said to have been his (ﷺ) foster sister, and he used to visit her in Madina. And (there was) Hamza, among whose daughters was Umama. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came back from the Umrat al-Qada', he brought her from Makka and married her to Salama, the son of Umm Salama. The implication of al-Qastallani's statement is that Hamza was his (ﷺ) foster brother, whom Thuwayba nursed with the milk of her son Masruh, and that she is not lawful for him (ﷺ). Rather, he himself also mentioned that she was presented to him and he said: "She is the daughter of my foster brother." And (there was) al-Harith, among whose daughters was Aruwa, wife of Abu Wada'a. And (there was) al-Muqawwim, among whose daughters was one also named Aruwa, wife of her paternal cousin Abu Sufyan ibn al-Harith.

They also mentioned for him (ﷺ) a number of paternal aunts and a number of their daughters. Among them was Umayma, and among her daughters was Zaynab, the Mother of the Believers, and she is the one concerning whom the words of Allah, the Exalted, were revealed: ﴿So when Zayd had no longer any need of her, We gave her to you in marriage﴾ [al-Ahzab: 37]. And Umm Habiba, who was the wife of Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf. And Hamna, who was with Mus'ab ibn Umayr, then with Talha, one of the ten (promised paradise). Among them was al-Bayda', and among her daughters was Aruwa, the mother of Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him), and Umm Talha, the two daughters of Kurayz ibn Rabi'a. Among them was Atika, and among her daughters was Qurayba bint Zad al-Rakib, Abu Umayya ibn al-Mughira. Among them was Safiyya, and among her daughters was Safiyya bint al-Harith ibn Haritha, and Umm Habiba bint al-Awwam ibn Khuwaylid.

As for the maternal uncle and maternal aunt, their mention is not well known. Yes, it is mentioned in al-Isaba: "Furay'a bint Wahb al-Zuhriyya, whom the Prophet (ﷺ) raised (in status) and said: 'Whoever wishes to look at the maternal aunt of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), let him look at this one.'" In it also: Fakhita bint Amr al-Zuhriyya, the maternal aunt of the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Tabarani related through the chain of Abd al-Rahman ibn Uthman al-Waqqasi, from Ibn al-Munkadir, "from Jabir: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: 'I gave my maternal aunt Fakhita bint Amr a slave boy, and I instructed her not to make him a butcher, nor a goldsmith, nor a cupper.'" Al-Waqqasi is weak.

And concerning Safiyya bint Abd al-Muttalib, it is said: she is the full sister of Hamza; their mother was Hala, the maternal aunt of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that is, Hala bint Wahb, as in al-Mawahib. We have not found for this maternal aunt any daughter other than Safiyya, his (ﷺ) paternal aunt. Likewise, we have not found daughters for those we mentioned before her. We have identified only one maternal uncle of his (ﷺ), namely Abd Yaghuth ibn Wahb, and we have not found a daughter of his. We have only found two sons: one of them is al-Arqam, who has a son named Abd Allah, who was a Companion who wrote for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and for his two companions. He was in charge of the public treasury in the caliphate of Umar (may Allah be pleased with him), and he was very dear to him, to the extent that Hafsa related from him that he said to her: "Were it not that your people would object to me, I would have appointed Abd Allah ibn al-Arqam as caliph." It is also said: he is the son of Abd Yaghuth, and al-Arqam is Abd Yaghuth. Al-Bukhari (agrees) with what we have said. He embraced Islam on the day of the Conquest. Some said of him: "the maternal uncle of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." Some people mentioned for this Abd Allah a brother whom they named Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Arqam and attributed companionship to him, but there is discussion about that. The second is al-Aswad, and the Prophet (ﷺ) applied to him the title of maternal uncle. It is related that he was one of those who mocked him (ﷺ), and Jibril (peace be upon him) intended to destroy him, but the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Jibril, my maternal uncle!" He said: "Leave him alone." He had a son, Abd al-Rahman, and a daughter, Khalida, who was among the righteous emigrant women, and he also applied to her the title of maternal aunt.

Al-Mustaghfiri related through the chain of Abu Umayr al-Jurmi, from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, from Ubayd Allah, as a mursal (report lacking a companion in its chain), that he said: "The Prophet (ﷺ) entered his house and saw a woman with Aisha. He said: 'Who is this, O Aisha?' She said: 'She is one of your maternal aunts.' He said: 'My maternal aunts in this land are strangers.' She said: 'This is Khalida bint al-Aswad ibn Abd Yaghuth.' He said: 'Glory be to the One who brings the living out of the dead,' reading it with emphasis (as mutaqqala)."

Musa ibn Ibrahim related from his father, from Abu Salama, from Aisha, a connected report similar to it. In this report and the one before it, "maternal uncle" and "maternal aunt" are applied to relatives on the mother's side, even if the maternal uncle is not her brother and the maternal aunt is not her sister. By this, what we mentioned earlier is confirmed, so remember that. And Allah, the Exalted, guides you. Beware lest you suppose that the matter is a matter of fard (an unquestioned rule), or that the address, although specific in appearance, is general in reality, so that the existence of daughters of paternal uncles and daughters of maternal aunts for other than him (ﷺ) suffices, as those supposes who are deceived by ignorance and confirm the maternal uncle by a lack of intelligence.

Now, the question has been frequently asked about the wisdom behind the singular form for "paternal uncle" and "maternal uncle," while "paternal aunt" and "maternal aunt" are in the plural. Al-Subki, as it is said, wrote a treatise on this called (al-Himma fi Ifrad al-Amm wa Jam' al-Amma).

Al-Khafaji said: I have seen among them weak statements concerning it, such as the statement of al-Razi that "al-amm" and "al-khal" are of the form of the verbal noun (masdar), and therefore they were not pluralized, unlike "al-amma" and "al-khala." It was also said that they were not pluralized so that they would be general when made into an idafa (construct), while "al-amma" and "al-khala" are not general because of the ta' of unity, and although it does not prevent generality in reality, it apparently contradicts it. And the words of Allah, the Exalted, in Surat al-Nur do not contradict it: ﴿the houses of your paternal uncles or the houses of your paternal aunts﴾ [al-Nur: 61], because it is according to the original form. Then he said: "Better than this is what has been said: that his (ﷺ) paternal uncles, al-Abbas and Hamza (may Allah be pleased with them both), were his foster brothers, and their daughters are not lawful for him; and that Abu Talib's daughter Umm Hani was not an emigrant." (End of quotation.) As for what he claimed to be weak, it is as he said. And as for what he claimed to be better than it, if it is as we have quoted it, without omission of anything as we found it in our copy, then there is nothing good in it, let alone being better. And if it has a continuation, then consideration of it, after having seen it, is up to you. I think, with all due respect, that it is not worth anything.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 50 (part 3 of 4):

One of the eminent contemporary scholars, the verifying (muhaqqiq) ulama, may Allah keep his time happy and his excellence ahead of his peers, said: It is possible that the singular "paternal uncle" (ʿamm) is used because he is in the position of a father; indeed, the word "father" (ab) is sometimes applied to him, and among its uses is in the saying of Allah, ﴿And when Abraham said to his father Azar﴾ [al-Anʿam: 74]. A father is only one, so the singular is more fitting for the one who occupies his position. The plural of "paternal aunt" (ʿamma) is according to the original form, and the singular of "maternal uncle" (khal) is so that it accords with the paternal uncle, while the plural of "maternal aunt" (khala), although she is in the position of a mother, is so that it accords with the paternal aunts. It is also possible that the singular of the masculine and the plural of the feminine is for the fewness of males and the abundance of females, and reports have indeed come that women are more numerous than men.

Another of those eminent scholars said, may the halls of knowledge never cease to be adorned by him and to give thanks for his favour: This is because of the verbal beauty in it, for between ʿamm and ʿammat, and between khal and khalat, there is a kind of paronomasia (jinas). And because his paternal uncles, upon him be prayer and peace, were, as mentioned by the author of (Dhakhaʾir al-ʿUqba), twelve uncles, and his paternal aunts were six. Had it been said "aʿmamika" (your uncles), it would be imagined that they were fewer than twelve, since it is a plural of paucity (jamʿ qilla), and the most that could be applied to it would be nine or ten according to one opinion. And had it been said "ʿammatika" (your aunt), the indication of their fewness would not have been established. Therefore the singular "ʿamm" was used and "ʿamma" was made plural. It was also said that "khalika wa khalatika" is used to agree with what precedes it.

I say: What predominates in my estimation regarding this is what Abu Hayyan related from the judge Abu Bakr ibn al-ʿArabi, that what was mentioned is a linguistic custom (ʿurf lughawi), in the sense that the custom of the lexicographers in such cases went on with the singular for ʿamm and khal and the plural for ʿamma and khala. We have followed up many of the poetry of the Arabs and have not found ʿamm when attributed to a son or daughter (ibn or bint) except in the singular or plural form, except singular, such as his saying:

Shaqiq came, carrying his spear across; indeed, the sons of your paternal uncle have spears among them.

And his saying:

A young man who is not to his paternal cousin like the wolf: if he sees his companion's blood one day, he devours it.

And his saying:

The daughters of the paternal uncle said, "O Salma, even if he is poor and destitute," she said, "even if..."

And his saying:

O daughter of my uncle, do not blame me and sleep, for my bed does not leave you one day.

And other examples beyond counting in number. As for the consistency of the singular of khal and the plural of ʿamma and khala when they are annexed to what has been mentioned, I am not confident of its matter. So if the matter in the mentioned cases is like the matter in ʿamm, then there is no answer beyond this answer.

The judgment of the judge is presumed to have been made only on clear evidence. Yet I do not absolutely state that a judge's ruling based on his own knowledge is unacceptable, nor do I issue a fatwa to that effect. Indeed, this judge has a well-known ruling concerning al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with him; may whoever was pleased with his killing be cursed, and no one approves of it except Yazid, may Allah increase his severe punishment.

And on the assumption that the matter regarding ʿamm and those with him is as he said, it is possible that the motive for the singular of ʿamm and khal is a return to a single origin, together with what exists among the males in terms of paternal and maternal kinship regarding the person related through them, of support and mutual aid. Therefore you see the person rushing to repel his affliction to the male paternal and maternal relatives, and that mutual support makes the plural as the singular in ruling. This consideration is strengthened there by the annexing of the offspring, such as "the sons and daughters," to that. Perhaps in the singular together with the plural of the annexed noun there is an indication that the sons and daughters, although they are sons and daughters of many persons in reality, are in the ruling of the sons and daughters of one person, and that each of the paternal and maternal uncles, because of his great compassion for the children of each, is as if he were a father to the children of each. What we have mentioned does not exist for the paternal aunts and maternal aunts. The plural of ʿamm and khal in the verse of al-Nur does not object to this, as is not hidden from one who has even a little light by which he is guided when matters become unclear.

It may be said regarding the wisdom here specifically: since the singular is the origin and the plural its branch, and the masculine is the origin and the feminine its branch, the masculine paternal and maternal uncles were brought in the singular, and the feminine paternal and maternal aunts in the plural. Thus two origins were combined in the first two and two branches in the latter two, by the ruling that a similar thing is attracted to its like, and that birds fall upon their own kind. How subtle is this gathering in the seat of the marriage occasion, for in it is an indication of equality (kafaʾa), and that the fitting thing is to join a kind to its own kind, as some verses require. And by my life, this is subtler than the plural of the masculine and singular of the feminine, so that each origin and branch are gathered together, and it agrees with what is in marriage of the gathering of a male, who is an origin, and a female, who is a branch. It is free of an indication to that fitting, pleasing union which is approved by every person of correct judgment. Moreover, in the plural of two origins in ʿamm there is agreement with what is in marriage of the gathering of the spouses, who are two origins, because of what is born from them. And if their gathering is considered in khal, whose kinship is through the mother, which is not counted in lineage, it agrees with the whole with what is in marriage of the gathering of an origin and a branch. Thus that is not lost entirely from the sublime composition.

Also, the shift from the singular to the plural in the sides of paternal and maternal kinship is an indication of what is in marriage of the transition of each of the husband and wife from the state of separation to the state of union. So may Allah the Exalted be praised for the sublimity of the revelation. This is what I have, and it is a spring flower that does not bear rubbing. Nevertheless, measure it against what you have heard from our contemporary masters, and choose for yourself what is pleasing. And Allah the Exalted knows best the secrets of His Book.

﴿And a believing woman﴾ in the accusative, as a conjunction to the object of "We have made lawful" (aḥlalnā) according to a group. The meaning of "We have made lawful" is neither the creation of an immediate lawfulness, nor a report of a past making lawful, but rather a notification of absolute permission encompassing what preceded and what follows, so the condition does not disturb that. This is like when you say, "I have permitted you to speak to so-and-so if he greets you." Because of the discussion in it, some said: it is governed by a verb that the preceding clause explains, that is, "and He makes lawful for you a woman" or "and We have made lawful for you a woman," and it is in the future because of the position of the condition. Abu Haywa read it in the nominative, on the basis that it is a subject (mubtada) and the predicate is omitted, that is, "and a believing woman, We have made her lawful for you too."

﴿If she gives herself to the Prophet﴾, that is, she grants him the enjoyment of her by whatever expression, without a dower. Ubayy, al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi, ʿIsa and Salam read "an wahabat" with the hamza opened, that is, "because she gave." It was also said: "whenever she gave" or "the period during which she gave," so that "an" and what follows it are in the sense of a verbal noun in the accusative of time. Most grammarians do not permit this except with the explicit verbal noun, such as "I will come to you at the emergence of the star," and not with the masdariyya particle. It is also permitted that the verbal noun be a substitute (badal) for "woman." Zayd ibn ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "idh wahabat," with "idh" an adverb of past time. It was also said: it is like it in the saying of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And it will not benefit you today, since you did wrong, that you are in the punishment sharing it﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 39].

﴿If the Prophet desires to take her in marriage﴾, that is, to possess the enjoyment of her by whatever expression, without a dower. This is a condition upon the first condition for the entitlement to lawfulness. So her giving herself to him, upon him be prayers and peace, does not make her lawful for him except with his desire to marry her, and this desire takes the place of accepting the gift. Ibn Kamal said: the desire mentioned is an expression for acceptance, and there is no way to take it literally, because the saying of Allah the Exalted, ﴿yastankihahā﴾ (he seeks to marry her), suffices from desire by its lexical meaning, and this indicates that the sin is for request (sīn lil-ṭalab). The statement of a certain eminent scholar on this, where he said: "the desire to seek marriage is a metonymy for acceptance," agrees.

It was said: "istafʿala" here is in the sense of "faʿala," so that "istinkāḥ" means "nikāḥ," lest repetition be imagined. In this there is an examination. The proponent of this view preferred to take the desire as the desire preceding the gift, on the basis that the construction requires the precedence of this condition. The scholars have said: if two conditions are combined, the second is a condition upon the first, later in wording but earlier in occurrence, and it is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl). From here the jurists said: if he says, "If you ride, if you eat, then you are divorced," she is not divorced unless eating precedes riding, so that the restriction of the circumstantial state is realized.

Al-Samin questioned this rule with respect to what is here, on the basis that they made that condition equivalent to acceptance, since the occurrence requires that. Then he mentioned that he presented it to the scholars of his age, and they found no escape from it except by saying that this rule is not universal but specific to cases where no indication establishes the lateness of the second, as in the case of "If I marry you, if I divorce you, then my slave is free," for divorce does not precede marriage, and what we are dealing with is of this kind. Then he said: whoever makes the second condition here prior has not been correct. I saw in the seventh section of (al-Ashbah wa al-Naza'ir al-Nahwiyya) of al-Jalal al-Suyuti, may Allah have mercy on him, a discussion by Ibn Hisham in which he mentioned that making the verse like the example, and placing them together under the issue of the objection of a condition to a condition, is what a group went to, among them Ibn Malik. He himself went to the view that the example belongs to the matter of the mentioned objection and not the verse, and he argued for it with what he argued. Then he mentioned the disagreement concerning the validity of the construction in which the objection occurs, like the example, and that the majority hold it permissible, and this is the correct view. The permitters differed about the determination of what the consequent that follows the two conditions is realized by, in three views:

The first: that it is realized only by the combination of two matters: one, the occurrence of each of the two conditions; the other, that the second condition occurs before the first. So in the example, divorce occurs only with the occurrence of riding and eating, with eating preceding riding in occurrence. He mentioned that this is the view of the majority.

The second: that it occurs by the occurrence of the two conditions absolutely. He mentioned that some scholars related this to him from Imam al-Haramayn, and that he later saw it related from others.

The third: that it occurs by the occurrence of the two conditions in order, so in the example she is divorced only if she rides first and then eats. He refuted each of the last two views.

For the construction on the first view he mentioned two positions:

The first: the view of the majority, that the consequent mentioned is for the first condition, and the consequent of the second is omitted, because of the indication of the first and its consequent upon it, and because that suffices for it and stands in its place. It follows that for the conditional to occur upon that, the second must occur before the first, since the consequent must necessarily come after the condition; thus the matter is the same for what stands in the place of the condition.

The second: the view of Ibn Malik, that the consequent mentioned is for the first, and the second has no consequent, neither mentioned nor assumed, because it restricts the first by a circumstantial state occurring in its place. So the meaning in the example is: "If you ride while eating, then you are divorced." In this there is that it departs from analogy, that it does not hold in "If you stand, if you sit, then you are divorced," and that the condition is remote from the view of the circumstantial state because of the future tense.

In sum, he extended the discussion on this matter, which is a famous issue mentioned by the scholars of legal theory and others, and what we have mentioned in it suffices here for the least that is necessary. So reflect.

Most scholars hold that the gift occurred, and they differed in identifying the woman who gave. According to Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada and ʿIkrima, she is Maymuna bint al-Harith al-Hilaliyya. In al-Mawahib it is said that Maymuna gave herself to the Prophet ﷺ, and that this is because his proposal reached her while she was on her camel, and she said, "The camel and what is on it belong to Allah and His Messenger ﷺ." This was in the seventh year after the battle of Khaybar, and he built with her at Sarif, ten miles from Mecca. According to this, the desire for marriage preceded the gift, and thus the statement of al-Samin is refuted.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 50 (part 4 of 4):

And on the authority of ʿAli ibn al-Husayn (may Allah be pleased with them both), al-Dahhak and Muqatil: she was Umm Sharik Ghaziyyah bint Jabir ibn Hakim al-Dawsiyyah. In al-Safwa (al-Safwa, a work of tafsir), it is said: "The majority hold that she is the one who offered herself in marriage to the Prophet ﷺ, but he did not accept her, so she did not marry until she died." In al-Durr al-Manthur (al-Durr al-Manthur, a work of tafsir), on the authority of Munir ibn Abd Allah al-Dawsi, it is reported that he, peace and blessings be upon him, did accept her.

And on the authority of ʿUrwa and al-Shaʿbi: she was Zaynab bint Khuzayma from the Ansar. In the pre-Islamic period she was called Umm al-Masakin (Mother of the Poor) because of her feeding them. This took place in the third year [after the Hijra], and she did not remain with him ﷺ except briefly, until she died, may Allah be pleased with her.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan related on the authority of ʿAʾisha (may Allah be pleased with her) that she said: "The one who offered herself to the Prophet ﷺ was Khawla bint Hakim, and he, peace and blessings be upon him, deferred her, so ʿUthman ibn Maz'un married her with his permission ﷺ."

Some have said: it is permissible that there were several women who offered themselves, for al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim) and others related on the authority of ʿUrwa ibn al-Zubayr that he said: "Khawla bint Hakim was among those women who offered themselves to the Prophet ﷺ." Then ʿAʾisha said: "Does a woman not feel shame to offer herself to a man?" Then, when the verse was revealed:

﴿You may postpone whom you will of them﴾. Aisha said: "O Messenger of Allah, I see that your Lord hastens to fulfil your desire." His words ﴿of those women who gave themselves﴾ are explicit that there were several of them. Some scholars denied that any gift actually took place. It was also said that His words ﴿if a woman gives herself﴾ indicate that the gift had not occurred and was only a hypothetical matter. Likewise, the indefinite ﴿a woman﴾ means that the purpose is to inform of the permissibility in this case, if it should occur. Some denied that it was accepted.

Ibn Sa'd related from Ibn Abi 'Awn that Layla bint al-Khatim gave herself to the Prophet ﷺ, and women gave themselves, but we have not heard that the Prophet ﷺ accepted any of them. What Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan related from Ibn Abbas, who said: "There was never a woman with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ who had given herself to him." This may mean that he did not accept, and it may mean that no gift was made. The mention of him ﷺ in both places by the title of prophethood, through a shift of expression, is for honour and to indicate that this is the basis for the establishment of the ruling. Thus it is specific to him, peace and blessings be upon him, in accordance with the specificity of the matter to him, as His words indicate: ﴿exclusively for you, apart from the believers﴾. This also implies that the giving of herself by a woman who gives was not out of greed for men or the fulfilment of desire, but in pursuit of the honour of serving him ﷺ and of dwelling in the source of virtue. From this it is known that the words of Aisha, "There is no woman who gave herself to a man who is better," and likewise her earlier objection, arose from the intensity of her jealousy, may Allah be pleased with her, towards the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. There is nothing strange in this, for the lover is jealous. Some lovers have said:

"I am jealous when I perceive a sigh in the quarter,
out of fear and dread that it may be for his love."

The accusative of ﴿exclusively﴾ is a verbal noun emphasising the sentence before it. Its agent, in verbal nouns, according to al-Zamakhshari, is not rare, like "al-'afiyah" and "al-kadhibah". Abu Hayyan claimed that it is rare. The more common view is that it relates to the permissibility of the woman who gives, meaning: its permissibility became exclusively for you, a pure exclusivity. Al-Zajjaj said it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from ﴿a woman﴾ because it is specified by the description, meaning: We made her lawful for you exclusively, not lawful for anyone other than you, in this world and the Hereafter. Abu al-Baqa' said it is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ﴿gave﴾, or an adjective of an omitted verbal noun, meaning: a gift that is exclusive.

It is also read in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: that is an exclusivity and a particularity for you, or: she, that woman, or the gift, is exclusive to you, not exceeding the believers.

The Shafi'is, may Allah be pleased with them, used this verse as evidence that marriage (nikah) is not concluded by the wording of a gift (hibah), because the wording follows the meaning, and since the meaning was specified for him, peace and blessings be upon him, the wording is also specified. One of the eminent scholars of our school said regarding this: the intended meaning of gift in the verse is the transfer of enjoyment without compensation, by any wording, not the transfer of it by the words "I have given myself." Since this is not explicit in transferring by this wording, it is not suitable to be the basis for the dispute about whether marriage is concluded by the wording of gift, either affirmatively or negatively. The meaning of the exclusivity of the permission mentioned for him, apart from the believers, is that it is realised in his case and not realised in theirs, since for them there must be the customary dower (mahr al-mithl).

The apparent sense of the words of the great scholar Ibn al-Humam is that the wording of gift is taken into account. He said in al-Fath: "Marriage has been reported with the wording of gift," and he cited the verse, then said: "The original position is the absence of specificity until evidence for it is established." His words ﴿exclusively for you﴾ refer to the absence of a dower, by the indication of its being followed by the explanation of the removal of hardship, since hardship does not lie in abandoning one wording for another, especially for the most eloquent of the Arabs, but in the obligation of wealth. And by the indication of its occurring in contrast to ﴿those whose dowers you have given﴾. The result is: We made lawful for you the wives whose dowers you have given, and the woman who gave herself to you without taking a dower, this quality is exclusively yours, apart from the believers. As for them, We have known what We have imposed upon them regarding their wives, etc., of dower and other matters.

Sadr al-Shari'a suggested the permissibility of its being connected to ﴿We have made lawful﴾ as a restriction on the lawfulness of his wives for him, to indicate that they are not lawful for anyone other than him, peace and blessings be upon him, and he concluded.

Some permitted that it be a restriction on the lawfulness of the female slaves also, to indicate that his female slaves, like his wives, are not lawful for anyone after him, peace and blessings be upon him. Others held that it is a restriction on the lawfulness of all that was mentioned before, meaning: the permission of what We have made lawful for you of those mentioned, under the stated restrictions, is exclusive to you, apart from the believers, because the permission of all of them under the stated restrictions is not realised for them; rather, what is realised for him is the permission of some of the enumerated under the known manner. Al-Zamakhshari chose this view.

In any case, His words ﴿We have known what We have imposed upon them regarding their wives and what their right hands possess﴾ are an interjection between the connected and the connected-to. The first, under all the aspects, is His words: ﴿so that there may be no hardship upon you﴾. The second, under the last aspect, which is the connection of ﴿exclusively﴾ to all the four permissions previously mentioned, is His words ﴿exclusively﴾, which emphasises the meaning of his exclusivity in what he was specified with, in that each of the exclusivities is from knowledge, and that this privilege is befitting only to the station of prophethood. So the meaning is: Allah, exalted is He, has known what is fitting from the standpoint of wisdom to impose upon the believers regarding wives and female slaves, and to what extent and manner it should be imposed upon them. So He imposed it, and He singled you out, glorified be He, with purity and the choice of what is better and more excellent in your worldly life, in that He, majestic is His majesty, made lawful for you categories of women to marry, and added for you the woman who gives herself without compensation, so that there would be no constraint upon you in your religion. The third, under the first aspect we mentioned, which is the connection of ﴿exclusively﴾ to the woman who gives alone, is His words, mighty and majestic: ﴿We have made lawful﴾. This is what Abu Hayyan preferred, and the matter of the interjection is in its own context. Some made the connected-to ﴿exclusively﴾ under all the other aspects, and the connection to it is by consideration of what it contains of the meaning of the establishment and realisation of the permission for him, peace and blessings be upon him, not by consideration of its being specific to him, because the basis for the removal of hardship is the first, not the second, which is an expression for its non-establishment for anyone other than him, peace and blessings be upon him.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: "His words ﴿so that﴾ and so on are connected to an omitted element, meaning: We explained this explanation and clarified this clarification, so that there may be no hardship upon you and it may not be supposed of you that you have sinned before your Lord, mighty and majestic. So there is no objection to this, though it is not free of objection. So reflect, and do not be heedless."

﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving﴾, that is, of abundant forgiveness, so He forgives whatever He wills of what is hard to guard against and other things, ﴿Merciful﴾, that is, of abundant mercy. And of His mercy, glorified be He, is that He widened the matter in the places where hardship might fall.

﴿You may postpone whom you will of them﴾, that is, you may delay whom you will of your wives and leave off lying with her, ﴿and take to yourself whom you will﴾, and bring close to you whom you will of them and lie with her. This was related from Qatada, and from Ibn Abbas and al-Hasan: that is, you may divorce whom you will of them and keep whom you will. Some said: the postponing and the taking-in, in their unrestricted form, encompass what is in both interpretations and what is mentioned in them, for that is only by way of example, and it is not without merit. In a report from al-Hasan, the pronoun in ﴿of them﴾ refers to the women of the Ummah, and the meaning is: you leave off marrying whom you will of the women of your Ummah, and you marry whom you will of them. He said: when he ﷺ proposed to a woman, it was not permissible for anyone else to propose to her until he left her.

From Zayd ibn Aslam and al-Tabari: it refers to the women who gave themselves, that is, you accept whom you will of the believing women who give themselves to you, and take them to yourself, and leave off whom you will of them, so you do not accept her. From al-Sha'bi is what this requires, for Ibn Sa'd and al-Bayhaqi in al-Sunan and others related from him, who said: "There were women who gave themselves to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He lay with some of them and postponed some of them, and they did not come near him until he, peace and blessings be upon him, passed away, and they were not married after him. Among them was Umm Sharik." That is the meaning of His words: ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them and take to yourself whom you will﴾. What supports the earlier point that it refers to the wives is what Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim and others related from Abu Razin, who said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ intended to divorce some of his wives. When they saw that, they came to him and said: Do not release us, and you are free in what is between us and you. Impose upon us from yourself and your wealth whatever you wish." So Allah, exalted is He, revealed the verse. He postponed some of them, and among those he postponed were Maymunah, Juwayriyah, Umm Habibah, Safiyyah and Sawdah. And among those he took to himself were Aisha, Hafsah, Umm Salamah and Zaynab, may Allah be pleased with them all."

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read ﴿tur'ji'﴾ with a hamzah, and according to al-Zajjaj this is better, though the meaning is the same.

﴿And whoever you seek﴾, that is, you desire, ﴿from those you have set aside﴾, that is, you have avoided. This avoidance is understood as being by divorce. ﴿Whoever﴾ is a conditional particle governing what follows it. His words ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾ are its response, meaning: whomever you seek from those you have divorced, there is no sin upon you in seeking her. Or it is a relative pronoun, and the clause is its predicate, meaning: she whom you sought, there is no blame upon you in seeking her. The intended meaning is the negation that there is any sin upon him, peace and blessings be upon him, in taking back a divorced woman. It was also said: ﴿whoever﴾ is a relative pronoun conjoined to the second ﴿whom you will﴾, and the intended meaning is other than the divorced woman. The meaning of ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾ is that there is no sin upon you in anything mentioned of postponing, taking in, and seeking, and the intended meaning is the delegation of all this to his own will, peace and blessings be upon him.

Some said: the intended meaning is leaving off lying with a woman without divorce, and the purpose of the verse is to explain that he has the right to leave off lying with whichever of his wives he wills, and to lie with whichever of them he wills, that is, of those he had not postponed and left off lying with, and to return to lying with the one whom he left off and set aside. So the one he set aside is the one who was postponed. The author of al-Kashshaf noted that the verse contains a comprehensive division covering all that is required: he, peace and blessings be upon him, either divorces or keeps. If he keeps, he either lies with her or leaves her and does not divide his time. If he divorces and sets aside, then either he leaves the set-aside woman alone and does not seek her, or he seeks her. The understanding of divorce and keeping, with their divisions, is through the unrestricted sense of postponing and taking in, in His words: ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them and take in﴾. The understanding of seeking the set-aside woman is from His words, glorified be He: ﴿And whoever you seek﴾ and so on. And when it is understood that there is no blame in seeking the set-aside woman by divorce and returning her to marriage, it is understood from this that the lifting of the marriage, in not returning her, is by way of greater reason. He indeed excelled in what he conveyed.

Some permitted that ﴿whoever﴾ be a conditional, with an omitted conjoined element and an omitted predicate, meaning: whoever you seek of those you have set aside, and whoever you do not set aside, are equal, and His words, glorified be He, ﴿there is no blame upon you﴾ are an emphasis of that. Its distance and forced character are not hidden.

Al-Hasan said: the meaning of ﴿whoever you seek﴾ and so on is: whoever of your wives who are with you has died, or whose way you have released, there is no blame upon you in exchanging her for one of those whom I have made lawful for you, so that you do not exceed the number of your wives who are with you. So it is in al-Bahr. It seems that he took ﴿whoever﴾ as a substitute, like the ﴿those﴾ in His words: ﴿Are you content with the life of this world instead of the Hereafter?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38]. And ﴿those you have set aside﴾ includes both those who died and those whom you divorced. Both are distant, and the second is far more distant than the first. Similarly is the consideration of what he considered of restrictions. In sum, it is a view whose attribution to goodness is distant, and more distant still is its attribution to the interpreter of the Qur'an, Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, as in al-Durr al-Manthur.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 51 (part 2 of 2):

﴿That is more suitable so that their eyes may be comforted, and they will not grieve, and they will be pleased with what you give them, all of them.﴾ That is, leaving the matter to your will is closer to comforting their eyes, to their joy, and to their being pleased, all of them, because the ruling is the same for all of them. Then, if you treat them equally, they will consider that a favour from you, and if you prefer some of them over others, they will know that it is by the ruling of Allah the Exalted, so their souls will be at rest with it. This is related from Qatadah (ra). The meaning of "what you give them" is what you do with them, so it includes leaving out sleeping with them and the division (of nights). It is related from Ibn 'Abbas and Mujahid that the meaning is that when they know that you have the right to bring them back to your bed after you have set them aside, their eyes are comforted, they do not grieve, and they are pleased with what you do of equal treatment and preference, because they know that you have not divorced them. The apparent meaning of this is that the thing pointed to is the knowledge that he (ﷺ) has the right to take them back. More clear than this in this regard is the statement of al-Jubba'i: that knowledge on their part, that when you set aside one of them, you have the right to take her back after that, is closer to their joy and the comfort of their eyes.

Some of the eminent scholars said: that the reference is to the leaving of the matter (to his will) is more suitable in wording, because "that" is for the distant, and that its reference is to taking them back is more suitable in meaning, because the comfort of their eyes is in fact by taking them back, so do not overlook this. "Al-a'yun" is the plural of paucity (jam' qillah), but here what is meant is the plural of multiplicity (jam' kathrah), and it seems that this was chosen because it better fits the number of the wives. Ibn Muhaysin recited "tuqirra" from "aqarra" (to cause to be comforted), with its subject being his pronoun (ﷺ), and "a'yunahunna" in the accusative as the object.

It was also recited as "tuqarra" in the passive form, with "a'yunuhunna" in the nominative as the deputy subject, and "kulluhunna" in the nominative in all of that, and it is an emphasis of the "nun" in "yardayna" (they will be pleased).

Abu Iyas Juwayyah ibn 'A'idh recited "kullahunna" in the accusative, as an emphasis of the pronoun in "ataytahunna" (you gave them). Ibn Jinni said: this recitation returns to the meaning of the common recitation "kulluhunna" with a dammah on the lam, because their pleasure, all of them, with what they were given, all of them, individually and collectively, is the same, so the two meanings are one, except that the nominative has a meaning, which is that in it there is an explicit statement in the wording that all of them will be pleased, while the explicitness in the irregular recitation is in their being given, although the actual state in both is one with the interpretation. End of quotation.

Al-Tibi said: emphasizing the subject rather than the object shows the completeness of their pleasure, even though the giving was not complete (in equality). In emphasizing the object there is a showing that, with the completeness of the giving, they are not complete in pleasure. The first is more eloquent in praise, because it carries the meaning of perfection, since the emphasis removes the suspicion of figurative usage in what is emphasized. End of quotation, so reflect.

﴿And Allah knows what is in your hearts﴾ is addressed to him (ﷺ) and to his pure wives by way of predominance (taghlib). What is meant by "what is in the hearts" is general, and it includes what is in their hearts of contentment with what Allah the Exalted has arranged concerning them, namely leaving the matter to him (ﷺ), and its opposite, and what is in his noble heart (peace be upon him) of inclination towards some of them over others. The statement urges effort in beautifying what is in the hearts. Perhaps his (ﷺ) being included in the address is for the comforting of their hearts. In al-Kashshaf it is said that this is a warning for whoever is not content with what Allah the Exalted has arranged in this matter and has entrusted to the will of His Messenger (peace be upon him), and it urges the harmony of their hearts, the purity among them, and agreement on seeking the pleasure of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the goodness of his noble soul. It is apparent that he (al-Zamakhshari) does not hold that he (ﷺ) is included in the address. In that case, either he would say that it is general for them and for all believers, or he would say that it is specific to them. This is probably the apparent meaning of his statement, and according to it the reason for the mention is not clear. Perhaps it may be said on the first view: the context does not clearly require the inclusion of all believers in the address.

Ibn 'Atiyyah said: the reference by "that" here is to what is in the heart of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) of love for one person over another, and the believers are included in the meaning. Perhaps it may be imagined that the address is to all the responsible (mukallafun), and the statement urges the beautifying of what is in the hearts regarding what Allah the Exalted has arranged for His Messenger (ﷺ) concerning the matter of his wives, and the removal of bad thoughts, by supposing that this is what wisdom requires, and that it is a sign of complete beloved-ness, and that its opposite is not to be imagined. For some of the heretics, like the Christians, criticized the great number of his marriages (peace be upon him), and his being in a position regarding women that was not permitted to his community, namely the permissibility of more than four, and not being bound to a rotation of nights for them, for example. They claimed that this is evidence of the predominance of sexual desire in him (peace be upon him), and that this contradicts the sanctity of soul that is part of the character of the prophets (peace be upon them). So they decided, may Allah the Exalted protect us, that his prophethood is denied, and that what he (ﷺ) did was not from Allah the Exalted, but rather it was only from him (peace be upon him). It is not hidden that those who say this, despite their disbelief, are ignorant of the degrees of perfection and deaf to the hearing of his reports (peace be upon him). Whoever examines the reports knows that he (ﷺ) was the most perfect of the prophets absolutely, because of the utmost perfection of his humanity and his sovereignty. The effects of the first perfection are marrying more than four and going round to all of them in one night. The effects of the second perfection are that he (peace be upon him) often spent the night and rose in the morning without eating or drinking, while he was at the highest degree of strength and not caring about leaving that. No one of the prophets (peace be upon them) has the combination of these two perfections as they were combined in him (peace be upon him). And his multiplying of wives has a great religious wisdom as well, which is the spreading of legal rulings that are hardly known except through them, together with the strengthening of the matter of his prophethood. For women can hardly keep a secret, and they are the most knowledgeable of people about the hidden matters of their husbands. So if his wives had come upon any hidden matter of his (peace be upon him) that harmed the rank of prophethood, they would have revealed it. And how can it be imagined that it could be concealed among them with their large number? "Every secret that passes between two spreads." And in not making the rotation obligatory for him (peace be upon him) there is an emphasis on this, as is not hidden from the fair-minded.

﴿And Allah has always been All-Knowing﴾ exceeding in knowledge, so He knows everything you show and everything you hide. ﴿All-Forbearing﴾ exceeding in forbearance, so He (glorified be He) does not hasten to respond to whoever does what He does not love, according to what his action requires of reproach or punishment, or He pardons what dominates the heart of inclinations and the like.

Here, in al-Bahr (of Abu Hayyan), the narrations agree that he (peace be upon him) used to be just among his pure wives in the division until he died, and he did not make use of anything of what was permitted to him, restraining his soul and taking the more excellent course. The exception was Sawdah, for she gave up her night to 'A'ishah and said: "Do not divorce me, so that I may be raised among your wives." Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Shihab that he said: it was not known that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) postponed any of them or set any of them aside after they were given the choice and chose him.

Al-Shaykhan (al-Bukhari and Muslim), Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i and others related from 'A'ishah that the Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him) used to ask permission from one of us on her day after this verse was revealed: ﴿You may postpone whom you wish of them﴾. She was asked: what did you used to say? She said: I used to say to him, "If that is up to me, then I do not want to prefer anyone over you." Reflect on this together with the previously mentioned consensus. And Allah the Exalted is the Granter of success.

﴿Lā yaḥillu laka al-nisā'u﴾ is read with the ya' (يَحِلُّ, masculine verb form), because the feminine marking of a plural is not real (غَيْرُ حَقِيقِيٍّ), and it is also separated from its verb by an intervening element. By "al-nisā'" (the women) is meant the genus (الجِنْس), which includes the single woman. The singular was not used because the word has no singular form from its own root. The word "al-mar'ah" (woman) includes the female slave (al-jāriyah), but she is not intended here. The restriction of "al-nisā'" to free women (al-ḥarā'ir) is by customary usage (bi-ḥukm al-'urf). The two Basran readers (al-Baṣriyyān) read it with the upper ta' (بِالتّاءِ الفَوْقِيَّةِ, feminine verb form). Sahl and Abū Ḥātim allow either reading. Whichever reading is adopted, the meaning is: the marrying of women is forbidden to you ﴿min ba'du﴾ (after this).

It has been said: meaning after the nine (التِّسْعِ) who are in your nikah today. Ibn Sa'd related from 'Ikrimah, who said: When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave his wives the choice, they chose him, so Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿It is not lawful for you to take women after these nine whom you have chosen﴾. That is, it became forbidden for you to marry others than them.

Abū Dāwūd in his Nāsikh (the book on abrogating and abrogated rulings), Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqī in his Sunan related from Anas, who said: When he gave them the choice and they chose Allah, His Messenger (ﷺ), He restricted him to them, so He, glorified be He, said: ﴿It is not lawful for you to take women after this﴾. Ibn Mardawayh also related from Ibn 'Abbās that he said regarding the verse: Allah confined him to them as He confined them to him (عَلَيْهِ الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ).

Some scholars supplied an elided genitive by way of choice (اخْتِيارًا): that is, "after their choosing Allah and His Messenger."

Al-Imām (al-Rāzī) said: this is preferable, and it seems that this is because it more clearly shows that the prohibition was an honour (كَرامَةً) for them and a thanks (شُكْرًا) for their good conduct. Another scholar allowed that the supplied phrase could be "after this day," and its consequence is the prohibition of all besides those whom he chose (عَلَيْهِ الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ).

It is related in al-Baḥr from Ibn 'Abbās and Qatādah, who said: When they were given the choice and chose Allah, His Messenger (ﷺ), He rewarded them by forbidding him other women and by their not being replaced, and Allah, glorified be He, abrogated by this what had previously been permitted to him of the latitude regarding all women. It is also related from Mujāhid and Ibn Jubayr that the meaning is "after the permission of women in general." It has also been said that the supplied phrase is "after the nine," in the sense that this number, apart from the specific nature of the counted items, is the limit (niṣāb) for the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), just as four is the limit for his community (ummah) among them. So the meaning is: it is not lawful for you to exceed nine.

﴿Nor that you should exchange them﴾: its original form is tatabaddalu, which was lightened by dropping one of the two ta's. That is: it is not lawful for you to substitute ﴿for them with [other] wives﴾, by divorcing one of them and marrying another in her place. So in the verse there are two rulings: the prohibition of exceeding [the number], and the prohibition of substitution. Its apparent meaning is that it is lawful for him (عَلَيْهِ الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ) to marry another woman in the event that one of the nine dies. If the purpose of the verse is the prohibition of all besides those whom he chose (عَلَيْهِ الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ), the verse indicates that if one of them died, it would not be lawful for him to marry another. The earlier statement of Ibn 'Abbās is very clearly apparent in this. It seems that His words, ﴿nor that you should exchange them﴾ etc., were for the purpose of removing the supposition that what was forbidden was only that he should take a co-wife (بِواحِدَةٍ مِنَ الضَّرائِرِ) in addition to [those he had].

In another report from 'Ikrimah, the meaning is: it is not lawful for you to take women after these whom Allah, glorified be He, named for you in His words: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful to you your wives﴾, the verse.
