So it is not lawful for him (ﷺ) beyond the four categories, such as Bedouin women (al-a'rābiyyāt) and strangers (al-gharā'ib), and he may take from them whatever he wishes. 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, al-Tirmidhī, who graded it ḥasan, and others related from Ibn 'Abbās something apparent in this, where he said in the report: And He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful to you﴾ up to His words, glorified be He: ﴿exclusively for you﴾, and what is other than that of kinds of women was forbidden.

'Abd Allāh ibn Aḥmad in Zawā'id al-Musnad, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Ḍiyā' in al-Mukhtārah, and others related from Ziyād, who said: I said to Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may Allah be pleased with him: "What do you think if the wives of the Prophet (عَلَيْهِ الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ) died, would it not be lawful for him to marry?" He said: "What prevents him from that?" I said: "His words, ﴿It is not lawful for you to take women after this﴾." He said: "He only made lawful to him a kind of women and described to him a quality, so He, glorified be He, said: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful to you your wives﴾ up to His words, exalted is He: ﴿and a believing woman﴾, etc. Then He, blessed and exalted, said: ﴿It is not lawful for you to take women after this quality.''"

On this view al-Ṭībī said: His words, glorified be He, ﴿nor that you should exchange them﴾ etc. are an emphasis of what precedes it, regarding the prohibition of what is other than the four categories explicitly mentioned. The pronoun in "bihinna" (with them) seems to refer to the categories mentioned in His words: ﴿O Prophet, indeed We have made lawful to you your wives﴾, the verse. The meaning is: it is not lawful for you to abandon these categories and turn away from them to other categories.

Shaykh al-Islām Abū al-Su'ūd (علَيْهِ الرَّحْمَةُ), after relating the aforementioned view, said: What refutes it is His words, ﴿nor that you should exchange them﴾, etc., for the meaning of making lawful the mentioned categories is making lawful their marriage. So the substitution with them would be making lawful the marriage of others in place of making lawful their marriage, and that is only conceivable through abrogation, which is not among human functions. End. So reflect and do not be heedless.

It has been said that ﴿nor that you should exchange them﴾ relates to the exchange (al-badal) that existed in the pre-Islamic period, when a man would say to another man: "Exchange your wife with me and I will exchange mine with you," and each of them would step down from his wife to the other. Something similar was related from Ibn Zayd, but al-Ṭabarī and others denied this view regarding the meaning of the verse, and said: The Arabs never did that at all. As for what has been related from the hadith of 'Uyaynah ibn Ḥiṣn, that he said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) when he entered upon him without asking permission while 'Ā'ishah was with him: "Who is this red-cheeked one (al-Ḥumayrā')?" He said: "'Ā'ishah." 'Uyaynah said: "O Messenger of Allah, if you wish I will step down for you from the lady of the Arab women in beauty and lineage." This is not an exchange, nor did he intend it; he only belittled 'Ā'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, because she was then a young girl.

And among the additions for emphasising the comprehensiveness (al-istighrāq), the prohibition includes the exchange of all or some.

His words, exalted is He: ﴿even if their beauty pleases you﴾ are in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the subject of "tabaddal" (exchange), and the meaning is: with the condition that your admiration for them is assumed. Its essence is: do not exchange them for wives under any circumstance. The apparent view of some scholars is that it cannot be a circumstantial clause from its object, namely "azwājan" (wives), and this was justified by its excessive indefiniteness (tawaghghul fī al-tankīr). This was objected to on the grounds that it contradicts the statements of the grammarians, for they allowed the circumstantial clause from an indefinite noun when it occurs in a negative context, since then it becomes generalised and its vagueness disappears, as al-Raḍī explicitly stated.

It has been said that indefiniteness is an obstacle to being a circumstantial clause here, because the circumstantial clause is analogised to the adjective, and the waw (و) prevents it from being an adjective, so it prevents it from being a circumstantial clause. It was objected that the necessity of this analogy is not granted, although al-Zamakhsharī and others allowed the waw to enter upon the adjective to emphasise its attachment. It was also said, as a reason for not permitting this, that when the circumstantial word is indefinite it must be placed first, and it was not placed first here. This was objected to on the grounds that this is not accepted in general for a clause linked by waw, because it has the form of a conjunction.

Ṣāḥib al-Kashf (al-Zamakhsharī) regarded it as permissible and mentioned that the meaning in both cases does not differ greatly, because when the verb is restricted, the restriction of its complements is necessary; the difference is only in primacy and subordination. The pronoun in "ḥusnuhunna" (their beauty) refers to the wives, and what is meant by them is those who would be substituted for his wives who are in his nikah (عَلَيْهِ الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ). So calling them wives is by consideration of what would occur to them. This is based on the view that the preposition "bi-" (with/for) in "bihinna" is attached to what is left, not to what is taken. If it were considered attached to what is taken, the pronoun would refer to the women, not to the wives. Among those whose beauty pleased him (ﷺ), according to what is said, was Asmā' bint 'Umays al-Khath'amiyyah, wife of Ja'far ibn Abī Ṭālib, after his death, may Allah be pleased with him.

In His words, glorified be He: ﴿even if their beauty pleases you﴾, according to what is related from Ibn 'Aṭiyyah, there is evidence that a man may look at the woman he wishes to marry, and there are reports supporting this. The detailed opinions on this are in the books of jurisprudence (kutub al-furū').

Scholars differed as to whether the verse indicating that women are not lawful to him (ﷺ) is muḥkamah (definitive, not abrogated) or not. From Ubayy ibn Ka'b and a group including al-Ḥasan and Ibn Sīrīn, and al-Ṭabarī chose it, and Abū Ḥayyān regarded it as apparent, that it is muḥkamah. From 'Alī, may Allah ennoble his face, Ibn 'Abbās, Umm Salamah, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk, may Allah have mercy on him, it is that it is abrogated (mansūkhah). This was also related from 'Ā'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her. Abū Dāwūd in his Nāsikh, al-Tirmidhī, who graded it ṣaḥīḥ, al-Nasā'ī, al-Ḥākim, who also graded it ṣaḥīḥ, Ibn al-Mundhir and others related from her that she said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not die until Allah, exalted is He, made lawful for him to marry from among women whomever he wished, except one who is a close relative (dhāt maḥram)," based on His words: ﴿You may postpone whom you will of them and take to you whom you will﴾. This is apparent in that the abrogating [verse] is His words: ﴿You may postpone﴾, etc. It is based on the interpretation that the meaning is: you divorce whom you wish and keep whom you wish. The way it abrogates on this interpretation is that by its generality it indicates that he (ﷺ) was permitted divorce and retention for whomever he wishes, so it indicates that he may divorce his wives and marry whomever he wishes from others, since the meaning of retention is not only the retention of those already married.

His words, glorified be He: "tu'wī" (you take in) is not restricted by "minhunna" (of them). So al-Khafājī said. There is something to be considered in this. It is necessary, on the view that abrogation is by this, to hold that its revelation came later than the revelation of the abrogated verse, since abrogation is not possible with precedence. This is evident. The precedence in the written text (al-muṣḥaf) does not cause a problem, because its arrangement is not according to the order of revelation.

Some said: the abrogating [ruling] is the Sunnah, and it is most likely that these were his actions (عَلَيْهِ الصَّلاةُ والسَّلامُ). Ibn Abī Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim related from 'Abd Allāh ibn Shaddād, who said regarding His words, exalted is He: ﴿nor that you should exchange them﴾, etc.: "That is, if he had divorced them, it would not have been lawful for him to substitute [others]. He would marry after this verse was revealed whomever he wished, and it was revealed while he had nine women under him. Then he married, after Umm Ḥabībah bint Abī Sufyān and Juwayriyah bint al-Ḥārith, may Allah be pleased with both of them."

The apparent view, on the basis that the verse was revealed as an honour for the chosen wives, a consolation to their hearts, and a thanks for their good conduct, is that there is no abrogation. And Allah knows best.

His words: ﴿except what your right hand possesses﴾ is an exception from "women," and it is contiguous (muttaṣil) according to the original linguistic usage, since he (ﷺ) is included in it, free women and slave women; and it is disjunctive (munqaṭi') according to customary usage, since in custom it is restricted to free women. ﴿And that you should exchange them for wives﴾ is explicit in it.

Ibn 'Aṭiyyah said: If "mā" is a relative pronoun referring to the genus, then it is an exception from the genus, and the preferred reading in it is the nominative (raf') as a substitute (badal) for "women," and the accusative (naṣb) is permitted as an exception. If it is a verbal-masdar "mā," then it is in the accusative position, because it is an exception from a non-genus of the first. End. This is not sound, because he said: "and the supposition is 'except the ownership of the right hand,'" and "milk" (mulk) in the sense of "owned" (mamlūk). When it is in the sense of "owned," it is not correct to affirm with certainty that it is not of the genus. Also, the accusative is not mandatory even if we suppose it is not of the genus in reality; rather the people of the Ḥijāz use the accusative and the Banū Tamīm use substitution. Whichever it is, the apparent meaning is that owned slave women are lawful to him (ﷺ), whether they were among what Allah gave him as spoils (afā'a) or not.

﴿And Allah is ever, over all things, Watchful﴾: that is, observing (raqīban, 'watcher') or watchful (muraqqiban), and what is meant is that He is guarding and aware of everything. So beware of transgressing His limits, glorified be He, and of going beyond His lawful to His unlawful, Mighty and Majestic.

[Page 67]

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 53 (part 1 of 3):**

﴿O you who have believed, do not enter the houses of the Prophet unless permission is given to you﴾ This begins an explanation of some of the rights that people have toward the Prophet (ﷺ) when they are in the presence of his wives, and the rights connected to the wives, may Allah be pleased with them. The connection of this to what came before is clear. According to most scholars, the verse was revealed on the day the Prophet (ﷺ) married Zaynab bint Jahsh.

Imam Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari, Muslim, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in his Sunan related, through several chains, from Anas, who said: "When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) married Zaynab bint Jahsh, he invited the people, and they ate, then they sat conversing. He appeared as if he was preparing to stand up, but they did not stand. When he saw that, he stood up, and when he stood up, those who were with him stood up, but three people remained seated. The Prophet (ﷺ) came to enter, but the people were still sitting. Then they got up, so I went and informed the Prophet (ﷺ) that they had left. He came and entered, and I went to enter, but he placed the curtain between me and him. Then Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter the houses of the Prophet﴾ [to the end of the verse]."

The prohibition (al-nahy) is for prohibition (tahrim). His, glorified be He, words ﴿unless permission is given﴾ are an exception (istithna') of the "emptied" type (mustathna mufarragh, an exception where the excluded element is left unspecified and the general category is implied) from the most general of states, with the preposition bi of accompaniment (bi'l-musahabah) understood. That is: "Do not enter it in any state, except while you are accompanied by permission."

Abu Hayyan permitted that the preposition be the bi of causation (bi'l-sababiyyah), so the exception would be from the most general of causes: "Do not enter it for any cause, except for the cause of permission." Al-Zamakhshari held that it is an exception from the most general of times: "Do not enter it at any time except the time when permission is given to you." Abu Hayyan raised an objection to this, that the use of the noun as an adverb of time (waqi' mawqi' al-zarf) is restricted to the explicit verbal noun (masdar sarih), not the verbal noun that is formed from a clause (masdar mu'awwal), so one does not say "I came to you when the rooster crows" (atitu-ka an yasih al-dik), but rather "I came to you at the crowing of the rooster" (atitu-ka sihah al-dik).

It is not hidden that the claim of this restriction is one of two positions held by the grammarians on the question. Indeed, it is the more well-known, and al-Zamakhshari is an imam in Arabic, who is not to be criticized with such an objection.

Some have claimed that the word "time" is implied in the structure of the sentence, so it is omitted by the deletion of the preposition, and that this is not a case of a verbal noun standing in the position of an adverb of time.

Some eminent scholars permitted that this is an exception from the most general of states without the preposition bi being understood, but rather by considering that the verbal noun is interpreted as a passive participle: "Do not enter it except being given permission." The fully formed verbal noun (al-masdar al-masbuk) may sometimes be interpreted with the meaning of the passive participle, as was said concerning His, exalted be He, words: ﴿And it was not [possible] for this Qur'an to be fabricated﴾ [Yunus: 37], meaning: "This Qur'an was not fabricated." Whoever says that the verbal noun having the meaning of the passive participle is not known in the interpreted form has not been correct.

It was said that what was mentioned contradicts the statement of the grammarians that the fully formed verbal noun is always definite, as Ibn Hisham clearly stated in al-Mughni. Al-Khafaji responded that the truth is that this is superficial, and that it may be indefinite, and he cited the words of Allah, exalted be He: ﴿What was not [possible]...﴾ etc.

His, glorified be He, words ﴿to a meal﴾ are connected to ﴿permission is given﴾. It is used with ila (to) even though it normally takes fi (in), as one says "he was given permission in such-and-such," because it has been construed with the meaning of invitation (al-du'a'), to indicate that they should not enter upon a meal without an invitation, even if explicit permission to enter the house has been granted, since not every permission is an invitation. It was also said that it is permissible that both verbs, ﴿enter﴾ and ﴿permission is given﴾, may have governed it, and this is something that is not objectionable.

His, exalted be He, words ﴿not waiting for its ripeness (ghayra nazirin inahu)﴾ mean: not waiting for its cooking and its readiness. One says: anā al-ṭa'ām yani'ī anyan, like qalā yaqlī qalyan, when the food has ripened and become ready. This was said by al-Zajjaj. Makki said: inahu is an adverb of time, an inverted form of an (ān), which means "time (hin)," so the nun was moved before the alif and the hamza was changed to a kasra; that is, "not waiting for its time (ānahu)," meaning its time, and the intended meaning is the time of its ripening and maturity, or the time of eating it. It is a circumstantial clause (hal) of the subject of "enter." This circumstantial clause is of the "emptied" type, from the most general of states, as you have heard in ﴿unless permission is given to you﴾. If this is made a circumstantial clause, then it is a synonymous circumstantial clause, so it is as if it were said: "Do not enter in any state except accompanied by permission, not waiting." The apparent meaning is that it is a circumstantial clause of anticipation (hal muqaddarah), but it may also be a concurrent one (muqarinah).

Al-Zamakhshari, after making what came before a case of the accusative of time (nasb 'ala'l-zarfiyyah), made this a circumstantial clause also, but he said, after the exception applied to both the time and the state together: "It is as if it were said: 'Do not enter the houses of the Prophet except at the time of permission, and do not enter them except not waiting.'"

Abu Hayyan objected to this, that according to the position of the majority, it is not permissible for anything to come after illa (except) in an exception other than the excepted item, the item from which the exception is made, or the descriptive adjunct of the item from which the exception is made. He then said: al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i permitted this in the case of the circumstantial clause, as in "They left except on Friday, departing from us." Thus what al-Zamakhshari said is permissible according to them. It is not hidden to one who reflects on al-Zamakhshari's words that this is far removed from treating the noble verse as similar to the example mentioned, because that is based on a reversal of order (al-ta'khir wa'l-taqdim), and his statement diverges from considering this in the verse. Yes, if he had limited himself to making ﴿not waiting﴾ a circumstantial clause of the pronoun in ﴿enter﴾, it would be possible to say that his meaning is: "Do not enter not waiting, except when permission is given to you," and the meaning would be that their entering without waiting for its ripeness is conditional on permission, while their entering while waiting is forbidden absolutely, by way of greater argument (bi-tariq al-awla). Then the exception is placed first and the circumstantial clause is placed later.

Some scholars objected to this, saying that it contains the exception of two things, namely the adverb of time and the circumstantial clause, with a single particle. Ibn Malik said in al-Tashil: "Two things may not be excepted with a single particle unless they are joined by a conjunction." Its apparent meaning is that this is not permissible, whether the exception is "emptied" or not, and whether or not the two things are governed by the preceding verb. So one may not say: "The people stood except Zayd, Amr," nor "What the people stood except Zayd, Amr," or "except Zayd Amr," nor "What stood except Khalid Bakr," nor "What I gave anyone anything except Amr a dang," nor "What I gave except Amr a dang," nor "What anyone took anything except Zayd a dirham," nor "What anyone took except Zayd a dirham." The discussion of this question, of what is correct among these constructions and what is not, and if it is correct, in what way it is correct, is long and broad.

What I incline toward is restricting the absolute statement of the grammarians, "two things may not be excepted with a single particle unless they are joined by a conjunction," to cases where the two things are not governed by the verb preceding the exception. Thus it is not permissible to say "What stood except Zayd except Bakr," for example, since a verb cannot have two subjects without a conjunction; nor "What I struck except Zayd Amr," for example, since "struck" cannot have two objects without a conjunction either. I consider permissible constructions such as "What I gave anyone anything except Amr a dang" and "What struck except Zayd Amr," without any need to commit to the substitution of two nouns for two nouns, like the verse:

"When we struck the nab-wood with the nab-wood, part of it against part, its canes refused to break,"

in the first, and in the second to assume a verb governing Amr, implied from what is mentioned in the second.

As for what Ibn Malik mentioned in the argument for the analogy with conjunction, where he said: "Just as two conjoined items are not implied after a conjunction particle, so two excepted items are not implied after an exception particle," this does not stand against us, for we say that in the case of conjunction it is permissible in such examples as "Zayd struck Amr and Bakr struck Khalid," definitely. So similarly "What I gave anyone anything except Zayd a dang." As for his statement that the exception is in the position of a separate sentence, because the meaning of "The people came except Zayd" is "The people came, none of whom was Zayd," this, as it has been said, requires that what precedes the particle should only govern what follows it in such constructions, because the particle stands in the position of "what"; this is not one of the excluded cases, and it is nothing, as is not hidden.

As for what is in the Amali of al-Kafiyah, that the "emptied" exception must have an implied general category, so that if two items are used after illa, either no general category is implied at all, which contradicts the rule of the chapter, or two general categories are implied, which leads to something outside analogy without basis; and if it were permissible with two, it would be permissible with more than two, which is clearly invalid; or one is implied for one of them and not the other, which leads to ambiguity in what is intended.

This was criticized by al-Hadithi, who said: "Someone may choose the third option and say: the general category is only implied for the item that comes immediately after illa, because it is the apparent 'emptied' exception, so no ambiguity arises at all." Abu Hayyan implied in the verse a deleted element and made ﴿not waiting﴾ a circumstantial clause of the pronoun in it. The implied sense is: "Enter, not waiting." This is what Ibn Malik's statement requires, since he made it obligatory in such examples as "What struck except Zayd Amr" to make Amr an object of an implied verb indicated by what is mentioned, and the sentence is a resumptive clause of explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), which came as an answer to a question arising from the first sentence: as if, when it was said "What struck except Zayd," someone asked, "Who struck?" and it was answered, "He struck Amr."

Our scholar Taqi al-Din al-Subki, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned in his treatise entitled "Forbearance and Deliberation in the Grammatical Analysis of ﴿not waiting for its ripeness﴾," and in it al-Salah al-Safadi says:

"O seeker of grammar in a time whose shadow is longer than the spear,
and what is adorned with it as a necklace, upon you is forbearance and deliberation."

The apparent meaning is that al-Zamakhshari said that only as an explanation of meaning. In reality, the excepted item is the verbal noun to which the adverb and the circumstantial clause are attached, so it is as if it were said: "Do not enter except with an entering accompanied by such-and-such." Then he said: "I am not saying that an implied verbal noun is the governing element for both, since the governing element is the 'emptied' verb, but I only intended to explain the meaning." This type of parsing is what we prefer in His, exalted be He, words: ﴿And those who were given the Book did not differ except after knowledge had come to them, out of envy among themselves﴾ [Al 'Imran: 19], meaning: "They did not differ except a difference after knowledge had come to them, out of envy among themselves." So "after knowledge had come to them" and "out of envy" are not excepted items; rather, the excepted item, namely "differing," falls upon both of them. This is like saying: "I did not stand except on Friday, laughing, in front of the amir, in his house." In all of these, the "emptied" verb is governing from the standpoint of grammatical construction, while from the standpoint of meaning they are like one thing, since together they are a part of the verbal noun contained in the negated verb. This is better than saying "they differed out of envy among themselves," because then it would not express restriction, whereas according to what we have said it does express restriction in it, just as it expresses it in His, exalted be He, words: ﴿after knowledge had come to them﴾. So it is a restriction to two things, but by the method we have described, not that it is the exception of two things, but rather the exception of one thing that applies to two things. The words of al-Zamakhshari may be understood in this way: his statement "the exception falls upon the time and the state together" is correct, since the excepted item is more general, because the more general applies to the more specific, and what applies to what applies is itself applied, and thus he escapes the objection raised against him from the grammarians' statement that two things may not be excepted with a single particle unless they are joined by a conjunction. End of quote. So reflect on it.

It was also permitted that ﴿not waiting﴾ be a circumstantial clause of the genitive pronoun in ﴿for you﴾. Al-Zamakhshari did not mention this. In al-Kashf it is said: if it were made a circumstantial clause of this, it would produce what he mentioned, in that it is a prohibition against entering at all times except at the time when a specified permission exists. Taqi al-Din said: it was not made a circumstantial clause of this, although it is permissible from the standpoint of grammatical construction, because it would become an anticipated circumstantial clause, and because they do not become prohibited from waiting; rather, that would be a condition on permission. The meaning is not that, but rather that they were forbidden to enter except with permission, and when they entered they were forbidden to be ones not waiting for its ripeness. Therefore, from the standpoint of meaning, it is impossible for the governing element to be ﴿is given permission﴾ or for it to be a circumstantial clause of its object. End of quote.

[Page 68]

It may be that this view has a broader perspective than what is found in *al-Kashshaf* (the commentary of al-Zamakhshari). Ibn Abi 'Abla read *ghayri* (غَيْرِ) with a kasra, treating it as an adjective (*sifah*) of *ta'am* (طَعامٍ, "food"), so that it agrees with a noun other than the one it refers to. The position of the Basrans on this is that the pronoun must be made explicit, so one says here *ghayra nazirin antum* (غَيْرَ ناظِرٍ أنْتُمْ) or *ghayra nazirin antum* in the dual or plural form (غَيْرَ ناظِرِينَ أنْتُمْ). The Kufans hold that omitting it is permissible when no ambiguity arises, as is the case here, and the explanation mentioned above is based on this. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i inclined the *alif* in *inahu* (إناهُ), taking it as a verbal noun (*masdar*) of *anā al-ta'āmu* (أنى الطَّعامُ), meaning "the food became ripe" when it reached its time. Al-A'mash read *inā'ahu* (إناءَهُ) with a long vowel after the *nun*.

﴿But when you are invited, then enter﴾: this is a *istidrak* (an exception or qualification, "but") to the prohibition on entering without permission. In it is an indication that the permission to come to the food is the invitation to it. ﴿And when you have eaten, then disperse﴾: that is, when you have eaten the food, then scatter and do not linger. The *fa'* (فَ) here indicates immediate succession (*ta'qib*), without delay, to show that their entry should be after the permission and invitation in such a way that eating begins immediately without a gap. The verse, according to what most exegetes hold, is an address to people who used to watch for the Prophet's (ﷺ) food, entering and sitting while waiting for it to be ready. It is specific to them and to those like them who do the same in the future. Therefore the prohibition applies only to one who enters without an invitation and sits waiting for the food without need. It does not indicate a prohibition on entering with permission for a purpose other than food, nor on sitting and staying after the meal for another important matter. If the address were taken as general, the entering and lingering mentioned would both be forbidden, and no one holds that.

This is supported by what 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from al-Rabi' from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "They used to watch for the time, then they would enter the house of the Prophet (ﷺ), sit down and talk, waiting for the food to be ready. So Allah revealed: ﴿O you who believe...﴾ the verse." Likewise is what Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Sulayman ibn Arqam, who said: "It was revealed concerning the ones who overstay." From this it has been said that it is the verse of the overstayers.

It has already been mentioned to you that ﴿to food﴾ may be governed by both verbs, *tadkhulu* (تَدْخُلُوا, "enter") and *yu'dhana* (يُؤْذَنَ, "be permitted"), and the matter on this is clear.

The *allamah* Ibn Kamal said: "The apparent meaning is that the address is general to non-relatives (*ghayr al-mahārim*), and the specificity of the occasion of revelation (*khusus al-sabab*) does not serve as a restriction (*mukhassis*), as is established in the principles of jurisprudence (*usul*). Yes, it would be a reason for restricting the permission by His words ﴿to food﴾, so that the illusion of taking its implication (*mafhum*) is dispelled." End of quote. In this there is room for discussion, so reflect upon it. The well-known account concerning the occasion of revelation is what we mentioned at the beginning of the discussion of the verse, from Imam Ahmad, the two Shaykhs (al-Bukhari and Muslim), and others. So do not be heedless.

﴿Nor those who linger for conversation﴾: that is, for the conversation of some of you with others, or for the conversation of the people of the house by listening to it. Thus the *lam* is causative (*ta'līliyyah*) or the *lam* that strengthens (*al-lam al-muqawwiyah*). *Mustaʼnisina* (مُسْتَأْنِسِينَ, "those who seek comfort/familiarity") is in the genitive case, conjoined to *nazirin* (ناظِرِينَ), and the *la* (لا) is extra. It may also be in the accusative case, conjoined to *ghayra* (غَيْرَ), like His words ﴿nor of those who are astray﴾ (al-Fatihah 7). It has also been permitted that it is a circumstantial clause (*hal*), either anticipated or contemporaneous, from the subject of a verb that has been omitted along with its subject, and this is conjoined to what was mentioned. The estimated meaning is: "Do not enter it, or do not remain, seeking comfort in conversation."

﴿Indeed, that﴾: that is, the staying indicated by the speech, or the seeking of comfort, or what was mentioned of seeking comfort and looking, or entering in a manner other than the one mentioned. The first is more suitable (*mulā'amah*) to the context (*siyaq*) and the preceding discourse (*sibaq*). ﴿Is an offense to the Prophet﴾: because it would prevent him, peace and blessings be upon him, from attending to some of his needs, together with the constraint placed upon the Prophet (ﷺ) and his household. ﴿So he is shy of you﴾: that is, shy of expelling you, by saying to you "Get out," or shy of preventing you from what would harm him, according to what has been said. The speech therefore has an elided genitive (*muḍāf* elided) to match His words ﴿but Allah is not shy of the truth﴾, for this indicates that the thing one is shy of is some meaning of the meanings, not their persons, so that negation and affirmation apply to one thing, as the arrangement of the speech requires. If the intended meaning were shyness from their persons, He would have said, "and Allah is not shy of you." So the intended meaning of "the truth" is their expulsion or the prevention of that. The word "truth" is placed in that position to glorify its aspect. The summary of the speech is that He did not abandon the truth and commanded you to leave. The expression "not being shy" is for the sake of *mushakalah* (correspondence in expression). It has also been permitted that the speech is by metaphor (*isti'arah*) or by a general metonymy (*majaz mursal*). Considering an elided genitive is what al-Zamakhshari and many others held, and it is what ought to be relied upon.

In *al-Kashshaf* it says: "If you say: being shy of Zayd for the purpose of expelling him, for example, is the literal meaning, and being shy of his expulsion is a broadening by making the source of the act like the relative clause. Both expressions are correct, and either may be used in place of the other." I say: What is meant is that one must consider the sense of expulsion. Either expulsion is estimated and made the object, which multiplies the pronouns and does not match the wording in negation and affirmation, or the genitive is estimated, which is fewer and matches. With the presence of the preponderating factor and the absence of an obstacle, there is no reason to deviate, so what has been mentioned is necessary.

Ibn Kamal said: "His words ﴿so he is shy of you﴾ are the causation of an omitted clause indicated by the context, meaning: 'And He does not expel you, so He is shy of you.' For this reason it begins with the particle of causation. If the meaning were 'he is shy of expelling you,' it should have begun with a *waw* (و, "and")." In this there is that, after granting what has been mentioned, the speech is still on the estimate of an elided genitive.

Some claimed that the original is ﴿so he is shy of you from the truth﴾ and ﴿and Allah is not shy of you from the truth,﴾ with the intended meaning of "the truth" being their expulsion. This is by *ihtibak* (a rhetorical device in which something is omitted in each of two parallel clauses, each supplying what is missing in the other). Both prepositions are not the same in meaning: the first is for beginning (*ibtida'*) and the second is for causation (*ta'lil*). He said: "Taking it that way is the most suitable for the inimitability of the revelation (*i'jaz al-tanzili*) and the Qur'anic brevity." What is wrong with this is not hidden.

A group read, as mentioned in *al-Bahr* (*al-Bahr al-Muhit*), ﴿fa-yastahi﴾ (فَيَسْتَحِي) with a kasra on the *ha'*, the imperfect of *istahā*, which is the dialect of Banu Tamim. The omitted element is either the middle radical (*'ayn al-kalimah*), so its pattern is *yastafil*, or the final radical (*lam*), so its pattern is *yastaf'il*. In *al-Kashshaf* it is read ﴿la yastahi﴾ with one *ya'* (لا يَسْتَحِي), and I think the reading with one *ya'* on the verb in both places is the case. Furthermore, the apparent meaning is the prohibition of staying for the one invited to food after he has eaten, if that causes harm to the master of the house. What has been mentioned is not restricted to when the staying is in the house of the Prophet (ﷺ). For this reason the burdensome guest is blamed among people and considered a disgraceful act by the wise.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with them both): "It is enough for you regarding the burdensome guests that Allah, mighty and majestic, did not bear them." In my view, like the burdensome guest mentioned is the one invited at a specific time with a group who arrives late without a substantial legitimate excuse, but only in order to wait and show his greatness among those present, while the master of the house cannot bring food to the attendees before his arrival, out of fear of him, or out of respect for him, or for something similar, so the attendees or the master of the house are harmed by this. We have seen many of this type, and we ask Allah, exalted is He, for well-being. Indeed His grace, glory be to Him, is great.

﴿And when you ask them﴾: the pronoun refers to the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ), implied by the mention of his houses, peace and blessings be upon him. That is: and when you request from them ﴿something (matā')﴾: that is, an object that is enjoyed, such as utensils and other things. ﴿Then ask them﴾: that is, request that from them ﴿from behind a screen (hijab)﴾: that is, a partition.

[Page 72]

al-Bukhari, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) said: 'O Messenger of Allah, the righteous and the wicked enter upon you, so if you ordered the Mothers of the Believers to observe the hijab...' So Allah revealed the verse of the hijab." 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) was keen on their veiling, and that was only out of love for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Ibn Jarir reported from 'A'ishah that the wives of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, used to go out at night when they went out to al-Manasi', which is a wide open ground. 'Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him) used to say to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Veil your women." But the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not do so. One night Sawdah bint Zam'ah (may Allah be pleased with her), who was a tall woman, went out after the 'Isha' prayer, and 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) called out to her in a loud voice: "We recognize you, O Sawdah," out of eagerness that the hijab be revealed. So Allah revealed the hijab. That is one of 'Umar's (may Allah be pleased with him) agreements with revelation (*muwafaqat*), and it is well known.

The Shi'ah counted what occurred from him (may Allah be pleased with him) in the report of Ibn Jarir among his faults, saying: "Because of the bad manners it contains and the embarrassment and harm it caused to Sawdah, the wife of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)."

The People of the Sunnah answered, after accepting the report's authenticity, that he (may Allah be pleased with him) considered there to be no harm in it because he believed a great good would result from it. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), though he was more knowing than him and more jealous, did not do that, out of waiting for revelation, and this is what is fitting to the perfection of his station with his Lord, mighty and majestic.

al-Bukhari in *al-Adab al-Mufrad* and al-Nasa'i reported from the hadith of 'A'ishah that she used to eat with him, peace and blessings be upon him, and some of his companions used to eat with them both. A man's hand touched her hand, and the Prophet (ﷺ) disliked that, so the verse was revealed. It is not far-fetched that the whole of what has been mentioned is a cause of revelation.

The hijab was revealed, according to what Ibn Sa'd reported from Anas, in the year five after the Hijrah. He also reported from Salih ibn Kaysan that it was in Dhu al-Qa'dah of that year.

﴿That﴾: the apparent meaning is that it refers to asking from behind a screen. It has been said that it refers to what was mentioned of not entering without permission, not seeking comfort in conversation upon entering, and asking for goods from behind a screen. ﴿Is purer for your hearts and their hearts﴾: that is, more purifying from the satanic thoughts that occur to men regarding women and to women regarding men, for seeing is the cause of attachment and temptation. In some reports: "The glance is a poisoned arrow from the arrows of Iblis." A poet said:

*"A man, as long as he has an eye that turns it
among the eyes of others, is subject to danger.
It pleases his eyelid what displeases his heart;
no welcome to a benefit that brings harm."*

﴿And it is not for you﴾: that is, it is not correct or proper for you ﴿to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾: that is, to do during his lifetime an act he dislikes and is harmed by, such as lingering and seeking comfort in the conversation that you used to do, and other such things. The reference to him, peace and blessings be upon him, by the title of messenger is to denounce that act, and an indication that it is far from what his station requires, since in the messengership there is what benefits them, which calls for repayment in kind, not harm.

[Page 73]

﴿Nor to marry his wives after him, ever﴾: after his death or his separation from them. This is like a specification after a generalization, for marrying the wife of a man after he has divorced her is among the greatest harms. Some people's jealousy over their wives is so intense that they wish for their wives to die so that they will not marry after them, especially the Arabs, for they are the most jealous of people. al-Zamakhshari relates that a young man killed a slave girl of his whom he loved, out of fear that she would fall into the hands of another after his death.

The apparent sense of the prohibition is that the marriage is invalid. The generality of "wives" (al-azwaj) shows that there is no distinction in this between a woman who has been consummated with and one who has not, such as the woman who sought refuge (al-mustaʿidhah) and the woman in whose side he saw whiteness, and to whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said before consummation: "Go back to your family" (ilhaqi bi-ahlik). This is what Imam al-Shafiʿi expressly stated and affirmed in al-Rawdah. However, Imam al-Haramayn and al-Rafiʿi, in al-Saghir, held as sound that the prohibition applies only to the one with whom he consummated the marriage, based on what is reported: that al-Ashʿath ibn Qays al-Kindi married the woman who sought refuge during the time of ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, and ʿUmar intended to stone him, but he was informed that she had not been consummated with, so he desisted without denouncing him. It is also reported that Qutaylah bint Qays, the sister of the aforementioned al-Ashʿath, was married by ʿIkrimah ibn Abi Jahl in Hadramawt, and her brother had previously given her in marriage on behalf of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Before he consummated the marriage, he took her with him to Hadramawt, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ died leaving her unconsummated. When this reached Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, he said: "I wanted to burn her house down over her." ʿUmar said to him: "She is not one of the Mothers of the Believers; the Prophet ﷺ did not consummate the marriage with her and did not put the veil upon her."

It was said: he was not argued against with this; rather, the argument was that she apostatized when her brother apostatized, so by her apostasy she was not among the Mothers of the Believers. Likewise, it is apparent that there is no distinction in this between those among them who chose this world, such as Fatimah bint al-Dahhak ibn Sufyan al-Kilabi according to the narration of Ibn Ishaq, and those who chose Allah and His Messenger ﷺ, such as the nine wives of his, upon him be peace, whom he left at his death.

Among the scholars there are two approaches concerning the permissibility of marrying those who chose this world: one is to extend the disagreement (tard al-khilaf), and the other is to hold categorically to permissibility, which was chosen by Imam (al-Haramayn) and al-Ghazali, may mercy be upon them both. It seems that whoever held the permissibility of marrying the unconsummated woman and the permissibility of marrying the aforementioned chooser of this world restricted "the wives" to those who were in his marriage at the time the verse was revealed and to those resembling them, and these were none other than the consummated wives who chose him, upon him be peace. If that is so, and if by the words of the Exalted "after him" (min baʿdihi) is meant "after his separation (from them)," then it follows that marrying any of those wives whom he divorced, ﷺ, is forbidden to the believers, and this is indeed the case.

From here, those who differed about whether his divorce was limited to three (talaq) disagreed: some said that a woman whom he divorced three times becomes lawful to him, upon him be peace, without an intermediary (muhallil). Others said that she never becomes lawful to him. The expression "the wives" (al-azwaj) apparently indicates that the ruling does not extend to a slave-concubine (umm walad / amah) whom he separated from after intercourse.

On this question there are three views. The third is that she is forbidden if he separates from her by death, as with Mariyah, may Allah be pleased with her, but she is not forbidden if he sold her or gave her away during his lifetime.

The prohibition of marrying his wives after him, upon him be peace, is one of his particular distinctions ﷺ. I have heard from some ignorant Sufis that they forbid a sheikh's wife to his disciple (murid) after the sheikh's death, and this is an ignorance beyond which there is no further ignorance.

﴿Indeed, that﴾ refers to what has been mentioned of harming him, upon him be peace, and marrying his wives after him, and the sense of distance in the demonstrative is to indicate the remoteness of their rank in wickedness and corruption. ﴿was in the sight of Allah﴾ in His judgment, mighty and majestic is He, ﴿tremendous﴾, that is, a grave matter and an awesome affair whose extent cannot be measured. In this is an exaltation by Him, exalted is He, of the station of His Messenger ﷺ and the obligation of his sanctity, alive and dead, which is not hidden.

Page 74

For this reason, the Mighty and Majestic went to great lengths in the warning when He, glorified is He, said:

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 54:

﴿If you disclose a thing﴾ — of that which has no good in it — upon your tongues, such as speaking about marrying them, ﴿or you conceal it﴾ in your breasts, ﴿then indeed Allah is ever Knowing of all things﴾, in complete knowledge, so He will recompense you for what proceeds from you of sins, the manifest and the hidden, without fail. This is the indication of the response (jawab, the consequent of the conditional), and the original sense is: "If you disclose a thing or conceal it, He will recompense you for it, for indeed Allah..." etc.

It has also been said that it is the response with the meaning: "I will inform you that Allah..." etc. The generalisation of ﴿thing﴾ in both places, together with the proof regarding the intended meaning, namely the establishment of His exalted knowledge of what pertains to His wives ﷺ, adds emphasis to the terror and intensifies the severity of the warning.

The occasion of revelation of the verse, as it has been said, is that when the verse of the veil was revealed, a man said: "Are we forbidden to speak to our paternal cousins (daughters of our paternal uncles) except from behind a veil? If Muhammad (ﷺ) dies, we will certainly marry his wives." In some narrations: "I will marry Aisha or Umm Salama."

Juwaybir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that a man came to some of the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ) and spoke with her, and he was her cousin. The Prophet (peace be upon him) said: "Do not stand in this position after this day of yours." He said: "O Messenger of Allah, she is my paternal cousin. By Allah, I did not say to her anything objectionable, nor did she say anything to me." The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I know that. Indeed, there is no one more jealous than Allah, the Exalted, and there is no one more jealous than I am." Then the man left, and then said: "She has upbraided me with the speech of my paternal cousin, so I will certainly marry her after him." Then Allah, the Exalted, revealed this verse. That man freed a slave, and was equipped with ten camels in the way of Allah, the Exalted, and performed Hajj on foot after his statement.

'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Qatada that Talha ibn 'Ubayd Allah said: "If the Prophet (ﷺ) passes away, I will marry Aisha," and then the verse was revealed: ﴿And it is not for you﴾, the verse.

Ibn 'Atiyya said: That the speaker was Talha, may Allah be pleased with him, is not sound, and this is what prevails in my assessment; I can hardly accept the soundness of it unless what is contained in the report of Ibn 'Abbas is accepted, which indicates great remorse. In some narrations, some of the hypocrites said when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) married Umm Salama after Abu Salama and Hafsa after Khunays ibn Hudhafa: "What is wrong with Muhammad that he marries our women? By Allah, if he dies, we will cast lots for his wives." Then it was revealed. By my life, that is not far from the hypocrites, and it is further from the sincere believers than the Pleiades (al-'Ayyuq) is far, especially whoever was among the ones given glad tidings, may Allah be pleased with them all. I have seen, from some of the eminent scholars, that the Talha who said what he said is not Talha, one of the ten, but another Talha, and the reported statement is not improbable from him. This is from the category of the confusion of names, so there is no difficulty.

﴿There is no blame upon them concerning their fathers, nor their sons, nor their brothers, nor the sons of their brothers, nor the sons of their sisters﴾. This is a resumptive statement (isti'naf) explaining who the women need not veil from. It is narrated that when the verse of hijab was revealed, the fathers, sons and relatives said: "O Messenger of Allah, shall we also speak with them from behind a veil?" So this was revealed. The apparent meaning is: there is no sin upon them for leaving off the veil before their fathers, etc. This is also narrated from Qatadah. From Mujahid: the intended meaning is that there is no blame upon them for removing the outer garment (jilbab) and displaying adornment before those mentioned. Included in their ruling is every mahram relative, by blood or by fosterage, according to what Ibn Sa'd narrated from al-Zuhri. Ibn Abi Shaybah and Abu Dawud, in his book on abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of one ruling by a later one), narrated from Ikrimah, who said: It reached Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, had veiled herself from al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with him. He said: "Indeed, his seeing her is permissible." The paternal uncle and maternal uncle are not mentioned because they are in the position of parents, or because the mention of the sons of brothers and the sons of sisters suffices in place of mentioning them. For the reason why there is no obligation of veiling between them and both groups is the very same as between them and the paternal and maternal uncles, namely that they are paternal aunts to the sons of brothers and maternal aunts to the sons of sisters. Al-Sha'bi said:

Page 75

They are not mentioned, even though they are among the mahram relatives, lest they describe her to their sons, and they are not mahram. Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated something similar from 'Ali, may Allah honour his face. Al-Sha'bi and Ikrimah disliked that a woman remove her head-covering in the presence of her paternal or maternal uncle, for fear that he would describe her to his son. In my view this opinion is weak, because it would apply to all women who are not mothers of mahram relatives, and I do not consider the narration from 'Ali, may Allah honour his face, to be authentic.

﴿Nor their women﴾, i.e., the believing women, as narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd and Mujahid. The attribution "their women" is in view of their being upon their religion, so they veil from non-believing women, even if they are People of the Book. In al-Bahr (Abu Hayyan's Tafsir al-Bahr al-Muhit): included in "their women" are mothers, sisters, all other relatives, and those who are connected to them among those who manage their affairs and those who serve them.

﴿Nor those whom their right hands possess﴾. The apparent meaning is male slaves and female slaves. Ibn Mardawayh narrated this from Ibn 'Abbas, and Imam al-Shafi'i adopted this view. Al-Khafaji said: the position of Abu Hanifah is that it is restricted to female slaves. On the apparent meaning, the mukatab (slave under a contract of manumission) was excluded. Abu Hayyan said: The Prophet (ﷺ) commanded that the veil be drawn between them and the mukatab, and Umm Salamah did so with her mukatab, Nabhan.

﴿And fear Allah﴾, in all that you do and leave undone, especially in what you have been commanded and what you have been forbidden. In al-Bahr: there is an ellipsis in the speech, and the sense is: "Confine yourselves to this, and fear Allah regarding it, that you not transgress it to something else." The shift in the speech from the third person to the second person carries added emphasis in demanding taqwa (God-consciousness) from them.

﴿Indeed Allah is ever, over all things, Witness﴾. Nothing hidden is concealed from Him, and circumstances do not vary in His knowledge, so He rewards deeds according to their state. Here it has been disputed whether it is forbidden to see the persons of women when they are covered. Some held that it is, and this is attributed to Qadi 'Iyad, whose words are: "The obligation of hijab is among what they have been singled out with. It is obligatory upon them without dispute regarding the face and the two hands. It is therefore not permissible for them to uncover these in testimony or otherwise, nor to display their persons even if they are veiled, except what necessity calls for, such as going out to relieve oneself."

Then he cited what is in the Muwatta' that when 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, died, Hafsah was screened by the women from having her person seen, and that Zaynab bint Jahsh had a canopy (qubbah) placed over her bier to screen her person. End of quote. Ibn Hajar, the hafiz, objected to this, saying: "There is no proof in what he mentioned for what he claimed, namely that it is obligatory upon them. After the Prophet (ﷺ) they performed Hajj and tawaf, and the Companions and those after them would hear hadith from them while their bodies were covered, though not their persons." End of quote. I myself consider it better to screen the persons, so it is not far-fetched to say that it is recommended for them and that it is requested of them more than of others.

In al-Bahr: 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, held that none should attend the funeral of Zaynab except a mahram of hers, out of regard for the veil. Asma' bint 'Umays informed him of a way to screen her on the bier with a canopy erected over it, and told him that she had seen this in the land of Abyssinia, so 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, did it. It is narrated that he did the same at the funeral of Fatimah, daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 56 (part 1 of 5):

﴿Indeed, Allah and His angels send blessings upon the Prophet﴾ is like a causal explanation for what the preceding speech conveyed of the great honour, the like of which is not known. The expression by means of the nominal sentence (al-jumla al-ismiyya) indicates permanence and continuity. It has been mentioned that the sentence indicates permanence when considered in its beginning, since it is a nominal sentence, and indicates renewal when considered in its end, since it is a verbal sentence (al-jumla al-fi'liyya). Thus its meaning is the continuity of the blessing and its renewal moment after moment. Its emphasis (by the particle inna) is for giving attention to the matter of the statement. It has also been said that it occurs as an answer to an implied question: What is the cause of this great honour? He is referred to as "the Prophet" rather than by his name ﷺ, contrary to the usual practice in God's narrating of His prophets (peace be upon them), to indicate what he ﷺ was singled out with of added majesty, nobility and exalted rank. This indication is emphasised by the definite article "al-" (alif-lam), which is used for specifying a known person, to indicate that he ﷺ is the well-known one who deserves this description. Some of the eminent scholars said: this is to indicate the cause of the ruling. The word "Messenger" (rasul) was not used in its place so that it would correspond with what precedes it, His saying: ﴿And it is not for you to harm the Messenger of Allah﴾, because the office of messenger is superior to that of prophethood according to the correct view on which the majority agree, contrary to Izz ibn Abd al-Salam. Therefore, linking the ruling to it (i.e., to the office of prophethood) does not indicate the strength of his entitlement, peace be upon him, to the blessing, in contrast to linking it to something lower than it while it is present in him. This is a subtle meaning which does not readily lead to an objection against it. The addition of "angels" (malaika) is for generality (al-istighraq).

It has been said: (His angels) and not (the angels), to indicate their great worth and their high honour by attributing them to Allah, the Exalted. This necessarily entails magnifying him ﷺ by what reaches him from them, since the great does not produce anything except what is great. Furthermore, there is in it an alert to their multitude and that the blessing from this vast host, whose extent none can encompass except their Creator, reaches him ﷺ throughout the passing of days and ages, along with its renewal at every time and moment. This is the most eloquent, most complete, most comprehensive, most perfect and purest form of magnification.

They differed regarding the meaning of blessing (salat) from Allah, the Exalted, and His angels (peace be upon them) upon His Prophet ﷺ, into several opinions. It has been said: it is from Him, Mighty and Majestic is He, His praise of him in the presence of His angels and His honouring of him. This was narrated by al-Bukhari from Abu al-Aliya and others, from al-Rabi' ibn Anas, and al-Halimi followed it in (Shu'ab al-Iman). His honouring him in this world is by raising his mention, manifesting his religion, and perpetuating the practice of his law; and in the Hereafter by granting him intercession for his community, multiplying his reward and recompense, and displaying his excellence before the first and last generations by the praiseworthy station (al-maqam al-mahmud), and by placing him ahead of all the near-stationed witnesses. Explaining it in this way does not preclude the conjoining of others, such as the family and companions, with him in it, because the honouring of each person is according to what befits him. And it is from the angels: supplication for him, peace be upon him, as narrated by Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Abi Hatim from Abu al-Aliya. It has been said: it is from Him, Exalted is He, His mercy, Mighty and Majestic is He. This was reported by al-Tirmidhi from al-Thawri and other people of knowledge, and was also reported from Abu al-Aliya and from al-Dahhak. Al-Mubarrad, Ibn al-A'rabi and the Imam al-Mawardi followed it, and he said: this is the most apparent of the views.

An objection has been raised based on what passed when speaking of His saying: ﴿He it is who sends blessings upon you, and His angels﴾ [al-Ahzab: 43], and the answer is the same answer. Also, the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) asked, as will come shortly, Allah willing, when it was revealed, about the manner of the blessing. Had they not understood a difference between it and mercy, they would not have asked about its manner, given that they knew the supplication for mercy in the tashahhud.

It has been answered: it is a specific mercy, so they asked about the manner in order to comprehend that particularity. And it is from the angels, as you have heard at the outset. This entails, according to this view and that, the use of a single word in two meanings, which many do not permit, such as the Hanafiyya. Those who hold to one of the two views and do not permit that kind of usage differed in escaping this in the verse. Some said: there is an ellipsis in the verse, and the original is: Indeed Allah sends blessings, and His angels send blessings; thus each meaning is conveyed by its own word. Another said: the multiplicity of the agent made the verb like a multiple verb. Sadr al-Shari'a said: it is possible that the meaning is one, literal, namely supplication, and the meaning, and Allah knows best, is that He, Exalted is He, supplicates for His own Self and the angels by bringing about good; this, with regard to Him, Exalted is He, is mercy, and with regard to the angels is forgiveness. In this there is a vagueness that is not hidden. A group of the investigating scholars said: it is escaped by means of general figurative usage (umum al-majaz), so that a general figurative meaning is intended, of which each of the meanings is a literal instance, namely: attentiveness to whatever is good for him ﷺ, the rectitude of his affairs, the manifestation of his nobility and the magnification of his station, or compassion and inclination of the heart.

Some of the eminent scholars said: the meaning of blessing differs according to the state of the one who blesses, the one for whom blessing is made, and the one upon whom blessing is made. The better view is that it is here placed for the common element, which is attentiveness to the one upon whom blessing is made, or the intention of the arrival of good. Another said: the correct view is that salat in the linguistic sense has one meaning, which is inclination (al-atf). Then, with respect to Him, Exalted is He, it is mercy; with respect to the angels (peace be upon them), it is seeking forgiveness; and with respect to the sons of Adam, it is supplication.

It has been criticised: inclination in its literal meaning is impossible for Him, Exalted is He; so, from considering it as attributed to Him, Exalted is He, and to the angels (peace be upon them), there follows what follows. It has been answered: we do not concede the impossibility, except when inclination in the Unseen is like inclination in the seen, which is not realised except by a turning of the heart and the like, which are attributes of bodies that are impossible for Him, glorified is He. We stand beyond the prohibition, for much of what is in the seen is a thing, and in Allah, Exalted is He, it is beyond that, and it is attributed to Him, glorified is He, in its true sense, as with hearing and sight, and likewise will.

The early Muslims (al-salaf) went to not interpreting mercy in regard to Him, Exalted is He, by either of the two well-known interpretations, although in the seen it is not realised except through what is impossible for Him, Exalted is He. Had that interpretation been made obligatory, there would have remained in our hands hardly anything that does not need it, except a little. What is related to this topic has been mentioned previously in more than one place in this book. It may be chosen that salat here is magnification of his ﷺ rank, accompanied by an inclination befitting Him, Exalted is He, and His angels. When it extends to him ﷺ and to any one of the believers, it is connected to each according to what suits him. The joining of Allah, glorified is He, and the angels in one pronoun does not contradict his ﷺ saying to the one who said: "Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger has been guided, and whoever disobeys them both has gone astray." He ﷺ said: "Evil is the orator of the people; you are one—say: and whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger." This is because such a joining from Him, Exalted is He, is purely an honour for the angels (peace be upon them), from which no deficiency is imagined. Hence it was said: when the like of this comes from an infallible one, it is said as in his ﷺ saying: "None of you believes until Allah and His Messenger are dearer to him than anything else."

Some of them said: there is no harm in this absolutely, and they criticised the orator because he paused upon "yas'hima" and stopped briefly. Evidence was adduced from a report of Abu Dawud. It has been said: it is ugly if it is in two clauses, as in the speech of the orator, and not ugly if it is in one, as in the verse and the speech of the Beloved, peace be upon him. In this there is discussion.

Ibn Abbas and Abd al-Warith, from Abu Amr, read "wa-malaikatuhu" (and His angels) in the nominative (raf'). According to the Kufans other than al-Farra', it is conjoined to the position (mahall) of inna and its subject. Al-Farra' stipulates for this conjoining that the grammatical case of the subject of inna be hidden, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 69], and as in the words of the poet:

"Whoever has his abode in Medina this evening, then I and Qayyar in it are strangers."

Whether the hiddenness of the grammatical case includes the defective noun (al-ism al-maqsur) and the noun construed with a pronominal suffix of the first person (al-mudaf li-l-ya') or is specific to the indeclinable is a matter of dispute. According to the Basrans and al-Farra', it is a subject (mubtada'), and the clause "yusalluna" (they send blessings) is its predicate, and the predicate of inna is omitted, being confidently understood from what follows it. The meaning is: Indeed Allah sends blessings, and His angels send blessings.

﴿O you who believe, send blessings upon him﴾, that is: magnify his station, inclining towards him, for you are more entitled to it. The apparent thrust of the verse is that it is to obligate us to imitate Him, Exalted is He, and this fits the unity of meaning together with the unity of wording. The reading of Ibn Mas'ud ("send blessings upon him as He sent blessings upon him") and likewise the reading of al-Hasan ("so send blessings upon him") is more apparent in what has been mentioned, so explaining "send blessings upon him" as "say: O Allah, send blessings upon the Prophet" or something similar is far-fetched.

Whoever explained it in this way meant that what is intended by the magnification commanded is what occurs with this wording or similar to it, of what indicates the seeking of magnification of his station, peace be upon him, from Allah, Mighty and Majestic is He, because the capacity of the believers falls short of fulfilling his right, peace be upon him. What came in the reports is guidance to the manner and description of that, not an explanation of the word "send blessings." This came in several forms, and the gathering of them is evident.

Abd al-Razzaq, Ibn Abi Shayba, the Imam Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ka'b ibn Ujra (may Allah be pleased with him), who said: "A man said: O Messenger of Allah, as for the greeting (salam) upon you, we already know it; so how is the blessing upon you? He said: 'Say: O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and upon the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings upon the family of Abraham; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious. O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed the family of Abraham; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious.'"

[Page 78]

Malik, the Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and others reported from Abu Humayd al-Sa'idi that they said: "O Messenger of Allah, how should we send blessings upon you? The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'Say: O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and his wives and his offspring, as You sent blessings upon the family of Abraham; and bless Muhammad and his wives and his offspring, as You blessed the family of Abraham; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious.'"

The Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and others reported from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri: "We said: O Messenger of Allah, this is the greeting upon you, we already know it; so how is the blessing upon you? He said: 'Say: O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad, Your servant and Your Messenger, as You sent blessings upon Ibrahim; and bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Ibrahim.'"

al-Nasa'i and others reported from Abu Hurayra that "they asked the Messenger of Allah ﷺ how they should send blessings upon him. He said: 'Say: O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, and bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You sent blessings and blessed upon Ibrahim and the family of Ibrahim among the worlds; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious. And the greeting is as you have known.'"

The Imam Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn Mardawayh reported from Ibn Buraida (may Allah be pleased with him) who said: "We said: O Messenger of Allah, we already know how to greet you, so how should we send blessings upon you? He said: 'Say: O Allah, make Your blessings, Your mercy and Your blessings upon Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You made them upon Ibrahim; indeed You are Praiseworthy, Glorious.'"

Among the other reports found in the books of hadith, and although some of the narrations mentioned in them are open to criticism, the apparent meaning of the question is that it concerned the manner (of sending blessings), as we indicated earlier. This is the view preferred by al-Baji and others, and al-Qurtubi affirmed it. It has also been said that the question concerned the meaning of prayer (salah) and the words with which it should be performed. What prompted them to ask in this way is that the greeting of peace (salam) had come in the tashahhud (the seated formula recited in prayer) in a specific wording, so they understood that the blessing too must be made in a specific wording. They did not resort to analogy (qiyas), because the wording of the text was easy to find, especially since in matters of remembrance (adhkar) the wording is observed as far as possible. The matter turned out as they understood it, for he (ﷺ) did not say the blessing as he said the greeting of peace, but taught them a different form. So it has been said. It may also be said, according to the first view, that when they heard the command to send blessings after hearing that Allah the Mighty and Majestic and His angels, peace be upon them, send blessings upon him (ﷺ), and understood that the blessing from Allah the Mighty and Majestic and from His angels upon him, peace and blessings be upon him, is a kind of honour befitting the station of that noble Prophet, upon whom be from Allah, exalted is He, the best of blessings and the most perfect of peace, they did not know what the befitting way of honouring that dignified one and lord of the wise would be, (with) blessings and peace that would encompass the reckoning. So they asked about the manner of that honouring, and he (ﷺ) guided them to what is known to be the best kind of it, and he is kind and merciful to them. He (ﷺ) said: "Say: O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad," up to the end of what is in some of the authentic narrations. In this there is an indication that you are unable to honour me as is fitting, so ask Allah the Mighty and Majestic to do so for me.

From here it is known that whoever does what he was commanded, by asking Allah the Mighty and Majestic to send blessings upon him (ﷺ), has brought the greatest kind of honour, because it includes the acknowledgement of inability to honour him as is fitting. It has been said, and it is attributed to al-Siddiq (Abu Bakr), may Allah be pleased with him, that "the inability to attain perception is itself a perception." Something close in general to what we have mentioned is the saying of one of the eminent scholars, which Abu al-Yaman ibn Asakir related and deemed good: "When Allah the Exalted commanded us to send blessings upon His Prophet (ﷺ), we did not attain knowledge of its excellence, nor did we reach the reality of what Allah the Exalted intends by it, so we left that to Allah the Mighty and Majestic and said: 'O Allah, You send blessings upon Your Messenger, for You know best what befits him and what You intend for him (ﷺ).'" End of quotation. Perhaps what we have mentioned is more subtle than that. The apparent implication of his (ﷺ) guidance to them to ask Allah, exalted is His station, to send blessings upon him is that the command is not fulfilled except by what includes asking that from Him, the Mighty and Majestic.

"O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad" suffices, because it is the wording on which the narrations agree in explaining the manner. It seems that the specific form, in wording and meaning, is not binding. For this reason, some who made it obligatory in prayer (and you will learn of it, God willing) said that just as "O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad" suffices, the wording reported is not specifically required. There is a dispute with some who held that "Allah bless Muhammad" (ṣallā Allāhu ʿalā Muḥammad) suffices according to the more correct view, unlike "bless the Messenger of Allah," which is not valid by consensus, because it does not attribute the blessing to Allah the Exalted, and so it does not have the meaning of what was reported.

In the Tuhfah of Ibn Hajar: the blessing "send blessings upon Muhammad" suffices if one intends by it supplication, as appears. Al-Naysaburi said: "Saying 'I have sent blessings upon Muhammad' does not suffice, because the rank of the servant falls short of that. Rather he should ask his Lord, glorified is He, to send blessings upon him (ﷺ). Then the one who sends blessings upon him in reality is Allah the Exalted, and calling the servant one who sends blessings upon him is a metaphor for asking Allah the Exalted to send blessings upon him (ﷺ). So reflect on it."

They mentioned that using the form of command is better than using the form of report. It was answered regarding the consensus of the hadith scholars on using the form of report that it is part of what we were commanded to do, namely to speak to people in what they recognise, since when the books of hadith are read, many common folk gather, and it was feared they would understand from the form of command that the blessing upon him (ﷺ) had not yet been granted by Allah the Mighty and Majestic; otherwise we would not ask for it to be granted to him, "the blessings of Allah and His peace upon him." So they used a form from which the attainment is immediately understood by them. Yet, while it keeps them from this confusion, it includes the request which we were commanded to make. End of quotation.

Its weakness is not hidden. The better view is to say that this is because their blessing, in most cases, came in the middle of a narrative statement, such as "The Prophet (ﷺ) said such-and-such" or "He (ﷺ) did such-and-such." So they preferred not to lengthen the interruption, nor to have the speech in two styles, because that involves departing from the familiar path. You rarely find in eloquent speech a supplicatory clause inserted in the middle except that it has a declarative form in wording, though there is a possibility of disturbing the listener's mind and slowing his understanding; and clarity of expression is among the things that must be observed. So reflect.

The apparent view is that the command is not fulfilled by "O Allah, magnify Muhammad with the magnification that is befitting," or similar wording that does not contain a derivative of ṣalāh (blessing), such as ṣalli (send blessings) and ṣallā (sent blessings). We have not heard of anyone counting one who says that as having sent blessings upon him (ﷺ). This is most evident when "Say: O Allah, send blessings upon Muhammad" is an explanation of His saying: ﴿Send blessings upon him and greet him with peace﴾ (Al-Ahzab 33:56). That is, "and say: Peace be upon you, O Prophet," and similar. This is the view of most of the eminent scholars.

As for the meaning of "peace be upon you" (al-salāmu ʿalayka), there are three aspects:

The first: safety from defects and afflictions for you and with you, that is, accompanying you and remaining with you. Thus salām is a verbal noun meaning safety, like al-ladhādh and al-ladhādhah, and al-malāmu and al-malāmah. Because peace includes praise, it is followed by ʿalā, not because of the sense of qaḍāʾ (decreeing), i.e., "Allah has decreed peace upon you," as has been said, since qaḍāʾ, like duʿāʾ, is not followed by ʿalā for benefit, nor because it includes the sense of authority and dominion, since that is far-fetched in this aspect.

The second: "peace" is one who constantly guards and protects you, takes charge of it and is its guarantor. Here salām is a name of Allah the Exalted. Its meaning, according to what Ibn Furak and others chose from several views, is "the One free from every defect and deficiency in His essence, attributes and actions." It has also been said: when salām is intended as one of His names, the meaning is "may you never be without good and blessing, and may you be safe from every disliked thing, because when the name of Allah the Exalted is mentioned over something, it bestows that." It has been said that the sentence on this reckoning is elliptical, with the omission of the genitive, i.e., "May Allah the Exalted protect you," and the meaning is a supplication for protection.

The third: submission to you. Here salām is from musālamah (peaceful accord) and non-opposition. The meaning is a supplication that Allah the Exalted make His servants submissive and humbly obedient to him (ﷺ) and to his law. Its being followed by ʿalā is said to be because it contains the sense of turning towards, for whoever submits to someone and yields to him has turned towards him. My preferred view is the first aspect.

It has been said that the meaning of "greet him with peace" (sallimū taslīman) is "submit to his commands (ﷺ) with submission." This is not far-fetched, but the apparent meanings of the reports and traditions require the earlier meaning, and perhaps for this reason most scholars took that view. The sentence is a declarative form whose meaning is supplication for safety and the request for it from Allah the Exalted for His Prophet (ﷺ). This has been questioned in the case where Allah the Exalted says "Peace be upon you, O Prophet" or similar, because supplication cannot be conceived from Him, the Mighty and Majestic, since supplication is a request, and it involves a requester, a requested thing, and one from whom it is requested, which are distinct matters. If His request, glorified is He, for safety for His Prophet (ﷺ) is from other than Him, then its impossibility is among the most evident self-evident truths. If it is from His own essence, the Mighty and Majestic, it would follow that it differs from His essence, and a thing does not differ from its own essence by necessity. This is the source of the saying of some: "In the peace from Him, the Exalted, there is a problem of great importance, so it deserves attention and not neglect. Who grasps its secret?"

It has been answered that request belongs to the category of volitions, and the one who wills, just as he wills that another do something, so too he wills that he himself do it; and self-directed request, even if it is not volition, is more specific than it, and volition is like the genus for it. Just as it is conceivable that the one who wills wills for himself, so too he requests from himself, since there is no difference between request and volition. The upshot is that the request of the Truth, exalted is He, from His own essence is an intelligible matter that each person knows from his own soul, as proven by the fact that he commands it and forbids it. He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Indeed, the soul commands to evil﴾ (Yusuf 12:53), and ﴿But as for one who feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from desire﴾ (Al-Nazi'at 79:40). Command and prohibition are two kinds of request, and they have been conceived from a human being toward himself by explicit text. So likewise the remaining kinds and types of request.
