Clearer than this is that request from Him, exalted is He, has the meaning of volition, and the volition of a person toward something from his own essence is conceivable on the basis of a conceptual distinction, and something like this suffices in this context. The meaning of "O Allah, grant peace upon the Prophet" is, as has been said, "O Allah, say peace upon the Prophet." It has also been said that its meaning is "O Allah, bring about or realize safety for him," and it has been said that it means "O Allah, make him safe from deficiencies and afflictions."

One of the contemporary scholars said: "The saying 'peace be upon you' and similar from Allah the Mighty and Majestic is for the bringing about and creation of safety through this wording, like what they said about the formulas of contracts." He chose that the meaning of "O Allah, grant peace upon the Prophet" is "O Allah, bring about safety or realize it for him," rather than "say peace upon the Prophet," in order to shorten the distance. So reflect.

It may be that the greeting of peace from Allah the Mighty and Majestic upon His Prophets, peace be upon them, is like His saying, glorified is He: ﴿Peace upon Noah among the worlds﴾ (Al-Saffat 37:79), ﴿Peace upon Abraham﴾ (Al-Saffat 37:109), ﴿Peace upon Moses and Aaron﴾ (Al-Saffat 37:120), as an indication that He, majestic is His dignity, placed them in such a state that prayers are made for them and praise is given to them.

The accusative of ﴿taslīman﴾ is because it is an emphatic verbal noun. He, glorified is He, emphasised the greeting but did not emphasise the blessing. It has been said that this is because the blessing is already emphasised by His informing that He and His angels send blessings upon him, while the greeting is not like that, so emphasising it with a verbal noun is fitting, since there is nothing else to take its place.

To this returns the saying of Ibn al-Qayyim: "The emphasis in both is present, though its aspect differs. He, exalted is He, informed in the first (verse) of His blessing and the blessing of His angels upon him, emphasising it with 'inna' and with the plural that conveys generality for the angels. In this there is such honour for him (ﷺ) as requires hastening to send blessings upon him without waiting for a command, in agreement with Allah the Exalted and His angels in that. For this reason it dispensed with emphasising 'yuṣallī' with a verbal noun. When the greeting was free of this meaning and came in the sphere of a bare command, it was fitting to emphasise it with a verbal noun to establish the meaning, and emphasis of the verb was placed in the position of affirming it. Thus in the blessing there is repetition in both report and request, and likewise in the greeting there is repetition in verb and verbal noun. Also, the blessing is placed before the greeting in wording, and placement indicates importance, so it was fitting to emphasise the greeting, lest it be imagined that there is little concern for it because it comes later." It has also been said that the speech contains ihtibak (a rhetorical device of omitting parallel elements from two clauses), and the original is: "Send blessings upon him, a blessing; and greet him, a greeting." So "upon him" was omitted from one of the two clauses, and the verbal noun from the other. The blessing was attributed to Allah the Exalted and His angels but not the greeting, and the believers were commanded with both. It has been said that this is because "peace" has two meanings, greeting and submission, so they were commanded with both since both are valid here. It was not attributed to Allah, glorified is He, and to the angels, lest it be thought that in relation to Allah the Exalted and the angels it means submission, which is impossible in His regard, and likewise in the regard of the angels.

[p. 81]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 56 (part 3 of 5):

It has been said: the prayer (salah) from Allah, glorified is He, and from the angels includes the greeting of peace (salam) in the sense of the salutation (tahiyyah), which cannot be conceived otherwise. So, in attributing the prayer to Him, exalted is He, and to the angels, there is an implication of the existence of the greeting in this sense. As for the prayer from us, although it too implies the salutation, we are addressed with submission (al-inqiyad), and the prayer does not imply that. Therefore, it was necessary to state it explicitly for us, because the prayer does not suffice in place of its two conceivable meanings that are required of us. Then it was said: this is better than what preceded it, because that is refuted by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Peace be upon Abraham﴾, and ﴿The angels will enter upon them from every gate, [saying], "Peace be upon you"﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 23-24], and these two are not refuted by this. Thus far, but there is a discussion in it.

Al-Shihab al-Khafaji, may Allah have mercy on him, said: A secret subtlety has appeared to me in the omission of emphasis on the greeting and its restriction to the believers. It is that the greeting upon him (ﷺ) means his being safeguarded from what harms him. So when this verse came after the mention of what harms the Prophet (ﷺ), and harm comes only from humans and has proceeded from them, the restriction to them and the emphasis were appropriate. And perhaps it may be said, though remotely, that the greeting of Allah, exalted is He, and His angels upon him (ﷺ) may have been known to the believers before the revelation of the verse, so it was not mentioned, and they greet in it for that reason. And that their being commanded to greet him (ﷺ) was also known to them, as was the manner of the greeting. This knowledge is indicated by what is narrated in several reports, that when the verse was revealed they said: "O Messenger of Allah, we have known how to greet you," and by this, as it has been said, they meant the greeting that is in the tashahhud. So when they were informed of the prayer of Allah, exalted is He, and His angels upon him (ﷺ) in the verse, stripped of the mention of the greeting, and this was followed by the command to pray, it was liable to cause neglect of the matter of the greeting. Or it was that its demand from them was abrogated (naskh), so they were commanded with it in emphatic form, to repel that suspicion. And Allah, exalted is He, knows best the reality of the matter. The command in the verse, according to most scholars, is for obligation (wujub). Rather, some of them mentioned the consensus (ijma') of the imams and scholars upon it.

The claim of Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari that it is for recommendation (nadb) by consensus is rejected, or interpreted as being applied to what exceeds one time in a lifetime. For al-Qurtubi, the exegete (mufassir), said: There is no disagreement on the obligation of prayer upon the Prophet (ﷺ) once in a lifetime. The detailed discussion of its command, after setting aside the view of its recommendation, is that the scholars differed about it. It has been said: it is obligatory once in a lifetime, like the statement of monotheism (kalimat al-tawhid), because the command is unrestricted and does not require repetition, and the essence is achieved by one time. This is the view of the majority of the community, including Abu Hanifa, Malik, and others. It has been said: it is obligatory in the tashahhud absolutely. It has been said: it is obligatory in every prayer. Some of the Hanbalis uniquely held that the opening supplication (du'a al-iftitah) is specifically to include it. It has been said: it is necessary to do it abundantly without restriction to a number, and this was related from the judge Abu Bakr ibn Bakir. It has been said: it is obligatory in every session once, even if the mention of him (ﷺ) is repeated many times. It has been said: it is obligatory in every supplication.

It has been said: it is obligatory whenever he (ﷺ) is mentioned, and this was said by a group of the Hanafis, including al-Tahawi, whose wording is: it is obligatory whenever his mention is heard from another or he is mentioned by oneself. And a group of the Shafi'is, including the Imam al-Halimi, the Ustadh Abu Ishaq al-Isfara'ini, and Shaykh Abu Hamid al-Isfara'ini. And a group of the Malikis, including al-Tartushi, Ibn al-'Arabi, al-Fakihani, and some of the Hanbalis. It has been said that this is based on the weak view in the principles of jurisprudence (usul) that an unrestricted command implies repetition, but this is not so; rather, it has other proofs, such as the hadiths in which there is supplication against him with humiliation, distance, and wretchedness, and the description with stinginess and rudeness, and other things that imply a threat, and this, according to most, is among the indications of obligation.

Many have objected to this view, saying that it contradicts the consensus that was established before its proponent, since it is not known from any Companion (sahabi) or Follower (tabi'i). And that on its generality it would follow that the listener could not devote himself to another act of worship, and that it would be obligatory upon the muezzin and the one who hears him, the reciter who passes by his mention, and the one who pronounces the two words of testimony (shahadatayn). And in this is hardship which the tolerant Shari'ah has come to reject. And that the praise of Allah, exalted is He, whenever He is mentioned, is more deserving of obligation, and they did not say so. And that it is not narrated from any Companion that he said: "O Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless you." And that those hadiths cited as proof for obligation came in the form of exaggeration in emphasizing this and demanding it, and regarding one who habitually neglects prayer.

This can be answered regarding all of that. As for the first, the proponents of obligation are among the imams of transmission, so how could they break the consensus? It is not sufficient to refute them that it was not preserved from a Companion or Follower. The refutation is only complete if a consensus expressly stating non-obligation is preserved, and how could it be? As for the second, it is denied, rather one can devote oneself to other acts of worship. As for the third, the proponents of obligation are bound by it, and there is no hardship in it. As for the fourth, a group expressly stated obligation with regard to Allah, exalted is He, too. As for the fifth, it has been narrated through several chains from several Companions that when they said, "O Messenger of Allah," they said, "May Allah bless you." As for the sixth, interpreting the hadiths in the manner mentioned is not sufficient unless its chain is explained, and they did not explain it. Then, as most of the proponents of obligation mentioned, it is an obligation of individual (fard 'ayn) upon every single person, and some of them held that it is a communal obligation (fard kifayah).

They also differed on whether the obligation repeats with the repetition of his (ﷺ) mention in one session. In some commentaries on the Hidayah, it suffices once according to the sound view. The author of al-Mujtaba said: it repeats. And with the repetition of the mention of Allah, exalted is He, it does not repeat. He and others distinguished between them by what is open to examination. It may be distinguished in that the rights of Allah, exalted is He, are based on leniency and latitude, and the rights of the servants are based on strictness and restriction as far as possible. And the claim that it is also a right of Allah, exalted is He, because He commanded it, glorified is He, arises from not understanding what is meant by the right of Allah, exalted is He.

It has been said: it is obligatory in the sitting at the end of the prayer, between the tashahhud and the closing salam (salam al-tahallul). This is the position of al-Shafi'i which is authentically attributed to him.

Al-Asnawi related that he had another view: that it is a sunnah in the prayer, which his eminent companions did not take into account. It was agreed with by a group of the Companions and the Followers after them, and the jurists of the cities. From the Companions is Ibn Mas'ud, for it is authentically reported from him that he said: "A man recites the tashahhud in the prayer, then sends prayers upon the Prophet (ﷺ), then supplicates for himself." And Abu Mas'ud al-Badri and Ibn 'Umar, for it is authentically reported from them that there is no prayer except with recitation, tashahhud, and prayer upon the Prophet (ﷺ). "If you forget any of that, then prostrate twice after the salam." From the Followers is al-Sha'bi, for it is authentically reported from him: "We used to know the tashahhud. When he says, 'And that Muhammad is His servant and Messenger,' he praises his Lord and extols Him, then prays upon the Prophet (ﷺ), then asks for his need." Al-Bayhaqi narrated from him: "Whoever does not pray upon the Prophet (ﷺ) in the tashahhud, let him repeat his prayer," or he said: "His prayer is not valid." And the Imam Abu Ja'far Muhammad al-Baqir, for al-Bayhaqi narrated from him something similar to what was mentioned from al-Sha'bi. And al-Daraqutni approved it, as did Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi and Muqatil. Rather, the hafiz Ibn Hajar said: "I have not seen from any of the Companions and Followers an explicit statement of non-obligation except what is related from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i, and this indicates that others were holding the view of obligation." And from the jurists of the cities is Ahmad, for two narrations came from him, and the apparent view is that the narration of obligation is the latter, for he said: "I used to hesitate about that, then it became clear to me that prayer upon the Prophet (ﷺ) is obligatory." And Ishaq ibn Rahawayh, for he said at the end of the two narrations from him: "If one leaves it intentionally, his prayer is invalid; if by forgetfulness, I hope that it suffices for him." This is a view among the Malikis, adopted by Ibn al-'Arabi among them, and it is perhaps necessary for those who hold its obligation whenever he (ﷺ) is mentioned, because his mention precedes it in the tashahhud. However, its obligation after the tashahhud for that reason does not imply that it is a condition for the validity of the prayer. Yet it is objected to those who say that al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, was alone in his view of obligation. As for his evidence, may Allah be pleased with him, for that, it is mentioned in al-Umm. His companions argued for it with several hadiths, some sound and some weak, and they composed treatises in defense of it and in rebuttal of those who criticized him, such as Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, al-Khattabi, al-Tahawi, and others. I consider criticism of such an imam to be a grave matter, and partisanship together with little investigation to be a dreadful thing. And the discussion of the greeting (salam) is like the discussion of the prayer.

Ibn Faris the linguist expressly stated that the two are equal in obligation, because each of them is commanded in the verse, and the command is for obligation in its literal sense, unless something arrives that diverts it from that. The best forms of prayer upon him (ﷺ) are what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) taught his Companions after they asked him, because he (ﷺ) does not choose for himself except the most noble and the most excellent. Hence al-Nawawi said in (al-Rawdah): If someone swears that he will pray upon the Prophet (ﷺ) with the best prayer, he is not fulfilling his oath except with that form. Al-Subki justified it by saying that whoever does it has certainly performed the prayer that is required, and has the good that is reported in the hadiths on prayer in that manner. Al-Rafi'i related from al-Marwazi that one fulfills it by saying: "O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, whenever those who remember You remember him and whenever the heedless forget him." Al-Qadi Husayn said: The way of fulfilling it is "O Allah, bless Muhammad as he deserves and is entitled to." Al-Barizi preferred that the best is "O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad with the best of Your blessings and the number of Your knowledge." Kamal ibn al-Humam said: Whatever forms are mentioned are all present in "O Allah, bless forever with the best of Your blessings our master, Your servant, Your Prophet, and Your Messenger Muhammad and his family, and grant him peace, and increase him in nobility and honor, and cause him to be brought near to You in the station on the Day of Resurrection." Ibn Hajar al-Haytami preferred other than that. Ibn 'Arafa related from Ibn 'Abd al-Salam that in the greeting upon him (ﷺ) it is necessary to add "peace" (taslim), such as saying: "O Allah, bless Muhammad and grant him peace," or "May Allah, exalted is He, bless him and grant him peace." It seems he took the apparent meaning of what is in the verse, and it is not a sound interpretation, as becomes clear upon slight reflection. It is related from a group of the Companions and those after them that the manner of prayer upon him (ﷺ) is not restricted to the text, and that whoever Allah grants the ability of clear expression, explaining the meanings with eloquent words, sound structures, and clear meanings, which indicate the perfection of his nobility (ﷺ) and the greatness of his sanctity, has that right. It was argued for with what 'Abd al-Razzaq, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Majah, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "When you pray upon the Prophet (ﷺ), then do it well, for you do not know, perhaps it is presented to him." They said: "Teach us." He said: "Say: O Allah, make Your prayers, Your mercy, and Your blessings upon the master of the messengers, the leader of the God-fearing, the seal of the prophets, Muhammad, Your servant and Your Messenger, the leader of goodness, the guide to goodness, and the messenger of mercy. O Allah, raise him to a praiseworthy station which the earlier and later generations will envy him for. O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Abraham and the family of Abraham, You are indeed Praiseworthy and Glorious."

[p. 84]

Concerning His saying, glorified is He, ﴿Send blessings upon him and greet him with peace﴾, there is, in my view, a subtle allusion to the desirability of beautifying the prayer upon him (peace and blessings be upon him), in that it came as speech that could form a hemistich of the meter al-Kamil (al-Bahr al-Kamil). So reflect upon it, for I think it is precious.

Al-Nawawi (may Allah have mercy on him) took the verse as evidence that it is disliked (makruh) to mention the prayer upon the Prophet without the greeting of peace, or the reverse, because the command to do both together appears in it. Some scholars agreed with him. It was objected that the hadiths on teaching indicate that the teaching of the greeting (al-tasleem) preceded the teaching of the prayer (al-salah). Thus he would have mentioned the greeting alone once before the prayer, in the tashahhud. It was answered that mentioning one alone at that time is no proof, because it did not occur from him (peace and blessings be upon him) intentionally. How could that be, when the verse explicitly mentions both? Rather, it is only possible that he taught them the greeting and thought they knew the prayer, so he remained silent about teaching them it, and when they asked him, he answered them (ﷺ) accordingly. This, as you see, is weak.

Al-Allama Ibn Hajar al-Haytami mentioned that the correct view is that by "dislike" is meant "that which is less preferable" (khilaf al-awla), since the specific prohibition that would demand it is not found. Al-Hamawi, from our companions, reported from Muniyat al-Mufti that according to us it is not disliked to mention one of them separately from the other. Then he said, quoting al-Allama Mayrak: "This disagreement concerns our Prophet (ﷺ). As for the other prophets (peace be upon them), there is no disagreement among scholars that it is not disliked to mention one of them alone. Whoever claims otherwise must produce an explicit transmission and will not find a way to it." End of quotation.

Some scholars stated that the dislike, according to those who hold it, applies only to mentioning one alone verbally, whereas mentioning one alone in writing, as occurs in the umm (the mother of the book, i.e., the written form), is not disliked. In my view, the use of the verse as evidence for the dislike of mentioning one alone, as you have heard, is extremely weak. Its maximum indication is that each of the prayer and the greeting is commanded absolutely, and it does not indicate a command to perform them both at one time, such as being performed together joined by a conjunction, so that whoever prays in the morning and greets in the evening, for example, has fulfilled the command. It is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Establish the prayer and give the zakah﴾, and ﴿Remember Allah with much remembrance and glorify Him﴾ [al-Ahzab: 42], and other commands joined by conjunction. Yes, most of the early generation (al-salaf) followed the practice of combining them, so I do not favor departing from it, together with the safety that mentioning the greeting after the prayer provides from a suspicion that hardly occurs except to sick minds, as is not hidden.

Regarding his (ﷺ) inclusion in the address, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, here there is a disagreement. Some said he is included. One of the eminent Shafi'is explicitly stated the obligation of sending blessings upon him (ﷺ) in one's prayer, and he mentioned that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to send blessings upon himself outside the prayer, as is apparent from hadiths such as his saying (ﷺ) when his she-camel strayed and a hypocrite spoke about it: "Indeed, a man from among the hypocrites rejoiced that the she-camel of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had strayed," and his saying when he offered to the Muslims to return what he had taken from Abu al-'As, the husband of his daughter Zaynab, before his Islam: "And Zaynab, the daughter of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), asked me..." (the hadith). So he mentioned the prayer and the greeting upon himself after mentioning himself. The possibility that this was from the narrator in the two hadiths is very remote. End of quotation.

Some scholars hesitated about his inclusion, on the basis that the contextual indication of the passage from ﴿O you who have believed, do not enter the houses of the Prophet﴾ up to here is evident in restricting this ruling to the believers and not to him (ﷺ). This was examined: what precedes this verse explicitly restricts it to the believers, but this verse itself has no indication of restriction. You know that the scholars of legal theory (usuliyyun) have several opinions regarding his inclusion in a formula of this kind: (1) that he is excluded absolutely, and this is anomalous; (2) that he is included absolutely, and this is the most correct according to a group of scholars; (3) that he is included except in what was issued with a command to convey, such as ﴿Say: O you who have believed﴾. I rely upon inclusion unless there is an indication of non-inclusion, whether the command to convey came first or not. Here, the preceding context (al-sibaq) and the immediate context (al-siyaq) are, as it appears, two indications of non-inclusion.

He expressed it as "those who have believed" rather than "people," which would include the disbelievers. It was said: this is an allusion to the fact that the prayer upon him (ﷺ) is among the most sublime and most beneficial means (wasa'il), and the disbeliever has no means, so he was not addressed with a word that includes him. The addressing of disbelievers with the subsidiary rulings (al-furu'), on the view that they are addressed, concerns only their punishment for them in the Hereafter. Moreover, the place of their obligation to them is where there is consensus upon them. For this reason, the addressing of them with these is excepted for their corrupt transactions and the like.

It is perhaps better that the expression is with this for what has been mentioned, together with what the context requires. In calling the believers with this style there is a stimulus to comply with the command, which is not hidden. The command to send prayers and greetings is among the special features of this community (ummah), so no other community was commanded to send prayers and greetings upon its prophet.

This, according to what is transmitted from Abu Dharr al-Harawi, was in the second year of the Hijrah. It was said: it was on the night of the Isra' (the Night Journey). You know that the verse is Medinan. 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir reported from Mujahid that when it was revealed, Abu Bakr said: "Allah has sent down nothing good to you except that He has made us share in it." So there was revealed: ﴿It is He who sends blessings upon you, and His angels﴾. The wisdom of the difference in style between the two verses is evident to the reflective. Sending blessings by us upon the prophets other than our Prophet (ﷺ), upon him and upon them be the blessings and peace, is permissible without dislike. There came, with a sound chain, as the linguist al-Majd stated, the hadith: "If you send blessings upon the messengers, then send blessings upon me along with them, for I am a messenger among the messengers." And in another wording: "If you greet me with peace, then greet the messengers with peace." The first has another route whose chain (isnad) is hasan jayyid (good, sound), but it is mursal (a transmission in which the companion's name is omitted at the end of the chain).

[p. 85]

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Qadi Isma'il, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in (Shu'ab al-Iman) reported from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Send blessings upon the prophets of Allah and His messengers, for Allah, exalted is He, sent them just as He sent me." Although it came by weak routes, it is acted upon in a matter of this kind, as is not hidden. As for what is reported from Malik, that blessings are not to be sent upon prophets other than our Prophet (ﷺ), his companions interpreted it to mean that we have not been commanded to worship by sending blessings upon them as we have been commanded to send blessings upon him (ﷺ).

As for sending blessings upon the angels, it was said that no explicit text about it is known, and it is derived only from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah mentioned just above, if it is established that Allah, exalted is He, named them messengers.

As for sending blessings upon others than the prophets and angels (peace be upon them), the opinions of the scholars have diverged concerning it. It was said that it is permissible absolutely. Al-Qadi 'Iyad said: "On this is the general body of the people of knowledge." It is argued for by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It is He who sends blessings upon you, and His angels﴾, and by what is authentically established from his saying (ﷺ): "O Allah, send blessings upon the family of Abi Awfa," and his saying (peace and blessings be upon him), when he raised his hands: "O Allah, make Your blessings and Your mercy upon the family of Sa'd ibn 'Ubadah."

Ibn Hibban authenticated the report that "a woman said to the Prophet (ﷺ): 'Send blessings upon me and upon my husband,' and he did so." In the report of Muslim: "The angels say to the spirit of the believer: 'May Allah send blessings upon you and upon your body.'" By this the statement of al-Khafaji in (Sharh al-Shifa) is refuted: "The sending of blessings by the angels upon the Ummah is not except through its following of him (ﷺ)." It was said: it is not permissible absolutely. It was said: it is not permissible independently, but it is permissible as a subsidiary in what the text has mentioned, such as the family (al-al), or what is attached to it, such as the companions (al-ashab). This was chosen by al-Qurtubi and others. It was said: it is permissible as a subsidiary absolutely, but not independently; this is attributed to Abu Hanifah and a group.

In (Tanwir al-Absar): "Blessings are not sent upon anyone other than the prophets and angels except by way of subsidiary." This admits of the dislike of sending blessings without a subsidiary as prohibited (tahrimen), or as disliked in the sense of abstention (tanzihan), or as being less preferable. But al-Biri from the Hanafis mentioned: "Whoever sends blessings upon others than them commits a sin and it is disliked, and this is the correct view." In a report from Ahmad: the dislike of this when done independently. The position of the Shafi'is is that it is less preferable.

Al-Laqani said: Al-Qadi 'Iyad said: "What the verifiers (al-muhaqqiqun) adopted, and to which I incline, is what Malik and Sufyan said, and what more than one of the jurists and theologians chose: that it is obligatory to restrict the Prophet (ﷺ) and all the prophets with the prayer and greeting, just as Allah, glorified is He, is singled out when mentioned with sanctification and exaltation, and others are mentioned with forgiveness and good pleasure, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him﴾ [al-Tawbah: 100], and ﴿They say: Our Lord, forgive us and our brothers who preceded us in faith﴾ [al-Hashr: 10]." Furthermore, this is a matter that was not known in the first generation; it was only introduced by the Rafidah concerning some of the imams, and resembling the people of innovation (al-bid'ah) is forbidden, so opposing them is obligatory. End of quotation.

It is not hidden that the prohibition of resembling the people of innovation is also established among us, but not absolutely; rather in what is blameworthy, and in what is intended as resemblance to them. So do not be heedless.

It has come from 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz with a hasan or sahih chain that he wrote to his governor: "Some storytellers (al-qussas) have introduced, in the sending of blessings upon their allies and clients, a practice equal to their sending of blessings upon the Prophet (ﷺ). So when this letter of mine reaches you, order them that their blessings be upon the prophets specifically, and their supplication for the Muslims generally, and that they leave aside whatever is other than that."

It is authentically reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "The sending of blessings by anyone upon anyone is not fitting except upon the Prophet (ﷺ)." In another report from him: "I do not know that sending blessings is fitting upon anyone from anyone except upon the Prophet (ﷺ); but for the Muslim men and women, one supplicates with forgiveness." Both of them admit of the dislike and the prohibition.

Those who prohibit argued that the word "prayer" (al-salah) has become an emblem (shi'ar) of the greatness and reverence of the prophets, so it is not said of others independently, even if it is true, just as "Muhammad, mighty and majestic" is not said, even though he (peace and blessings be upon him) is mighty and majestic, because this praise has become an emblem of Allah, exalted is He, and no one shares in it with Him.

They answered what has passed by saying that it came from Allah, exalted is He, and His Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him), and that they may specify whom they will with what they will, and this is not for anyone other than them except with their permission, and no permission from them in this has been established. For this reason Abu al-Yaman Ibn 'Asakir said: it is permissible for him (ﷺ) to send blessings upon others absolutely, because it is his right and his station, so he has freedom in it as he wishes, unlike his community, for they have no right to prefer others to what belongs to him. But the author of al-Mu'tamad from the Shafi'is disputed this, saying there is no proof of exclusivity. Al-Bayhaqi understood the position of prohibition as applying when this is made as glorification and a salutation (tahiyyah), and its permissibility as applying when it is a supplication and a seeking of blessing (tabarruk). Some Hanbalis chose that sending blessings upon the family is legislated as a subsidiary and permissible independently; that sending blessings upon the angels and the people of obedience generally is also permissible; and that sending blessings upon a specific person or group is disliked. Even if it were said to be prohibited, it would not be far-fetched, especially if this is made an emblem for him alone without his equal or one better than him, as the Rafidah do with 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face. There is no harm in it at times, as he (peace and blessings be upon him) sent blessings upon the woman and her husband, and as he (peace and blessings be upon him) sent blessings upon 'Ali and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, when he entered upon him while he was covered. Then he said: "By this distinction the evidences are harmonized." And you know their harmony without what has been mentioned.

The greeting (al-salam), according to many, in what has been mentioned, and in (Sharh al-Jawhara) of al-Laqani, quoting the Imam al-Juwayni, is in the sense of the prayer, so it is not used in reference to an absent person, nor is it singled out for anyone other than the prophets (peace be upon them). Thus one does not say "'Ali, peace be upon him," but says "may Allah be pleased with him." And this is the same regarding the living and the dead, except in the case of a present person, where one says "al-salam," or "salamun 'alayka," or "'alaykum." This is agreed upon. End of quotation. In the report of consensus upon this, there is room for examination.

In Ad-Durr al-Mandud, it is said: The salam (greeting of peace) is like the salah (blessing) in what has been mentioned, except when it is addressed to someone present or offered as a greeting to a living absent person. Others distinguished between them, saying that salam is prescribed for every believer, unlike salah. This is a distinction that begs the question, so it is not accepted. There is no proof in the salam "upon us and upon the righteous servants of Allah," because it is reported in a specific context, and nothing else shares its meaning. Moreover, what is in it occurs as a consequence, not independently.

Some scholars investigated the matter and said, with an addition, something whose gist is as follows: The salam that encompasses both the living and the dead is that which is intended as a greeting, such as the salam given upon meeting or upon visiting a grave. It calls for a response, which is either a communal obligation (wujub kifayah) or an individual obligation (wujub 'ayn) for the one present in person, or for his messenger or letter in the case of the absent. As for the salam that is intended as a supplication from us, asking Allah the Exalted to grant peace to the one for whom it is offered, whether it is phrased in the third person or the second person, this is the kind that is specific to the Prophet (ﷺ) over the rest of the Ummah. Therefore, no one else among them is greeted with it except by way of following him, as the Taqi al-Subki indicated in Shifa' al-Gharam. In that case, our saying "upon him be peace" resembles our saying "upon him be blessings," in that what is meant is peace from Allah the Exalted. Thus it carries an indication of the honour found in salah, in that it is a request that the one greeted be granted peace by Allah the Exalted, as in salah. This is the kind of salam that al-Halimi claimed is the meaning of salah. End of quotation.

There is disagreement over the permissibility of invoking mercy (rahmah) upon the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn 'Abd al-Barr held that this is prohibited, but this was refuted by its occurrence in authentic hadiths, the most authentic of which is the hadith of the tashahhud (the testimony recited in prayer): "Peace be upon you, O Prophet, and the mercy of Allah and His blessings." Another is the words of the Bedouin: "O Allah, have mercy upon me and upon Muhammad," and the Prophet's (ﷺ) approval of this. Another is his (ﷺ) saying: "O Allah, I ask You for a mercy from You... O Allah, I hope for Your mercy, O Ever-Living, O Self-Subsisting, by Your mercy I seek relief." In the preface of al-Shafi'i's Risalah, the wording is: "(ﷺ) and he showed mercy and honoured."

Indeed, the implication of his statement, as in the hadith of the tashahhud, is that permissibility applies only when the word salah or salam is joined to it; otherwise it is not permitted. Among those who adopted this view is al-Jalal al-Suyuti. Al-Qadi 'Iyad even transmitted it in al-Ikmal from the majority. Al-Qurtubi said: "This is the correct view." Al-Ghazali, may Allah have mercy on him, firmly held that it is not permitted to invoke mercy upon the Prophet alone. He said: "It is not permitted to ask mercy for the Prophet." Supporting this is the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Do not make the calling of the Messenger among you like the calling of some of you to others﴾ [al-Nur: 63]. Although salah carries the meaning of mercy, the prophets were singled out with it to honour them and distinguish their lofty station above others. Moreover, in their case it does not mean mercy in its general sense, but something more specific, as you have heard above.

Yes, the apparent meaning of the Bedouin's statement mentioned earlier, and the Prophet's (peace and blessings be upon him) approval of it, is permissibility even without joining it to salah or salam.

Ibn Hajar al-Haytami said: "This is what is apparent (yattajih), and his approval mentioned above is specific, so it takes precedence over the general ruling implied by the verse." Then he said: "The statement of those who say it is not permitted should be understood to mean that they intended the negation of permissibility in the sense of equal standing on both sides, so it is valid to hold that such invocation is disliked (makruh) or contrary to what is better (khilaf al-awla)." Zayn al-Din, in his Bahr, mentioned that they agreed that one should not begin by saying "may Allah have mercy on him" (rahimahu Allah). I say: What is appropriate is that this should not be said as an opening phrase.

Al-Tahtawi, in his glosses on al-Durr al-Mukhtar, said: "It should not be permitted to say 'may Allah forgive him' or 'may He pardon him,' because this implies a deficiency. This is what I incline toward, although supplication for forgiveness does not necessarily imply that a sin has been committed; it may be for an increase in ranks, as is indicated by his (peace and blessings be upon him) seeking forgiveness one hundred times a day and night. Likewise, supplicating for forgiveness for a young deceased child in the funeral prayer. Similarly, it appears that 'may Allah pardon him' (afa Allah 'anhu) is the same, even though it occurs in the Qur'an, since Allah the Exalted may address His servant however He wishes."

I hold that the ruling on invoking mercy upon the angels, peace be upon them, is the same as the ruling on invoking mercy upon him (ﷺ). As for whoever is disputed concerning his prophethood, such as Luqman, it is said regarding him: "may Allah be pleased with him" (radi Allah ta'ala 'anhu), or "may Allah bless the prophets and him, and grant them peace" (salla Allah ta'ala 'ala al-anbiya' wa 'alayhi wa sallam). This is the matter. Many other discussions remain on this topic, and mentioning them would make the discussion extremely long, so they should be sought in their proper sources. Allah the Exalted is the Granter of success, and in His hand, glorified be He, are the reins of verification.

﴿Indeed, those who harm Allah and His Messenger﴾. By "harm" is meant either committing what They do not approve of, such as disbelief and major sins, used metaphorically (*majāz*, figurative usage) because such acts are a cause of harm or a necessary result of it. This holds even though, with respect to Him, exalted is He, the harm is considered in relation to Him in comparison with others, glory be to Him, since that suffices for the connection (*ʿalāqa*). It has been said that harming Allah means the saying of the Jews, the Christians and the polytheists: "The hand of Allah is chained," "the Messiah is the son of Allah," "the angels are the daughters of Allah," and "the idols are His partners," exalted is Allah far above that by a great exaltation. It has also been said that it means the words of those who deviate concerning His signs, glory be to Him, and that it means the making of images, and something corresponding to this has been related from Ka'b. As for harming the Messenger (ﷺ), it has been said that it is their saying: "He is a poet, a sorcerer, a soothsayer, a madman," and far be it from him, upon him be blessings and peace. It has also been said that it is the breaking of his front tooth (*rubāʿiyya*) and the wounding of his noble face, which occurred at the Battle of Uhud. And it has been said that it is their slander concerning the marriage to Safiyya bint Huyayy. The truth is that the meaning is general in both cases. As for harming him, upon him be blessings and peace, specifically, it is in its literal sense (*ḥaqīqa*), and the mention of Allah, mighty and majestic is He, is to glorify him (ﷺ) by declaring his nearness and that he is His beloved, specially chosen by Him, to the extent that what harms him harms Him, glory be to Him, just as whoever obeys him obeys Allah, exalted is He. It has also been permitted that the harm be in its literal sense and that the speech contains an elision of a word (*ḥadhf muḍāf*), meaning "they harm the friends of Allah and His Messenger," but this is not correct. It has been said that it is permissible for the word to carry both the metaphorical meaning with respect to Him, exalted is He, and the literal meaning with respect to His Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace. The multiplicity of the object (*taʿaddud al-maʿmūl*) is like the repetition of the verb, so the matter of combining the two meanings becomes lighter, to the extent that some have claimed that it is not among the prohibited kinds of combination, but this is not correct.

﴿Allah has cursed them﴾, meaning He has expelled them and removed them far from His mercy, ﴿in this world and the Hereafter﴾, such that they hardly obtain any portion of it in either of them. In the Hereafter this is evident. As for this world, it has been said that it is by His preventing them from increased guidance. ﴿And He has prepared for them﴾, in addition to that, ﴿a humiliating punishment﴾, which will befall them specifically in the Hereafter.

﴿And those who harm the believing men and the believing women﴾, meaning they do to them what they are harmed by, ﴿in words or deeds﴾. Restricting it by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿without their having earned it﴾, meaning without a misdeed for which they deserve harm according to the Sharia, after it was stated absolutely in what came before, is to indicate that the harm of Allah and His Messenger (ﷺ) occurs only in what is unjust, whereas the harm done by these people is both of this kind and that kind.

It is related that Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said one day to Ubayy: "O Abu al-Mundhir, last night I recited a verse from the Book of Allah, Exalted, and it struck me in every way"

﴿And those who harm believing men and believing women﴾. By Allah, I punish them and beat them. He said: "You are not one of them. You are only a teacher and a corrector."

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿الَّذِينَ﴾ (alladhina, "those who") is a *mubtada'* (the subject of a nominal sentence). His saying, glorified is He, ﴿فَقَدِ احْتَمَلُوا بُهْتانًا﴾ ("then they have borne a slander") means a shameful act. It was said: it is like a slander, that is, a lie that stuns the person because of its enormity in sin. It was also said: "they have borne a slander" means a dreadful lie, if the harm was by speech. ﴿وإثْمًا مُبِينًا﴾ ("and a manifest sin") means clear and evident in its report. The *fa'* (ف) entered because the relative clause (al-mawsul) includes the meaning of a conditional. It was said that the verse was revealed concerning hypocrites who used to harm Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, and make him hear what has no good in it.

Ibn Juwaybir related from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, who said: It was revealed concerning Abd Allah ibn Ubayy and some people with him who slandered Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) gave a sermon and said: "Who will excuse me regarding a man who harms me and gathers in his house those who harm me?" Then this was revealed.

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that it was revealed concerning those who criticized the Prophet (ﷺ) for taking Safiyya bint Huyayy, may Allah be pleased with her. And from al-Dahhak, al-Suddi and al-Kalbi: it was revealed concerning fornicators who used to follow women when they went out at night to attend to their needs. They would only approach slave women, but sometimes they would approach free women out of ignorance or feigned ignorance, since all of them were alike in dress and clothing. The apparent meaning is that the verse is general, covering all that has been mentioned and all the rumors of rumor-mongers that will come. It also contains evidence of the sanctity of believing men and believing women, to the extent that it does.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid concerning this verse that he said: Scabies will be inflicted upon the people of the Fire, so they will scratch until the bones show, and they will say: "Our Lord, for what has this befallen us?" It will be said: "For your harming of the Muslims."

Others related from Qatada, who said: Beware of harming the believer, for Allah, exalted is He, protects him and becomes angry on his behalf.

Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in (Shu'ab al-Iman) related from Aisha, may Allah be pleased with her, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to his companions: "Which usury is the greatest in the sight of Allah?" They said: "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said: "The greatest usury in the sight of Allah is violating the honor of a Muslim person." Then he (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And those who harm believing men and believing women without their having earned it﴾, the verse.

﴿يا أيُّها النَّبِيُّ﴾ (O Prophet). After Allah, glorified is He, described the bad state of those who harass [the believers], as a deterrent to them from harassment, He commanded the Prophet (ﷺ) to tell some of those who were being harassed to do what would, in general terms, prevent their harassment: to cover themselves and to be distinguished from the places where harassment occurs. So He, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿Say to your wives, your daughters, and the women of the believers, that they should draw their jilbabs (outer garments; sing. jilbab) over themselves﴾.

It is narrated from more than one source that free women and slave women would go out at night to relieve themselves in the open fields and among the palm trees, without any distinction between free women and female slaves. In Madinah there were debauched men who would pursue female slaves, and sometimes they pursued free women too. When they were challenged, they would say: "We thought they were slave women." So free women were commanded to differ from slave women in dress and covering, so that they would be modest and be known, and thus no one would covet them.

The jalabib (jilbabs) are the plural of jilbab. According to what is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, it is a garment that covers from the top down to the bottom. Ibn Jubayr said: it is the miqna'ah (a headcovering). It was also said: it is the milhafah (a wrap). It was also said: it is any garment a woman wears over her other clothes. It was also said: it is anything with which she covers herself, of cloth or otherwise. They also recited:

*She wrapped herself in a cloak of the darkness of the night.*

It was also said that it is a garment wider than the khimar (headscarf) and smaller than the rida' (upper wrap). The idna' (drawing near) means bringing close; one says *adnani*, meaning "he brought me close." The verb has been given the meaning of letting down or draping (al-irkha' aw al-sadl), and so it is followed by ʿala (over), as appears to me. Perhaps the reason for this implicit meaning is to indicate that what is required is a covering which still permits them to see the path when they walk. So reflect on this.

Abu Hayyan transmitted from al-Kisa'i that he said: i.e., they should cover themselves with their wraps, drawn tightly over them. Then he said: by "tightly drawn" he meant the meaning of idna'. In al-Kashshaf, the meaning of ﴿yudnina ʿalayhinna﴾ is "let them lower [their garments] over themselves." It is said that when a woman's garment slips from her face, one says: "Draw your garment over your face." Sa'id ibn Jubayr explained it as "let them let down [their garments] over themselves." In my view, all of this explains the resulting meaning. The apparent intention of ʿalayhinna is over all their bodies. It was also said: over their heads or over their faces, because what used to show of them in the pre-Islamic period was the face.

There was disagreement about the manner of this covering. Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and others transmitted from Muhammad ibn Sirin, who said: I asked ʿUbaydah al-Salmani about this verse, ﴿yudnina ʿalayhinna min jalabibihinna﴾, and he lifted a wrap he had and covered himself with it, covering his whole head until it reached his eyebrows, and covering his face, and he brought out his left eye from the left side of his face. al-Suddi said: she covers one of her eyes, her forehead, and the other side [of her face], except for the eye. Ibn ʿAbbas and Qatadah said: she twists the jilbab above the forehead, fastens it, and then turns it down over the nose, and even if her eyes show, she covers the chest and most of the face. In another narration from the Rabbi (Ibn ʿAbbas), transmitted by Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh: she covers her face from the top of her head with the jilbab and shows one eye.

ʿAbd al-Razzaq and a group transmitted from Umm Salamah, who said: When this verse was revealed, ﴿yudnina ʿalayhinna min jalabibihinna﴾, the women of the Ansar went out as if there were crows upon their heads, from the sobriety of their dress, and they wore black garments.

Ibn Mardawayh transmitted from ʿA'ishah, who said: May Allah the Exalted have mercy on the women of the Ansar. When the verse ﴿O Prophet, say to your wives and daughters﴾ was revealed, they tore their coarse woolen wraps and wrapped themselves in them, and they prayed behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) as if there were crows upon their heads.

The min here is partitive (lil-tab'id), and according to al-Kashshaf this permits two possibilities. The first is that the "part" refers to one of the jalabib, and drawing it over them means that they wear it over the whole body. The second is that the "part" refers to a portion of it, and drawing it over them means that they veil themselves, covering the head and face with a part of the jilbab while letting the rest hang over the rest of the body. Women, by customary usage, are specifically the free women, and the occasion of revelation requires this, and what follows in the verse clearly indicates it. Therefore the female slaves of the believers are not included in the ruling of this verse.

It is narrated from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that a non-free woman should not veil herself. Ibn Abi Shaybah transmitted from Qilabah, who said: During his caliphate, ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab would not allow any slave woman to veil herself, and he would say: "Veiling is for free women, so that they will not be harassed." He and ʿAbd ibn Humayd transmitted from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, saw a slave girl veiled, so he struck her with his whip and said: "Take off the veil! Do not imitate free women." It came in some narrations that he, may Allah be pleased with him, said to a slave woman whom he saw veiled: "O wretch! Are you imitating free women?"

Abu Hayyan said: "The women of the believers" includes both free women and slave women, and temptation with slave women is greater because of their frequent movement in public, unlike free women. Therefore removing them from the general category of women requires clear evidence, end of quote. You know that in our school, a free woman's face is not 'awrah (what must be covered), so it is not obligatory to cover it, and it is permissible for a non-mahram man to look at it if he is safe from desire absolutely; otherwise it is forbidden. Al-Qahstani said: looking at a young woman is forbidden in our time, even without desire. As for the ruling on another man's female slave, even if she is a mudabbarah or umm walad, it is like the ruling for a mahram: it is permissible to look at her head, face, leg, chest, and upper arm, if one is safe from desire on both sides. The apparent meaning of the verse does not support what has been mentioned regarding free women, so perhaps it is to be understood as a demand for a covering by which free women are distinguished from slave women, or from chaste women in general from others. So reflect.

﴿Yudnina﴾ may be the object of the saying, and it is a statement with the meaning of a command; or it may be the answer to the command, in the manner of ﴿Tell My servants who have believed to establish prayer﴾ [Ibrahim: 31]. In the verse there is a refutation of those among the Shi'ah who claim that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) had no daughters except Fatimah, may Allah the Exalted bless him, his father, her, and grant them peace. As for Ruqayyah and Umm Kulthum, they were his stepdaughters (raba'ib), peace and blessings be upon him.

﴿That﴾, i.e., what has been mentioned of drawing close and covering, ﴿is more suitable﴾, i.e., nearer, ﴿that they will be known﴾, i.e., distinguished from slave women, who are the objects of men's pursuit and harassment. It is also permissible to keep "known" in its own meaning, i.e., more suitable that they be known to be free women, ﴿so they will not be harmed﴾ by people of ill repute who pursue them, on the assumption that they are slave women.

Abu Hayyan said: i.e., that is more preferable so that they are known by their chastity, so that no one pursues them and they do not encounter what they dislike, because when a woman is covered and modest to the utmost degree, no one approaches her, unlike the woman who shows herself off, who is regarded as a target for desire. This is an explanation based on his opinion regarding women. In any case, al-Subki said in his Tabaqat: Ahmad ibn ʿIsa, one of the jurists of the Shafiʿi school, deduced from this verse that what scholars and nobles do by changing their clothing and turbans is good, even if the early generations did not do it, because in it there is a distinction for them so that they are recognized and their words are acted upon. This is a subtle deduction.

﴿And Allah is ever Forgiving﴾, abundant in forgiveness, so He forgives whatever may occur of failure in covering. It was also said: He forgives what has passed of their negligence.

This has been objected to: if the negligence in the matter of covering before the revelation of the verse is meant, then there is no sin before it arrives in the Sharia; and if negligence in other matters is meant, so that the sense is "Allah is abundant in forgiveness, so He forgives what has passed of their sins and their committing what He has forbidden absolutely," then this is not appropriate to the context. It is permitted to mean negligence in the matter of covering, and the command to it is known from the verse of hijab by implication, but this, as you see, is weak.

﴿Merciful﴾, abundant in mercy, so He rewards whoever obeys His command among them with what He alone deserves. It was also said: merciful to them after repentance for failing to cover after the revelation of the verse. It was also said: merciful to His servants, in that He, glorified is He, takes into account in their interests such particular matters as these.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 60:

﴿If the hypocrites do not desist﴾ from what they are upon of hypocrisy and its rulings that necessitate harm, ﴿and those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ who are a people in whom there was weakness of faith and little steadfastness upon it, from what they are upon of wavering and what follows from it of that which holds no good, ﴿and the agitators in the city﴾ from among the Jews neighboring it, from what they are upon of spreading bad news about the expeditions of the Muslims and other fabricated rumours that lead to harm. The root of al-irjaf (agitation, spreading rumours) is tahrik (stirring) from raj fa (the quaking), which is the earthquake; false reports are described by it either because they themselves are shaking and unstable, or because the hearts of the believers tremble and are disturbed by them. The difference between the conjoined items is, as we have mentioned, in essence, and this is what the apparent sense of the conjunction requires.

Ibn al-Mundhir and others transmitted from Malik ibn Dinar, who said: I asked Ikrimah about "those in whose hearts is a disease," and he said: they are the people of immoral acts. Ata' likewise explained them thus. In another narration from him, he said: they are believing people who had in themselves the desire to commit fornication; so the disease is the love of fornication. And if the agitators are explained according to that which you have heard, the difference between the conjoined items will also be in essence.

Ibn Sa'd transmitted from Muhammad ibn Ka'b that "those in whose hearts is a disease" are the hypocrites, and this is the well-known description of them. He also transmitted from Ubayd ibn Hunayn that "those in whose hearts is a disease" and "the agitators" are all the hypocrites; then the conjunction is with unity in essence and difference in attributes, in the manner of: "He is the king, the lord, and the son of the brave." It is as if it were said: If the gatherers of these ugly attributes do not desist from being characterised by them, which leads to harm, ﴿We will surely incite you against them﴾ i.e., We will surely urge you to fight them and expel them, or to do what compels them to exile, and We will encourage you to that. It is said: aghrahu bi-kadha, meaning he urged him to take it by encouraging him toward it. Al-Raghib said: ghurriya bi-kadha means he became attached to it and clung to it, and its origin is from al-ghira' (glue), which is what something is stuck with; and aghraytu fulanan bi-kadha means I made him cling to it. And from Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that it means: We will surely empower you over them.

﴿Then they will not remain as your neighbours in it﴾ is a conjunction upon the answer of the oath, and thumma (then) indicates a gradation in rank and indicates that exile and separation from the neighbourhood of the Messenger ﷺ is the greatest and most severe thing that befalls them. ﴿in it﴾ i.e., in Medina; ﴿except for a little﴾ i.e., for a period of time or a little neighbourhood, for the interval until their condition becomes clear regarding desisting or not, or so that they may gather their families and themselves.

In the verse, according to al-Intisaf, there is also an indication that whoever is obliged to vacate a dwelling owned by another for a lawful reason is given a respite, the time needed to move himself, his property and his family, for a period of time until another dwelling becomes available to him according to his effort. The accusative of ﴿qalilan﴾ [a little], according to what we have indicated, is either as an adverb of time or as a verbal noun; it has also been permitted that it be an accusative of circumstance, i.e., "except as a few humiliated ones," and its state is not hidden from one who has discernment.

Al-Alusi's commentary (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 61:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Cursed﴾ (mal'unina) is in the accusative by way of dispraise, meaning "I dispraise those cursed," or it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of the subject of ﴿they shall not be your neighbours﴾. The exception (al-istithna') includes it according to the one who considers such a construction permissible, and the discussion of this was already presented at His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿except when permission is given to you for a meal, without waiting for its preparation﴾ [al-Ahzab: 53]. Ibn 'Atiyya made the meaning, on the circumstantial reading, "they shall be expelled as the cursed." It was also permitted that it be a circumstantial qualifier of their pronoun in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿wherever they are found﴾, meaning "wherever they are confined and overpowered," and it seems to mean "wherever they are found, characterised by what they are upon." ﴿They shall be seized﴾, meaning they shall be captured, and from this comes al-akhidh (the captive) for the prisoner. ﴿And be slain with thorough slaughter﴾, meaning they shall be slain with the most thorough killing.

It has been read as "qutilu" (with the lightened form), in which case ﴿taqtilan﴾ is a verbal noun not of the expected pattern (masdar 'ala ghayr al-sadr).

The circumstantial reading was objected to on the basis that the conditional particle's following element does not govern what precedes it, absolutely. This is one of the grammarians' positions on the question. Their second view is that it is permissible absolutely, and their third is that it is permissible to front the complement of the response (jawab) but not the complement of the condition (shart).

It was also permitted, on the assumption that ﴿qalilan﴾ is a circumstantial qualifier, that ﴿mal'unina﴾ be a substitute (badal) for it. Abu Hayyan criticised this by saying that substitution by a derived noun (mushtaqq) is rare. He then said: "The correct view is that ﴿mal'unina﴾ is an attribute of qalil, meaning 'except a few who are cursed,' and ﴿qalilan﴾ is an exception from the waw in ﴿they shall not be your neighbours﴾, and the conditional clause is also an attribute, meaning 'subdued, overcome.'" End quote. And it is, as you see, [weak].

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 62:

His saying, Most High: ﴿The way of Allah concerning those who passed away before﴾ is an emphatic infinitive (maṣdar mu'akkid), meaning: Allah, Most High, established this as a sunnah (sunnah, a settled way or practice) among the earlier nations, namely the fighting of those who strive in corruption among a people, their expulsion from their homelands, and their subjugation wherever they are found, while they are characterized by that.

﴿And you will not find﴾, O Prophet, or O whoever is fit for such finding, ever, ﴿any change in the way of Allah﴾, in His constant custom, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿a change﴾, because it is founded on the basis of wisdom; so He, exalted is His majesty, does not change it, and far, far is it that anyone other than Him, glory be to Him, could be able to change it. Whoever examines the reports of the earlier generations will come upon a great matter in their mistreatment of those who spread corruption among them, and it is as if human natures are inclined to mistreat and subjugate them.

In the tafsir of al-Fakhr (al-Razi): ﴿And you will not find for the way of Allah any change﴾, meaning this sunnah is not like a ruling that is changed and abrogated (naskh, abrogation), for abrogation occurs in rulings, whereas actions and reports are not abrogated. As for al-Suddi, he has a strange statement on the verse which I do not think anyone has held.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him that he said concerning it: Hypocrisy was of three kinds. One is the hypocrisy like that of Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul and his counterparts, who were among the notables of the Ansar; they were shy of committing fornication, protecting themselves by that
Page 92
(their souls), and they are the hypocrites in the verse. The second is the hypocrisy of those in whose hearts is a disease, who are hypocrites: if fornication was available to them, they committed it, and if it was not available, they did not pursue it or concern themselves with it. The third is the hypocrisy of the spreaders of rumours (al-murjifin), who are hypocrites: they overpower women, follow their traces, and overcome them against their will, and then commit fornication with them. These are the ones who overpower women.

﴿Then We would surely incite you against them﴾: He, glory be to Him, says: We would surely make you aware of them. Then He said, Most High: ﴿cursed﴾. Then the verse is separated: ﴿wherever they are found﴾, doing this deed of overpowering women, ﴿they shall be seized and killed with slaughter﴾.

Then al-Suddi said: This is a ruling in the Qur'an that is not acted upon. If a man or more than one man followed the trace of a woman, overpowered her against her self, and committed fornication with her, the ruling concerning them would not be flogging or stoning, but that they be seized and their necks struck.

﴿The way of Allah concerning those who passed away before﴾: thus He used to deal with those of the nations who passed away. ﴿And you will not find any change in the way of Allah﴾. So whoever overpowers a woman against her self, overcomes her, and is killed, there is no blood-money (diyah) upon his killer, because he is the aggressor. End of quote.

It is apparent that the hypocrites, and those in whose hearts is a disease, desisted from what was the object of the prohibition, namely the harm that their condition entailed, but the spreaders of rumours, I mean the Jews, did not desist, so fighting and expulsion came upon them.

In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit by Abu Hayyan): It is apparent that the hypocrites, meaning all who are mentioned in the verse, desisted from what they used to inflict upon the Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers, and all of them concealed themselves and refrained out of fear that what the oath was sworn upon would befall them, namely incitement, expulsion and killing. This is related from al-Jubba'i. And from Abu Muslim: they did not desist, and the incitement was realised by His saying, Most High: (Strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites) [al-Tawbah: 73, al-Tahrim: 9]. In this there is a problem: expulsion and killing did not befall the hypocrites, and the striving in the verse is verbal. It was also said: they did not abandon what they were upon and were not wholly prohibited from it, nor was the threat fully carried out against them. Do you not see their expulsion from the mosque, His prohibition from praying over them, and what descended in Surah Bara'ah? And some claimed that none of those mentioned desisted at all, and the threat was not carried out against them; in this is evidence for the invalidity of the view that the threat must necessarily be executed in the Hereafter, and this threat would be conditional upon His will. And in this is much remoteness.

﴿They ask you, the people, about the Hour﴾, that is, about the time of its establishment and occurrence. The polytheists used to ask the Prophet (ﷺ) about it, seeking to hasten it, mockingly; the hypocrites asked to provoke him; and the Jews asked to test him, because they knew from the Torah that it is among the things God, exalted is He, has concealed. So they asked him, upon him be prayer and peace, in order to test him: whether it would coincide with a revelation or not.

﴿Say: Its knowledge is only with God﴾. He, glorified is He, does not make anyone aware of it, neither a nearly-brought-near angel nor a sent prophet. ﴿And what will make you know?﴾ This is a separate address to him (ﷺ), not included under the command, brought to show that although it is unknown, its coming is expected soon. Here *mā* is an interrogative in the nominative position as the subject of a nominal sentence, and the clause after it is the predicate, meaning: "What thing will inform you of the time of its establishment?" The sense is negative: nothing whatsoever will inform you of it.

﴿Perhaps the Hour is near﴾, that is, perhaps it will come into existence and be realized at a near time. Here *qarīban* (near) is in the accusative of time (*ẓarfiyyah*, adverbial accusative of time), and its use in this way is common. The verb *takūnu* may be a complete verb (*tāmmah*, not requiring a predicate), and it may also be an incomplete verb (*nāqisah*, requiring a predicate). If *qarīban* is taken as the predicate and understood as an adjective rather than an adverb, then its masculine form is because it is originally an adjective of an unstated masculine predicate that refers to the feminine subject, and it is not itself the predicate; that is, "perhaps the Hour will be a near thing." It is also permissible that this is in observance of the meaning, since *al-sāʿah* means "the day" or "the time."

Abū Ḥayyān said: It is permissible that this is because the implied phrase is "perhaps the establishment of the Hour," so *al-sāʿah* is considered in *takūnu*, hence the feminine form, while the omitted genitive noun *qiyām* (establishment) is considered in *qarīban*, hence the masculine. Its remoteness is not hidden. It has also been said that *qarīban*, being of the *faʿīl* pattern, is the same for masculine and feminine, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the mercy of God is near to the good-doers﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 56], and what this entails has already been discussed. In the statement there is a warning to those who mock and hasten, and a rebuke to those who test and put to trial, and the explicit mention (*al-iẓhār*) of "the Hour" in place of a pronoun (*al-iḍmār*) serves to magnify the matter, reinforce it, and emphasize the independence of the sentence, as has been pointed out.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 64:

﴿Indeed, Allah has cursed the disbelievers﴾ without restriction, i.e., He has expelled them and removed them far from His mercy, both in this world and in the Hereafter. ﴿And has prepared﴾, i.e., readied, ﴿for them﴾, in addition to that, in the Hereafter, ﴿a blaze﴾, i.e., a fire of intense kindling, as the intensive form (sighah al-mubalaghah) indicates.

Abiding therein forever, they shall find neither a protector (ولِيًّا), one who takes charge of their affairs and guards them, nor a helper (نَصِيرًا), one who gives them support and delivers them from it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 66:

﴿On the Day their faces are turned over in the Fire﴾ is a time-adverb (zarf) governed by "non-finding" (ʿadam al-wijdan, i.e., the failure to find [a helper] mentioned in the preceding verse). It has also been said that it governs "abiding forever" (khalidin), and it has been said that it governs "helper" (naseer), and it has been said that it is an object (maf'ul) of the verb "remember" (udhkur), meaning: on the Day when their faces are turned about in it from one side to another, like meat being roasted in the fire or cooked in a pot, so that the boiling turns it about from one side to another; or on the Day when their faces change from one state to another, so that hideous appearances succeed one another upon them due to the severity of the terrors; or on the Day when they are cast into the Fire upside down and head-first. The specific mention of the faces is because they are the most honoured of the limbs, so this carries greater abhorrence of the matter and greater dread of the calamity. It is also permissible that the faces be an expression for the whole body.

Al-Hasan, ʿIsa and Abu Jaʿfar al-Rawasi read «tuqallabu» with a fatha on the taʾ, and the original form is tatuqallabu, so one of the two tas was elided. Ibn Abi ʿAbla read it with both (tas) in accordance with the original form. Ibn Khalawayh transmitted from Abu Haywa that he read «tuqallibu wujuhahum» with the verb attributed to the pronoun of majesty (the divine "We") and «wujuhahum» in the accusative as the object. ʿIsa of Kufa read «tuqallibu wujuhahum» with the verb attributed to the pronoun of the Blaze (al-saʿir), by way of extended usage (ittisaʿan), and the faces in the accusative.

﴿They will say﴾ is a resumptive statement (istiʾnaf) built upon a question arising from the description of their dreadful state, as if it were said: "What will they do at that time?" So it is answered: "They will say, full of regret over what they have missed: ﴿O would that we had obeyed Allah and obeyed the Messenger!﴾ so that we would not be afflicted with this punishment." Or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in (their faces) or from the faces themselves. It has also been permitted that the verb "say" be the governor of "the Day".

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 67:

﴿And they will say﴾ is conjoined to ﴿they say﴾. The shift to the past tense form indicates that this statement of theirs is not continuous like their earlier statement, but is rather a kind of excuse-making, by which they intended a kind of gratification through doubling the punishment of those who led them to this dreadful place and cast them into that painful torment, even though they knew it would not be accepted on their behalf to secure their deliverance from what they were in.

﴿Our Lord, indeed we obeyed our masters﴾, that is, our kings and rulers who take charge of the management of the great majority among us, ﴿and our elders﴾, that is, our chiefs from whom we took the arts of evil. This was in contrast to what they had wished for, namely obedience to God Most High and obedience to the Messenger. The "masters" (sada) and the "elders" (kubara') are two distinct groups, and expressing them under the headings of lordship and greatness serves to strengthen the excuse; otherwise they are in a position of contempt and humiliation.

They mentioned obedience to the masters first because they had the power to subdue them should they not obey them, so this was more deserving of precedence in a context of excuse-making and seeking gratification. It has also been said that the masters and the elders are one and the same group, and the conjunction is of the type found in His saying "and she found her husband at the door" (wa-alfa qawlaha kadhiban wa-mina). By them are meant the scholars who instilled disbelief in them and adorned it for them. It is reported from Qatadah that they were their leaders in evil and in polytheism.

Al-Hasan, Abu Raja', Qatadah, al-Sulami, Ibn 'Amir, and the general body of readers in the Friday mosque of Basra read ﴿sādātanā﴾ (our masters) in the plural of plural form, which is shadhdh (irregular), like buyutat (houses/families). It is said that this indicates abundance. Furthermore, that sāda is a plural is the well-known view; it has also been said that it is a collective noun (ism jam'). If it is the plural of sayyid, it is also irregular, since they have explicitly stated the irregularity of fi'la as a plural of fa'il. If it is the plural of a presumed singular, sā'id, it would be like kafir and kafara, but this too is irregular, because fā'il is not pluralized as fi'la except in the sound (healthy-lettered) forms.

﴿So they led us astray from the way﴾, that is, they made us go astray from the true path by what they called us to and what they adorned for us of falsehoods. The alif is for lengthening the vowel, as in ﴿and we obeyed the Messenger﴾.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 68:

﴿Our Lord, give them double the punishment from the torment﴾ That is, two punishments, each of which multiplies the other in punishment: a punishment for their own misguidance, and a punishment for their misguiding us. ﴿And curse them with a great curse﴾ That is, a severe, mighty curse. For greatness is used metaphorically for magnitude, as in ﴿Great is the word that comes out of their mouths﴾ [al-Kahf: 5]. Magnification is also derived from the tanwin (nunation) in the word. The majority of readers recited "kathiran" (كَثِيرًا) with the three-dotted thā' (ث), meaning abundant in number. The opening of the supplication with the vocative, repeated, serves to intensify the earnest pleading and the seeking of a response.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 33, verse 69:

﴿O you who have believed, do not be like those who abused Moses﴾. It is said: it was revealed concerning what happened regarding Zaynab bint Jahsh, may Allah be pleased with her, and his (ﷺ) marriage to her, and the words he heard about that which hurt him, upon him be prayers and peace. ﴿So Allah cleared him of what they said﴾. That is, of what they said, or of what they uttered. In either case, "saying" here means "what is said," and what is intended is its actual referent in reality. Allah's clearing him of that means the manifestation of his innocence from it, and the falsity of what they attributed to him. This is because what follows from their harm is the manifestation of his innocence, not his innocence itself, since innocence precedes it. The verb is used metaphorically for its manifestation. "What is said" in the sense of "its content" is very common and widespread. So the meaning is: Allah manifested his innocence from the blameworthy matter they attributed to him, upon him be peace. It is also said: there is no need for what has been mentioned, for when Allah manifested his innocence from what they fabricated against him, their words concerning him were cut off, so he was cleared of their saying. This is on the basis that (barrahu) means "freed him from their saying" by cutting it off from him. This has been objected to: even apart from its artificiality, cutting off their saying is not the goal in itself; rather what is intended is its cessation because of the manifest falsity of it. What has been mentioned must be taken into consideration. The matter they attributed to him, upon him be peace, refers to a defect in his body.

Imam Ahmad, al-Bukhari, al-Tirmidhi and a group narrated through the route of Abu Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Moses, upon him be peace, was a man who was shy and very modest; no part of his skin was seen out of bashfulness. So those among the Children of Israel who harmed him said: 'He only conceals himself this much because of a defect in his skin: either leprosy, or a swelling of the testicles, or some other affliction.' Allah wished to clear him of what they said. One day Moses, upon him be peace, was alone, so he placed his garments on a rock and then bathed. When he finished he approached his garments to take them, but the rock ran off with his garment. Moses, upon him be peace, took his staff and went after the rock, saying: 'My garment, O rock! My garment, O rock!' Until he reached a group of the Children of Israel, who saw him naked, in the finest form Allah had created, and thus Allah cleared him of what they said. The rock stopped, he took his garment and put it on, and began striking the rock with his staff." That is the meaning of His saying: ﴿O you who have believed, do not be like those who abused Moses, so Allah cleared him of what they said﴾.

It is also said: what they attributed to him, upon him be peace, was the killing of Harun. Ibn Mani', Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn Abbas, from Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said concerning the verse: Musa and Harun, upon them both be peace, ascended the mountain, and Harun died.
